I am not really sure what else they would have access to.
T/DCC Mark Travis: There would be no identifier as to address, contact details and things like that. None of that kind of private information is held in the system.
It is just a name and a picture.
T/DCC Mark Travis: It is an identification.

It is just one picture, but there could be access to a system with a whole lot of pictures in it, and they could then say, “These are the people the police are interested in”, which you might not want to disclose to the public generally.

​ ​ Ms Lindsey Chiswick: ​ That comes back to the fact that the watchlist created for the deployment is kept for only 24 hours and is specific to that case. Even if they accessed it, they would not have access to the whole system of images that the police have as part of their custody image database.
A good question, which I will not go into, is that a person could, effectively, be part of a watchlist without being visibly part of it, but that is for another day and another witness.
You have been using the word “dissident”, but if I substitute the word “protester” , is the answer the same?

T/DCC Mark Travis: Yes, the answer is the same. The concern that we would have as professional police colleagues would not be the accessing of this data but the accessing of wider police data, the police national database, which is the system that holds the breadth of information that allows you to understand the picture of an individual, where they are, who they are and their associates. Accessing something like that would be fundamental in terms of those risks, which is why we have such significant safeguards for those elements. What we are talking about here—I am not saying that it is not significant to the individual—is a small snapshot of that data, which is divorced from what we call their nominal data. For example, a hostile state knowing who an individual was would be able to identify a photo and match the photo, but if you did not know that, because you were not a hostile state, it would have no bearing or no benefit in an intelligence picture for anybody.

Professor Yeung, do you want to come in on all this? I wonder whether there are any useful international comparators. I say “useful” because there are different legal systems. If they are not comparable, one does not necessarily have a read-across.

It is useful to locate the discussion that we are having in this room within the larger international context. I am sure that everyone is familiar with objections to the use of this technology by civil society organisations. For example, in Europe alone, it has been banned entirely in Luxembourg and Belgium. The AI Act will basically ban it in Europe once it is enacted, subject to very limited law enforcement exception, requiring higher judicial authorisation and only for specific serious crimes. It is much more limited than the way it is currently being used in the UK. It is used everywhere in China and it is the norm. There is a question about whether that is the kind of political community that we wish to be, and that is where we need to be mindful of the fact that we are an outlier as a democratic state in the pace at which we are embracing these technologies.
We have mentioned ethics committees, and one could say that we should have started with questions about ethics.

Q12 This has been a really interesting session, not just with the specific focus questions but raising some very broad issues that we clearly cannot deal with today. The more it has gone on, the more I realise how important an ethics focus will be. Given the lack of an agreed legal foundation, ethics becomes, in a way, the place where a lot of these issues can be raised. Perhaps I could ask Karen about the use of ethics committees. Is there a common framework for them? Do they just spring up ad hoc? How do they operate? Can you tell us something about them?

That is a really good question, although I do not have specific expertise. A study was done and reported in August this year, for which I can give you the reference, into the 43 policing localities and, it turns out, based on the survey, that a substantial majority of police forces have an ethics committee. There is no generalised framework or structure. They were largely divided into two types. The first type used their ethics committee largely as a kind of expert panel for ad hoc ethical dilemmas. The other type incorporated ethics committees into their internal governance structure and they incorporated a whole range of types of reporting, which included human resources questions, for example. There is quite a diversity of ways in which such committees are set up. They are increasingly used. There is no obligation to use them, and, of course, the advice from an ethics committee is not binding.
I will defer to Guy, because I know that we are short of time and he will take this forward.

Q13 I have some specific questions that require yes or no answers. They are first directed to Deputy Chief Constable Travis. The South Wales Police ethics committee is an independent committee. Do we not need a national data ethics model on a statutory basis, with national guidance?

T/DCC Mark Travis: I want to answer your question accurately, so I need to use more than one word; I apologise. We have an internal and external ethics committee who support us. The complexity of this area of business, which has been highlighted today and has just been discussed, would be beneficial if there were a form of central reference that had subject matter expertise in a complex area. Whether that is statutory, or how that is formed, is a recommendation or decision for other people, but would we want to have that facility and that support to make effective decisions? I think that would be of benefit to us.
I did not realise that you had two committees. Can you explain the difference?

T/DCC Mark Travis: The internal ethics committee consists of people from our own organisations who make observations and recommendations about challenging questions. The external ethics committee is made up of professionals, predominantly with a professional educational background, who form a committee and who then, if necessary, they can go directly to the chief constable with any form of challenge.
They are dealing with what I call the policy rather than the day-to-day issues.

T/DCC Mark Travis: They deal with everything, in the way that Professor Yeung described, from policy and procedure through to staffing issues, issues around equality, all sorts of things. They have looked at the issue of—
Their decisions are minuted . Am I correct?
T/DCC Mark Travis: They are minuted and they are publicly shared.
If the force decides not to follow a recommendation, is that minuted or a matter of public record?
T/DCC Mark Travis: Yes.
Good. Can I turn to the Metropolitan Police? Who appoints the members of your ethics committee?
It is the London P olicing E thics P anel (LPEP) , and I believe that it is appointed by the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime.
Does it publish minutes?

Yes, it does, on the MOPAC website. It commissioned a report on the Met’s use of live facial recognition, which is also published, including the response by the Met about how it is going to meet the five conditions for the ethical deployment of the technology. That is all available on the website.
Presumably, the Metropolitan Police is not obliged to follow a recommendation—or is it?

It is not statutory, but why would we not follow five very good and sensible recommendations for the ethical deployment of the kit? I think, from the MOPAC oversight perspective , when it comes to new and innovative technology—or sensitive processing, as it is in this case— it would check and oversee that we are responding to the LPE P recommendations.
Is it a matter of public record if there is non-following by the police?
We have written to show how we would follow it. I cannot imagine a circumstance where we would not.
Well, it has not happened yet.
We could write to them and tell them that we would not.
All right. Would you also agree that it would be helpful to have national guidance, possibly on a statutory basis?

I think that there is some work across policing—it is not my area of expertise—to bring together a national data ethics board. That would be very useful. Other places that we go to are the CDEI—the Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation. The Alan Turing Institute has been really useful with help and advice on data ethics. There is some national work, but I am not sure how advanced it is.

We have slightly overrun but let us see whether any members have further short questions, presuming on your ability to stay for another two minutes. For some members, this is something of a revelation. It certainly was to those of us who were on the committee a couple of years ago, doing this work. As Baroness Henig said, the more questions you ask, the more questions you want to ask. Is there anything that the witnesses would like to leave with us that they feel we have not properly covered or that they would like us to amplify?

T/DCC Mark Travis: The last question was in relation to oversight and scrutiny. The police and crime commissioner structure in south Wales and the mayor’s structure in the Metropolitan Police are very keen to get this right, on the back of the complexity that exists around the position. We are very keen, as police officers, to get it right, and you have suggested a number of things today that we will take away and consider. We are very open to suggestions and recommendations on how we move this area forward. We recognise the significant impact of the use of the technology, which is why we are so determined to manage it in the most effective way we can. Thank you for your time.

I have a few brief comments. One of them is the importance of recognising that, because the technology operates at scale, it has the capacity to change the default political and constitutional culture and environment in which we move about lawfully in public spaces, and that, I think, is easily lost in these discussions. I just want to remind the committee of that.

The second piece that I want to emphasise is that, even though the claim is that the intervention is minimal, we need to remember that there is a really stigmatising effect in being singled out by a police officer as you are going about your lawful business in public. As a non-white woman, I am very conscious of how that can have a differential impact as I move about the world, particularly in airports, for example, in a very troubling way. I want to remind the committee of the reality of that experience.
That is the point that Lord Beith was making, although I am not sure whether I would catch you at the January sales or a football match, Lord Beith.

To all our witnesses, thank you very much. This is a very short inquiry, too short for the subject, but it is the best that we can do in the time we have available before the membership of the committee changes. We wanted to use this opportunity to pursue points that we identified a couple of years ago, but knowing that life and technology move on, it is quite hard to keep up and be on top of it . Thank you all very much indeed.

[1] The witness has clarified that her point was as follows: “ You can see the attractions for control within that, and that is why I think that we need to have a specific legislative regime that provides clear and effective safeguards to ensure adherence to respect for democratic rights and freedoms and the rule of law .”

sessions.w: Confederation of Passenger Transport; Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency; Local Government Association

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Accessible transport: legal obligations , HC 82
Wednesday 22 November 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 22 November 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Iain Stewart (Chair); J ack Brereton; Sara Britcliffe; Karl McCartney; Grahame Morris; Gavin Newlands; Greg Smith ; Mick Whitley .
Questions 79 – 11 1
Witnesses

III : Keith McNally, Operations Manager, Confederation of Passenger Transport; Loveday Ryder, Chief Executive, Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency; and Councillor Linda Taylor, Vice-Chair , Local Infrastructure and Net Zero Group, Local Government Association.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Confederation of Passenger Transport
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Keith McNally, Loveday Ryder and Councillor Linda Taylor.
Q79 Welcome to our third panel this morning. Could I ask each of you to introduce yourselves and your organisation, please ?
Good morning. I am Keith McNally, operations director at CPT , the Confederation of Passenger Transport, the trade association for the bus and coach sector.
I am Loveday Ryder , the chief executive of the DVSA —the Driv ing and Vehicle Standards Agency. We look after drivers, vehicles and enforcement activity on the roads.
Councillor Taylor: Good morning. I am Linda Taylor. I am the leader of Cornwall Council but I am here representing the LGA. I am the vice-chair of the local infrastructure and net zero board .

Q80 Thank you very much and welcome to you all. Linda, we have heard in the course of our inquiry many complaints about street clutter, poor maintenance of pavements and e-scooters all combining to make the public realm harder for people with disabilities to navigate. Can you tell me a little abou t how local authorities apply the public sector equality duty when it comes to the streetscape?

For a lot of local authorities it is a challenge. I am going to use local experience. In most places like Cornwall, there are A-frames, chairs and furniture. If local authorities have not trained the appropriate person who is able to go out and issue tickets , which is a costly process , they have nowhere else to go. The easiest answer that we see happening is a default position to the legislation that London has in relation to enforcement of street pavement activity. It seems sensible to have that default position.
Q81 Could you tell us a little more about how that works in London and why it is not applicable elsewhere ?

My understanding of what happens in London is that if there is pavement parking, in particular, you can be issued with a fixed penalty. Local authorities outside London could have that ability , but they would have to train specific officers to deal with it , whereas i f it was a default position, it would make accessibility easy to implement across the whole of the UK.
Q82 Would that be welcomed generally across local authorities?

Definitely. It would be cost-effective and it would allow local authorities to make sure that pavements were kept clear. It is not just for disability. Where there are joined-up cycle routes, it could be to protect the cycle routes. In Cornwall, we are very passionate in delivering our active travel , but we need very clear legislation. It is there for you : default position, please.

Q83 Thank you. To follow up that point, you referenced active travel. There is lots of money being spent on redesigning streetscapes. How well are the needs of people with disabilities taken into account when th ose are being designed?

As an example of where there is a very obvious failure, just over Westminster Bridge, outside County Hall, there is a floating bus island, where there is the pavement, a cycle lane and then a bus stop on an elevated bit of pavement. It is safe as regards cyclists not being in the same path as buses and other traffic, but when people with a visual impairment come off the bus there is a very dangerous crossing point , with bikes often going at high speeds. Th at has been flagged to us as a particular problem. Clearly, the needs of visually impaired people were not taken into account when that was being designed. I use that as one example. Generally, how well does involving disabled people work in the design process?

Being parochial, and going back to what we do in Cornwall — I know other local authorities follow our lead — we implement a decision wheel called doughnut economics from Kate Raworth. It is a decision wheel that we demonstrate for every decision we make that has an impact on our residents. Disability is a characteristic that is built into th e decision wheel. We look at all aspects so that we can see that the decisions we are making are right and proper and do not disadvantage other sectors in our community. That is our guidance.
Q84 Is that specifically for Cornwall or is it a standard practice across local authorities?

We introduced it and a lot of local authorities have adopted the model. It is not just for travel; it is every decision we make. We look to see, with our protected characteristics and with our community, that the decisions we are making are right for everybody. It is an incredibly useful too l. Happy to send it to you.
Q85 We would be very interested to see that.
Typically , who would you consult? What types of groups would you consult when making design decisions?

Most road schemes have to go out to consultation, especially for active travel. We have extensive consultations , and that happens with the majority of local authorities. It is beholden on the local authority to make sure that they engage and identify. If there is somebody not responding, in Cornwall we absolutely actively make sure that we engag e with every person who could be impacted. We go out and talk.

Q86 The first question is particularly for Keith. It is about some of the transport used for home to school transport , rail replacement bus transport and things like tha t, a lot of which is currently exempt from the Public Service Vehicle s Accessibility Regulations. When do you expect those sorts of vehicles to come into compliance and reach compliance with some of th e legislation?

As an industry, we are very much committed to improving accessibility. We have demonstrated that over the years. Where the regulations were well understood, the delivery of compliance has been very good. Where the problem arose is, as you say, on certain home to school services and rail replacement services, where the regulations were not as well understood. A problem developed where there was an insufficiently compliant fleet to deliver all those services in a compliant way. Hence the need for the medium-term exemptions currently in place.
Q87 How medium term is medium term? It has been going on for quite a while, has n’t it?
They run through to 2026.
Q88 Do you expect that we will be entirely compliant by 2026?

I do n’t, if I ’m honest. We have put forward a proposal, as part of the D fT call for evidence on PSVAR , which are the regulations on public service vehicle, bus and coach accessibility. That proposal is that what we call open-door services — services that anyone can get on, whether it is a local bus service, long-distance express coach or, indeed, a rail replacement service — should be compliant in the future. Most of them already are.

The other element of the proposal is that where services are closed-door and the passengers are known about in advance , which are largely home to school services , those services would be compliant on the basis of demand. Where there was an accessibility requirement, it would be provided for.

Q89 Are we sufficiently meeting those needs? Every year, there are children who do not have their transport in place soon enough ; I am sure colleagues have similar issues. There does not seem to be a sufficient supply of vehicles with the accessibility requirements for children who have a disability. Is a more widespread issue the lack of vehicles suitably adapted to facilitate home to school transport?

We are playing catch-up, in effect, because coaches do not have to be accessible by law. Coaches, when they are used on services that are in the scope of the regulations, need to be compliant. As I say, it was not understood that certain services that were in scope were indeed in scope. That is to do with some of the complexity around the regulations, the way they were written and the way the home to school market has changed over the years since the regulations were originally written. At the moment, it depend s on whether a separate fare is paid as to whether the service is in scope of the regulations or not.

Our proposal is that that aspect will be swept away, so that if a service was what we describe as regular , and ha d a timetable, such as a home to school service or a works service operating on a daily basis , it would be compliant on the basis of demand, whether or not a separate fare was paid. That complexity would be taken away.

Q90 I understand that. The question I am asking , though, is whether we are sufficiently meeting demand. That seems to be a wider issue. The other thing I want to ask you about — maybe Loveday might be able to give some stats as well — is the scale of th e issue? How many vehicles out there are non-compliant with this legislation?

We believe that there are in the region of 10,000 to 15,000 vehicles used on home to school services. Many of those —most of them — would be covered by the medium-term exemption s. The default position in 2026 is that many of th em would come into scope. We probably have between 3,000 and 4,000 coaches that are PSVAR-compliant at the moment. There are more coming on stream all the time , with new vehicles and existing vehicles that are adapted. As I say, we are playing catch-up in the context that the covid pandemic hit the coach industry very hard and made it more difficult to invest.
Q91 Loveday, is your data at DVSA showing an improving picture?

We do not hold data on that, per se. The Department collates the numbers of the medium-term exemptions that there are. My understanding of that is there is a requirement that each year the percentage of compliance will go up or it will not be granted for the next year. I agree with Keith that we should see an improving picture between now and 2026, certainly.
Q92 You are not responsible for ensuring that those vehicles are compliant with some of the public sector equality duty and accessibility requirements .

We work with operators to make sure that they are in compliance where they have buses on services that are in scope. That means that we work with them right from the beginning, with a new operator seminar, where we make sure that they are educated and the drivers are trained. We work through content in the theory test. Every one of the things, the touch points that DVSA has with a PSV, we check , either to make sure that there is a medium-term —
Q93 You are not collecting data on any of it .

We have data on the number of checks that we do and then the number of offences. I cannot tell you, in total, as a percentage of the fleet, how compliant it is. For example, we did 5,100 roadside checks on PSVs in 2022 -23. Of that number, we found 14 accessibility offences. That 5,100 is about 6% of the fleet. When you take out earned recognition, which is for our best and most compliant operators , and we do not pull th em over at roadside , the equivalent is that we pull over about 8% of the non - earned recognition fleet each year.
Q94 What are the consequences for those operators and vehicle owners? Is there a fining regime that you implement? What is the consequence?

We take intelligence from the roadside . We take intelligence from complaints that we receive from the public. We put that through a triage process. We certainly log them all and then we work our way through th em . O ur approach to enforcement and our strategy is always that the best approach is to b egin with education.

By and large, operators want to be compliant, so we start with educating, providing additional information, helping them to comply and making sure that they know what they are supposed to be doing. If it becomes a theme or there is evidence that they may be, perhaps, wilfully not doing it, we use our investigative powers, do targeted checks on operators, maybe visit operator premises and look for evidence that their systems are right and that it is not a systemic or a wilful failure by an operator. If we think, at that point, that there is an issue, we refer it to the traffic commissioner s. The traffic commissioner s are the regulator and they make a decision based on the merit and proportionality of th e particular case, as to whether to take it forward under their powers .

Q95 Mi ck Whitley : Good morning, panel. My question is to Linda. How do local authorities procure accessible home to school transport if the vehicles used by local providers are exempt from the accessibility legislation?

The exemption is a little bit of a lifeline until 2026 for local authorities to be able to operate , but a lot of local authorities struggle to get appropriate vehicles under the requirements for accessibility.

The bigger picture, if I may, is that we have the Education Act section 19 which is absolutely directional in how local authorities deal with and deliver transport for SEND children. One thing becoming very clear is that that requirement is growing every year. Looking at the pressures f or local authorities, for most of them school transport is a real, big issue. In 2019, the deficit was £111 million and it is growing seriously every year.

One thing I would ask that some consideration is given to is that, apart from the requirements under SEND, local authorities are working to very antiquated school transport legislation from 1944. That seriously needs to be looked at to help provide a better system, per se, for school transport. When local authorities are not able to get vehicles that meet accessibility needs, that adds to the additional costs to make sure, under the education Act, that they get SEND children to school. It is a picture that is escalating every day.
Q96 Are local authorities that are unable to provide accessible vehicles in breach of the public sector equality duty?

They have th e fallback position of the exempt, which will run until 2026. It is an absolute challenge. They have to provide transport so that is wh y they are going out to taxis, which is quite a gold-plated service. That i s an additional cost.

For local authorities, once they have been able to procure a service that meets the accessibility requirements, there is th e challenge of making sure that they enforce what I call the street furniture, the drop-down pavements, making sure that it is very clear. There is a lot of work to be done there as well.
Q97 Thank you. The last question is to Loveday. Cracking name that, by the way, is n’t it?
Thank you.
Q98 Could you explain the DVSA’s function and approach to enforcing the Public Service Vehicle s Accessibility Regulations?

Yes, absolutely. As I answered previously and building on that, what we have aimed to do, with PSVAR, is to build it into all the processes we run and all the interactions we have with operators of PSVs; starting from a new operator seminar, working through our road to earned recognition scheme and making sure that we check KPIs monthly. The two-year audits have PSVAR as part of them. Obviously, there is the annual inspection of a vehicle — the MOT-equivalent for PSVs . PSVAR is built into that as well and it is checked as to whether the equipment is on the vehicle.

When we do roadside checks, as I said before, we look at the equipment, and check that it is working. Of course, there are some constraints in doing roadside checks , in that we do not go with a full coach or bus. It needs to be a place where the passengers can safely alight before we do the check. We tend to use places like coach parks, stadia or motorway service areas. When we do check s like that, we check not only the vehicle itself, but the operation of equipment . We make sure that drivers know h ow to do t hat and what their duty is in a roadside check.

If we get intelligence that there is a problem, we follow up, as I said, with operator premises visits, where we talk to any drivers we can find. For us, it is about satisfying that the vehicles in scope are compliant , the equipment works and that drivers are trained appropriately, and that the operators themselves have the right processes and systems. It is an end-to-end thing for us.
Q99 How many public service operators have you enforced again s t in the past year for non-compliance with the regulat ions?

If you take annual tests, there were 69,000 vehicles that were tested. That includes those that would be, perhaps, coaches on scheduled services, and it includes out-of-scope vehicles. Of those, 33 failed on PSVAR items in 2022 -23 ; 13 then passed after rectification, so it is quite small numbers. On the roadside checks, again in 2022 -23 , we found, of the 5,100 we pulled over, 14 accessibility offences. So far this year, we have had three. They are relatively small numbers that we see.
Q100 What concerns do you have, as a regulator, about accessibility in the sector?

The traffic commissioners are the regulator in this space. In terms of our enforcement, if I think about areas where we would like to see improvement, one of the thing s we will be looking at is how passengers can make complaints. We hear a lot of reports from customers that they find it difficult to navigate the system. There is Bus Users UK, and a separate set-up in London.

We tend to respond to the complaints that are about the vehicle and the way the equipment is working on the vehicle. We are going to try to streamline our complaints process, signpost it to make it a bit easier and set up something that gives people feedback that their complaint is logged. That is an area we can do. The other thing we have done in the past is to hold awareness sessions. In 2021, we had a special accessibility awareness week. We look to do more things like that, using more intelligence-led work and using ANPR to try to investigate better. They are all sensible things.

We are going to invest in some wheelchairs. On our roadside checks, we will be able to go with a wheelchair and get the driver to demonstrate that they know how to restrain it adequately, and get it on and off properly. There are lots of things we can do.

Q101 A number of local authorities are now introducing what are known as DRT service s, demand responsive transit, that sit between a bus service and a taxi , where you have an app to summon a vehicle to come and collect you and others. To what extent are those services covered by existing accessibility regulations? Is there a gap that needs to be addressed?

In Cornwall, the delivery of a bus service is incredibly challenging ; we absolutely have to work to a timetable. If other local authorities are using exempt vehicles to address the suggestion you have just made, which is a very good suggestion, they have a bit of a dilemma. If those exempt vehicles have capacity, they have to make a decision: are they going to sell the spare seats to family members ? If they were to do that, to think more about the impact on the climate, the vehicle would lose th e PSVAR exemption. It sounds good. It is a model that needs to be followed but it is not as easy to implement, especially in a lot of local areas where transport is not as available and freely subsidised as in parts of urban areas. It is a challenge.
Q102 Keith, Loveday, do you have any views on the DRT provision?

PSVAR regulations apply to vehicles with a seating capacity of over 22 , so 22 or less are exempt. Many DRT services have fewer than that number of seats , so they are exempt. Many of the services provided are probably accessible, even though they are out of scope , so provision is made for wheelchair users and others with accessibility needs. I do n’t have any data on the proportions of which would be accessible and which not .
I do n’t have anything to add on that.

Q103 Thank you. The last issue I wish to cover in this session is the enforcement of regulations with regard to taxis carrying people with disabilities, particularly people with assistance dogs. The law is very clear that the passenger has the right to take their dog or other animal with them , but we hear many cases where that is not happening. What is the problem in enforcing that law , Linda?

I am sorry to keep going back to where I can give evidenc e. In Cornwall, believe it or not, it is not such a big issue. We have had very few cases where the local authority has had to go out and enforce.

An issue I would like to raise is that where taxis have been licensed outside their particular area, it is a real big problem for local authorities to deliver enforcement. One consideration could be that local authorities license the vehicles and, if they are licensed within that local authority, it can enforce and m ake sure that the requirements under the law are absolutely delivered.
Q104 For taxis operating in another local authority area, who has responsibility for enforcement? Is it the local authority where the taxi is licensed or the one where it is operating?
It is the local authority where it is licensed.
Right, okay.
It causes problems . It can cause problems especially if there is a local area where taxis coming in know there is a lot of business, like coastal resorts.
Q105 It is a big issue in Brighton, is n’t it?
Yes. If the local authority had the ability to license, it would absolutely be able to enforce. At the moment, that is a little bit of a concern for many local authorities.
Q106 Talk me through that. To give your example, say someone in Liskeard —
Well done.

Q107 — wants to get in a taxi that is licensed by Plymouth, a different authority, and they make a complaint to Cornwall Council, what rights do you have as a council to take that up with Plymouth to get them to enforce?

We do not have any legal enforcement . However, because of the close proximity of our two areas, our transport department would absolutely make sure that the licensing authority of that vehicle —for example , Plymouth — is made aware of the issues. As the local authority for Cornwall, we cannot enforce complaints.
Q108 Should it be mandatory for all authorities to take proactive steps to identify non-compliance —for example , doing mystery shopping or other such measures?

I would suggest that where data show s that there is an issue, it would be absolutely appropriate. It is a really good suggestion to do mystery shopping , but a local authority that does not have those complaints should not have the burden of doing mystery shopping. A local authority will know if there is an issue, because it understands its community . Obviously, if complaints escalate, it is a really good idea to take a mystery shopper exercise.
Q109 Finally, should it be mandatory for all local authorities to maintain a list of all their accessible taxis under the Equality Act?

Absolutely. People’s health in some parts is not improving. It is really important that they know wh ich taxis are accessible just to make their life easier as they mov e around. Also, it is assurance that if the local authority is listing accessible taxis, it is because it knows about them. That is incredibly important for standards as well.
Thank you very much. Do colleagues have any last questions?
Q110 I have a quick one for Councillor Taylor. It is very kind of you to offer to share with the Committee the model you have in Cornwall. We w ould be interested in that.

To go back to the earlier point about floating bus stops, A-frames and street clutter, you mentioned the position in London. Things are getting worse with the advent of scooters, e-scooters and electric bikes littering the pavements. A little while ago, a number of us, at the invitation of the Royal National Institute of Blind People and Guide Dogs for the Blind, did an exercise where you wear a blindfold, go on to a talking bus and walk through a shopping centre or a neighbourhood centre to have th e lived experience of what it is like for someone who is blind or partially sighted. I thought that was incredibly valuable. I had bruises on my shins from falling over the A-frames and the chairs that were placed outside without any consideration of what obstructions mean for people with disabilities. Have any of the panellists done that?
No.
Q111 It is valuable, honestly; it is a good insight. No pun intended .
I think it emphasises the point, if I may, about delegated powers coming from London to the rest of the UK to d eal with pavement furniture.
I understand that. Point well made.
Thank you.
Thank you all for your time and evidence this morning. We have had a packed morning, with lots of information to digest. Thank you, again, for coming before us.

sessions.iT: Keeping the power on: our future energy technology mix
sessions.w: Richard Coulson (Wood Recyclers’ Association); Philipp Lukas (Future Biogas); Eddie Wilkinson (Melton Renewable Energy); Angela Hepworth (Drax)

segs.tx: Energy Security and Net Zero Committee
Oral evidence: Keeping the power on: our future energy technology mix , HC 116
Wednesday 13 December 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 December 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Angus Brendan MacNeil (Chair); Vicky Ford; Mark Garnier; Mark Pawsey; Lloyd Russell-Moyle; Alexander Stafford; Mick Whitley.
Questions 200 - 329
Witnesses
I : Angela Hepworth, Commercial Director, Drax ; Richard Coulson, Chair, Wood Recyclers’ Association ; Philipp Lukas, CEO, Future Biogas ; and Eddie Wilkinson, CEO, Melton Renewable Energy.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Wood Recyclers’ Association
– Future Biogas
– Melton Renewable Energy
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Angela Hepworth, Richard Coulson, Philipp Lukas and Eddie Wilkinson .

Q200 Good afternoon and welcome to the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee. This is our third session in our keeping the power on inquiry. Today we have a session on bioenergy. I see four witnesses in front of me and I will ask them, as I always do, name, rank and serial number, starting on my left.

Good afternoon. I am C hair of the UK Wood Recyclers’ Association. Our members represent the entire supply chain for UK waste wood. We were formed in 2001 and our members represent over 90% of the volume of UK waste wood we process each year in the UK.
Excellent, thank you very much.
Hello, I am the Commercial Director for Drax. We generate renewable power from biomass and we are looking to develop carbon removals from biomass in the future.
Thank you very much. I think we have heard of Drax.
Good afternoon. I am the C hief E xecutive of Future Biogas. We are an anaerobic digestion operator running a dozen plants, injecting around 0.5 TWh of green gas into the grid in the UK.
Excellent, thank you very much. Finally, you have been stuck out on the edge there, I apologise.

That is fine. CEO of Melton Renewable UK Ltd. We are quite a unique operation, a portfolio of five biomass power stations, unique in the nature of the fuel being land neutral, sustainable, UK-sourced biomass, including 500,000 tonnes per annum of poultry litter . We are also unique in our longevity. We have been in operation since 1992 , with our first power station based at Eye.

Q201 Grand. Thank you all for coming here this afternoon. T o kick us off I will probably start with Mr Wilkinson, because I have great sympathy for where you are sitting at the end of the table there . W hat role should bioenergy play in and outside of the power sector in 2030 and , say , 2050 as well?

I think it is an important contributor to power generation and keeping the lights on, which is the subject of this Committee. C urrently, as an industry, biomass contributes between 6% and 10% of demand. UK demand is somewhere between just under 30 GW and up to 50 GW . W e are about 2.8 GW to 3 GW, so we are about 6.5% to 10%. We would like to grow that capacity. As things currently stand, we will be a diminishing share of UK power production based upon lack of support and lack of incentives , in reality, between 2030 and 2035.
We will probably investigate that further, but just briefly from Philipp Lukas.
What role should it play in the power sector?
Yes.

Probably very little, because we make gas and it will be much more valuable, we think, to inject that gas into the gas network and use it for decarbonisation of heat, which thus far has been a trickier thing to do.
Fascinating, thank you. Angela Hepworth.

I would say that biomass has a critical role to play in the power sector. The big benefit of biomass is that it can provide reliable, dispatchable renewable power, so it can provide the power that we need when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining. It plays a critical role in the system today, maintaining security of supply and enabling us to displace fossil fuels . O ne of the critical things about biomass is if we keep generating from biomass now, we can use it as a source of carbon removals in the future. That is what Drax is looking to do at its power station in north Yorkshire. We want it to be a source of carbon removals, taking carbon out of the atmosphere and putting it permanently underground.
Yes, I will touch on that in just a second. Richard Coulson.

Engineered removals is certainly important, but I see biomass’s role in the future as essential. It is not only about the baseload power. Our members produced around 3 TWh of baseload from waste wood last year for the UK. It is not just about the carbon savings. We have equated that our sector, from waste wood alone, saves 734,000 tonnes of carbon compared to the marginal fleet. That could increase to 3.5 million tonnes with backers, but what sets us apart is that we are missing something, which the biomass strategy picks up. We provide a vital environmental service in making full use of the UK waste wood resource.

Q202 Thank you very much. Philipp Lukas, Angela Hepworth touched on the bioenergy and carbon capture and storage, but what regions and sites and scale of site do you think are well suited to the bioenergy with carbon capture and storage?

In the case of anaerobic digestion, it will always be a much smaller industry in the size of its plants than biomass power stations. The material that we use, be it waste or be it grown crops, is generally produced in a very local proximate area and our material never travels much more than, on average, five to seven miles to the plant and then back to the field in terms of the fertiliser out the back of our digesters.

As for carbon dioxide, we think that each anaerobic digestion plant—and we believe there could be several hundred built in the UK— could collect between 10 and 25,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide, which could be aggregated for sequestration. V ery briefly, the anaerobic digestion is a bit like brewing. Instead of making alcohol and carbon dioxide—the bubbles in the c hampagne, if you like—we make methane and carbon dioxide, then before we inject the methane into the grid, we strip off the carbon dioxide, but as it has been absorbed the previous season by the plants it is biogenic CO 2 so it is a carbon removal if we were to take it for sequestration.
Q203 Angela Hepworth, you mentioned CCS or BECCS around presumably Drax in north Yorkshire. Do you want to expand on that a little more?

We have our existing facility up in north Yorkshire with four biomass units. Our aim is to convert at least two of those to bioenergy with carbon capture and storage. We would like the first of those units to come online in 2030 and the second by 2035. It is a fabulous location for carbon capture and storage because we can be part of the cluster up in the Humber and Tees region and there is a brilliant resource in the North Sea to enable us to store the CO 2 permanently underground. With the existing power station there and such excellent storage resources, it is the obvious place to locate a BECCS facility and provide a source of permanent carbon removals.
Q204 How dispatchable would such a power plant be to add balance to the grid and basically to meet needs?

If you fit carbon capture and storage and it becomes a source of carbon removals, probably you want to run the unit ’ s baseload because its key function is as a carbon removals technology and you want to maximise the potential of the carbon removals. One of the great things about the Drax site is, as I say, we have four units on the site at the moment so you could have a perfect complement with two units of BECCS providing baseload carbon removals and two flexible biomass units sitting alongside them, which would provide you with your dispatchable flexible power.

Q205 In August this year, the Government published their biomass strategy. I am wondering if each of you can give us your views on the strategy . W hat do you think of it? I will perhaps start with Mr Coulson and move along.

Our sector welcome s the strategy. The one important thing that it recognised is that biomass comes in all shapes and forms. It is not just about large-scale pellet combustion. It also includes waste, so we are very supportive of that. It recognises the role that bioenergy has to play and how the role can improve with BECCS. We particularly were supportive of the four key pillars that it introduce s in respect of net zero, sustainability and resource management, which suits our sector. We score well on those criteria.

What we didn’t appreciate is that there still is no clear detail there. The power BECCS business model has been removed away from our scale of fleet. We have about 50 plants in the UK, ranging in size from 1 to 65 MW , and we only have one option in our greenhouse gas removal model . T he detail is not there. Some of the plants will drop out of the ROC regime in 2027 and urgent business decisions need to be made now to keep that plant online.
Q206 What would you have liked to see that was n o t there?

We need some investor confidence, so we need clear detail on what the greenhouse gas removal schemes will provide and how they will operate. We are at the point now with some plant that it might be too late—
Q207 You are waiting for Government to tell you what to do; is that what you are saying?
No. We have been lobbying long and hard for them to tell us what the business models are, the detail of the scheme.
Q208 But you have told Government what you want?
I believe so, yes.
T hey have n o t responded?
We need urgent clarity on what that model will be.
Q209 What was your view of the strategy?

We welcome the strategy. We thought it was an excellent overview of the role of biomass. It confirmed that biomass has a critical role in the power sector now, and it confirmed that going forward the priority use for biomass should be around BECCS. For us, that was excellent.

The key thing for us is seeing the next steps. The biomass strategy said that Government would be publishing further details on a sustainability framework. That is very welcome. We are waiting to see that and the follow-up steps with relation to getting BECCS confirmed and getting the contractual arrangements in place. We are looking for Government to confirm that we should be online as a BECCS unit in 2030 and to finalise the details of the business model.
Q210 Does it provide the certain future that your company would be looking for?
It provides the right vision for the future. What we now need is the practical implementation steps.
Q211 T here is an outline, giving a direction of travel. Like Mr Coulson, do you want more detail?
What we need is the follow-up, practical implementation steps in terms of agreeing the framework to support power BECCS and getting a contract in place.
Q212 Mr Lukas, what did you think of it?

We thought again the focus on BECCS was very positive. That is the future of any form of biomass use. We were very keen on the common sustainability framework because, as an operator, we are now moving into an unsubsidised world, so we are selling our gas with subsidy. As a result, we need rigorous sustainability evidence for our corporate customers.

We were a bit disappointed that there was a focus on perennial crops and not annual crops that fit into the rotation, in particular because we believe there is a huge opportunity there to help decarbonise UK farming . It could bring into UK farming cropping opportunities that on the one hand may replace some of the income lost to subsidy that has gone, and at the same time will help the journey of the farm to lower use of inputs—diesel, fertiliser, sprays—and to the formation of soil organic matter, soil carbon. Generally , anaerobic digestion a s a tool to improve the carbon balance of the farm wasn’t yet recognised in there.
Q213 Did it look far enough forward for you? Was there more detail you wanted?

There could have been more detail. There is still a binary approach to land use: it is either for food or for fuel. We think both of those need to be considered in the round, which is something we have taken up .
Tell me what you mean by that.

There is an opportunity in an annual cropping regime to use crops grown for anaerobic digestion and the digestate that comes out of the back of the digester to improve the organic balance of the farm, so soil organic matter, as well as to reduce, through amendments to the way that cropping is done, the use of diesel, the use of imported fertilisers, which obviously have a high carbon footprint and those sorts of things. That was missing from the biomass strategy. I will grant that that is something that is a relatively new approach. It is our business model that we have been pursuing now for two or three years and it is something we have been discussing with DEFRA.
Q214 T hank you. Mr Wilkinson, your thoughts?

It was a bit of a cur ate’ s egg, so good in parts and not in others. I t was positive that it recognised the environmental benefits that biomass plants can provide in dealing with annual waste arising from , say , the poultry industry . R ather than getting it spread to land and leaching into watercourses , the things that happened in the River Wye over in the west—that doesn’t happen in the east because 500,000 tonnes of litter are managed by us, so it is well managed—and the propensity it gives to , say , avian flu, the disposal route for the litter is important in that regard. That was positive .

However, what it didn’t go on to say is that it will be supported beyond 2027 . A t the moment that management tool will be gone in 2027 because the operating costs of a biomass fleet will exceed the revenue that it can receive. There is a gap there in terms of how that will be sustained beyond 2027. Yes, there are abatement revenues coming downstream in maybe the mid-2030s, but there isn’t a roadmap or an opportunity to stay in business for those eight years or so between 2027 and the mid-2030s.
Q215 Are you suggesting that the amount of biomass power will reduce because there isn’t the—
I can guarantee it will reduce because the subsidy isn’t—
Q216 By a factor of how much? How much do you think it is likely to fall between now and 2035?

Power BECCS covers two out of about 54 power stations, granted there is a large power station that it will support, so that is fine, but the other 52 I would suggest will be uneconomic on a sliding scale between 2027 and 2037 as the ROC regime falls away.
Q217 Y ou are telling us that the existing biomass - generated power will fall out of use over the next few years because of the G overnment ’s strategy?
Yes. I can guarantee our units will fall away come 2027.
Q218 Does everybody else share that view, that the proportion of our electricity generated by biomass will fall over the next few years as a consequence of the Government’s strategy here?

We should view the ROC scheme as a real success. It has built a fleet of modern environmentally compliant waste wood plants across the country to handle all UK waste wood, let alone the baseload power. We are on a cliff edge now. We have a great graph that shows the ramp-up of the plans and now there is no future, there is no support post-ROC on what will happen. That is what I tried to intimate in my last answer . We need the detail now to transition from one scheme to another and maybe transitional support. It might be too late for Mr Wilkinson’s plants to make the investment decision and get the planning to instal l BECCS by 2027. We need some transitional support to get from ROCs to the future.
Q219 Very quickly, Angela Hepworth and Philipp Lukas, do you share this view, that the proportion of our electricity coming from bio means is likely to decline?

For Drax and other large biomass generators, Government have confirmed that they want to put in place transitional arrangements from 2027 to enable them to transition to BECCS. I am confident that we should have an arrangement in place that will enable us to continue generating at Drax.
Y ou see Drax continuing for many years ahead?
Yes.
Q220 Okay. Mr Lukas.

I am not qualified to speak on particular ly power, but on anaerobic digestion I think there is a good argument to say that on a post-subsidy regime for biogas for anaerobic digestion, there will be a continuation in many plants unsubsidised.

Q221 Ms Hepworth, given that the carbon release by burning woody biomass at Drax is unlikely—probably impossible—to be resequestered before 2050 and definitely not in the area in which the carbon was released, is the UK decision to support large-scale bioenergy sabotaging our efforts to achieve net zero in reality, no matter what it says on the paper?

Maybe I can answer that first of all in relation to biomass and then in relation to BECCS. Biomass is counted as zero-rated carbon emissions at the stack and there are very good reasons for that . It is critically important—and this is a key point I wanted to make today—that people understand the difference between biogenic carbon and CO 2 that is produced by fossil fuels. If you are taking carbon from fossil fuels, you are extracting carbon that has been in the earth for tens of millions of years. If you didn’t extract it, it would remain in the earth, but instead you are pumping CO 2 into the atmosphere. Now, if you are using biogenic CO 2 it is part of a natural carbon cycle. The material that we are using is a by-product of the timber industry. If that material was left in place it would either be burnt as waste or it would decompose in any event and the CO 2 would be released, whereas we can use it to displace fossil fuel.

Provided it is part of a sustainable forestry practice and the trees are regrown, the minute you start regrowing the trees, they are absorbing the CO 2 from the atmosphere again. That is why biomass now is counted as zero-rated at the stack because it has a neutral impact on carbon stocks. In the future we will be able to use our BECCS facility to take carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere via trees, via our power station , and store it permanently underground. The Climate Change Committee, the National Infrastructure Committee and the National Grid are all of the view that it is essential that we have carbon removals from BECCS if we are going to meet net zero.
Q222 Carbon imported from wood abroad, you are right, it is treated as zero when it is import ed and then at the stack. Does that not give a false equation of our national picture of being net zero?

No. As I said, it is counted as zero-rated at the stack in terms of the carbon emissions, but there are supply chain emissions associated with producing and transporting biomass. In order to get the support that we get at the moment via the renewables obligation and the CfD, there are strict supply chain thresholds that we have to come underneath. At the moment the threshold is 200 kg per MWh and we are at 96. That is our total supply chain emissions. We are very transparent. All the information about our supply chain emissions is on our website . T he key thing is to compare it with the alternative options. If you compare our 96 g per KWh in total emissions from biomass, the equivalent for gas is around about 400. The equivalent for coal is over 1,100. Even taking account of our supply chain emissions, we are a very low-carbon option.
Q223 The supply chain emissions are accounted in terms of net zero, including the growing of the trees?

We take account of the full supply chain emissions and publish details of the supply chain emissions. They are required to come under a particular threshold in order to get renewables support in the UK.
Q224 Just so I am clear, you are saying that it is not true that the import of trees from abroad is treated as zero for the purpose of the national emissions?
Biomass as a technology is zero-rated at the stack, but the full supply chain emissions are counted where they occur.
Q225 Where they occur. So while we are producing demand abroad, they get the hit and we don’t? It is not very fair, is it?
If there are supply chain emissions that are created abroad, that is where they are counted. That is in accordance with international accounting practice.
Q226 But all your wood is from abroad, isn’t it?
The bulk of our wood comes from the US and Canada.
Q227 N one of that then is counted as UK emissions?
The supply chain emissions are counted where they occur and that is in accordance with international accounting practice.

Q228 Just answer the question rather than giving me waffle. Just say, “Yes, they are not counted as UK emissions”. The waffle degrades you; it doesn’t help you. Yes, that is fine. Thank you very much.
Burning wood now with the idea that trees will be grown again in the future, those trees will not reach maturity for many years, maybe 50 or 60 years. Is that net zero in anyone’s mind?

One of the interesting things if you are looking at the impact of trees on carbon stocks is that trees absorb more CO 2 as they are growing than when they are mature. If you use material from forests and if you have replantation of those forests afterwards, from the minute you replant a tree, it is absorbing CO 2 from the atmosphere.
Q229 It is absorbing more CO 2 than you have burned? No.

It is absorbing more CO 2 as it grows than when it is mature. If we step back and look at this at a forest level, I completely appreciate that using material from forests and using that in power stations seems counterintuitive. People worry about that, but if we look at the impacts of the forest industry and what has happened in the US, if you look back over the last 70 years or so, the use of forestry products has increased, but so has carbon stocks in forests. If you manage forests, they are more effective at absorbing CO 2 from the atmosphere and the biomass industry can play a valuable part in that.
Q230 Do you have a programme that you are monitoring to ensure that the forests are increasing where you are purchasing from?
Yes. It is a requirement when we are sourcing biomass that we are able to prove that the carbon stocks in the forests are either neutral or increasing.
Q231 You can guarantee that for all your products?
T hat is one of the requirements, for example, under the S ustainable B iomass P rogramme that we use for our products.

Q232 I will touch on this and I think Vicky Ford will touch on this , too . I think you had a subsidy of about £1.7 million a day in 2022 at Drax. You are the UK’s single largest emitter of CO 2 — the eighth largest in Europe — releasing something like 12.1 megatonnes of CO 2 in 2022. For a bit of context, it is double the UK’s second-biggest emitter, which is Pembroke power station , which emits less than half of that at 5.3 megatonnes. You are still putting CO 2 into the atmosphere and that CO 2 will not be recaptured in the next 30 years, will it?
In terms of the carbon impact, as I say, we are using carbon from sustainable biomass. So long as the impact we are having in the forest—

Q233 Yes, but the point is I know where it is coming from and those trees wouldn’t do it i n the next 30 years. The concerns that people have about rising CO 2 in the atmosphere is what is going in by 2050. This is the temperature rise. You are n o t doing anything about removing that CO 2 . You are emitting 12.1 million tonnes of CO 2 a year into the atmosphere, which isn’t coming out of the atmosphere anytime soon. It is like the CO 2 that is coming out of the gas-powered station as well. Isn’t that correct?
Maybe something that would help to put it in context is if I took a little bit—
But will that come out of the atmosphere? What you burnt last year, when is that coming out of the atmosphere?

If as a result of managed forestry practices we are replanting trees or the forests are replanting trees, then from the minute those trees are replanted they will be absorbing CO 2 from the atmosphere again.

Q234 But shouldn’t we be finding an energy source that is not burning and putting CO 2 into the atmosphere? Because the atmosphere doesn’t care whether the CO 2 came from Drax or from , let’s say , the No. 2, the Pembroke power station .
No, the atmosphere and the planet really do care. They care because—
What, it can discern between your CO 2 and its CO 2 ?

What you need to look at is the impact of the overall process. As I say, if you are burning fossil fuels, you are taking material out of the earth where the carbon has been stored for tens of millions of years and the net impact is to take carbon out of the earth and put it back into the atmosphere. If you are using carbon from forests, then you are using carbon that is part of a natural regeneration cycle and the impact is neutral.

Q235 Hold on. The carbon that is going into the atmosphere, where we are concerned about the global temperature rise in the next 30 years, whether that is being emitted by you or by a gas power station, it is still CO 2 in the atmosphere. Would we not be better trying to produce power and energy from non-carbon sources full stop, non-carbon emitting sources into the atmosphere? Whether you are burning it from trees that were grown a few years ago or trees that were grown millions of years ago, you are still putting CO 2 into the atmosphere.

We need to make the most of all low-carbon energy sources, so biomass has a role to play as part of a balanced mix. We should be making the most of our resources of wind, solar and nuclear, but the point about biomass is it provides renewable power, low-carbon power, at times where the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining. As I say, the carbon impact is neutral, so the carbon impact of using biomass is neutral.

Q236 Over what period? Hang on, there is a very important point. You keep saying it is neutral, but it is neutral over a specific period. This is the point, so what is the specific period over which it is carbon neutral?
It is carbon neutral in the context of a continuous cycle.
Q237 No, no, no. You start today and you start pumping out carbon. You plant the trees and all the rest—I completely understand your logic, but I think the point we are trying to get to is how long .
Before that carbon is taken back.

I t starts becoming zero carbon at a certain point once the trees have reached a certain maturity. What is the length of the cycle that gets it started? Because obviously once you stop producing it, the tree will carry on growing. What is the delay factor? How many years is the delay?
I don’t think I can answer the question in those terms because as soon as you replant trees they are absorbing CO 2 and when they are regrowing—
Somebody must have worked it out.
Q238 Some people tell me it is between 44 and 115 years. W ould you agree that it is possible that it is between 44 and 115 years before that carbon is recaptured?
That is not the way I see it at all because the trees are immediately starting to recapture CO 2 .

Q239 You don’t disagree with that, you just don’t see it that way. There is a final point I just want to raise. Bloomberg had an interesting investigation into Drax , where it saw Drax was avoiding the CfD system — which would have returned £639 million to consumers , which they were due — by putting less production into an area that was producing under the CfD scheme and where production costs were capped . I nstead it sold some of its biomass pellets on the open market, where prices were very high due to the high energy prices. Was Drax gaming the system, as Bloomberg seem to indicate?
No, we absolutely were not. Again, if I give you the context for that, that was during the energy crisis. W e were facing—
Yes, when you could game the system , if it was possible.

—unprecedented circumstances in terms of what was happening to gas and power prices, but also what was happening to the availability in the price of biomass. During that period we had constrained biomass availability. We had hedged our ROC units in advance. The issue with the CfD unit during that period is because of what had happened to power and biomass prices, for substantial periods during that time it would have been uneconomic to run, but we always made sure that it was available to run if it was needed, if one of the other units had broken down or if the system was tight. When the power was needed from the CfD unit, we generated from the CfD unit. Over that period, we returned £45 million to consumers and we were the largest single generator of renewable power during that period.
£45 million is a bit less than the £639 million I quoted, but anyway, time defeats me. I will go to Vicky Ford. I might come back on it.

Q240 Ms Hepworth, please will you stop using this line, “As soon as you plant a tree, it starts taking carbon out of the ground”? We all know that the amount of carbon from a huge mature tree is infinitely higher than a little tiny sapling you have just planted in the ground, so let’s just stop using that phrase.

You claim that Drax is only burning waste wood. “Panorama”, The Daily Telegraph, CBS News, they have all had senior journalists show entire forests being cleared for this waste wood industry that Drax is part of. It is a scandal, isn’t it?
T he bulk of the material we use comes from sawmill and forest residuals.
The bulk, not all. Thank you.
It is something like 98% if we want to be specific about it. L ast year 98% of the material we used came from residuals from sawmills and—
Q241 Where does that statistic come from?
It is a statistic that is available on our website. We published—

Q242 It comes from you. Thank you very much. Now, in terms of how long it take s to replace the carbon from the trees that you have cut down, a Chatham House estimate put that period at 104 years. There are other analysts who say it is nearer 190 years. We need to reduce carbon this year, next year and every year up to 2050 to meet net zero. How can it be acceptable that you are getting the carbon reduction benefits now when the payback period is well past 2050?

As I say, I can only reiterate that if you have managed forestry, it is a more effective way of absorbing CO 2 from the atmosphere. I would like to come back. You mentioned the “Panorama” programme and that was talking about the impact—
And The Telegraph and CBS.
Yes, okay. Let the witness speak.

That was talking in particular about forestry in Canada. Last week I had the privilege to be out at COP and I was able to talk to some people who are in the Canadian forestry sector. The biggest threat to forests in Canada comes from wildfires. Last year Canada lost 19 million hectares of forest due to wildfire, so that is forest that is literally going up in smoke. We all saw on the news the impact that had on communities that had to be displaced, the smoke in the atmosphere and the carbon impacts of that. Canada needs to manage its forests in order to prevent wildfires from happening. It identifies how forestry can play a part in that and we are a very small part of that process, but managed forestry is critical to keeping forests as forests.

Q243 I absolutely get the need to manage forestry and to clear brushwood and create waste wood from that process, but later we will get on to whether there needs to be better regulation and monitoring of whether you are burning waste wood or burning virgin forest.
Your own advisory board, we have been told, has recently said that Drax should stop calling burning trees carbon neutral. Do you have a comment on that?

Our independent advisory board is made up of academic scientist experts. What they said is that biomass per se can be carbon neutral. It depends on the way you are managing your forests. What they recommended we do is some more specific work to look at the impact of biomass supply chains on forests and that is the follow-up work that we are doing. They did not say that biomass per se cannot be carbon neutral, but they encouraged us to do more work on the impacts.

Q244 My understanding of what you want to do is continue burning the wood, which you say is from sustainable waste wood sources , and then take the carbon from that and deploy that into CCS, which you said is an excellent opportunity because your location is so close to the North Sea. If it is such an excellent opportunity, why in March of this year did you announce that you had paused your CCS development plans?

Our CCS development plans are going at pace. W e have already invested over £50 million in the development of BECCS in the UK and we are very much looking forward to having our first unit online in 2030.
Why have we been told that in March you said you had paused it?

What we said in March was that we were looking forward to hav ing more certainty from the Government and that in order to progress with our investment we needed greater certainty and clarity from Government about their intentions with respect to BECCS. The Government have made very positive progress since then in the development of their strategy, so we are confident that we will have our BECCS online in 2030.

Q245 Angela, can I just go back to something you said right at the very beginning when you were talking about the dispatchability of energy from biomass? Clearly , it is very important and you made a very important point about wind and solar. As I understand it, there is 8 GW of biomass capacity in the UK, but at the moment only 3 GW is being used on the grid. Why is 5 GW of capacity of this great energy source not being used?
I can only speak for Drax power station , but we run when the system needs us. There are times when you need more biomass on the system than others and that will depend—

Q246 H ow does that work? Because ultimately right now 46.4% of our energy use is gas, so we all agree we don’t like gas, we all agree that gas is wrong. That is 19.6 GW of power, so we have 5 GW that could reduce that gas capacity quite significantly. The question is why. Look, I am slightly giving you a hard time and you are not responsible for the market, but can anybody explain why it is that we are using an extra 5 GW of gas when we could be using an extra 5 GW of biomass, if biomass is such a good product?

I would agree with the principle that using biomass is better than using gas and we should be prioritising biomass generation ahead of gas. I can’t speak to what is going on in the market that means that plants aren’t being dispatched at any given time.
Q247 Can I just check that your CfD value is £139 per MWh ? I s that right?
In today’s money that is about right, about £130.
Q248 The current electricity price is around £90. I appreciate we have to move forward with decarbonisation, but right now you are quite expensive.

Right now it is above the market price, but Drax, in common with other renewable generation, is given a supplement to the market price. Yes, we are given payments in the market for generating renewable power, but so are other renewable generators. The market price is only a fraction of what it takes to deliver renewable on the system.

Q249 Sure. Sorry, can we get back to sustainability? Richard, why don’t we chat to you for a bit and give Angela a chance to have a glass of water? O n this whole issue of sustainability of the production of biomass, what are the processes for assessing if the biomass supply is genuinely sustainable? Is there a way that we can work this out? Yes, have a crack.

What I am conscious of is there are concerns over the sustainability of biomass, yes, and the issues that you have highlighted at the moment , the whole sector is tainted by those concerns. We welcome the strategy . T here will be another consultation next year and they will look to strengthen sustainable claims. We are very supportive of that. Moving forward, the way we envisage that, it should be risk-based and proportionate. A one - size - fits - all approach w ill not work for everyone.

For our sector, for UK waste wood, domestically sourced waste, there are no Ofgem reporting requirements. There are DEFRA waste reporting requirements. We need to appreciate that some of the UK waste wood fleet will have to burn a proportion of forestry residues. The terminology is important. Drax do es no t burn waste wood. I represent post-consumer waste wood, material that has been used. Drax use preconsumer—
This is old plywood sheets, old pallets, that stuff?

Yes, a bit of furniture and the like. For domestic UK waste wood there are no Ofgem reporting requirements, but there are DEFRA environmental waste reporting requirements. Some of the fleet have to fire with a proportion of virgin materials. It might be a permanent requirement or an operational requirement. Where the fleet is using domestic UK forestry residues, the current Ofgem reporting criteria are sufficient enough in respect of the carbon chain, the location of where the materials come from and the material . I f you envisage moving forward for our sustainability reporting criteria, if you count simple boxes to say it is UK waste, it is UK domestically sourced, there should be further criteria and further questions to answer to pacify these concerns because the public perception is t a inted over biomass.

Q250 It is, you are right, and it has an implication on things like ESG - compliant governance. I s there an audit trail that checks all this stuff? I am deliberately giving you a break, Angela, but if you want to chip in, feel free.
We all have to do annual Ofgem reporting.
Q251 How is that audited?
It is independently audited. We use companies like Black & Veatch .
Okay, that is fine. The same for Drax, yes.

We are not woody biomass, we are mainly poultry litter, which is animal bedding , straw and faeces. In terms of sustainability, in order to get the ROC support we have to prove it is biomass and we batch test everything that comes in and test the biomass content. It has to be 99 . X per cent, so it has to be 100% biomass, effectively. In addition to that, in order to be sustainable, we are measured against Ofgem’s sustainability requirements, where each consignment of fuel on aggregate needs to be less than 55 grams of CO 2 per megajoule of energy in that fuel . F or the fleet I represent, we average about 12, so we have about 80% headroom against that. For the waste products such as litter, the answer is zero, because it is a waste product in the greenhouse gas calculation for Ofgem purposes. That is audited on an annual cycle by PwC.

Q252 Angela, because I am running out of time, just following on from the discussions you have had with my colleagues about this cycle , whether it is 40 years, 140 years or 1,040 years, if the Government were to suddenly turn around and say that wood cut from forests — or even waste wood, as we are discussing — had to be immediately carbon neutral, you would be in trouble, wouldn’t you?
As I say, our view and the Government’s view i s that burning biomass is carbon neutral today.

Q253 It obviously isn’t. It is over a cycle. I completely accept the cycle, but it obviously is n o t day by day. Let’s assume this is a 30-year cycle, and it is probably more than that, there will come a point. If you started doing this—I can’ t remember when you started, but let’s say it was 2010—in 2010 and by 2040 it will be carbon neutral . W e get that , t hat is fine, but if the Government turned around and said, “We are not happy with that. We are going to make it different on the cycle” you wouldn’t be able to produce carbon neutral power if you had to be carbon neutral immediately.

As I say, the right way to look at this is in terms of the impact it has on forests. If the impact today is carbon neutral or carbon positive on forests, then that is the right way to think about the carbon impacts.
Look, I do understand what you are trying to say but this language is difficult.
With respect, all we are going to get is her view on that. Vicky Ford.

Q254 I understand the Government rel y on third party sustainability audits to try to understand whether or not the biomass is being harvested sustainably. What are your views—Angela, I will give you a break—on whether or not those audits are accurate enough, good enough, high enough quality? Do the Government rely on that too much? What are your views?

I can’t comment whether they are or aren’t today, but the debate suggests the perception is damaging us. There are concerns and those concerns need to be answered. With the sustainability consultation next year, that will be our recommendation. There needs to be robust certification to answer that perceptional question.

Q255 Angela, is your point that if you are taking a tree that had otherwise already fallen on the ground and is, therefore , going to rot into carbon now, then you might as well burn it? If you were going to take that tree and it is putting the entire forest at a risk of forest fire because the trees are all too dense and it needs to be cleared for firebreaks, then you might as burn it; is that your point and that is why it is carbon neutral now?

You are right in saying the counterfactual, if you like, if we weren’t using the material. As I say, I come back to the fact that what we are using is the by-product of the timber industry, so we are never the primary driver of what is happening in the forests. Before the biomass industry, a lot of this material was burnt as waste. Now, if you are going to burn this material, it is far better to use it to displace fossil fuels than to just burn it by the roadside where the forests are located.
Q256 What monitoring do you do to make sure that it is waste?

People have talked about the reporting and the auditing that has to be done in conjunction with renewable schemes in the UK. We provide monthly and annual reports to Ofgem. Those are independently audited and almost all the material that we use is also SBP certified. The Sustainable Biomass Programme is a certification scheme that was set up specifically for woody biomass and it is very far-ranging in what it covers. It covers the carbon impacts and where the material is coming from. As I say, almost all the material is independently audited against that standard as well as the auditing we do before we submit information to Ofgem.

Q257 We have been told , according to the Financial Times, which I tend to trust, that Ofgem is currently investigating whether Drax is in breach of its biomass sustainability rules. Do you want to comment on that?

Yes, I am very happy to. We have to provide a lot of data relating to sustainability to Ofgem. It is looking into the way that we have provided some of that data. It has already confirmed that there is no indication that we have breached any of our sustainability criteria, but it is just looking into the way that we have provided that data.
It would be helpful to get that from Ofgem, Chair.
