Very good, thank you very much. We will move on to Alexander Stafford.
You have had a tough time today, haven’t you, Angela?
That is quite all right. Honestly, I think that it is right that the power sector and our industry comes under scrutiny, so I am honestly very happy to answer questions.
Q258 How are things going in Drax? How are profits?
W e run a profitable business, and as a result of having a profitable business we are able to invest in our plant and invest in BECCS.
Q259 It was very profitable last year, wasn’t it? How muc h profit did you make?
I don’t have the numbers to hand, but we certainly did make a profit on our operations. Some of that money went back to the Government , though , under the electricity generator levy.
Q260 I have the numbers here. I think you made £731 million profit in 2022, up from £398 million in profit in 2021. That is a huge increase, isn’t it, coming up to double?
We were able to increase our profits but, as I say, as a profitable business we are able to reinvest the money.

Q261 No, it is good. As a Conservative, I am very pleased that you are making a profit, but my question is in that period where you almost doubled your profits, Bloomberg basically said you cut generation deliberately to exploit the loopholes to increase profit at the sake of cutting down production . That is great business sense, don’t get me wrong, but your claim in your evidence today that you are doing all this out of the goodness of your hearts to increase security and low carbon, surely it is best to just keep burning the carbon, keep burning the pellets and make less profit , but better for the planet.

The Bloomberg article was dealing with a period over the energy crisis and during those times the amount of biomass that we were able to access was constrained. As a result of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and what happened to gas prices and electricity prices, they had also put pressure on biomass markets. We were not able to source as much biomass as we would usually source, so we ran the ROC units. We had hedged those units in advance, but we had the CfD unit on standby and ready to generate power when it was needed. When it was needed on the system, it was generating power and it was returning money to the consumers.
Q262 Y ou are saying if you had access to more pellets, you would have burnt more; is that correct?

For some periods during that time it would have been uneconomic to run the CfD unit, so if we had been running the CfD unit, we would have been running it at a loss. That is about what was happening with power prices, but biomass prices had escalated markedly during that period , too. We ran it when the system needed it, but if it wasn’t needed, we were not going to run a unit at a loss.

Q263 Let’s just get this right. D uring the period, you—quite rightly, as a business—decided to not burn the pellets because you would make a loss of business, but when you could burn them, you burnt them again. I just find that quite hard, to go from the period where you are very worried about not being profitable, but in that same year you almost doubled your profits. Explain to me how that makes sense overall.

During that period electricity prices in the market rose and a number of generators were able to increase their profits. In response to that, the Government implemented the electricity generator levy and we were required to pay money back as a result. In terms of how we were operating during that period, we were just operating in accordan ce with the rules of the market, so we dispatched our units in the market, we got renewables obligation payments—
Q264 I am not questioning that you are operating within the law in the market, but you were selling the pellets, weren’t you?
We were not a net seller of pellets during that period.

Q265 That is interesting; that is different. I am trying to get to this point of what Drax , as a business, operate because what you have been telling the Committee today is that what you are doing, the whole idea is fundamentally trying to help the environment, to take carbon out of the atmosphere and provide an alternative security of supply, yet there are so many reports now that you are selling pellets. Your profits have doubled, coming up to close to £750 million in profit in that same period. Are you being honest with us when it comes to the purpose of the company and what you are doing or are you just taking from the UK taxpayer—everyone around this table, everyone who is watching on television—just for the sake of, I don’t know, some profit?
The purpose of the company is fundamentally to enable a net zero future.

Q266 The purpose of Drax is to enable a net zero future, not to make money? I always thought the purpose of a company is to make money. Bear in mind you did have quite a large dividend to your shareholders last year. There is nothing wrong that, I am a Conservative, but you are either making a profit in your company and you want to make money, great, or your main purpose is to save the planet. What is it?

Those two things are related. Our purpose is to enable net zero, to generate low carbon power and carbon removals. As I say, if we are going to get to net zero, carbon removals are essential. That is a key part of our mission. In order to do that, we need to be a profitable company because we need to invest. You have been talking about profits. Over the coming year we are looking to invest around £500 million in maintaining the power station and in developing carbon removals. It is by being a sustainable, profitable, growing business that we are able to make the investment we need to provide secure low-carbon power and carbon removals.

Q267 You are saying you want to make this profit to maintain your power station because that will help the planet. Surely you are investing in your power station to make money. Once again, I have no issue with this, but you have to be honest with us about what you are doing. My big issue is from 2021 to 2022 you almost doubled your profits , a t the same time as you weren’t providing as much power and security to the UK, yet you are sitting here saying what you are doing is the best for the environment. I just want a bit of honesty from the company while you are here . W e have already had answers today about what you are doing, about the fact —in your view— that out of the chimney it is carbon neutral . C learly , it is not carbon neutral, frankly. Now you are not being straight on the purpose of the company.
Bioenergy and biomass—and this may be a question for everyone—what is the main purpose? Is it necessary or is it just purely another way of taking money from taxpayers for yourselves ?

T o give Angela a little break, and back on the topic of keeping the lights on and net zero, on Monday afternoon, as per the E nergy D ashboard, the UK was using 40 GW of power, of which half came from gas and a couple of per cent came from coal. If we are going to keep the lights on and get to net zero , we need to produce 40 GW of power . It will not be 223 g of CO 2 per KWh now and zero tomorrow, there is a gradual process to get there, so what we need to do is get demand down and decarbonise the demand that we have. They are the two things we need to do. Forget wherever it comes from at this stage. The average on Monday afternoon of carbon into the atmosphere was 223 g —it is an estimate, it is not measured instantaneously—of CO 2 per KWh , of which, as Angela mentioned earlier on, gas is around 400 g per KWh , coal is about 900 g , biomass is accounting for 120 g , so it is surely better to swap out gas and coal, which are over the average, and swap in things that are below the average, which includes nuclear, biomass, wind and solar , which are all important, as is the dispatchable power.

I think that the focus of this industry and this group is to decarbonis e and reduce the amount of carbon being pushed up into the atmosphere over time and then by 2030, 2035, if you can capture the CO 2 as well, you have a further reduction . N ot every industry will get to net zero. Aviation is unlikely to, maritime won’t, so if this industry can capture carbon, it offsets those industries that can’t, so capturing that carbon is important. I think the target for 2030 is 5 to 7 million tonnes, which they probably achieve through power BECCS, but the 23 million tonne target of 2035 will not be achieved unless we start capturing CO 2 from biomass. Whether you like it or not and argue with the science, the way it is accounted for, we need to capture carbon from biomass.

The biomass that is already there will be diminishing and there will be less opportunity, so if you take my fleet, we could capture 1.5 million tonnes if the infrastructure was there and the market was there for the carbon pricing, but it isn’t. The other thing that isn’t there is any incentive for us to stay operating beyond 2027 . Y ou have focused on EBITDA and profit. Come 2027, my E B ITDA and profit w ill be negative. At that point I will be switching off. I won’t be selling pellets, I just won’t be operating , because I will be making a loss to do so.
Q268 You mentioned EBITDA. What is your EBITDA this year or last year?
Last year was roughly about £34 million, which was significant debt repayment.
It does sound a very profitable business, getting involved in the pellets.

Q269 I will j ust check one thing before we move to Lloyd Russell-Moyle. You said in response to Alexander Stafford a second ago that you were not a net seller of pellets over this period. That would indicate to me it was a sleight of hand that you were maybe selling pellets in that period. Not a net seller, but there might have been periods when you were a net seller, but if you draw the time for a month rather than a year and a half or whatever, you might have been a net seller of pellets for part of that period.
No, we were not a net seller of pellets, but—
Were you selling pellets?
If you want me to get more details, perhaps that is what I can come back to the Committee with.
Q270 That would be grand, thank you. You had also said you could not make a profit on that. Just to check, your strike price was £139; is that right?
Yes, and the issue is the difference between the reference price and the strike price over that period and how that compared with biomass prices, so that is the issue.

It would be interesting to see the price of pellets against that strike price, but I will happily accept some correspondence afterwards. Thank you. Lloyd Russell-Moyle, apologies. We will take account of this time.

Q271 It would be interesting to know how many pellets you normally buy, how many pellets you bought during that period and how many you sold during that period and then post so we can see, not netted off, what was happening there. I think the suspicion is that you bought/stockpiled and had pellets. You then did n o t need them or you realised you could get more , because there was a global shortage , by selling them rather than by burning them.
The other thing I was not quite clear about when you answered was that you said the CfD unit was not profitable, but you still burnt some of those pellets in your other units, didn’t you?
Yes, so the RO units were profitable to run during that period. The CfD unit sometimes was, but quite a lot of the time was not.

Q272 Is n’t the point of CfD that sometimes you will not get it so great, other times you will get it good, but you have a more stable fixed price ? T herefore , you saying , “We are not going to do the CfD in the bad times, we will only take the good times” is a deliberate manipulation of the CfD, in principle .

No. The point about a CfD is that it is intended to be a revenue stabilisation mechanism and to make sure that you always get the revenue you need to make a unit profitable. Now, if you are applying that—
Q273 Over every day or over the course of the arc of having that unit?

The point about when it is applied to something like a wi n d farm, a wind farm is effectively a zero marginal cost plant, so it does not have a fuel input. If you set a strike price for a wind farm, in any conditions that wind farm should be profitable to generate. The issue with biomass is you have an input, which is the fuel, and that has a cost associated with it. If you set the strike price, if the strike price is set at a particular level and then biomass go es through the roof, then you can find that it is not economic to generate with that unit.

Q274 Yes, but the point of market stabilisation with inputs is that sometimes you will gain heavily because that strike price is much higher than what you would need in the market, but other times it is lower. Otherwise why on earth are we doing CfD in a market where you are happily burning with your other units?
CfDs in general are intended to ensure that you can always cover your operating costs and make a reasonable profit.
Q275 Every minute of every day?
With something like a wind farm that doesn’t have an input fuel—
No, I get that. On every minute of every day you are meant to be making a profit on the CfD unit?
The idea is that when you are generating, it should cover your costs and a reasonable operating margin. The issue with biomass is—

Q276 My question is: what timescale should you be making a profit? Every minute of every day that you are operating that unit you are meant to be making a profit or over the period of time of the CfD? Maybe I have misunderstood the CfD. I get that it is meant to make sure that it is stabilising, but are you saying that every single second an action that you take with that unit has to make a profit?
The CfDs were never intended to force generators to operate at a loss.
Not for any second?
I t is up to individual generators how they dispatch their units, but in general they are intended to ensure you can cover your operating costs and a reasonable margin.
Clearly , the CfD was made badly. We will have to ask the Department.
Annual profits seem to have been up, so—

Q277 Yes. One suggestion would be a recommendation that the CfD change there because clearly it is being manipulated. Look, one of the things that you have mentioned a number of times there is, quite understandably, that wood pellets are being traded internationally and sometimes the price goes up and sometimes it goes down. Just like when we had the natural gas crisis, wood pellets were affected in a similar order. Does that not mean that wood pellets might well be useful for other forms, but in terms of energy security they are just as vulnerable to market fluctuations and price gouging as gas?

What matters to consumers is the overall price of generating using different technologies. We have had some work done for us by economic consultants, Baringa, recently looking at the cost of generating using biomass as opposed to other generation technologies. If our power prices stay at something like the same level and we end up with support after 2027 to continue to run our biomass generation units, then that will most likely save consumers money. The point is: how does it compare with the cost of generating from other technologies? Biomass looks like it will be a good option in terms of saving consumers money over the longer term.

Q278 How do you protect against market fluctuations? I grant where it is domestically produced, where it is waste material, all that area, whether it is pure waste material, post-use waste, I get it there, but with virgin or material that is from production waste, that is liable to market fluctuations.
The best way we can protect against that is to lock in long-term contracts, so—
Q279 Do you not do that already?
Yes, we do that already and we are looking to secure more supplies post-2027 on a long term—
Q280 How long are your long-term contracts at the moment ?
Oh gosh, I think that is another where I would need to get back to you. There are different contracts and different contract layers.
I think it would be very interesting to know how long your contracts are for pellets , if you could get back to us. However, you do have long-term contracts at the mo ment ?
We do have long-term pellet contracts.
Q281 That means that you have locked in suppliers for long periods of time?
Yes. As you can imagine, some of our contracting is done long term, some of it is done on spot markets. That is a commercial strategy for—
Q282 It seems strange then a short-term price fluctuation means you turn off the CfD system again , but you had long-term contracts in place anyway, but let’s get the figures of that.

Richard, I would like to come to you, but others can answer as well. How much can we increase the amount of biomass that we are importing without driving environmental degradation in the regions producing biomass? Yes, I get that waste biomass does not have that, but there comes a point , doesn’t there, where we are not producing enough waste to run , so we have to move to either virgin or imported ? How do we protect from that meaning that we are n o t just degrading our environment?

In respect of the waste wood industry, and it applies to what you have just been discussing, we are producing the baseload power in a carbon-friendly way, but we have that environmental service. Each year the UK produces 4.5 million tonnes of waste wood. Last year, 2.7 million tonnes of that went to energy recovery, some with heat and power. We can’t simply stop. We have to keep the supply chain and the wheels moving from our local rubbish tips to the factory wall. The wheels need to turn and the turbines need to turn. We are proven to offer that service, a reliable—
You have another 2 million tonnes of headroom.

No, because our membership of the Wood Recyclers’ Association encompasses the whole industry. We have reuse and recycling outlets . T he likes of the panel board industry consume 1 million tonnes. It will take some sawmill residues to manufacture chipboard MDF.
Q283 I see, so the maximum there is 2 million tonnes that you could provide ?

The UK produces, on average, dependent on the economic cycle, around 4.5 million tonnes a year. Last year the sector consumed 4.3 million tonnes, so there is a spare marginal 200,000 tonnes. There is still the capacity in the UK waste wood biomass fleet to use that. It wouldn’t produce a lot ; it would produce about an extra third of a terawatt. What we could consider is that as we move out of the ROC regime and the 90% biomass threshold, we might be able to introduce other waste. Currently , England exports about 1.5 million tonnes a year of the likes of SRF and RDF.

One last important point, please. I am not sure we can rely on imports going forward. Last year we imported something like £11 billion worth of timber products, the third largest in the world. The World Bank has noted that timber demand will quadruple by 2050. What we should concentrate on is DEFRA’s tree-planting plan and all Confor’s good work. It has a target to plant 30,000 hectares a year. I think we managed 13 last year. We have resources at home.

Q284 Angela, if I may just bring the spotlight back on to you again , following on from an avenue that Lloyd has opened up , which is very interesting, this whole thing about the CfD. Let me get this right: you buy in at variable prices. Either it could be a spot price or it could be a long-term contract, but you buy your biomass pellets, your biomass energy, from an open market, be it either directly with producers or in the spot market. The CfD marke t was designed for those energy product ions where there is no input cost in terms of what you buy. For example, if you have a wind turbine, you have a cost of development, but the wind doesn’t cost you any thing ; ditto with a solar farm. Your model is very similar to a gas-fired power station where you are buying gas either on a long-term contract or on a spot price , where you are then selling into the market. How did you manage to get a contract for difference in the first place when your business model is typical to a gas power station, not to a renewable generator?
Good point.
I guess I would come back to the fact that the situation in the market during the energy crisis was just extraordinary.
We will leave it there.
In the normal course of events—
Hang on. What I am after is a fundamental question: your business model doesn’t fit the CfD market at all.
It had fit the CfD pretty well until we hit an energy crisis.
Only if you turn on and off.

But there is an issue about the fact that we are different in terms of other forms of low-carbon generation because we have a fuel input price. That is something that is worth reflecting on in terms of the best way of support ing biomass.

Q285 All right. I have slightly missed that, but I do want to get to the bottom of this because it is a very important point. Eddie, I will come to you on different things, but it is a very important point. The CfD market does not fit your business model, so how are you selling into the energy market through CfD?
The CfD has worked very well when energy markets were stable. The CfD did not work so well in an energy crisis.

Q286 T he CfD s are designed for energy production where there is a cost of setting up that energy production but there is no input cost on the energy that goes into it. You could have two wind farms. An offshore wind farm costs more than an onshore wind farm and , therefore , you have to have a CfD that reflects the cost and a return on your capital. Sorry, I was an investment banker, which is why I am being boring about this. You got a return on your capital employed over whatever it is, a 10 or 15-year period, what everybody agrees on , and that is very predictable. Yours is a completely unpredictable model because you have a variable price of your input . T hat is the point. You are no different from a gas-fired power station in as much as you do n o t know what your input cost s are , so your model—
We are a—

Hang on a second. If you were taking in energy at a certain price, putting up a margin on it and selling it at another price, you would have a constant output, a constant profit, and that would be understandable. This is the point that we can’t get our head around: how is it possible that your business model ever became suitable for CfDs?
Biomass is different from gas in that we are undertaking long-term contracting, so—
You can do that with gas as well. You are running a treasury operation in terms of—
Let her answer the question.
Sorry.
Eddie wants to come in as well.

CfDs definitely work for power generation sources that have zero short - run marginal costs. It can work for power stations like ours with variable input costs if those costs are relatively stable. It could also work if you had some way of adjusting the strike price in relation to the input fuel price. That is another way a CfD could work if you had an adjustment mechanism.
Q287 What we can’t understand is why did the profit go up when you had high input prices?
Yes. That is the long and short of it, isn’t it?
The long and the short of it. That is it , not long or short—
The units that were more profitable were the RO units w h ere the power price was up.
Q288 You switched off your CfDs then. You decided not to play the CfD game when the price was high and then when the price was low you played the CfD game. That is having your cake and eating it.
No. As I say, during that period we were the largest generator of renewable power in the country, so our priority is keeping the lights on.

I think how it happened was when the RO scheme closed to new generation projects, the CfD was the mechanism for how the Government supported them and that is how you ended up with the CfD. That was your question, “How did you end up with the CfD?” The ROC wasn’t available, so CfDs were provided. It is for other people to judge whether the system was gamed or not.

Q289 I think we are all agreed that it feels wrong that at the peak of the energy crisis Drax cut its production, but because of the way Government subsidies work through the CfD and other mechanisms, Drax’s profits went up. Therefore , the way that the Government subsidy works through CfD s and other methods needs to be looked at again. Do you agree, Angela, yes or no?

No. To be clear, we didn’t cut our production. We were generating on the RO units. The CfD unit always generated when it was required and we were the largest provider of renewable power during that period.

Q290 I think that is inconsistent, from what I heard out there. Anyway, before I get to my main question, Philipp, we were also in a time of food insecurity and rising food prices. Does Future Biogas use edible food? If it does or might do, how do we make sure it doesn’t use edible food and it is using waste products?
We do produce less food in the UK than we used to, absolutely. That is largely because we import strawberries at Christmas.
Not the question. Do you use edible—

Future Biogas uses whole crop maize, whole crop cereals. Future Biogas grows those on fields where in principle you could grow food crops. However, they are grown as part of a farming rotation and that is an important part of the benefits of anaerobic digestion. It is the opportunity to grow profitable break crops that help with cultural control of things like invasive weeds and—

Q291 Y es, you do grow edible food. Thank you very much. I want to get on to carbon capture and storage. How economically sustainable are the Government’s proposed business models for bioenergy with CCS? Who wants to go first?
There isn’t a market at the moment . Power BECCS is for units—
I can’t hear, sorry.
Power BECCS is for units above 100 MW, which restricts access to power BECCS, and you also need—
Is it only me? I am really struggling to hear what you are saying.

I am saying that the current model, power BECCS, is only appropriate for anything above 100 MW. Anything below is ruled out and you have to be close to a pipeline, so there isn’t a market at the moment. There isn’t a revenue stream you can hang your hat on.

On units above 100 MW, when we convert Drax power station , what Government have said is they will put in place a two-part contract for difference structure. There will be a contract for difference for the renewable power that we produce, but also for carbon. A t the moment carbon removals, negative emissions, cannot access the ETS market. They can access voluntary carbon market revenue, but that market is quite small at the minute . T he intention is that over time we will be able to get more of the revenue we need from the carbon market and the requirement for any Government support should diminish over time.

This is where we need clarity now. My members are in the exact camp as Mr Wilkinson’s. We are handling 3 million tonnes of domestic waste. Once the ROCs phase out, I am not sure where that 3 million tonnes will go. I think Mr Wilkinson mentioned 600,000 tonnes of poultry litter. I am not sure you can spread that to land. We are trying to move away—
Q292 Do you want to re-explain that, Eddie, as simply as you can in language that I could explain to people down at the Dog and Duck ? What is the problem?

Every year the poultry industry — so the chicken that ends up in Asda or Tesco or Waitrose — produces litter. On a cycle, those sheds are cleared out and have to be dealt with. Every year , annually, the poultry industry for your broiler bird, which is what we eat, produce s very roughly 1 million tonnes, probably a little bit less. We take over 500,000 tonnes of that, the a risings, and put it through our biomass units. If we are not operating, the ships with the wood pellets will still turn up at the dock or they won’t, depending on the support mechanism. Whatever you do with that support, that litter will still arise.

The only issue will be if we haven’t received the support we won’t be there to take it, so you will have a lot of the poultry industry looking to where they will spread it . It will get spread inappropriately or it will get stored to wait for the land to dry out and be spread and there will be peak nitrogen runoff into watercourses and rivers. The rivers eventually will suffocate and die, which is what is happening at the River Wye currently.
I was trying to ask you about the carbon capture elements of this.

We do n’t capture carbon at the moment . If we are still operating in 2035 and the infrastructure is there to do the transport and storage, we would invest in the carbon capture, capture it and store it. If we are not there in 2035 because we have not been supported, we will not be there to capture it and it is in the plan to close down .
Q293 I am guessing y ou are concerned about your financial stability now.
Yes. We are keen to implement carbon capture, but we do not have the opportunity to do it now and will not have the opportunity to do it in the future.
Q294 What is the reason you are concerned now?
Come April 2027, if I lose my RO support, my power station units will be uneconomic because their operating costs will be below the revenue they receive—
Because your RO support runs out in 2027.
Yes, and we will not be there to capture carbon or generate power. That impacts 2.8 GW of production.
Q295 You would say that at the moment there is not a lot of financial sense in investing in the unabated bioenergy generation that you have because you do not have a vision of what happens post 2027.
I have a vision. It is not one that is being shared or put into legislation.
You do not have a Government vision on post 2027.
Yes. We are discussing with Government Departments, but at the moment it is being batted between DESNZ and DEFRA. At the end of the day, the litter will be in the—
Q296 Can I get back on to the CCS elements of this? How financially viable or economically sustainable are the different models we have had for bioenergy with CCS?

From an anaerobic digestion point of view, there is about 1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide currently produced in the industry, almost all of which, over 90%, is relatively pure. It could be collected relatively easily. The opportunity is to make considerably more than that. Two or three years from now, if we had a sequestration facility in the UK, if we had somewhere to take it, that could be collected and sequestered. I believe that it is possible, on the basis of voluntary market demand for high-quality carbon removals, to be done commercially, possibly even without subsidy, albeit a kick - start would not hurt.
Q297 You have such confidence that this could work that you have signed an MOU with Northern Lights in Norway.
Correct.
Q298 I have been to see that and it is not yet up and running, but you think—

No. That is also delayed, so it is now a neck-and-neck race between UK facilities — potentially HyNet and Teesside — and Norway. There will be facilities in the North Sea but it is very difficult to tell whether it is 2027, 2028 or 2029.
Q299 By 2035, how will the cost to consumers of electricity from bioenergy CCS compare with wind and solar?
It is hard to do that exact comparison because you are getting carbon removals as well as renewable power. The question is how it compare s with other ways of decarbonising .
Q300 I will put it to Philipp. It is difficult for you to do it for Drax. How do you think your bioenergy CCS compares to wind or solar?
As briefly as you can, Philipp. Thank you.

Yes. In another decade I think that biogas will stand unsubsidised because people will be willing to pay more for clean heat than they do today, partly because of the UK Ts and other mechanisms like that.

I would like to say that the cost of BECCS is the cheapest way to achieve net zero. Again, Baringa did some analysis for us that said, compared with other pathways to get to net zero, it would save the UK over £10 billion.
Q301 How close are we in the UK to building a full-scale BECCS plant? Maybe Philipp is the one for this, I do not know.

We have two projects in phase one. At the moment , they are both expecting to go to final investment decision next year—July, September, take your pick. There are a few other political headwinds that might occur in 2024, as members might be aware, that could impact that. That is certainly the plan at the moment . Both schemes say that they could be ready to sequester CO 2 in 2027. HyNet has a lower infrastructure requirement because it has a lot of the offshore facilities but Teesside requires a lot of the offshore facilities to be built. Certainly, it is technically feasible to do it if we make the decisions to do it.
Q302 A slight question is required. How much energy do you require to capture a tonne of carbon?

The production process for anaerobic digestion makes a methane molecule and a carbon dioxide molecule and we then split them through a sieve before we inject the methane in the grid, so the high-concentrate CO 2 is actually already there. We have a low energy requirement for liquefaction. We estimate that if you were to offset the residual inputs—if you take 100 tonnes of CO 2 for sequestration, 5% to 6% of that would be required to offset the residual aggregation , liquefaction , transport to facility and so on. Therefore , 9 5 % of your biogenic CO 2 is then sequestered beneath the North Sea.
Q303 You are not needing an extra CfD for that then, because it sounds quite cheap.

The total cost of doing all that is in the hundreds of pounds. We will either need to sell certificates in the region of £300 to £500 a tonne, which is very high, or we will need to get some support. Over time, I expect those costs to fall. The transport and storage costs for offshore facilities will fall with volume. It is very different whether a facility is sequestering 1 million tonnes or 10 million tonnes. The marginal tonne of CO 2 through HyNet, Teesside or whatever is considerably cheaper than the first tonne, having built all that infrastructure.

Q304 When it comes to Drax, if Drax is running BECCS, I understand you could do power generation or CO 2 power of maximum capture, but you cannot do both. What is the compromise and what extra CfD are you looking for? You are currently £139 per megawatt hour, I understand. What would you look for then?

On your first question about power generation and carbon capture and storage, the carbon capture process requires some energy input. At the moment , each unit generates something like 650 MW. To capture the carbon from that unit will take about 200 MW.
Q305 Would a third of the power production of your unit have to go into carbon capture?
Yes, but that is more efficient than the alternatives, such as direct air capture.

Q306 You have your CfD for all the 600 MW, and you are taking 200 MW to capture the carbon. Would you need a further CfD on top of that or would the CfD of £139 that you already have to produce the 200 MW do?

The Government suggested that they will put in place a CfD for power and a CfD for carbon. That would need to cover the total cost of the project, but then it depends on how you allocate the cost between the power and the carbon.
Q307 Are there any particular technical obstacles that you have come across? I know there have been delays, so a bit further on that.

No. From a technology and a project-readiness standpoint, we are doing extremely well. We have the existing biomass power station operating. Carbon capture and storage is a well - proven technology. We also had two pilot plants at the project running, which have proved that we can capture the CO 2 from the biomass flue gas. All the elements of the chain have been proven. It is just a matter of getting the green light to put them together.
Q308 It will cost £31 billion over 25 years. Does that ring a bell?

We have not got as far as working out what the cost would be because we need more details of the business model before we can do that. We are at an early stage in our discussions about that with Government.
Independent energy analyst Ember ha s a figure of £31.7 billion for the 25 years.
I do not recognise those numbers. We are still in discussion with Government about the business model so it is too early to say what the costs of the project will be.
Vicky Ford, do you want to come in briefly on this point or are you happy?
I have had lots of questions.

Can I please add, Chair, that we actually have members who are seriously looking to invest in the technology today? We have Evero , a 22 MW biomass plant in Ince Marshes . It has selected the technology for BECCS and will start the planning process next year.
Q309 Is that big enough for 22 MW?
It will cover the scale of that. It should be operational for the end of the decade. We also have the likes of MVV.
Q310 Would you also say a third of your energy might need to be taken to run?
I am not sure of the exact figures, sorry, but we could certainly try to come back to you on that.
Q311 How is the carbon going?

Evero is situated next to HyNet. It should be in track one. MVV in Ridham, Kent, is trying to work with local industries to form a group to make the transportation of the gas commercially viable. We have not talked about BECCUS. T here are projects such as Chinook Sciences out in Nottingham who have working technology to take hydrogen from biomasses. That plant works in America today. They have a pilot plant in the UK.

I think that the important point to make, though, and our members are exactly the same as the gentleman at the end, we do not know what the future is. Some of our members will drop out with the subsidy regime from 2027. We need some transitional support now and we need the future greenhouse gas removal models to be flexible and inclusive.

The size of our plant makes it attractive to test an emerging technology, to improve it, and to build a UK contractor set with UK skills. You could use our fleet to fine tune and make the most of this technology. Let us move from BECCS to BECCUS . Let us get the full advantage out of it.

Q312 Angela, you will be pleased to hear you are off the hook for the next two questions if that is all right. Everybody else, you are not. I will turn to biomass energy using waste feedstocks. Will this be a significant part of our future energy mix? Do we have enough waste feedstock for biomass energy?

We certainly have enough biomass f eedstock for the current 2.8 GW that we produce and we have enough for my portfolio, which is about 111 MW in total. I would not advocate creating waste just to create a biomass power station, but I think that in the long term chickens will do what they do, people will eat chicken, so I think that process and the other f uel we use a lot of is straw —
Q313 These are chicken droppings, yes?

Yes, chicken droppings in bedding. We also burn a lot of straw. Straw is produced as part of the wheat production process annually —you take the wheat and we take the straw with a revenue stream for farmers as well. There is no reason why that process, production , output and electricity generation should not continue into the future, apart from the lack of support, whether it is economic or not from that perspective.

I should also point out another factor. We produce 70,000 tonnes of fertiliser per annum. Early on in the discussion Philipp mentioned that we are reducing imports of fertiliser by producing a PNK- rich natural fertiliser from the ashes from the poultry litter.

For the anaerobic digestion industry, there are certain things where we will not see big increases or opportunities. Sewage sludge will not suddenly increase or decrease. In the food waste space, we are already processing 5 million to 6 million tonnes, and that is the DEFRA target for overall food waste at the end of this decade. In animal manures, there is a lot of animal manure out there but there are two things to bear in mind. First, we probably need to reduce livestock holdings overall in the UK between now and 2050. Secondly, a lot of the livestock in the UK is outside, so you do not really have the opportunity to —you cannot put nappies on cows, if you like.
You could try.
I would rather you than me.
I will leave it to you.
You have volunteered it first.

Okay. We see the big opportunity in sustainable rotation that helps improve food crops, reduce fertiliser inputs, build soil carbon, and helps to build the resilience of UK farming to the effects of climate change.
That is a good point. Animal waste on fields does fertilise.
Of course. I t does , yes .
Q314 Okay. To a certain extent, you are in competition with —
In the right proportions.

Yes. Eddie would rightly argue that animal manures from chicken and poultry are very concentrated , whereas cattle are out on the field in the west country. That is where the issue arises. You have these very concentrated locations of manure arising s , particularly in poultry.
Q315 What do waste feedstocks look like? What is that comprised of? This is to both of you.
In the anaerobic digestion industry, it is source collected food waste—banana peels, catering waste, all that stuff.
Q316 Is it the stuff you put in a compost heap?

Yes, exactly. There is an element of green waste that comes into that. In Scotland and Wales, we have effectively 100% collection of food waste. In the UK we are hoping to get there in 2026 or something, but at the moment we have about 45% collection. You may have it at home ; I do, some people do not. In sewage, it comes out as sewage sludges. The bulk of animal manures is very thin slurries—the urine and faeces of cows, pigs and so on—which does not have a huge energy content, is a lot of water to transport around and, as I say, often arises out in the field. In certain operations, such as house d pigs and house d poultry, you have very concentrated dry matter—very high - energy waste s comes out of straw bedding for broilers, for instance, which is what Eddie looks after.
Q317 There are different challenges in how you ship it around ?
Absolutely.
Q318 What is the best ? W hat has the least challenges?
The best thing to do is to put all organic waste that you can collect back to land after they have been through an anaerobic digestion or a combustion process.
Collecting and transporting—

That is the thing. With wet wastes, such as slurries, it is quite complicated. With very dry wastes, such as chicken manures and food waste, it is much less so because they arise in places where you can collect them, conurbations particularly.
I am not sure my operators would suggest we have dry arisings. They are always complaining it is too wet, to be fair.
It is dr y in slurries.

It is dr y in slurries —i t is about 35% to 45%. Our feedstocks are, as I say, animal arisings, poultry litter, horse bedding, and straw and meatball meal from the rendering industry. It is reasonably unpalatable stuff to discuss around the dinner table, but that is what we deal with.

Six million hectares of the UK is farmed, arable land that needs profitable rotational options with a whole raft of new soil health regulations coming through from DEFRA—which has a completely changing subsidy regime—all of which means that we need new opportunities for farmers.
I would like to reiterate that this stuff will arise in the UK whether we are here or not, and it needs managing. That is my plea and my ask here.
Q319 Do you use slaughterhouse waste?
The animal will go to a rendering facility and we take the renderings , the meatball meal , so effectively, yes, but it goes through a process first.

To clarify, not all waste can be spread to land. Post-consumer waste wood and certain cartons have environmental legislation to stop it. We are at near full capacity. We are proud that in the UK last year we either reused, recycled or recovered 95% of UK waste wood. The majority of it went to recovery. There is a 200,000 tonne gap. We talked about imports and exports. There is a debate to be had there now. Our country exported 150,000 tonnes of wood waste resource last year , I think. Should we keep that on our own shores now?

Q320 This is a slightly different question. Given the fact that we have all this waste — and it is good that we are using it — should we prioritise the use of this waste for the more difficult to decarbonise activities rather than the relatively easy ones? I am not a scientist, but if it is easy to take chicken guano and turn it into energy, it might be trickier but more useful to turn it into jet fuel for aviation, for example. Is that possible and should we prioritise it?
I am not a scientist but having come across the varieties you get from winter to summer, I imagine that that would be a difficult process. Scientists might want to correct me. I am not sure.

Certainly , from an anaerobic digestion point of view . B ecause we produce biomethane that we inject into the grid, we contribute to decarbonising heat, which thus far has been considerably more difficult to decarbonise than electricity.

That is potentially BECCUS . We have talked a lot about BECCS. W ith w hat we have today, BECCS would be great but BECCUS is the true pinnacle. These use the size of our fleet to scale up the technology and make full use of biomass materials.
Q321 Should we grow more biomass?
Yes.
Q322 How does that work in competition with available land to grow food and raise not only crops but also cattle and livestock? At what point does the competition become complicated?

DEFRA has the target to move to 30,000 hectares of plant in a year . Confor launched a really stimulating report recently, using Forestry Commission work, that showed we have sufficient low-risk land in the UK to meet those targets. I think that I mentioned that we harvested 10 million tonnes last year from a plant of 30,000 hectares . There is considerable room for growth there. Some of that material can go through our mills to use more timber in construction, which will naturally produce more wood residues. When you sustainably manage and harvest a forest, there will be small roundwood and brushwood. We should make use of those resources.

In arable farming, if you moved to a regenerative farming model there is an opportunity, particularly because we have seen over the last couple of years profitable opportunities fall away . R apeseed in the east of England , in particular , is no longer as interesting as it was because the chemicals have fallen away, and we have flea beetle infestations and soil-borne nematodes around root vegetables and sugar beet, which are grown too close in the rotation. We need other profitable opportunities in the rotation so we can get back to high-yielding, high-quality food crops.
Q323 On the outputs, you produce biomass crops. How do they compare in price? Presumably , it is cheaper to produce it locally than to import that type of thing.
From our point of view, because our feedstocks are generally quite wet, they are all local. You would not transport them very far.
Q324 Take wood pellets, for example. It is much easier to grow them locally than it is potentially to ship them in from Canada .

Is the volume there? S hould we make more use of it? It is a balance . W hen you harvest a tree, there will be residues that you can use to make pellets out of the brush, the small roundwood and diseased timber, so that ticks two boxes.
Q325 What appetite is there among farmers to produce these crops?

An e ver-growing appetite. This year , particularly , farmers were paid £180 a tonne for their wheat, but they paid £600 a tonne for the fertiliser that came through last year. Given that subsidies are moving from what used to be £3 billion out of the CAP to about £1 billion out of Treasury, the economics of farming are challenged and any profitable rotational options available are interesting, particularly if they help on the decarbonisation path. That is the crucial thing. A lot of buyers—the big food companies and so on—are now starting to look into the carbon footprint of their supply chain, in particular, the farming supply chain. That is where opportunities to increase soil organic matter and soil carbon are crucial.
Q326 Looking at the market potential, then, if you have £600 per acre for energy crops and you have £150 per acre for food crops, presumably if everybody goes—

No, that was the price you are paid for your wheat and the price you have paid for your fertiliser to make that wheat. T hat is out of context ; I apologi se . I am saying that you are paying a high price for your fertiliser but not getting a high price for your wheat in the global markets right now. It was the other way around last year. Farming is very volatile. To take some of that volatility out at the same time as making the transition to low-carbon farming, removing the diesel use, the fertiliser use and building up soil organic matter is what is interesting.
Q327 Yes, but I am talking about farmers start ing to produc e energy crops.

The gross margin you get out of an energy crop such as ours is lower than you would get from a first wheat, and considerably lower than you would get this year from sugar beet. It is a break crop. It is not a main crop. It is not nearly as economically attractive as a good healthy blackgrass-free first w heat.
Q328 Okay, thank you. From the farmers ’ point of view, they will not all suddenly stop producing food.
No.
Brilliant. That is it. Thank you very much.

Q329 I have a quick one. I think it is to you, Richard. I do not know if you have a view on this, but last winter when energy prices were so high, there was a trend of investing in a home wood burner for a lot of people. I have been told that it was very bad for air quality in urban areas. Do you have a view on that?

That is a completely different sector from the WRA. That would be the Stove Industry Association . I think that the general principle is that as long as they are using properly seasoned timber in modern , well-maintained boilers, then no. There are places that are off the grid that need some sort of heat, so I still see there is a place for that.
Trying to make sure that wood is well seasoned is an important issue.
Yes. A quality fuel in a quality application. There is an industry that offers that. The Stove Industry Association would help you with those questions.

Thank you. We have reached the end of our session. Thank you all for coming. I hope that you enjoyed it, Richard, Angela, Philipp and Eddie. These are the questions that come up and it is our job to probe. I hope it was not too personally uncomfortable. Thank you again.

sessions.w: Amanda Blanc (Aviva Plc); Nishma Gosrani OBE (Bain & Company – Financial Services)

Members present: Dame Angela Eagle (Chair); Dr Thérèse Coffey; Stephen Hammond; Keir Mather; Siobhain McDonagh; Anne Marie Morris.
Questions 131 - 181
Witnesses
I : Amanda Blanc, CEO, Aviva Plc and Women in Finance Charter Champion; Nishma Gosrani OBE, Partner, Bain & Company.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Amanda Blanc and Nishma Gosrani .

Q131 This afternoon we are pursuing our inquiry into sexism in the C ity. We have two distinguished guests to give us some evidence today. Welcome to the Committee . I wonder if you would introduce yourselves for the Hansard reporters.
Thank you, Chair. I am here in my capacity as co-author of the women in finance charter blueprint , a pro-bono initiative led by Bain & Company where I am a financial services partner.
I am Amanda Blanc. I am the group CEO of Aviva in the UK and I have been the Government’s women in finance charter champion since March 2021.

Q132 Thank you for giving us your time today to give evidence on this extremely important issue. I want to start with Amanda. What do you see as your biggest achievement as the women in finance charter champion?

I have been doing the role since March 2021. First of all, thank you very much for doing the inquiry. It is much appreciated and it is good that we follow up from the inquiry that was done in 2018. A number of things have happened. If we have a look at the data from the women in finance charter , we have 400 signatory firms representing a million employees from financial services. The percentage of women in senior roles, in the two years that I have been in the role, has moved from 33% to 35%.

The thing I am most proud of is the blueprint, which Nishma and I authored last year. We pulled together a group of accountable executives into a taskforce. All of the major financial services firms were represented and one of the key things that came out of that was that people did not know what best practice was. E verybody was trying lots of initiatives. Nobody really knew what was actually delivering major success.

We surveyed 100 representative accountable executives of firms and we produced the blueprint, which came out with a document with four pillars of things that we believe are best practice in firms we have surveyed. It is, in essence, a good guide to what good firms should do to move the dial. I am incredibly proud of that. We have also held events for women in finance accountable executives and brought the industry together on what is clearly a very important topic.
Q133 Nishma, do you have anything to add on the importance and significant of the initiative that you are a part of ?

There are a couple of things I would add to that. Between m e and Amanda, we have been speaking to in the region of 40 executive committees across the large global merchant banks, the UK retail institutions as you would imagine , such as Nat W est and Lloyds Banking Group , the large insurers and the asset managers, as well as the market infrastructure firms.

As Amanda said, we have covered a large footprint there and a large workforce across the UK financial services industry. Many of these institutions have been disseminating elements of the blueprint, taking each of those pillars and marking themselves against each of the five areas that we have outlined in the work programme. A number of trade bodies—you heard from the ABI a couple of weeks ago—have also taken the blueprint and looked at how they might spread that across their members.

There has been huge uptake of the blueprint this year and, as Amanda pointed out, this came from realising that there has been an improvement in the numbers —as you have pointed out in the various sessions—of 1% to 2% CAGR, which, in my view, is very modest and insignificant .
Q134 What can you achieve by pursuing this initiative in your remaining time as charter champion , Amanda?

Genuinely, we have to keep moving on those initiatives that we actually believe are going to make a real difference. Too often, in many aspects of life, everybody is looking for a silver bullet to fix what is clearly a difficult problem. T he issue here is that , clearly , there is not a pipeline of women who are coming through to senior management roles. W e have to systematically look at all the component parts of what needs to be addressed , whether that is in recruitment, in the way we retain and promote women, in the culture and the behaviour or in the way that we then measure it. I would be continuing to push on that point .

Aviva, for example, has 40% women in senior management. We have 46 % women on our exco and 42% on our board . We have implemented a large number of these initiatives and we believe that they are actually making a difference. In many respects, that is proof positive that, if you do implement the initiatives, you can make progress.
Q135 Nishma, do you have anything to add?

Through the accountable executive taskforce meetings that Amanda has referred to, we often found that many institutions were collecting data—60% of signatories collect data—but only 20% of those qualitatively and quantitatively analysed that data. Having this collaboration across the industry, where we are able to share best practice, was hugely beneficial, particularly for smaller institutions.

Amanda and Aviva hosted an event attended by many of the smaller charter signatories and we were able to share a lot of these best practices. We recognise that collecting data can be an expensive process if not managed effectively or outsourced, so this enabled them to ask some of the bigger houses to aid them in doing that . On the back of that consultation, we also developed an industry-first dashboard, which enables organisations to track and measure data .

To give you an example of that, what we found from conversations we were having with the global investment banks with large footprints in the United Kingdom was that they were doing lots of initiatives, but did not have enough executive sponsorship over those initiatives . There were lots of fantastic, glossy initiatives that were not giving return on investment. We were suggesting that actually you need to track and measure these initiatives , and probably do fewer of them . You are much more likely to achieve better investment as a result , if they are manged effectively .

This process of consultation, through the work that Amanda has done and set up as part of the accountable executive taskforce and beyond, has been hugely beneficial, in my view. Through the data and research, we can see that laying out the four pillars for these institutions has been incredibly helpful for them.

Q136 Colleagues of mine are going to come on and ask in more detail about the blueprint , but I wanted to ask you a few more general questions. As part of this inquiry, we have taken evidence privately from groups of women who have told us about some of the difficulties they face working in the financial services sector. That is across the board. It is not only banks. It is across the entirety of financial services.

I have to say , we were extremely shocked by some of the evidence that we heard in those roundtables , up to and including sexual assault, bullying, sexual harassment, a general impunity for the perpetrators and a requirement, for example, that those who have been subjected to this should have to make a complaint and perhaps give up their career as a re sult of it. There i s a series of well-known bad apples that nobody ever does anything about. Even if they are moved out of a particular department or from firm to firm, the same behaviour is perpetrated.

Does this sound familiar to you? Increasing the number of women who are in financial services and increasing the seniority of the jobs they do , one would hope , would have some kind of answer to this in the long term but, meanwhile, we are losing vast numbers of women who experience this and have to leave the industry, give up their career and go elsewhere. W hat should we be doing about this?

I did my own research as well. I put out a LinkedIn post about two weeks ago saying that I was going to come to the inquiry , and I have been inundated with hundreds and hundreds of private messages from women who have had, I have to say, predominantly poor experiences . That is incredibly disappointing and some of the stories were incredibly sad . Some were absolutely appalling around unwanted advances; when they announce that they are pregnant, people saying things like, “Well, that is a bit inconvenient, is n’t it?”; being followed to hotel rooms and things like that.

I do genuinely believe that, from a behavioural perspective, we do need to act and we need to act authoritatively to avoid the situation you have just described, Chair, which is that the man stays and the woman leaves the organisation . What is the answer to that? First, there are a lot of very positive male allies in financial services and I have experienced that myself. I have been in a situation where I have had a pregnancy test in one hand and a job offer in another , and a boss who says, “You still join ”.

I have had very positive experiences . However, many women do not. Part of this is about the way that firms deal with a speak up. Every individual firm has to be accountable for any allegations such as this. The women in the firm have to know that there is a process for speaking up, that that process will be acted on, that everything will be investigated and that the actual person who did wrong will leave the organisation and not the wom a n.

We have had experiences like that at Aviva, where the wo man has stayed and the man has gone. I genuinely believe that it is about firms making sure that they do behave appropriately and take accountability, as well as, of course, being backed up by regulation and various other things, which I would agree definitely have a role to play here. The numbers, when we did the survey for the blueprint last year, showed that physical abuse was around 28% in financial services, in the firms that we surveyed, and verbal abuse was 43%. Those are 10 percentage points higher than in other industries. Clearly, there is an issue here .

From my own personal experience, at my own AGM a number of years ago I experienced verbal abuse as a woman. I have also worked in sport and had very misogynistic comments and behaviour directed towards me there. We have also seen the example of the CBI and various others. We are dealing with a societal issue , which is definitely amplified in financial services.

Q137 No body is denying that there is sexism, abuse , sexual assault, misogyny, or bullying in other areas . This inquiry is about its prevalence in financial services and y ou have pointed out that it is worse in the financial services sector than more generally. In the course of this inquiry, we are trying to discover what we can do and how we can bring together the entire financial services industry to have an effect on the outcome, rather than bemoan it .

We can all bemoan it. Our predecessor Committee bemoaned it in 2018 and it has not changed. Certainly, talking to women , nothing seems to have changed very much in reality for the last 20 years. It is lagging behind. Nishma, what can we actually do , apart from bemoan it and wish that individual companies had better ways of dealing with it?

The two hearings prior to this have talked a lot about culture and I do have to come back to that today. A culture of senior management making bold interventions to remove unacceptable behaviour is the way forward. As part of the blueprint , we have had that conversation with a number of chief executives who strongly advocate for zero tolerance towards exclusionary behaviour . I know it is much harder in practice to implement than to say it.

There are two other things that have come up in the work we have done around the blueprint. One is additional regulatory intervention. Chair, I am aware from the conversation that took place yesterday with Mr Rathi and Mr Alder that they are looking into this . Thank you for your robust questioning there . I do believe that the regulator, through the diversity consultation paper , is now taking this seriously. I strongly believe that the UK regulator has a tough regime and, if it is taking this seriously, it will take action , but I do think, in the way that Mr Rathi said yesterday, it need s the backing of the courts.

A combination of three different things is applicable here : a culture of senior management making bold interventions ; additional, targeted regulatory intervention ; and a role for boards to play in challenging their chief executives and the executive committees. Looking at the skillset of boards , some culture expertise across boards, not just financial expertise, will be instrumental in making changes here.

Q138 If the FCA do es develop a more robust approach to this —although, again, its approach seems to be about collecting data rather than doing anything—you would end up with a situation where an individual victim or their supporter in a firm would have to whistle b low to the regulator about what was going on in the company. That is asking an awful lot of someone who wishes to have a career , lasting a long time , in financial services , if they are known as the whistleblowers who told the FCA what was happening in their company . That is not something you are going to want to put on your CV, is it?

No, a bsolutely not , but that is why I believe that the individual accountability has to rest with the board of the firm and with the management of the firm to create the right culture. The process of whistleblowing has to be and is confidential to protect the whistleblower, so that there is a proper investigation , and where it is a more serious matter , whether it is racial discrimination or sexual harassment , you have experts who help, to make sure that that comes to the right conclusion and there are consequences for those individuals for bad behaviour.

I have and I chair an individual accountability review panel , which deals with those allegations and deals with the consequences for the individual who does that . It should not be that the woman has to leave the organisation , because the process should be run confidentially. The regulator should be the backer to that, should that not work.

Q139 I am new to this Committee , but it is great to see you both. Thank you, Amanda and Nishma, for what you are doing in this. I really appreciate that it is probably quite a significant extra to the standard day job. It feels a little bit déjà vu . I apologise to my colleagues if I stray a little bit into pipeline. A decade ago, I led an inquiry with a colleague at the time about the executive pipeline of talent. Amanda M ack enzie from Aviva gave evidence at the time and a variety of others.

The charter is focused on increasing female representation in senior roles. To what extent has it had an impact on improving that gender equality more broadly in financial services firms? The pipeline is going to be key to who is going to reach that level. I will try not to stray too much into the pipeline, because my colleague is going to go into that.

The pipeline is absolutely critical to getting more women into senior roles. When we have done research into this, we have found that we are losing women much earlier i n their careers than we originally thought. Many firms have interventions for senior women . They have sponsorship programmes , senior leader programmes, mentoring—you name it. Firms have lots of initiatives.

When we look ed at the data and did some data analysis, using the Aviva cohort of data, we found that women were leaving the organisation in much more junior roles. Why was that? It was because they felt that, when they were taking breaks—often maternity breaks—when they came back, they were not being supported. When they came back, they came back in less senior roles or part time and then were written off by the middle management.

It is very, very important that the interventions you put in place support the women when they come back, but also support middle management and lay out the rules around the fact that women have to be progressed , especially very capable women. It is about identifying your talent much earlier on and t r acking it right the way through. We all know that, at a graduate level, the intake is pretty much 50/50. It is just two steps on from that that the problem happens .

Q140 That seems to reflect perhaps why female representation in senior management of signatories of the charter , the people who are really thinking about this, has only moved from 33% to 35%. It is a blip, really. Is there another reason why progress may be slow?

Since the charter was put in place in 2016, it has moved from 27% to 35% . I do believe that, if you are going to move senior women into senior financial services roles, they have to be not only behaviourally capable, but also technically capable. To become a senior manager, to run an insurance firm or a bank, you have to go through a regulatory process to test your regulatory competence.

You are not going to be able to jump from one role to another role without going through a series of other roles in between. It is not going to be fixed overnight. You have to make sure that you keep the women in the organisation through all of those different layers.
Q141 I am going to share with my Committee colleagues a link to the report I did with another former MP.

You are spending a lot of time and of course lots of firms are signed up. There are over 400 signatories now and people are still joining every year. I want to understand, Amanda, in particular, what you have been able to do to try to expand the list of signatory firms. Frankly, a re there any firms on there where you either had to twist their arm or no amount of twisting means they are coming on? What can we do to encourage them as a parliamentary C ommittee?

It is a ve r y good question. The number of firms is 400 with a million employees. There are 2.5 million employees in financial services, of whom two-thirds work outside of the City. In all of this, we also need to remember there are lots of women who work outside of London and are also subject to some of the things that we see here today.

All of the major firms have signed up to the initiative. They do not need their arms twisted. If you look at the data in the charter , they all see it as strategically important. By the way, even if you just look at it from a financial perspective, the recent BlackRock survey says that firms with diverse workforces have better profits by 2% per annum. McKinsey’s work supports that. There is a financial rationale as well as it being the right thing to do.

The focus has been on improving those firms that have willingly signed up and that really want to improve . What we have seen is that many of them have actually improved and are very close to their target. I think something like 70% of these signatories have a target of 40% and are pretty close to that. We have moved from something like 33% two years ago to 40%. It can be done, but you have to be absolutely laser focused in the way that you do it.

There is no non-diverse hire at Aviva without it being signed off by me and the chief people officer , not because I do not trust my team, but because I want to make sure that the process followed for that recruitment has been diverse, has been properly done and is not just a phone call to a mate to say, “Would you like a job? Pop up and we will fix it up for you ”. A lot of work has been done to make sure you get those numbers right .

Q142 The 2022 Treasury review of the charter suggests that just over a third of signatories covered all of the points the Treasury expects to be included in the annual updates on their websites. Some people may then think perhaps signing up is just a tick-box exercise . What can be done for people to perhaps take that element more seriously?

One of the biggest challenges is the link to pay, which is the fourth requirement of the charter . Firms struggle a little more with that. S ome firms have done that and other firms have not. The report is taken seriously. When we annually review, we have the opportunity to point out those that are struggling.

The bigger issue is that those that star t off struggling tend not to recover. My view would be that the focus of effort needs to be on those firms that are signed up, want to do good things, but perhaps do not quite know how to do it. That is why we produced the blueprint , because we felt that many firms did not know what the right thing to do would be in recruitment, in retention, et cetera .

Q143 Some other colleagues are going to come on to the blueprint shortly . As you say, one of the principles is about ensuring that pay is linked to delivery against internal targets on diversity . We all know in business you get what you measure. Tell us more about how we can help reinforce that as being a positive rather than being something that is a bit too complicated.

It is definitely not complicated. I n my long-term incentive plan, I have an objective to hit the 40% and I do not get that proportion of the long-term incentive plan unless I do that. I have cascaded that to my senior team and they are all very focused on that. We discuss this at every exco meeting that we have. Once a month, we deep-dive on the numbers and we look at how many recruitments and promotions we need to make to get to the target.
You are so right that, in financial services, what gets measured gets done. This needs to be treated just like any other business issue . If it was, we would get better outcomes.
Q144 Nishma or Amanda, what is the extra tool in the toolbox that we should be inserting to help pull that lever, so we get the senior executives working on it?

As Amanda said, it is pretty simple and formulaic . This has to be treated like any other business problem and any executive should be measured in the way that it would be measured to solve a business problem. Both non-financial and financial metrics ought to be included as part of their key performance indicators and the way that they are remunerated. This would make up part of that compensation package.
Q145 Is this a push for investors or NEDs ?
It is a combination of all of them .
It is across the board.

Q146 As an aside , I know it has been said that, with young people and more senior people not being in the office, they have not been able to absorb. Do you see that as a potential reason for the slowing of progress on some of the measures in this charter ?

In a way, Covid has had pros and cons. It sanctioned flexibility because, prior to that, you would find that women would be working flexibly and men would be in the office. Post- C ovid, it is much more balanced. The bigger issue we need to watch—and the data does not show this yet—is that, over time, women might go back to more flexible working while men re appear in the office more frequently. Obviously they would be disadvantaged by that.

On the whole, it was a great leveller. We need to make sure that it is maintained. Certainly, the absorption of experience is something that is done in a physical way. You do not do that in a Microsoft Teams meetin g, as enjoyable as they are. You gain a lot more by listening. I was an underwriter listening to other underwriters. That is how you learn. That physical presence is very important.

Q147 Good afternoon and thank you for coming this afternoon . Can I go back to some of the evidence you have given, both in written and oral form, this afternoon? In your written evidence to us, you said that it will be 27% to 35% over seven years. You explicitly say that progress has been and remains too slow.

There are two questions that I wanted to ask. Th é r è se has already asked a little bit about the pipeline. I n terms of the gaps of what could be done to make sure that that pipeline is fuller , you talked about training, monitoring, mentoring, et cetera . Is there anything else missing that we should be really looking at?

One thing that we have not touched on is equal parental leave. If you have a really good equal parental leave policy where the men take up the parental leave in the same proportion that the women do, it makes a very, very big difference in terms of allowing other women to come back to work, but also showing that you are an organisation that takes these things seriously.

Aviva introduced equal parental leave in 2016. Since 2019, over 80% of the dads, the men, in Aviva have taken six months ’ parental leave. I do believe that that makes a massive difference. Those policies around flexibility of working and parental leave make a really, really big difference in terms of making it an environment where women feel there is a shared responsibility of childcare , because that is one of the very, very key things.

There are two things that I would add to that. The first is proactive, formal sponsorship for women, sponsored at the executive level. We have 100% take-up of that at Bain & Compan y and i t has been hugely effective across the organisation. The second is conducting frequent pulse surveys. At the moment, we are seeing a number of financial services institutions still using annual surveys for their employees, which, frankly, are very outdated. Employees have left by the time that you see the survey results, as you know.

At Bain, we do that on a weekly basis. When I have conversations with executives and committees about that they said, “That is very expensive, is n’t it, to run that process on a weekly basis?” but, if you look at the cost of hiring an individual and retaining the individual, you will know that it makes a lot of sense to do that. Those are the two that I would certainly p oint to.

Q148 Again g oing back to your written evidence , you said that, in terms of the pressures on the business, there needs to be a clear business case on cultural issues. You also said that intensified effort from Government is needed in terms of the pay . What are we missing and what should we be telling the Government they need to do more of?

From a Government perspective , simplifying some of these parental policies and encouraging the implementation of these policies is very important. At the minute, quite often a woman will be pregnant and she will not even be able to find the maternity policy when she is looking for it on the website. Making these things front and centre , and encouraging firms to be very clear and very fair , is very important.
I would not have anything else to add to that.

Q149 You also spoke about it being 50/50 at graduate and lower at middle management. Would it make any difference if the charter explicitly referred to middle management , in terms of its scope , as well?

I do not know the answer to that. I would expect that firms monitoring at a senior level would have to be monitoring the middle management, in order to know whether they are going to achieve the pipeline. In many respects, looking at one bit of it in isolation is not really going to help you. I guess f irms would say that that is just more data being submitted . I do not know. We would be happy to do it, obviously.

Q150 I would like to raise that I am new to this, so I have not heard some of the previous evidence but, from what I have read from our Clerk’s notes and the Committee preparation, a number of people have suggested that the target of 37% for senior management , which we have talked about, becomes an even bigger problem if you are disabled or from a non-white racial background. What improvements do es the charter need to alter that target and get it changed, so that people are more careful about abiding by it ?

We believe that, as women are 50% of the population, if you address the women problem, you will hopefully also address some of the other issues around ethnicity and disability . We do believe that there should be a natural improvement as a consequence of that.

One of the other areas we need to look at is the socioeconomic data. One of the things we will feed back to the regulator on the D & I consultation is that it is a missed opportunity to not capture , on a mandatory basis, socioeconomic data. I do feel that that is a group that is not really captured at the moment and, really, we should be looking at the profile of the individuals who are getting through to senior management roles. T hat is another area of real focus , but naturally by dealing with the women issue you will get a natural uptick in the other areas.

The recent survey from the F inancial S ervices C ulture B oard told a very nuanced story, as you will know, around ethnicit y versus gender and the issues and challenges were amplified. O ne of the things we did not look at as part of the blueprint was the intersectionality focus around some of this, but we should certainly think about that as we review the charter principles .
