Oral evidence: PSNI data breaches , HC 47
Wednesday 13 December 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 1 3 December 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sir Robert Buckland (Chair); Stephen Farry; Sir Robert Goodwill ; Claire Hanna; Tony Lloyd; Carla Lockhart; Jim Shannon ; Bob Stewart .
Questions 299 - 3 15
Witnesses
I: Sinead Simpson, Chief Executive, Northern Ireland Policing Board; Deirdre Toner, Chair, Northern Ireland Policing Board; Edgar Jardine, Vice-Chair, Northern Ireland Policing Board .
Examination of w itnesses
Witnesses: Sinead Simpson, Deirdre Toner and Edgar Jardine .

Q299 This is a meeting of the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee. I am delighted to be joined for our first evidence session on the data breach issue relating to the PSNI by members of the Northern Ireland Policing Board. We have Deirdre Toner, the chair of the board, Edgar Jardine, vice ‑ chair, and Sinead Simpson, the chief executive of the Northern Ireland Policing Board, who are all together, online with us. Welcome. M a y I begin by asking each of you for your initial reaction to the findings of the independent review that I think we are still all digesting?

Our initial reactions are that we welcome the report. It is a large body of work, which we appreciate. It was a critical incident, which we were always going to acknowledge, and the impact cannot be underestimated . I n an organisation that protects physical and personal security , w e needed to prioritise data information security.

We commissioned the joint report to see how it happened and how it could not happen again. The report is clear that there were numerous contributing factors and not one sole area of accountability and a series of systems failures with individual actions across a number of parts of PSNI. Fundamentally, as the author notes, the PSNI is basically not seizing opportunities to better proactively secure data and identify it in a modern way. Clear visibility on the data, equal to people and money, was top of the agenda.

Although the responsibility lies with senior information holders in the PSNI, this is about learning, future proofing and not apportioning blame. The report found, as we say, that PSNI does not possess the appropriate skills at a tactical level to drive the data security in the organisation. Investment in people and technology will be needed.

There are lessons here for all police services and the wider public sector, given the issues identified around audit and information governance. This really is a roadmap for the future and was commissioned to provide future assurance on best practice. There is learning here for everyone in terms of serious questions in terms of internal processes and audit provision within PSNI from which the board takes assurance.

Looking forward, we will consider the findings, the principles that are fair and need to be teased out to produce an action plan, through our committees and board, in partnership with PSNI and continuing contact with the author. It is key that we continue engagement with staff, officers and the associations, rebuilding confidence internally and externally.
Q300 Vice-chair, what are your observations?

I echo what the chair has already said. I would add that the report identified significant threads in terms of the work and focus on external threats and the need to balance that with additional work on the internal threats to the organisation. That is probably a lesson not only for PSNI but indeed for all our police services and any organisation that holds personal data.

There was a significant point for me in terms of the learning and training. There were a couple of points around that. First, there seemed to be an emphasis on generic training, whereas much more targeted training around use of Microsoft and Excel spreadsheets and so on would have been called for. The second thing that struck me was the need for specialisms around this area. Traditionally, it would seem that people were promoted or moved into posts to deal with FoI , data protection and so on. The message I took from the report in relation to that is the need for much more focused training and more specific professionalism around data management, data science and so on.

Good morning. T he chair and the vice-chair have covered the key issues for us as a board. In terms of my initial response to it, as has been said, it definitely came across as a wake ‑ up call not just for Police S ervice of Northern Ireland but for policing generally. The one thing I would add is that, when we met with the staff who were affected by the breach, the Police Federation, the superintendents and NIPSA, we were very struck by the impact that this had had on their members.

A big issue that came across in that early meeting with them was their desire to make sure that the page was not turned too quickly on this event and that everybody moved on. I was comforted by the fact that, in some ways, the report represents a large body of work that we will all now need to take time to think about how we are going to deliver, by PSNI, and how we are going to monitor and oversee at the board. For them, there should be some comfort that there will now be a focus on this issue and on getting it right. That would be the one thing that I would add.

Thank you very much indeed for those openers. The themes that we want to warm to are not so much individual responsibility but the overall culture in relation to freedom of information and how preventative work is going to need to be carried out here. There is then your role as a board and your responsibilities as well.

Q301 This question follows on neatly from the point that Sinead Simpson has just made about the impact on staff. We heard yesterday from representatives of serving officers and ancillary staff. I was particularly struck by the evidence we heard from S uperintendent Gerry Murray for the Catholic officers and how some officers who are forward - facing have not had so much impact, but a lot of the officers were living within communities without people necessarily knowing what they were doing. You are obviously aware of that. What could we do more to address some of those problems? We heard that some were even going to leave the force. It would be a great shame to lose that experience.

For us as a board, we were very keen in the early days after the breach to have early engagement with the staff associations to hear their views. Yes, we would have heard first - hand some of what you would have heard yesterday from the staff association representatives. The board was extremely concerned about the impact that this was going to have on staff.

We know, and indeed I think that the f ederation said yesterday, that there is a broad spectrum of reactions to this. Some people are already in front ‑ facing roles and it might not have had such an impact on them, but there are a lot of others, including on the police staff side, who maybe did not sign up for such a level of visibility and were impacted. As a board, we intend to continue with that engagement. We reached out in the hours after the report was published and we hope to get direct engagement with the staff associations over the coming days.

In terms of the work that has been done, the response from PSNI immediately after the data breach covered a number of angles. There was a criminal investigation. There was work to take information down and to devalue the information. A large body of work was done by PSNI, which members were impressed with, around reaching out to staff, the referrals into an emergency response threat group, the opportunity to avail of an employee assistance programme and referrals into occupational health, as well as supports on the security side. We might touch on it later but the news in the last couple of days that money has been made available for the universal offering is obviously welcome.

I do not think that we on the board would say that all of that makes the impact go away. It absolutely does not. We will want to focus over the coming months on how we can help ensure that this does not happen again. Those things certainly go some way to addressing the impact on staff.

Building confidence in the PSNI is an issue for the whole of society. I was very taken by comments made by Archbishop Eamon Martin after the breach. He was interviewed on Radio Ulster and offered unequivocal support for the families of police officers from his community. He went on to say that policing “is considered across the world a noble vocation, something that should be natural for our young people to consider and we all need to play our part in making that a reality” . Going forward, that broader, unequivocal community support for policing and the PSNI is going to be critical.

From my perspective, I agree with my colleagues. It is about keeping it up high on top of the agenda, in terms of not letting it slip. It is very important to realise that public servants who work as police officers and staff are exceptional in their approach to their jobs and what they do. We cannot underestimate their involvement. We keep in contact. We work with them and find out what the impact is on a range of different areas on the particular job that they do in a very difficult environment.

Q302 It is nice to see you, Deirdre, and Edgar and Sinead as well. I am sure that you have watched the Polic e Federation at the meeting yesterday. You will have heard what it said. It is quite incredible, is it not? This left hand here does not know what this right hand here is doing. In relation to the P olicing B oard, if we are going to move forward in a positive fashion, if that is possible, the arrangements on data between the P olicing B oard and the PSNI have to be a wee bit more hand in hand perhaps. The upgrade role of our deputy chief constable also has to be part of that. Also, I believe that the need to prioritise data, information and cybersecurity is not recognised at a strategic level. What plans does the P olicing B oard intend to make to improve, and improve greatly, what has happened?

A bit of context is that the Policing Board is not an operational board. We work as an accountability body to oversee the policing plan and make sure that the assurances that we seek are within the PSNI’s strategic management board and its risk registers. That is an area where, as big public bodies, the same as every other one, we must seek assurances, because we are a small organisation overseeing quite a big organisation. That is an area where we need to highlight that that is our role. I do not underestimate the impact on that .

We have a series of different issues where we have resources that have been cut over a long time. DoJ has not had an uplift in nearly 10 years. We have police officers who have stretched responsibilities and jobs, and policing staff as well.

The other thing is that we can see from the report that the PSNI’s focus on cybersecurity is very strong and actually a lesson to a lot of other organisations. Internally, there is work to be done across skills, capability, maybe training and gaps in understanding in terms of modern approaches to dealing with such issues in terms of data protection. All that can be accomplished in an action plan, jointly agreed, I suppose, through the Policing Board as well, coming to us to see what the practicalities are and how we measure that and keeping it high on the agenda of the operational board from the PSNI, but also in terms of our committees and resources committee and looking at what good could look like.
Q303 In t he conversations that have taken place between you , the PSNI and the federation, you have agreed a platform and a way forward. I presume you have, anyway .

On that , there are 37 recommendation s . We have had the report just for about five days or so. There is a piece of work to be done to go through those recommendations and identify how they will be implemented . I would envisage then that the board would have this on the agenda going forward, so that the implementation plan, as the chair has said, will be monitored very carefully.

I know that the chief constable already invited the review team back in in a year’s time to provide its assessment of progress. Clearly, we will want to look at that very carefully and take assurance from the team in terms of how the implementation plan has worked out .

If I could just add, in terms of our monitoring , the report makes a clear recommendation that there should be KPIs and a reporting regime between PSNI and NIPB. Part of the implementation plan and our monitoring of it will be developing, along with PSNI, what those key performance indicators should be. As the vice-chair says, we will then integrate that into our committee structure as appropriate.

The board oversees a nd monitors recommendations regularly . We have human rights reports. We have CJINI reports and reports from other bodies. We have mechanisms for funnelling that work through our committees. As the vice-chair said, at least for a period of time before we integrate it into business as usual , we want to continue to treat it as a critical incident and keep it on our board agenda for a number of months yet.

I have the permission of the C hair to speak in relation to police pensions. I will make the comments and expect you to come back to me. Regulation 40 of the 2006 PSN I injury benefit regulations 2006states that the pension of police officers under these regulations shall be payable in respect of each year as from the date of his retirement. It is qualified by regulation 10 (2), which refers to any period before the officer becomes disabled.

What is the Northern Ireland P olicing B oard ’s understanding of the process by which the board determines the date upon which the applicant became disable d ? Secondly, by what process does the board’s resource committee arrive at decisions in relation to retrospective injury on duty awards? Thirdly, the board’s business plan outlines four key objectives. Number 4 describes the objective as to deliver independent, fair and transparent processes for former and serving officers in line with police pension, injury, benefits and appeals legislation. To what extent, and by what means, is the board achieving this? Fourthly and lastly, it has been stated that the board is facing considerable financial challenges at present. To what extent has this impacted upon the board’s approach to deciding whether to grant a retrospective injury on duty award?

I have been in touch with you over this matter for some time. I suspect that it is the last reason. You cannot hide behind financial challenges on what is right and what is wrong. My suggestion to the Policing Board is to stop messing about. Reply to the conversation. Sort out the injury benefit pensions for police officers and do it soon. I have it on record with the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee today . I want ed to do that so that you know what we are talking about. The public will have heard it as well, so we expect to have an answer and a solution to these matters.

I am not expecting there , members of the board, necessarily a detailed answer to those questions. You have come to give evidence about the data breach. They have been asked. If you were able to provide a response in writing, the Committee would be content with that. Is that a l right?
I would be happy, as chief executive, to come back. We could maybe get from the C lerk the detail of those points from Mr Shannon , and t hen yes, we will come back in writing.
Yes , absolutely. That is no problem.
We will make sure that those are furnished to you.

Q304 Good morning. The chief constable at least in part resigned as a result of the data breach. The PSNI review has now been published, as you say, not long ago , but it is now in your hands. When can we expect the review of the board to be published and its leadership and operations held to account?

In the aftermath of th e scoping judgment, as the Member rightly says, there were a number of issues that they wanted to focus on . Obviously in the immediate aftermath of the previous chief constable’s resignation we were focused on bringing stability to the service through the appointment of an interim and then a substantive chief constable. The n , yes, the review of the board and the review of the service executive team structure were issues that the board wanted to see focused on.

As it is a review of the board, it is obviously not appropriate for the board to take the lead on that. We have, over recent months, secured agreement from the Department of Justice, which is prepared to act as the independent commissioners, if you like, for that review. The D epartment has agreed to take that forward for us. We have been afforded the opportunity to feed our views into what the terms of reference might be, but the Department and the person or persons appointed by the Department will have the final say on that. That is where that is and I do not have a timetable as yet to share with the Committee.

Q305 I take that point. An external review makes sense. However, you are in a position to be self-examining within this process. One comment that was made is that these issues around data handling and IT , et c. , were not on the board’s agenda. It is a real question for you all as to whether that is an accurate description.

Also, importantly, I have been in the position myself very equivalent to the role you have. IT is extremely difficult for those of us who are not experts. Do you have the expertise in house to be able to perform the role that you have of scrutinising the operation of the PSNI? It is not just enough to say that you are a review body. You are, but have you the capacity and the people in house on the board to advise you who can make sure that you can adequately scrutinise the progress of the PSNI in this area?

The independent review report suggested the appointment of a board member with particular expertise in this area . There is a deficit in expertise. There is no question about that. I do not know whether that is the best solution to it. Alternatives would include identifying someone who would come as a periodic adviser when this issue was on our agenda, or indeed, as is happening over the next year, where the people who undertook this review would come back and assist us in terms of reviewing progress and so on. Yes, t here is a need for additional expertise. We need to discuss within the board and with the Department how best that could be acquired and procured.

To go back to the point that you made at the very outset, the board is an accountability body. Management of information governance in PSNI , though , is for PSNI. The report is very much about a collective responsibility and the board is absolutely in that space , but just to highlight , on the point that information and data management is not on the board’s agenda , t he board, as the accountability body, derives assurance from the internal mechanisms. PSNI has its own audit and risk assurance and its own internal audit programme. It would only be where those processes flag an issue up that it would make its way on to the board agenda. That is in compliance with the T reasury guidance around risk management.

I just say that by way of explanation as to why it was not on the board’s agenda at the outset. The report shows that there are issues , certainly, in terms of training , roles and responsibilities and operating procedures, but definitely issues around internal governance that I hope this report will now allow us to get right, going forward.

Q306 Are you sure that that is a satisfactory response to say that it is only if PSNI internal processes flag something up that the board would take an interest? It does not seem to me that that is the way that the board ought to operate .

T he primary objective of the board is to hold the PSNI to account for the delivery of efficient and effective policing. We primarily do that through our policing plan. We go out, consult with the community and identify what the priorities are for the community in Northern Ireland . That drives the content of our policing plan.

In terms of the work of our committees, those are driven by our statutory functions, such as our human rights monitoring. We would also be driven by major strategic work areas within PSNI, such as financial planning and people management. There would also be a focus through committees on issues that are being flagged up through the risk process. I would not want to suggest that the only way in which things make their way on to the agenda is through that sort of risk management process. There is tha t range of other means by which they can come on to our agenda .

In terms of board oversight, there are a range of different mechanisms across the different committees as well that touch on data and information governance in terms of the HRA and privacy in policing report, for example. There are a variety of human rights reports that touch on individual protection of data and protection of community data or data that is held. There are a range of areas there where we scrutinise the PSNI from its corporate plan on a couple of different reports that are reoccurring right across the committees.

Q307 I appreciate the engagement with us. Looking at the report overall, I wanted to clarify whether you are satisfied with the timeline of the incident specifically. Are there any questions that you think have not been either addressed or satisfactorily concluded on in relation to what happened in those few days in August?

It was a critical incident that we had to react to very speedily across a range of different partners and bodies. It was appropriate that everybody was engaged, primarily the people who were affected, first and foremost. We cannot underestimate that. As soon as we could physically action responses, they were done.

We have had a range of meetings between August and now, collating the board together to make decisions collectively, which it is our responsibility to do. We have had over 20 official meetings, never mind committee meetings, to be able to action a range of areas in terms of getting things done properly in the right order in the right way, so that this can be an effective process that can be measured and monitored and that decisions are made at the right time. There are 37 recommendations.

Q308 I just want ed to confirm what the report sets out happened in the run-up to the incident and the incident itself . A re you satisfied with the explanation given of the issue around closing tabs, deleting tabs and all that? A re you satisfied with the explanation and is there anything else you would have liked addressed in the report?

In the situation from the report, and from the author as well, you can see that there were a whole range of different areas across a range of different teams and parts of the organisation that contributed to this, not necessarily one area that is at fault. There is a lot of learning across this area that can be there for a lot of other organisations as well. I would accept that no organisation is perfect and that we now know that there are a variety of areas that need to be improved for the PSNI to ensure that this does not happen again .
Q309 Sinead or Edgar, I did not know whether either of you want ed to add anything further .

I thought that the report was comprehensive. As we have already said, there is learning in it for the organisation, for ourselves and for many others across the public sector. The board discussions that we have had on the report over the last number of days have turned very much to a focus on, “How do we get on with the job of work that needs to be done?” and developing a costed implementation plan to take that forward . I felt that the report was comprehensive.

I would agree with that. We engaged some independent experts ourselves as a panel to provide us with additional advice. Overall, the report has been well received. No doubt it is very challenging for all of us and probably for a lot of other bodies as well . We think that we can move to a position where we have very significant confidence in how data is managed, shared and used within the PSNI.

Q310 Good morning to our witness es . I think that it was you, Edgar, who referred to the 37 recommendations that were made. That is a lot of recommendations. I appreciate that the board is still going through these. Do you have any sense of the prioritisation that is required in terms of delivery of those, which are most important and which are probably slightly lesser in terms of their impact and significance? S econd ly , just to clarify, Sinead , the board’s function in this regard, presumably at some stage the PSNI will need to put in place an action plan for implementation of the recommendations. Could you clarify the board’s role in terms of either the compilation or, perhaps more relevant, the oversight of the implementation of said action plan?

The first point would be that the report emphasises that data protection and management should be up there with finance and HR i n terms of key assets available to any organisation , including PSNI . In terms of key issues that might assist going forward, clearly the internal governance and management within PSNI is a critical issue. I know that it has already responded to that by elevating the SIRO role to deputy chief constable level.

There is a further recommendation, which is quite significant, and that is the importance of developing a standard operating procedure for dealing with FoI . There seems to be no shortage of instruction s, guidance and so on, but it did not seem to have been pulled together in a way that was helpful to the staff who were managing it. That is reflected in the fact that there had been an opportunity when the National Police Chiefs ’ Council had on two occasions been in contact with police services in relation to safeguarding data that was being released. That did not seem to get through or was not implemented . That whole governance issue and the standard operating procedure are two of the matters.

The third is how training is conducted and the need for more targeted and specific, rather than generic, training for people who are dealing with it. Related to that is recognising data management as a profession with very specific skills that need to be acquired and developed. In terms of the board’s function, as some of my colleagues have said already, when we develop an action plan , the board will be wanting to keep that on our agenda going forward, ensuring that actions that are due to be taken are taken and to go further and look at the impact of those.

If I could point to the recommendation that I read out earlier, the authors ask us to develop a set of KPIs. Once we see the implementation plan, we can then work on the KPIs. That will dictate and drive how we manage it through our committees, whether we need a separate group or, depending on the content of the plan, funnel it through our existing committee structure.

The one thing I would add to what the vice-chair has said , and picking up on points that committee members have made, is that, over and above the fact that the report author is planning to come back to have a look, we will want to, as a board, collectively decide whether we want to buy in some expertise to assist us in the same way as we do in relation to HR or human rights issues. That would be the additional point I would make.

One further critical issue for me in the report picks up on the point that the vice-chair has made around the visibility. There is a recommendation for a data board. It would seem to me that that would be pretty central to making sure that the rest of the recommendations that the vice-chair has mentioned get driven forward. Whether it has an existing governance mechanism that could be morphed into a data board or whether it needs a fresh set-up is something we wish to discuss with the leadership team in the coming days.

To add to that on the human side, our colleagues yesterday spoke about the capacity and capability of staff and the workloads that staff and police officers have. We have to be very aware of building capability and understanding and support across all those teams and work with the PSNI to make sure that that capability and support is there.

Q311 That is a very good segue into my next question. I want ed to get a sense in terms of resourc ing, first in terms of delivery of the recommendations . Do you see a potential impact in terms of either additional human resources or financial implications for any of the recommendations as such?

You touch on a very significant point . The Northern Ireland Fiscal Council last year reported on the justice budget in Northern Ireland. Between 2018-19 and 2024-25, it was scheduled to increase by 3.6%. The equivalent functions in GB will increase by over 33%, so there is a real issue. There has been a financial crisis with PSNI long before there was a data breach crisis.

Also, as you are aware, through the Barnett consequentials, when money comes to Northern Ireland it is allocated by the Department of Finance, not necessarily from where those consequentials came from but in terms of assessed need there. In respect of that as well , justice has had a very difficult number of years in terms of budgets . Resourcing will definitely be an issue going forward, but the priority that the review team ascribed to getting this right will be very influential in terms of how resources are allocated.

Q312 There are two elements to the very particular financial implications from the data breaches themselves. One is the implementation of the action plan in terms of any particular changes that need to be made. Probably t he wider issue, which has been well articulated previously, is around the wider costs to the PSNI of mitigating the impact of the data breach in terms of managing people’s potential security requirements and the wider issue about potential compensation. You are all aware of potential legal challenge in that regard .

Without discussing the merits of that, can you maybe update us on your understanding of where things are with highlighting this within the Northern Ireland Office and Treasury around any particular bespoke funding to try to address those pressures? Some of them may well be in - year. Some may well have a tail over several years .

Can I echo the point that has been made previously ? A lot of these issues are not purely a Northern Ireland responsibility, given that there is a residual UK responsibility around policing and some of the implications here are national security implications . There is a very ready lead-in for the U K Government to take on some of this responsibility.

As you are aware, th at bid has been made to the T reasury. As a board, we very much welcomed the support of colleagues in DoJ, DoF and Treasury. The bid, as was articulated last time that we were with the Committee, is between £27 million and £32 million. That is to d eal with the data breach . That is not any potential fine. That is not litigation.

We welcome the fact that that money has recently been made available for the universal offering. PSNI had to take some measures for a particular cadre of staff in the early days afterwards , but this universal offering will now allow them to deal with the more general issues that people have . In terms of further funding , my understanding is that PSNI will need to work out the implementation plan and then have further conversations with Treasury around funding of those. I suppose that we are heartened by the support that there has been already and by the release of the £5 million for the universal offering. On the point that you make, Mr Farry, we are not involved in the conversations but our understanding of the discussions is that people are very mindful of their responsibilities and the impact that this has had more generally.

Q313 Thank you to the panel for your comments this morning . I would want to be associated with the comments of my colleague, Mr Shannon, in relation to the retired injuries payment. It is important that the board grasps this. I know that you have said that you want the information on it, but you already have the information because this has been raised in Parliament on a number of occasions. I would go further and ask that you meet with some of these officers who are so badly impacted by this ongoing lack of action by the Policing Board .

In relation to the report, I have a very quick question. In my mind, one big thing is that the issue with the PSNI’s handling of data has been that it has not transformed its systems or its estates . I n y o ur mind, as the Policing Board , what can you do to help facilitate th at transf ormation of systems? Ultimately, we are still dealing with policing that was 20 years ago.

We all know that things have moved on. I know that, even in my own constituency, as an elected representative the way that people contact me and use technology is so different. If you take a constituency office, 20 years ago it would have been a drop - in. It would have been a walk - in. Now it is through Facebook and social media. It is instant, overnight and all the time. What do you feel should be done more between the Policing Board and policing to try to transform our services?

W hile there is a lot of work to be done, we need to recognise that significant change and transformation has taken place over recent years . Currently, as you say, the contact is different than it was 20 years ago, but our contact centres are dealing with something like 500,000 calls every year. They are dealing with about 20,000 999 calls every year. They take a domestic abuse call every 17 minutes. Technology has been really very important in assisting them. There has been a roll-out of secure laptops, which allow officers to report directly, rather than having to go back into the station again.

A lot has happened, but there is a lot to happen yet. One area that the report focused on particularly was the HR system, the SAP system. That has been patched, changed and modified over the years to a point where it is beyond its normal lifecycle. We need to acknowledge that that is one area that will need to get priority and that the board will be wanting to keep on top of as things go forward.

I would stress a point that has been made by the chair and others. T he operational responsibility for all this lies with the PSNI and the chief constable. I would just mention of the importance of ensuring that our police service is resourced properly going forward.

I will add just two points. The parts of the report that are probably transformational include some that the vice-chair is referring to — the replacement of SAP and the use of the data warehouse, the building foundations section of the report . There is probably also a large price tag attached to them. T he board would want to be understanding P S NI’s business case to change and transform and to then, when we are satisfied, be supportive of those business cases.

The other point might not be quite in the transformational space, but is in terms of helping to improve anyway. There is a lot of work going on nationally through the NPCC. You can see, smattered throughout the report, a number of references to PSNI engaging and utilising some of those networks that are there . I have heard others in policing refer to it as almost free consultancy. We would want to make sure that that is tapped into.

Q314 I want to ask a final question. I appreciate the difference between strategic oversight and operational responsibilities, but sometimes there is an overlap. Sometimes, the operational matters are reputational for the entire force. There is a big question underl y ing all of this , not about the process by which people understand Microsoft but why in the first place there are so many FoI requests and so many FoI requests from members of the very same force . As a board, have you asked questions about that? If not, why not? Here is a suggestion. Could that not be a theme for you to explore proactively with the PSNI , with an aim to reducing the overall number of FoI s in the first place and, frankly, dealing with the question of trust between officers and the senior police that we hear so much from the evidence that has come before us thus far?

Y our point is well made. In terms of the policing plan, there are a lot of areas there that can touch on support. In terms of why those FoI s are coming forward, it is a very legitimate question. They have been discussed across committees and I welcome that . I welcome that thought.

On another area, if you are talking about the actual report itself , talking about the culture, data, skills and talent, there is a link there in terms of how the board scrutinises that across HR, skills and abilities, the different cultural audits and the different areas that we examine across the work that we do. That will support and enable this .

The federation people yesterday were very helpful in this regard . A lot of the FoI s seem to arise almost as a precursor to an industrial tribunal or whatever. Part of the answer to that is a more aggressive publication scheme , where you do not need it .

The caution I would put in there is that, very often, in compe nsations you are dealing with relatively small numbers. The risk of disclosure of individuals is something that is taken into consideration normally in F o Is, but particularly around small compe nsations .

In a conversation that we had with the members of the senior team last week, they already take on board the fact that 20% of FoI s are from their own people about their own processes. Notwithstanding the point that the vice-chair has made, they very much are on the page of wanting to find a way of getting some of this information out. It would be good practice in an open, transparent organisation . It is already on the ir radar. When we are looking at the KPIs, we will absolutely take on board your suggestion, Chair , of a reduction in FoI numbers overall .

Q315 Yes. You c ould have a really constructive , proactive role in holding the PSNI to account in year - on - year reduction in F o Is because of the publication of information that, by dint of it being answered by FoI , is in the public domain anyway, or should be .
That is very true.
Thank you very much indeed to board members for the evidence . We are grateful to panel 1. We will say farewell and compliments of the season to you . We wish you well in your work in the year ahead.

I : Simon Hoare MP, Parliamentary Under - Secretary of State (Local Government), Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities ; and Liz Owen, Deputy Director for Registration and Franchise, Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities.
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Simon Hoare MP and Liz Owen.

Welcome, everyone, to this morning’s session of the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Select Committee. This is our final evidence session in our inquiry into electoral registration and the challenge we have in this country , where there are an estimated 8 million people — maybe even a few more — who are entitled to be registered to vote but do not appear on the register. That is the issue we will look at today. We have the local government Minister, Simon Hoare, with us today . I will come to you and your official in a minute, Simon.

To begin with, I will ask Committee members to put on record any interests they may have that may be relevant. First of all, welcome to Tom Hunt, a new member of the Committee. I think you have put your register of interests as in the register before us today ; t hank you very much. We will go around the table now and put on record any particular interests we have that may be relevant to this inquiry. I am a vice-president of the Local Government Association.
I employ a councillor.
I am a member of the One Nottingham board.
I am vice-president of the Local Government Association and I employ a councillor in my office.
I employ two county councillor s in my constituency office.
Okay , fine . That is all the particular interests , as well as the ones on the formal register.
Minister, thank you very much for coming this morning. Would you like to introduce the official who is with you today?
Liz Owen is the brains of the outfit. Anything that sounds a bit tricky I shall pass to Liz, but hopefully between the two of us we can answer your questions.

Q232 The first question is quite obvious and is the reason why we are doing this inquiry. Eight million people who could be registered—that was one estimate and I think the Electoral Commission said recently that it might be as high as 9 million—are not on the register. Does that concern you?
Yes.
Q233 That was the easy question. I suppose the next question is: what are you going to do about it?

Yes, of course i t is a concern. I take a rather old-fashioned view that there is almost a sacred majesty in voting and therefore anybody who is entitled to vote should at least be on the register. Whether they then exercise their vote is of course a matter for them to decide.

There isn’t a silver bullet, Mr Betts, as you know , with your long experience as a local authority leader and as a Member of Parliament. There are a number of tools and there are a number of organisations that are involved. Local authorities of course play a key part in local promotion. They are the best people to know their communities and where certain initiatives may be required.

There are p artner organisations . O ne might think, for example, of organisations like the National Union of Students , which is very important in driving registration among young students in our universities and colleges. The charity sector s are quite involved in encouraging people to think about registering. The Electoral Commission, which I met yesterday, obviously plays a big part with big TV ads. The Government can support and augment. We can use the gov.uk site to promote registration.

Social media has a huge influence, of course, which we forget at our peril. You will recall the biggest spike in registration before the 2019 general election followed hot on the heels of a Facebook post that it had promoted, which effectively said, “You have X number of hours” or days or whatever it was , “before the deadline for registration”.

It is something where you cannot say the job is done because in every generation and in every year there is a new cohort of people who need to be told what to do. We do not think that the figures now , with the IER system introduced in 2014, in any way show a change from prior to its introduction. There is always work to do by an awful lot of people.

Q234 Minister, you have accepted that it is worrying that 8 million people are not registered who should be or could be. You have just described what the current system is. You have not indicated any potential change that you might like to see to improve it.

If you are talking, Mr Betts, about the process by which somebody can get on to the electoral register, there are, as we know, two principal ways of doing that. There is online, which the vast majority of people do. There is the paper forms that local authorities use , and there is an element of local design and promotion that sits around that. The thing that a lot of people do not know about is that you do not have to fill out a form either digitally or o n paper to get on to the electoral register . O n the proviso that you provide the information that is required , o ne can just write a letter to their local authority to say, “I wish to be included on the electoral register . ”
I don’t think it is the method of registration that causes me or the Government concern. It is about focus ing more resolutely on how you make people aware of the process and get them to utilise it.

Q235 You have just described all the ways that people are made aware and it still does not work. Have you no interest at all or no intention to make any changes to the system to try to tackle the 8 million people?

I do not want to default to an easy answer . H owever, one can take a horse to water but one cannot make it drink. You can promote as much as you like . Y ou can advertise ; y ou can have public awareness campaigns. Think of the great work that the commission does in television advertising, online promotion and so on. We cannot force people if they do not wish to register. We should also be aware that of course contained within the figures are a number of people in our country who for primarily faith reasons do not take part in the democratic process.
Minister, I do not think there are 8 million Jehovah’s Witnesses missing .

Chairman, no, and I did not say there was , but you have to try to unpack the figure. There are, for example—somebody can do the maths—139,106 Jehovah’s Witnesses in the UK, 6,000 Rastafarians, 16,000 Exclusive Brethren or Plymouth Brethren, 8,200 Christadelphians—
How many does all that add up to?
Somebody can do the maths for me because I do not have the running total, but it certainly does not run up to 8 million.
I don’t think it runs up to 800,000.
It doesn’t; y ou are right. What I am saying is that there are a number of factors that play into people—
Okay , l et’s get back to this.
You have to raise the awareness—

Q236 Yes, but we have been trying that. Other countries manage to get registration figures in excess of 96% or 97%. We are below 90%. Have you no interest in looking at what anybody else does to see if they do it better?
We would always look to other countries to see what they do. Canada is an interesting example.
Yes, we have been there to look at that.

Yes, Canada is an interesting example. I will never say in whatever sphere of elections that we have alighted upon the most perfect system and there is no scope for change. I think that anybody who ever says that is a certifiable idiot. There is always room for change, for evolution, for iteration and for learning from others. It is important that it is nationally bespoke and not just some off-the-shelf response. Yes, of course it can always remain fluid and we are always open. As I say, I was talking yesterday to the commission on a variety of subjects. If any company comes up with a stellar idea that can be deployed at pace in order to promote registration, we will of course give it thought.
Okay. We may look at some stellar ideas of other people.
I look forward to your report on this, which hopefully will be a Lord Young of Graffham report, which is : don’t just bring problems, bring solutions.
Well, you never know. Let us look at and explore one or two options and ideas. Kate, over to you.
Q237 The Electoral Commission has identified a form of assisted registration that could be implemented. Do you have any concerns about this form of registration?
I might ask Liz to start off and talk about that.
I am assuming that you mean prompts from other government services. Is that what you are referring to?
Yes.

As you know, over the last two or three years the Government’s particular focus in relation to elections has been working on bringing forward measures to improve the integrity of the electoral system. In terms of assisted registration, there are some interesting ideas there. We have done a piece of work with our colleagues in HMRC to include information about the register to vote service on the letter that goes out when somebody gets a new national insurance number . I would say that in principle those ideas are interesting. Over the last few years, working on electoral integrity has been a higher priority for this Government.

I would also point to, for example, when HMRC—which commu nicates, as we know, with a huge number of people—sends out letters to notify people of their national insurance number, it will signpost people that that number is required if you wish to register to vote , so t here is some signposting. I think there is a danger if one is just relying upon the agency of g overnment with which you are interacting — it could be the DVLA, the Passport Office and so on — to effectively then make the leap to assist in electoral registration . T hat might be quite a flimsy base upon which to launch a strategy.

I also make this point, and it goes back to whether you think —and I am sure we all do — that the act of voting is an important part of our citizenship. It is part of the contract between the citizen and the state. People should think about registration to allow them to take part in our democratic processes. I think there has to be a certain amount of personal responsibility and motivation to do that, going back to the Chair’s initial question. That interest has to be prompted by a whole variety of promotion points, but in essence it is part of that relationship between the individual and the state if they wish to take part as an active democratic citizen.

Q238 Of course you are right. You talked about campaigns just before an election, but it could be much smoother. It can be quite daunting for people to go online and register with all the evidence that you need. Are you suggesting that you would not support further assistance because you think people have a duty to register?

I think t he primary motivator—again, you have to have the information to make you think about doing it, so once you have that I do not think it is unreasonable to expect the individual to make the effort to join the register themselves. It is part of that contract, as I say.

Ms Hollern, I entirely take your point about trying to avoid spikes, which is why it cannot be one of those things where you say, “Here is a stream of work” and it lasts six months, box ticked, job done. It is an iterative process because you have to consider people qualifying to get on to the register. It is an annual ongoing event. The people who would most like to avoid dramatic spikes in registration — so having a calmer approach — are of course the electoral registration officers themselves. We will all appreciate as political practitioners the huge amount of pressure that those staff are under in the immediate run-up to a general election or any election. They want to ensure as best as they possibly can the accuracy of the register. The integrity of the register is important. If you suddenly have a massive spike, let’s say as a result of a campaign that has been singularly or solely focused at younger voters , and you have that dramatic spike in university cities, the EROs would much prefer to see that as a nice steady approach to life.

I was just trying to look at the figures. Facebook, for example, ran a campaign between 22 and 25 November 2019. The peak was 659,666 applications to register to vote in just one day, so that was a phenomenal volume of people for EROs to deal with. A nice steady workload and a nice steady workstream is to be preferred. However, if there are spikes, as the 2019 registration process demonstrated very clearly, they can cope. The blood pressure may go up a wee bit , but they can cope.

Q239 I am sure you are aware that the Welsh Government introduced a Bill in October to consider bringing in automatic voter registration, which seems a very sensible approach. It reduces the spikes and it verifies a lot of the information that is held. What were your feelings on that?

I am in a freethinking spirit at the moment. As I understand it, it is on the agenda for me to discuss and learn more for when we have our inter-governmental ministerial meeting. However, you speak to a generally important point and it speaks back to the point that I ma de earlier. If one thinks that this system is utterly perfect and cannot be reformed in any way, that is a very arid way to start any conversation. Of course we will look and listen and learn and speak to and engage with Edinburgh or Cardiff or other parts of the democratic world , because technology and citizen expectations change. It is a fluid thing and therefore our systems have to have that baked in , whereby there is the opportunity to deliver change. I would suggest that if you look at the legislation the Government have brought forward in recent times, it does suggest an appetite to respond to demands for change in changing circumstances.

Q240 Minister, I have a quick follow-up. You will be aware that there are a large number of people who have come to this country from despotic regimes. They are very nervous about putting anything around identity to authorities. What action are you taking to enable those people to feel confident that they should register?

Mr Blackman, that is a key and important point. It is certainly one I learned when I chaired the Northern Ireland Affairs Select Committee , with refugees going to live in Northern Ireland. W e never really think about the innate suspicion of people in uniform and officialdom and authority when you have come from a country where they are agents of the state , who will dob you in at a moment’s notice and would sell their granny for a gold epaulette .

F unnily enough, we were discussing this with the commission yesterday. They do quite a lot of work , but there is room for doing more , and that is with faith leaders . Faith leaders are hugely important in saying to their communities—I hope it is not on a false premise — that those communities will welcome newcomers into their area and bring them into the fold to provide support and advice and so on . I t is a very key thing to do.

I also think that , without creating work for our teachers, in areas such as yours in Harrow, where you have a lot of children of new people coming into the UK, it is the role of the education sphere to say to our young people that authority is not something to be feared. It is something to be respected, it is something to be admired and it is something to be trusted, but feared is not part of it. There are a number of things that can play into it, but it is a hugely important point. People from very despotic regimes will be particularly partial as to who they share their data with , their date of birth or any information that could lead to “their collars being felt”.
We will move on to the use of data with Natalie Elphicke.

Q241 Building on that very point, the evidence from Professor James is that , in relation to cyber-security , overseas actors could purchase the data that we have in the open register and compile it into a single dataset for malign purposes. Building on the question about confidence in the use, security and privacy of data that is provided by individual citizens, could you explain why you do not support the abolition of the open register?

The first thing to say, Ms Elphicke, is that the Government always seek to ensure up-to - date, contemporary security measures for the individual electoral registration digital service . We always look to best practice and there is a vast amount of work that is done across government and across Departments to make sure that that is in sharp focus and being thought about. There have been, as we know, several changes in this arena in recent years. In 2020 the IERDS moved to a cloud-hosted environment, adding substantial robustness and security to the service , in keeping with our Government Digital Service cyber-security cloud principles.

Q242 Sorry, could I just stop you there? This is a question a b ou t the open register. This is a question a bout people having the ability to purchase information that people have provided, not about people breaking into g overnment systems, as has been known from time to time. I would be grateful if you could address this : why not abolish the open register?

Any individual organisation, as you know, before 2002 could ask for a copy of the electoral register and there were no restrictions on how it was used. The High Court in the Robertson v . Wakefield judgment in 2002 made some suggestions for change, which then led to the edited register.

T here is an important point here about the need to safeguard, which again is why we think it is rather important that people do registration principally of their own volition. Those who would classify themselves as vulnerable—one automatically thinks of violence against women and girls, that arena of policy, but also vulnerable young adults who may be fleeing an abusive home environment and so on—want to be very careful with how they use their data. The law now governing access to the register was changed to provide two versions of the register, the electoral register and the open register, which is also sometimes known as the edited register. The full electoral register is available only to certain persons and bodies specified in law and can be used for electoral purposes, law enforcement, jury summoning and credit checking. There are different rules governing the electoral register as far as Northern Ireland is concerned.

Q243 I think the Committee is aware of that, thank you. G iven that this information is available in the open register, why would the Government be opposed to abolishing the open register ? T he Electoral Commission, Professor James — who, as I mentioned, gave some expert evidence on this —and the Electoral Reform Society , p eople who know a lot about this are saying it is a problem having an open register. Can you confirm that it is the Government’s position that you will retain an open register?
That is the current position of the Government , with no intention to change it.

Q244 Moving to your “ no intention to change it ” , I understand from your comments earlier that you said that it was the EROs, the electoral registration officers, who had the responsibility to keep accurate records. What is the Government’s responsibility in relation to the accuracy of electoral information?

I think our first responsibility is to set clear rules, guidance and regulation and to ensure that we engage regularly with practitioners who are learning directly from the field delivering down on the ground elections—
Q245 You are p roviding guidance and training. A re you saying that the Government do es not have a direct role in—
Each local authority is responsible for maintaining its own register. We do not—
It is the local authorities ; i t is not the Government .
We do not have a national—
Thank you. Moving on to the issue of the complete register—
Ms Elphicke, the point I wanted to make, if I may, is that we do not have a national register. One can deploy a perfectly acceptable argument for a national register .

Q246 Indeed, and I was coming on to that. Let’s just explore that. I understand from the comments you made earlier that it is not the Government’s position that they have a responsibility for accuracy and it is not the Government’s responsibility to have a complete register. I wanted to explore this by reference to the example that you gave of HMRC. If HMRC is involved, as you have recognised it is, do you think that the information that HMRC is providing — “ You need this information ” or “Y ou can register” — is adequate for such a pivotal democratic role that you have expressed to us in very effusive terms?

Adequate as far as the role of HMRC is concerned, yes. Adequate as a total communication strategy, no. As I hope I set out in an earlier answer, there is not a silver bullet on this. People will pick up information from a whole variety of sources and it is important to make sure that those who want to help to drive up registration numbers—and I think broadly people do ; n obody, I would think—
Q247 Do the Government want to?
Of course.
I was not sure from your earlier comments.
I think I made that hugely clear in my first answer to Mr Betts’s question.
Q248 In relation to that question, what is the Government’s target percentage to drive that up to?
Our ideal target is of course 100% of eligible voters.

Q249 A hundred per cent— but you have already expressed that there are a number of people who you think should not have to register. If it was 100% , why would you not just have compulsory registration?

No, what I said was 100% of eligible voters, which does not necessarily mean 100% of everybody over the age of 18. There are some who do not qualify because they are foreign nationals. They would qualify by age but not by category. There are those who qualify by age but decide not to register because their religious beliefs preclude them. I think it has to be an arena of exhortation rather than compulsion.

Q250 In relation to the information or access to this vital role in our democracy, you would acknowledge that there are some people in our society who might move more frequently than others, who might not be able to access this information. In the Government’s engagements, HMRC being a good example, why would Government not allow an opportunity, for example, when submitting a tax return for someone to tick a box to say, “Yes, please add me to the register”?

Because HMRC does not administer the register. If we had a perfect system of data handling — and I don’t think anybody ever would have a perfect system of data handling — the idea of HMRC registering people to vote and then passing on those details to the—

Q251 I have not suggested it registers. I have suggested that there is an opt-in process as part of the tax return. That is not it registering, although there is an argument to have a national register. To the question, why could it not indicate that and that be the process? Why do Government have a passive role in this?

They could , but principally we have the commission, which is, as you know, an independent body that leads principally on these matters. It is the job of Government to set the rules and the regulations. One can construct, I readily accept, a perfectly cogent argument that supports the idea of a national register administered by central Government. There are some people who might have general questions about the efficacy of that, and the morality of that, if you will.

It also presupposes that in terms of the communications campaigns that central Government— the man or the woman in Whitehall— would know better as to how best to target specific campaigns to motivate people to vote. We do take the view — and whether you agree with it or not , I still think it is a perfectly respectable position to take — that in the spirit of localism, local officials are the people who are best placed to know the intricacies of their communities and to target bespoke and specific campaigns to drive up registration in those “harder to reach” groups.

Q252 I know we are going to move on , but just to be clear about the question, this is about Government’s communication with individuals and the exercise of their democratic right and the role of Government, which is already providing information. From your answer, you are saying that that passive role of information is as far as the Government are prepared to go.
No, I would not describe it as passive , because that suggests an air of relaxed complacency.
Surely not.
W hat , from His Majesty’s Government?
Surely not.

No. We are conscious of the part we have to play. We help to facilitate best practice between EROs and others to learn from experience. There are elements of financial support that Government can provide in certain areas to advance that. We have an engaged role to play. It is a role that we take very seriously , but it is not our sole responsibility because it presupposes in the first instance that every person in the country takes as gospel information that is given to them by the Government. Other people will want to go to other sources for authenticity and verification and the like.

I am not a golfer , but just as I am told you wouldn’t turn up on a golf course with one club in your bag — you would have the full set of clubs that you could play —so there are a lot of— [ Interruption. ] No, it is a perfectly acceptable metaphor . [ Laughter. ] The point I am making is that there are lots of clubs in the bag of driving up electoral registration. I think it would be folly to rest it all entirely on central G overnment a n d a centrally administered national register.
Moving on to the issue of how we do it now, Mary.

Q253 If I may, before I go on, another metaphor is having all the tools in the toolbox . S urely one of the tools that could be considered, given that you have already said that local administrations are best placed to know their local communities, is perhaps looking at the system in Canada , where there is a box that is ticked on tax returns and that information is communicated with local administrations through a unique number. It is always worth looking to see whether we have the full range of tools in our toolbox, Minister.

Ms Robinson, I agree entirely. The Department is very familiar with the Canadian model, which seems to work very well. These things are kept under review. As I say, it is iterative and organic . If you are saying— and I am not suggesting that you are — “L et us bring in these changes for 2 May and the subsequent g eneral e lection , ” I think there has been a significant amount of change in how we are conducting our elections going forward , as kicked off in May of this year. To now have a wholesale root-and-branch change around with regards to how the register is compiled might be the straw that breaks the camel’s back.

If I may also add, Minister, we did some work looking at what could be done to encourage under - registered groups to register. It would have been about four or five years ago now, looking particularly at younger people and people who move house regularly. We did quite a lot of research and provided some funding for outreach organisations . We generated some materials providing insights on how to engage with those groups, which are all on gov.uk, which we then promoted out to EROs to use. When we stood back and took stock of the work that we had done it was simply unclear whether that action by central G overnment was having an objective impact , so at that point we decided not to undertake any further work. Ministers decided not to undertake any further work in that area.
Q254 Thank you for that clarity . I think we may move on to more about that later, but clearly if something is found not to work it is worth looking at why and what else might.

Meanwhile , we have the annual canvass, which basically is every year, writing to households asking whether they are still there and inquiring who is eligible to vote. The Electoral Commission found that one-third of households whose electoral details have changed do not respond to a canvass. Is the annual canvass therefore an effective tool ? O r are you considering alternative methods? If so, what may they be?

Are we considering changes , or are changes under consideration at hand at the current time? The clear answer to that is no. I have certainly heard from EROs the questions that they have about the efficacy of the annual canvass in terms of input versus output. I think it is certainly something that I will be giving thought to , as to whether that is the best way to do it, whether we should retain it but change it in some way, or whether we can add anything to it to make it a more robust exercise , but it does take up quite a lot of time.

I think it is quite useful , and I am certainly persuaded on this point , that in areas of relatively high churn, areas with a lot of quick turnover in the rented sector, it can play a useful part. I also think it is helpful for EROs and their team to then craft their wider communications campaign where they need to make specific interventions to try to drive up registration.

Q255 What may those interventions mean? It is those areas of high churn that need to be targeted. What would that targeting look like? Clearly if one third of people are not responding to the annual canvass , that is a deficit in our democratic process.

I think it would be horses for courses. Again, this speaks back to the overall benefit of having the registers managed, maintained and compiled locally. Let ’s say , for example , you are dealing with part of a city — part of an electoral area — that has a lot of students and they will have a very quick churn. You could easily see the electoral team reaching out to the National Union of Students, for example, to the college principal or the university people to say, “What can we do collectively to try to drive up registration?” Students are quite a challenge, because a lot will say, “Look, I will only be here for three years. I am a temporary citizen. I either will not vote at all or I will try to vote back at home . ” Again, students must be able to decide which register they wish to be on. It is that sort of intervention.

If you were dealing with an area with a very identifiable demographic, it may well be — speaking back to the point I discussed with Mr Blackman— religious leaders or faith leaders who could play a part in helping the registration there. There may be people in the voluntary and charity sector who can play a part and help as well. Again, I think that just underscores the importance of that local knowledge and information and in a very bespoke way devising communication campaigns, different in all areas—some with similarities and of a complementary nature , of course—with the overall uniting ambition of driving up legitimate registration.

Q256 I am sure we will go on to explore more how more engagement can be achieved. Meanwhile, is it sensible to carry on with the annual canvass? Are you comfortable carrying on with an annual canvass that clearly is not getting the people registered who need to be?

As I say, I think it plays a part. Since 2020 , under the reformed annual canvass — I am looking at my briefing note here — all EROs upload their registers to the IERDS at the start of the canvass period . T hat is 47 million entries in total. O bviously not all of those are generated from the annual canvass , but they play a part. I think they play a part in three specific ways: accuracy, awareness and alertness as to where specific communications need to be targeted. From that perspective they can play a useful part, but I take entirely the point that we hear from some EROs. They will raise the question about effort versus output and that is something that we will of course keep under review and keep alert in our discussions.

O n the one third of non-responses , as you mentioned , I believe that is in relation to the proportion of households where the data shows there has been a change in their details . I believe that for the 2022 canvass that was 24% of households, so we are talking about a non-response rate of 8% of households when you look at households overall. There were always non-responders to the canvass before it was reformed in 2020 , and of course since it was reformed. There are very few silver bullets here. What the reformed canvass did was give EROs more tools to use to contact those households, so now they can use email and they can phone them, as well as writing to them and knocking on their door.

This year we are in the third year of normal running of the reformed canvass, because obviously 2020 was highly disrupted by c ovid . W e have an evaluation that is running at the moment. There will be a final report on that early next year. We have published two already so we are keeping it under close review. My overall view is it is a little early to say . W e are giving time for the changes to bed in, see how they have landed and then consider whether further changes are required.

I have t wo statistics, if I may. Satisfaction among the EROs has increased by over 20% during the survey and review period. The one area that remains in the negative is the effectiveness of the door knock. It is the door knock that is the area we would need to have a look at. That would be data rather than hunch - driven , and I think that is quite important.

Q257 The door knocking is a very expensive and ineffective way to gather information. You mentioned the areas with high churn —where if someone knocks on your door in the middle of November , by March they have gone anyway . I think it is something that probably needs to be looked at quite urgently if we want accuracy and engagement to get people to use their democratic right to vote.

I agree , and I think the Government indicates that by the fact that they are conducting an evaluation on the effectiveness even of the reformed annual canvass process. It is one of those areas where there is efficacy and effectiveness in it. Have we maximised those? To use Ms Robinson’s phrase, are we using the right tools in the box to achieve that? We will listen to what practitioners on the ground say and to their suggestions as to how we can achieve the end objective, which is maximising the number of people who want to go on the electoral register. Is it the right way? Is it the best way? Are there other ways ? If so, what are they? The Government are open - minded on that.

Look, we have a system — we will come on to the issue of young people in a second, which is another major problem — where effectively we are putting most of our effort into writing to people whose circumstances have not changed. They live at the same address and they are going to send the forms back because most people who send the forms back are already registered at that address. The people who are moving and churning, that is where the effort should go. That is why we should look at Canada .

I spoke to the previous Secretary of State for Oregon the other day, which was the first state in the United States to bring in an automatic registration system . It uses data to identify where people have moved and then follow them up. Either they tick a box to say, “Yes, you can share my data with the registration officers , ” or they have an opt - out system where it is shared unless they say no. They put all their effort into the people whose circumstances have changed.

The other thing is that , as we said, if you are on the register in Canada , you do not get taken off unless you move to another address. Here , many people get taken off the register simply because they have not responded to the form, even though they have not changed. That happens. The EROs operate a different policy. If you do not respond in two years , you are off. In Canada you have a registration number for voting and it stays with you for life. You do not get taken off the register; you get moved to another address.

I will certainly look at that two - year point that you raised, Chair. That is new to me, so we will look at that . If we may , we will write. As I say, the system we have is the system we have and in broad terms it works. Could it be changed? Yes. Could it be changed , and to what? That is one question. Could it be changed over what timeframe? That is another. I am not sitting here — I do not think any Minister would — and say ing , “No , our system is absolutely perfect and there is nothing we can do to change it or make it better . ” We are living in a very fluid world, which is why we are always open to the experiences of other jurisdictions to see what they are doing. I think that is broadly the right approach to take.
That is helpful and we may encourage you down that route. We will see what is in our report when we make suggestions to you. Let us move on to the issue of young people, which is another challenge.

Q258 Thanks, Minister, for the evidence. I am still none the wiser, so I think the good thing is that you can put the golf clubs away, because the repo r t on electoral registration from this Committee is coming down the line, so that should give you lots of food for thought.
I look forward to it.

I want to touch on engagement and accessibility. I think we have a real issue in the country with regards engagement politically and there is a huge amount of apathy, which is very worrying. If we look at some of the figures, levels of completeness continue to increase with age for voter registration, remaining lowest for the 16 - to - 17 year age group. In Great Britain, completeness for this group has dropped from 45% in 2015 to 16% in 2022. That is quite devastating. As you said , it is the cornerstone of democracy and we have this level of apathy. Are we removing barriers for young people who are voting for the first time?

You are right to point to th at cohort , and this is not something that we are alone in experiencing. There is a growing block of evidence that tells us about the wider lack of engagement in party politics among the young. That seems to be common to all liberal democracies. Whether it is hard baked or a temporary phenomenon , I don’t know. I hope it is temporary. In part that may speak to a huge level of support and interest in joining single - issue pressure groups, but not getting involved with the general political arena.

I have always thought more can be done in our schools to tell people about the responsibility of being an active citizen. I will share briefly , with the leave of the Chair , something that was seared into my mind immediately post the 2016 referendum. I had voted to remain part of the European Union. I was walking across from Parliament to go to something and there was a massive demonstration of predominantly young people. I am not quite sure whether it was a compliment or not, but someone said to me, “You look like a Conservative MP, ” so I said, “Guilty as charged , ” and we got into a huddle of about 20 young people —I will not ask for a Division on whether it was a compliment or not — all of whom were on the electoral register and only 10 of wh om had voted. I asked what the other 10 had done , “We posted on Facebook. We put something on social media . ” T hey had not manned a stall, they had not delivered a leaflet, they had not done anything to support the campaign that they were passionate enough to come out on the streets to protest about , and had not been thoughtful enough to engage in the process. When I pointed out that returning officers do not count posts and likes and things on Twitter, there was a lightbulb moment. There is a huge amount to do.

The worrying thing is — because I don’t think it is necessarily about registration — that even when first or relatively young - ish voters, in their first or second year on the register, are on the register , their turnout is disproportionately lower. When you consider we have postal votes, proxy votes and a very long election day of 7 am through to 10 pm, I would suggest it is not lack of opportunity. Registration to vote digitally is very easy and straightforward and this is a supposedly digitally connected cohort of our fellow citizens. I don’t know if it speaks to something more underlying.
Q259 What are we doing to reach what that reason is? You give me reasons why they can do it, but why aren’t they doing it ? W hat are the Government doing to get to the root of that problem?

You ask me to consider why they are not. A s I say , for some it may be, “A curse on all your h ouses. Politics does not change anything but I will join a pressure group . ” That is certainly a phenomenon. T his is where there is that active role of, “I did not understand that I needed to be on a register to vote , ” and the commission, if you remember, did some very good ads underscoring that .
