segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: HS2 : p rogress update , HC 85
Thursday 30 November 2023 , Birmingham .
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 30 November 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Iain Stewart (Chair); Jack Brereton ; Grahame Morris; Greg Smith.
Questions 334 – 344
Witnesses
I : Trevor Gould, Railway Lead, Stone Railway Campaign Group ; and Trevor Parkin, Engineering and Environmental Lead, Stone Railway Campaign Group .
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Trevor Gould and Trevor Parkin.

Q334 Welcome to the Transport Committee here in Birmingham , rather than our usual place in the House of Commons. Before I start today’s proceedings, I would like to place on record , on behalf of my colleagues and the staff of the Committee , our sadness at the passing of Alistair Darling , who served as Secretary of State for Transport for four years from 2002. We pass on our condolences to his friends and family.

The purpose of today’s session is to continue our scrutiny of HS2 . W e would like to record our thanks to HS2 Ltd for showing us some of the works around Curzon Street here in Birmingham. Could I invite our first panel to introduce yourselves and your organisations for the record, please?

Good afternoon. I am the engineering and environmental lead for a local group in Staffordshire. It has just changed its name; it is now the Stone Railway Campaign Group. We have been working on the HS2 project for seven years and have given evidence on four occasions in Parliament, three times to the House of Commons and once to the House of Lords. I am a mining engineer and an environmental impact assessment specialis t , and I have worked in the industry for 30-odd years.

Afternoon. I am the railway lead for the same organisation as Trevor Parkin. I had been involved in the HS2 project for about three or four year s before the SRCG was inaugurated and I have been in railway operations for probably around 50 years, so I have a great breadth and depth of knowledge in that area of operation.

Q335 Thank you ; we are grateful for your time this afternoon. We are particularly interested in hearing from you to get your opinion on the consequences of the Government’s decision to cancel phases 2a and b of the HS2 project, which of course would have gone through your area. To begin with, could I invite you to give us your opinions as to what the consequences of that decision might be for the West Coast Main Line and related connections , and what else might we need to guarantee future capacity for that line?

I will start. We have forensically analysed the HS2 proposals — not only the engineering and environmental proposals but also the consequences for the West Coast Main Line, particularly in terms of services to west coast destinations. We think that rather than increase the capacity on the railway network in the north, HS2 would have done precisely the reverse. The evidence for that is the comparison between the Avanti timetables that we currently have in the north-west via the West Coast Main Line and what HS2 is proposing , or what is in the DfT's strategic outline business plan. Those proposals have been updated over the years, but if you do a direct comparison, over 75% of west coast stations would have ended up with a far inferior service, not only compared to London but where we are in Staffordshire. We currently have one train —or one and a half— an hour from Stafford to London. That is the Liverpool Lime Street service. Stoke-on-Trent enjoys two trains an hour, which is the Manchester service.

HS2's plan would be to remove all of those P endolino trains because there wouldn’t be capacity for them and to replace them with one single train that would terminate in M acclesfield , having gone through Stafford, crawled up the Norton Bridge line, through Stone at 25 miles an hour, stopped at Stoke and then terminated at Macclesfield. T he service to the north-west would be far inferior. Edinburgh wouldn’t get any trains with HS2’s current proposals and eight other stations would see a dramatic reduction in their levels of service, including places like Carlisle, Glasgow, Wigan, Warrington and Lancaster.

We think that the decision is an excellent one and we think that with some improvements to the West Coast Main Line—not big improvements, but relatively strategically targeted ones—we can take HS2 trains to the destinations they should have gone to in more numbers than was being offered by the HS2 proposals.
I would like to turn to what those alternative projects might be in a moment but, Mr Gould, do you have anything to add to what your colleague has just said?

Yes. Originally , and for many years , I was a great advocate of the HS2 project. I fully support the idea in principle and I still think that it is important that high-speed trains are segregated from freight and slower passenger trains, but unfortunately this HS2 is not the way to do it ; it does not do what it says on the tin. It does not release capacity north of Birmingham , it does not improve connectivity because of that , and it certainly does n’t level up if you start investing in the south and building northwards. As a result, I started looking at alternative options because we need, as Rishi Sunak originally said, to put it on pause, but then start building further north while we have another look at this because this is just not the way . T his is not the answer.

Q336 Just briefly, because we don’t have a huge amount of time this afternoon, can you summarise what type of other enhancements might need to be done , what the broad cost estimate of those might be, the time delivery , and what additional capacity it might release in the future?

The first thing that needs to happen is that the H andsacre Junction needs to be properly constructed so that HS2 joins onto the fast lines. That was the original proposal as part of phase 1 in the hybrid Bill of 2013. At the time it was described as the least disruptive to the West Coast Main Line and the cheapest option. Then in 2019 , HS2 decided , bizarrely, to join on to the slow lines. It did an options analysis, which has not been published publicly, so we have not seen it, but it only looked at six options, which all joined onto the slow lines. T hat affects the capacity on the slow lines, which is where the freight and the local trains are. I have heard it said that the HS2 changes were to save money and to simplify the connection. If you look at the engineering of the two schemes, I can’t see how it can come to that conclusion. It needs a much longer viaduct to cross over to the West Coast Main Line to create the Handsacre Junction on to the slow lines. It needs to return to the original proposals. We have not seen the costs of the Handsacre connection to the junction, either of them, and I think it would be useful to see that options appraisal published in full.

With t he stub end of phase 1, if you like, which continues over the Trent and Mersey Canal at Fradley Junction, there are nearly 2 kilometres of railway that are no longer required under phase 2a and I suspect that you could s ave at least £500 million by not constructing that. I went out there the other week and had a look at what is happening on the ground, and apart from a very large embankment that is constructed on that stub end, there is plenty of opportunity to return to the original plan for Handsacre . It just needs that design to be worked up in accordance with the HS2 original proposals. I can not see it would need any additional powers because the phase 1 powers are still in place. That is the first thing.

One of the issues on the line in that area is the Shugborough Tunnel, which is only two tracks and was built in the 1840s. That tunnel is underneath the historic gardens and in the AONB, but it is only 710 metres long and you could put another tunnel through the hill that it goes under and take four tracks up the West Coast Main Line to Crewe. But the big thing that we think should happen—Trevor will probably talk about this in more detail—is to go back to the HS2 plan of the Crewe consultation, which was to have the independent lines on the west side of Crewe s tation upgraded so that you could put the platforms there and take passenger traffic. I will hand over to Trevor and he can say a little bit more about that.

J ust as an addendum to what Trevor was just saying, under current HS2 plans even now trains to Stoke-on-Trent only terminate at Macclesfield. They go through Stafford and on to Stoke-on-Trent. With our plans, we can reach Stoke-on-Trent seven minutes faster than HS2 can, using HS2's trains, but that would require this great separated junction at Col wich and running up the Col wich line. That is the current route of the Pendolino to Manchester and that route is by far the shorter and quickest to Stoke-on-Trent. Under HS2's plans, that route becomes redundant, which sounds ludicrous — a section of the West Coast Main Line becoming redundant because the only commercial traffic on it is the Pendolino trains to Stoke-on-Trent. If those trains are diverted via Stafford because of the HS2 plans, there is no reason for having that section of the West Coast Main Line. You can see that is just a nonsense.

A s regards the Crewe section, I see that Andrew McNaughton has very helpfully submitted some written evidence to you in support of what he was saying two or three weeks ago . I agree with a lot of what is said about the Crewe area. The approach to Crewe from the south certainly needs the fourth track to be reinstat ed into the throat of the station to allow more trains to run into the station area . That would require the western island of Crewe s tation to be reintroduced, tracks to be re-laid there and a reconfiguration of the track layout — I hope you know a little bit about that now that Professor McNaughton has done that work — and also the platforms to be lengthened . Our plans rely on those four tracks, those extra platforms and the longer platforms, so we have no issues with any of that at all.

The big issue we have is that it is only incremental capacity improvements at Crewe. You can certainly get more trains in from the Shrewsbury line, but they have to terminate at Crewe. They can not get beyond Crewe because of the issues at Crewe North Junction, which I will come to in a second. You can get more trains in from the Chester line with fewer conflicting moves and those trains can access the West Coast Main Line, but the big issue is Crewe North Junction. Crewe North Junction is already up to maximum capacity. Network Rail made a statement a few years ago — in 2016 —w hich I will not read through because it says a lot of uncomplimentary things about North Junction, but putting it simply you can't get any more trains through without withdrawing services. HS2 plans to put more trains through that junction.

O riginally, as Mr Parkin has mentioned, the plan was to put a double-faced island platform on the independent lines, which is a set of four lines that runs to the west of Crewe s tation. It only carries freight trains at the moment . There are two lines to Liverpool and two lines to Manchester. Those lines head into tunnels underneath the north end of Crewe s tation and emerge , but t he Liverpool lines emerge on the West Coast Main Line going north and t he Manchester lines emerge in the Manchester direction and on to Manchester. We propose that we should resurrect th e plan for a double island platform face there so that passenger trains from the Manchester direction can use those tunnels and still call at Crewe by using the independent lines platforms, the new platforms. That would release capacity to allow the extra HS2 trains that the company wishes to run to go through the north j unction without having to withdraw any passenger services.

We also recommend that at least one per hour of the local Crewe to Manchester services, which also cause conflicts at Crewe North Junction, is routed through the independent lines tunnels to call at those platforms. That would allow those services to run southbound to Stafford, for instance. At the moment , nowhere in Staffordshire has access by rail to Manchester Airport. This would be an ideal opportunity to correct that for 2 million people. The route of the Cardiff to Manchester train would also be safeguarded. That approach is from the Shrewsbury end, but that one conflicts with every track in Crewe s tation. It would not conflict with any tracks in Crewe s tation if the independent lines were platformed.
Q337 Have you had any thoughts about what other potential enhancements could be delivered as a result of the savings that have come from the cancellation of phase 2?

Yes. We have developed a series of papers. One is very close to our locality and that is what used to be called the Stoke to Market Drayton line. This is a section of 13 kilometres of railway that used to connect the West Coast Main Line at Stoke through Newcastle-under-Lyme, which is one of the largest towns in the country without a railway station after the Beeching cuts of 1965 , to the West Coast Main Line at Madeley . I f you don’t know where Madeley is—I am sure you do, Jack—Madeley is only 12 kilometres south of Crewe. The reopening of that line and some minimal upgrades between Stoke and Derby and beyond, some of which are already in the Network North plan, would see a lot of freight traffic able to bypass the West Coast Main Line and address the bottlenecks that currently exist and come out just south of Crewe. That is one of our plans.

We are also looking at the alternative to the Northern Powerhouse Rail proposal. Currently, the idea is it shares 24 kilometres of railway with HS2 phase 2b between Manchester, Piccadilly and High Leigh, which is to the west, not far from the M6 motorway. That is a very circuitous route. We think a far more direct route between Liverpool and Manchester and Manchester and Leeds could be achieved for a lot less money. The £12 billion that has been earmarked in the Network North plan for potentially NPR, I don't think that money will go any further than the HS2 piece and it certainly will not stretch to Liverpool.

The alternative, with a through station at Manchester—which the Manchester authorities are desperate for—I think is the only sensible investment in terms of Northern Powerhouse R ail, rather than a turn-back station where trains have to pull into Manchester Piccadilly and pull out in the opposite direction. That is a far better proposal and a far better option than what is currently on the table with NPR.

Q338 In terms of some of the other things that the Committee has been looking at , we particularly have concerns about the road safety audit process. You may have seen that we recently had a letter back from the e xecutive c hair of HS2, following the Chair's writing to express some concerns, particularly in Staffordshire with some of the road safety audit process. I think you have had some involvement in this and dialogue with HS2. What are your thoughts on the current process that HS2 has used around road safety audits and in terms of the letter—if you have seen it—that we have had back?

I understand the Chair of this Committee wrote to HS2 on this issue with particular reference to Yarnfield Lane, which is one of 20 schemes on the phase 2 a project. Yarnfield Lane was probably the biggest of those projects because it was a new bridge over the M6 motorway. It was a 1.2 kilometre diversion of the existing lane between the village where I live and our main local town, which is Stone. We gave evidence back in 2018—in fact, our transport expert gave evidence—on two occasions, where we pointed out that we were very concerned about the outline design of Yarnfield Lane and whether it was feasible. The issue came to a head in the early part of this year, when we met with HS2 just before the phase 2a pause took place . W e now have the design plans from its contractors and consultants. These are the first detailed design plans.

We have analysed these plans and the basic point is the proposed road is just unsafe. It is not just unsafe because we don’t like the idea of this lane, but it is unsafe in terms of UK technical standards. I am sure that the Committee will be aware that under the DMRB process, there are lots of design standards that road designers have to adhere to when designing new roads or new junctions. These are CD 109 and CD 123. The whole process is governed by the road safety audit process, which again is set down in a UK technical standard, GG 119. T hat requires the relevant highway authority to be what is known as the overseeing organisation.

The problem with these HS2 roads is that the h ighway a uthority has been pushed aside from this process and effective ly HS2 has appointed itself as the overseeing organisation. The reason why the overseeing organisation should be the h ighway a uthority is because it is the h ighway a uthority that adopts the roads. We have evidence that Yarnfield Lane fails UK technical standards in about 10 ways, yet it got through the road safety audit stage 1.
Q339 Has that process not been sufficiently robust ?

We don’t think the process has been properly followed. It is not appropriate for the developer to be marking its own homework ; I think that is a phrase you have used before. It is just totally inappropriate. If that is a problem on a road on phase a, which now doesn't look like it will take place, what will the position be all along phase 1, where there have been plenty—

Q340 We have heard evidence previously —for example when we visited Buckinghamshire — that there are concerns in other parts of the country about whether that process is being followed properly and about the safety of some of those roads.

I t is very important. This is a very serious issue because we are talking about the safety of the public on these roads and there needs to be full transparency with this. We have asked, through freedom of information, to see the involvement of the highway authority — in our case, Staffordshire County Council — on this issue and we have been refused on three occasions now by HS2. The Committee has asked for this information — full details of what correspondence and minutes of meetings that took place. I note that the response that was received last week from the executive chairman of HS2 just said there was a meeting on 2 November last year . The road safety audit process should have started in 2018 or even 2017 when the roads were first alluded to. If the county council ha s not been involved until November 2022, it does demonstrate a serious concern for us that it has not been allowed to properly scrutinise these roads. I would stress very strongly that there is a big issue here and that HS2 need s to be far more transparent than it currently is willing to be.

Q341 I want to ask both of you about your experience of, as you say, giving evidence at the h ybrid Bill Committee. First I would like to ask about your feelings in terms of the engagement of HS2 with those giving evidence. What is your experience in terms of how HS2 has listened and considered some of the suggestions and genuine issues that have been put forward about how it could improve the project both in terms of listen ing more to the issues of residents and environmental issues, but also in terms of reducing the burden of cost for the taxpayer?

We started on this back in 2016. Just to give you a bit of background, I have been involved in environmental impact assessment since it was first invented in the late 1980s , and I have managed and authored a lot of major development environmental impact assessments. The reason why we first got involved—or I first got involved—in this was because of the proposed Stone railhead which , by any engineering standard or any planning standard , is not a feasible operation, never was and never should have been considered.

The problem is when you try to give evidence on this subject. I have been at public inquiries in the past and have been under cross-examination. We were hopeful at the beginning when we started this process. First we tried to have a dialogue with HS2, which it cut short. It wasn’t interested in listening to what we had; we had an alternative much more feasible location to put a railhead. Setting that aside, when we went to the House of Commons and then to the House of Lords, it was all extremely rushed. We had a QC the first time we went and we were giving literally two weeks of evidence in the space of five hours on the first occasion. Most of that time is taken up by HS2’s legal counsel interrupting the evidence that we are giving .

U nfortunately the problem I have is that those Select Committees do not have access to independent experts, so the tendency is to believe w hat HS2 say s as if it is the gospel. I think that is not just our experience ; it is the experience of many others. I think the problem is the hybrid Bill. If you have a major infrastructure project of this magnitude for any other kind of major development, there is a process called a development consent order, which is managed by the P lanning I nspectorate , where technical professionals from both sides can make the case.

That doesn’t happen with a hybrid Bill. In effect, before you even get to petition or turn up in front of the Committee , it has had its Second Reading and it is already deemed to be approved, so the best that you will ever get is a bit of tinkering around the edges . A ny substantive changes HS2 is not interested in . Y ou just don’t get enough time to make a technical case and the people who are making the judgment don’t have the technical knowledge on which to make the judgment. It is a very frustrating process.

I have analysed HS2’s environmental impact assessment in great detail and although it is a staggering amount of paper and a huge amount of baseline information, which for phase 2 has cost over £500 million , as I understand it, there is no proper methodology for assessing any environmental topic and no proper assessment. The conclusion is already drawn before you even walk in the room and that is incredibly frustrating if you are an environmental professional, as I am.
Mr Gould, do you have any points to add to that?

Yes. Although those sound like strong words, the position is , I think , that Mr Parkin is being a little bit reticent. I do have major issues with the candour of HS2 officials. It is not going beyond the pale to say that it is almost deliberately misleading in terms of what they tell Select Committee members. I gave my railway evidence for most of the morning the first time that we went down the House of Commons Select Committee, chaired by James Duddridge , now Sir James Duddridge , and it seemed that the evidence that was put forward against me by HS2 in the afternoon was in part—it would not be too strong a word to say— fabricated during the lunch hour. That is the opinion that I have and I think that is probably where we stand.

We have tried to engage with the company many times. Had it been more open and honest with us and listened to us with our ideas for Aldersey’s Rough instead of the Stone railhead, we would have been working with it , if it had said, “ Y es, there are better ways of building this railway than our ideas . ” B ut no, it carried on irrespective of what evidence was put in front of it, trying to make a silk purse out of a sow’s ear. T hat was when I unfortunately lost my support for HS2 , because I could see that it was not in the public interest. It does not do what it says on the tin.

If I could make one point about the whole process, it is describe d as a quasi-public inquiry situation, so more time is need ed for giving evidence. The critical thing about the way that should work is that you should be examined in chief , if you have a representative such as a KC , and then you should be subject to potential cross-examination , and the same should go for the witnesses for HS2. We were not allowed at any point to cross-examine the HS2 witnesses and what we considered to be highly misleading evidence found its way into the special report. It is not a proper process.

We also believe that it is not the job of the advocates to be giving evidence. That is quite wrong. It is the job of the witnesses to give evidence. You can watch hours and hours and hours of HS2 proceedings of phase 2a and phase 2b and you will see the advocates effectively answering the questions for HS2. The witnesses make only occasional appearances. Remember the advocates don’t have to swear the oath; the rest of us do. That is a part of the process. It is very important that when statements are made there is an opportunity to cross-examine and that was never permitted . T hat is a big failing of the process, but the main thing is there needs to be greater involvement from technical specialists and it needs to be run by the Planning Inspectorate, in my opinion.

Q342 One final question about the unwinding of the process of phase 2. In particular , there have been concerns about radio silence from HS2 , and a lack of engagement with parish councils and their concerns about the length of time that it will take to unwind , all while costs continu e . What do you think about the unwinding of the phase 2 process now, those compounds and the handing back of land to landowners?

On phase 2a, unless you were down at the southern end at Lichfield, most of the works have been enabling works or environmental works, so there have been a lot of minor road closure s or temporary lights and we have quite a few compounds for gas main diversions — that kind of stuff. Since the announcement by the Prime Minister, there is not only no communication from HS2 — or minimal communication — to say, "We are still looking of the implications of the decision , " but there is no evidence of the removal of any of their paraphernalia from any of these sites. We are in touch with quite a lot of landowners and the landowners are pulling their hair out about this.

There is an issue about the compulsory purchase s . Some people who had been subject to compulsory purchase have receive d money ; some people have not. Their land has been compulsorily purchased without any payment. They cannot get access to some areas of their land and they are extremely inconvenienced. Some of these people are suicidal because of the way that they have been treated because it is just deplorable, yet there is still radio silence about that. There is still no effort on the ground to do anything to remove any of these things. T hat has to change. I think the decision has been made, the safeguarding needs to be lifted , and it needs to be lifted along the whole railway.

The NPR route, which uses part of phase 2b, is not a serious proposition to be able to deliver, so I think the safeguarding needs to be lifted, the blight needs to be removed from people's lives and HS2 needs to get on with it. It just seems to be dragging its feet. I don't know whether it is part of saying , "If we can wait long enough, somebody might change the decision after a general election , " but as far as the people in the area where we live are concerned , it need s to communicate, it need s to leave and it need s to remove all of its stuff soon.
Grahame, do you have any supplementar y questions ?

Q343 I have a couple of points, some of which were raised with us in our consultation with parish councils yesterday. Mr Parkin, you mentioned the use of the tilting of Pendolino trains and HS2’s decision not to utilise that. Could you elaborate a little bit on the implications ? This session is HS2 scrutiny — it is one of the six-monthly sessions that we do — but we are doing a broader inquiry about the lessons we can learn in how best to deliver nationally important strategic infrastructure, so your comments about the hybrid Bill procedure are very relevant. As someone who has served on the 2b h ybrid Bill Committee — that was from Crewe to Manchester Piccadilly — I understand exactly what you are saying and I believe the criticisms are legitimate.

As we have started this inquiry on strategic infrastructure schemes and what happens now with the appraisal system, it is interesting that you mention technical appraisals and people who are properly qualified to put forward the case for and against particular schemes , rather than leaving it to professional advocates and laypeople like me to make a judgment. I think there is merit in that.

W e received evidence from an academic—I think only yesterday—and he set out this “ how, why, when, who ” approach, which I thought was very interesting, particularly on HS2 and national rail way infrastructure. When we talk about Pendolino trains and maximum speeds, for example, when it was decided that the high-speed line from central London to Manchester should run at 330 kilometres per hour, that had major implications for the route, the type of trains , the capacity and interchangeability.

Do you have any particular thoughts on whether at the very outset it would have been a dreadful thing if the maximum speed of the trains was 250 kilometres per hour? It would still have been faster than the intercity trains and the time saving would have been marginal, but had that allowed the completion of the route, it would have been tremendously beneficial.
Can I ask for slightly shorter questions and answers, please?
Yes. I am sorry, Chair.
We have quite a lot to get through this afternoon . T hank you.

The first thing I would say is that this railway is overspecified . We had to have the shiniest, fastest railway ever built in the UK when it first came about. It was never about capacity with the original intention; it was about speed. Certainly the re are pressures on the railway, if you are running trains at a speed that is far greater and you have to go in straight lines, which is why there is no tilting technology. I agree that it would have been far better . I f you wanted to increase capacity — if that had been the objective from the first point — you would never have come up with this plan for a high-speed railway in its current form.

With phase 2, I think there is an opportunity to go back to what we need. We need to be able to take trains without being delayed and quite often that is just a question of having four tracks or electrification or better signalling or whatever. Take the Northern Powerhouse Rail example. What is the objective? The objective is to get from Liverpool to Manchester and Manchester to Leeds and Leeds to York, so you want to go in a straight line. You would not be able to get out of second or third gear in a high-speed train because there are only 40 miles between Liverpool Lime Street and Manchester Piccadilly, or even 30 miles if you go the route we suggest. It is crazy. It should have been down- specced .

It is too late for phase 1, but for phase—well, not phase 2 because it is not going to happen, but for NPR and all the other schemes that should be brought about, this is about getting from A to B. What passengers want is to be able to get on a train and go somewhere. The problem with HS2 is it just goes to Birmingham; it goes to Manchester. Trevor talked about the situation at Crewe. None of the Manchester-bound trains, HS2, stops at Crewe. If you withdraw the south Wales train and one of the northern trains, you will barely be able to get a train from Crewe to Manchester. It is ridiculous. It is the wrong plan. I know it is 14 years in, but it is not too late to change.
Might I add a little bit to that?
Quickly, please.

The Pendolino trains get from Handsacre Junction to Glasgow anywhere between 11 minutes and 13 minutes faster than the HS2 trains because they have tilt technology. Tilt technology does take more maintenance . It makes the trains heavier so they need more power, so the specification has to be higher, but you are saving on time. Because the project has been cancelled, it gives everybody the opportunity now to look at the specification, to look at everything that HS2 is providing and say, “Right, let’s draw a line under what we have done. What do we really need out of this? Let’s make the right decisions from now on. Do we need tilt technology? Do we need the trains to stop at the stations whe re the Pendolinos stop?" and so on instead of just ploughing on.
Greg, do you have any last questions?

Q344 One very brief one. If we can go back to the points, Mr Parkin, that you were making earlier about the way decisions are made on projects like this , it seems to me that inherent in the hybrid Bill process—and indeed, other shiny thing decisions that Governments make— is that you have a row about the concept and the real design doesn’t come until much later. I was struck this morning when we visited the gigantic waste of money just outside the window from this building where we are sitting right now, the Curzon Street construction. There was an admission at one point, “Oh well, we didn’t know the land conditions until we started digging . ” For someone in your position who has such expertise in environmental impact assessments, surely no infrastructure project should proceed where you don't even know the land conditions on which you will be building.

Yes. If you were building a nuclear power station or you were building an airport, you would be doing your ground investigation in advance of coming up with your proposals. Unfortunately, with HS2 the route was decided based on BGS plans, geological plans, a lot of which geology dates from a century ago and is only updated when somebody drills some boreholes.

The Stone railhead is a classic. The Stone railhead is in a location that is a disaster for ground conditions . People should have realised that when they looked at the BGS plans because I could see it b ut when they drilled some boreholes and found artesian water shooting up into the air, they had 30 metres of what is called head, glacial material, which could be running sand moving through to massive boulders. The engineering that would be required to put a railhead there is phenomenal, but they did not want to listen to, “There is an alternative halfway up a hill on good solid rock”.

You are right : it is essential that you understand what you are building on before you come up with a proposal . A ny other developer who doesn’t have a bottomless pit of money being provided by the taxpayer would have done that. If this was a private sector venture and you had to borrow money from the banks, you wouldn’t be able to say, “We want to build a railway, but we are not quite sure exactly where we are going and what we want to do with it and we don’t even know what the timetable will look like. Can we have £100 billion?” or maybe £150 billion, which is where we are with HS2.
Can I thank you both very much indeed for you r time this afternoon and the evidence you have given, which will add to our collective knowledge as part of our inquiry? Thank you very much.
Thank you for the invitation.
Thank you.

sessions.iT: EU Entry/Exit and the UK border

segs.tx: European Scrutiny Committee
Oral evidence: EU Entry/Exit and the UK border , HC 169
Wednesday 29 November 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 2 9 November 20 2 3 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sir William Cash (Chair); Richard Drax; Dame Andrea Jenkyns; Mr David Jones; Gavin Robinson; Greg Smith .
Questions 1 - 4 0
Witnesses
I : Luke Petherbridge , Director of Public Affairs, ABTA — The Travel Association; Phil Smith, UK Coach Manager, Confederation of Passenger Transport UK .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses : Luke Petherbridge and Phil Smith .

Q1 Good afternoon and thank you for appearing to give evidence today. In July, we heard from the P ort of Dover, G etlink and Euro s tar on the EU ’s soon to be introduced e ntry /exit s ystem . A s they facilitate juxtaposed border controls at their sites, they will feel the impact of e ntry /e xit acutely. T hey told us about their particular concerns and preparations regarding the introduction of the system. Did you watch that? I presume you did.

Toda y, we will look at how e ntry /e xit will impact the travel industry more generally, including passengers departing from the UK , from traditional non -juxtaposed ports , for the EU / S chengen a r e a. We are especially interested in the preparations that airlines and coach operators are making to ensure that travellers are aware of the upcoming changes and your views on your own and the Government’s responsibilities in this regard .

With the system now stated to be introduced late next year, we hope to hear further details on what it will entail. We appreciate, however, that this information is for the European Commission to provide and the UK Government to e licit. We will also ask about related systems , such as the EU’s ET IAS and the UK’s ETA , and we will ask for the thoughts of the travel industry on what seems like a proliferation of new digital border systems.

Our overriding concerns are , first, that the UK Government are providing the support and advocacy that your members require ahead of such a major change and , secondly, that next year does not roll around with the trave l ling public unaware of the new EU entry requirements that they are going to be facing.
B efore we get started , then, for those watching at home, would you mind briefly introducing yourselves?
Luke Petherbridge : My name is Luke Petherbridge . I am director of public affairs at ABTA —T he Travel Association.
I am Phil Smith. I am here on behalf of the Confederation of Passenger Transport. We represent around 500 coach operators across the UK . I am the UK coach manager in that organisation .

Q2 By the way , as we go through, we want to look at the practical side of this . In the coach industry, these are big coaches. How will you handl e that? C an people come out of the coaches ? Do you have some ingenious method of speeding things up that you have put forward to the G overnment and to others , which they are not taking notice of ? It seems to me quite extraordinary , with modern digital facilities , that it is taking so long. You might believe that is the case ; maybe you think there is no way around it . I wanted to introduce that as a thought.

I f you think you have something practical to say on that subject, feel free to say it . W e are hearing from a lot of colleagues that the mechanics of checking people out , really because of the nature of coach travel in particular , is probably the biggest problem . Is that right? Please do throw something out into the arena on that subject, if you feel you would like to do so , or if we have not asked th at question in the way you think it should be asked .

I am asking the first question. A s a Committee , we are experts in UK - EU affairs . O ur expertise does not , with some exceptions —I am looking to my right — stretch to travel and tourism . F or our benefit , w ould you briefly describe your respective industries, explaining those aspects that make them unique, which in a funny kind of way is what I was trying to refer to just now , and say why a fluid UK - EU border is important for you and your members ?

Luke Petherbridge : O ur members are UK travel businesses, primarily intermediaries . T hey are not always the carrier s themselves. There are some exceptions to that, but they will primarily be tour operators or travel agents that have purchased travel arrangements from other providers. T hey are not in charge of the airline , the rai l operator, ferry operator or whatever the case may be.

T his matters to us quite simply because about 77% of all outbound UK holidays — our members primarily sell outbound holidays , but they do also sell some domestic holidays — go to the European Union. I t is by far our largest outbound market . Therefore, we need to ensure that the flows between us and the European Union continue in a free fashion.

Q3 You have made t hat clear . To offer a thought on the theme I was putting forward before, why can people not be checked at an earlie r stage in the journey — i n other words , when they are going towards the port , rather than at the port ?

Luke Petherbridge : Yes, the fundamental reason for that is that it is written in regulation that the check has to occur at the border . I f there are checks prior to that, they have to be verified at the border. In reality, for coach travel , that means scanning the passports of each individual . E ven in the event that there was an app or something that allowed some of the information from passengers to be taken downstream , you would still need to take fingerprints at the border , because there is not the technology to do that.

Q4 Do you have any technology that will enable you to speed up that part of the process? You could do it from the depot from which the coach made its way to the border , though I know t here is always the problem of people im personating other people and all that kind of stuff . Is this something you have been giving a lot of thought to?
Luke Petherbridge : I suspect that the industry’s solution — Phil might expand on this — would be to take this away from the border and do it in a mobile fashion .
Q5 Will you deal with this later ?

Yes. It is interesting that you should raise this , Sir William. W e were told in one of the HM Government workshops run by the Home Office that it would be a possible option for a frontier official to come on board the coach and use a tablet or an iPad to scan passenger s’ faces . I believe that has since been dismissed because of the angle that the device would have to be held at in order to take an accurate image . T he issue about space on board vehicle s for officials to move back and forth was also cited as a difficulty.
Q6 T hat is assuming they are sitting there in the coach for this purpose. If they somehow did it as they went into the coach , they could be static .

I will come to that as well. Passport scanning technology is already available . T wo of the ferry operators are using it for their own internal process of embarkation , when passengers leave the UK on coaches through the narrow straits . F or the two ferry operators concerned, that save s a great deal of time when the coach arrives at the f rontier on the quay side at Dover Eastern Doc k s.

A s a layman and not a technological expert, I would have thought that between the European Union and the UK Government it might be possible to develop some form of application to process at least a part of the EES process. I accept it might not solve the issue of fingerprints. I believe it is written into the regulation that , despite the pass enger having to pass through one of these kiosks to have their passport read biometrically and to have their fingerprints taken , et cetera , t hey still have to present to an EU state —
Q7 No one took my fingerprint yesterday when I came back from Madrid . You go through a visual recognition system. T hey do not ask you to put your finger on a bit of blue ink.

Luke Petherbridge : It is part of the new system that is coming in . W ith the EES, finger prints will be part of the biometric checks that are required. That is not in place yet. It is due to co me in at the back end of next year .
Q8 I am thinking out of the box , or in the box , really. I cannot understand why there is not a simple solution to this . Is it a frustration for the people on the coaches and so on ?

We would be very pleased if a proportion of the EES process could be conducted away from the bo rder itself . G iven the tech app developments that have tak en place at two of the ferry operators — the third one is probably working on something as well — some adaptation of that by the EU, because it is an EU scheme at the end of the day, ought to be possible to remove at least some of the more routine bits of EES, such as the sca nning of the passport .

We are reliabl y informed that each initial transaction through one of the kiosks will take up to 1.25 minutes , because everything has to be downloaded . T he person is then clear for the next three years . If they get a new passport or the three years expires , the next time they go through , it all has to be done again. I t is going to be a rolling ball , inasmuch as the re will always be people with new passports; there will always be people who have not been before . A nything that can be done to take some of this process away from the physical border would be very welcom e .

Q9 C ontinuing with the theme of the Chairman’s questions , it is clear that the fingerprint and photograph position is going to be difficult . C an you take us through some of the other impacts the entry/exit system is going to have , particularly on your sector, Mr Smith , and on the wider travel sector , Mr Petherbridge ?

In terms of coaches , currently everybody has to get off the vehicle and have their passport ink - stamp ed. D epending on the physical ability of the people on board the vehicle, that can sometimes be a quicker or slower process .

With EES , that time is going to be increased significantly , because everybody is going to have to tro o p through a kiosk. The re will be the inevitable issues about some people not realising what they have to do once they get into it , because it will be the first time they have done it. Even if it is not the first time , they will still struggle . There will be a further queue to present themselves to the f rontier officials so they can have their passport scanned. It will slow the whole process down.

The pivotal issue for us will be how many kiosks are going to be physically present at Dover Eastern Docks. For us, that is the location that really holds the key to the future of international coach travel post EES. If we get this wrong, I can see international coach travel becoming very difficult to maintain on a consistent basis in volume , because s o much of the traffic go es through Dover.
Q10 What does your modelling show to be the expected delays for a coach when the passengers in all 52 seats or whatever are fresh to the system?

It is a good question. It really depends on the number of kiosks that are installed . For example, if there are six kiosks, it could take 12 to 15 minutes to get one coachload or 50 passengers through . If there are fewer, i t is going to take longer.

We see spikes in coach traffic through the narrow straits at certain times of the year, such as post Christmas when the schools go skiing and then again at Easter . T he two main spring and summer school holidays create additional peaks as well. J ust to give you an example , we believe around 70 , 000 coaches a year go through Dover and the Eurotunnel altogether . I t is about 3 million passengers. T hat is not evenly spread. If you went down there today , you would probably only see one or two coaches .

A s we know from past events and the media coverage they attract when things slow down , it does not take a great deal of disruption to the pattern of processing for difficulties to arise , with all the result ant problems in the town of Dover and the impact it has on the people who live there who have to go about their normal business.

Q11 Just before I bring Mr Pe th erbridge in, there are clearly other borders that coaches cross . Where in the world offers the best solution for this? Is it the United States to Canada or the United States to Mexico? The s e ar e countries that are pretty well renowned for having secure borders.

It is difficult to find an example . It might be worthy of further investigation to look at USA - Mexico , but it is not really a like-for-like comparison. The narrow straits are very unique because of the coach volume. I am sure coaches go through the US bo rder into Mexico and Canada, but this concept of coaches going across into the EU has been developed over 70 years . It is a very popular means of travelling internationally , particularly for school groups and older people who do not like to fly. I t is very eco - friendly. As an industry we distribute about five times less carbon than a journey by air . I t would be a real shame if what is really an administrative challenge de stabilised and ultimately destroyed the international coach travel market.
It was not a particular challenge before we regained our sovereignty either.
Indeed, ye s .

Luke Petherbridge : I will pick up on what Phil was saying . It is about volume and velocity. If we look at the juxtaposed borders, particularly at Dover but also for the Eurostar, there is not the capacity to have large numbers of people dwelling at those border checks. It is the juxtaposed nature of the border checks that makes them unique. As Phil said, I am not sure there is an international comparison that quite works because of th e juxtaposed nature of the border.

F or us, the primary concern around the entry/exit scheme is pinch points . Y es, it is about the juxtaposed borders in particular, but picking up on what Phil said about seasonality , this is true of all travel and tourism . We should not dismiss the risk of disruption in aviation, particularly at small regional European airports or those that have very large volumes of UK travellers at specific times , whether that be the summer peak , during half-term holidays in October and February or , indeed, over Easter.

When we look at the specific sectors that we have concerns about within our membership —Phil touched on this a couple of times — school travel in particular does have a reliance on short strait s travel , particularly through Dover at the moment. Eurotunnel has reduced its capacity for coach travel, which has pushed more coaches into Dover. B ack at Easter we saw what happen s when full border checks are enforced . There were significant delays .

O ur members in the school travel sector have very long lead - in times. That is very important. They have 12 - to - 18 - month lead - in times and booking windows for schools who book these trips. If you have significant delays one year, it knocks on over more than one season. You are then looking at dissuading t ravel l ers in future years , who look at it and think , “ I cannot have kids from this school sat at the border for hours on end . ” We saw delays of 11 to 15 hours over the Easter period. There are safeguarding concerns when children and other vulnerable groups of travellers are on those coaches .
Q12 You mentioned emissions. I do not know enough about this to know whether you are into electrical power systems in coaches. Is that on the agenda at all?
I t is on the agenda , as is potentially hydrogen . I could probably spend the whole afternoon telling you about where that is going.
I j ust wanted to know that , because you did mention e missions. An electric- operated system would be a great improvement.

I would say one other thing about international coach travel at the moment and zero - emission vehicles . T he range s available from electric vehicles specifically are still quite challenging , in terms of some of the long distances that these vehicles have to travel across Europe once they have crossed the border.
It is the p erfect time to say that Wrightbus in Northern Ireland do es a great range of battery -powered electric vehicles.
It is working on a zero-emissions vehicle.
Q13 Thank you, Chair , for that . There are no advertisements from Parliament , and I have no interest to declare.

Gentlemen, we heard back in July from John Keefe at Getlink . He talked about not only the severe delays associated with the entry/exit scheme , but the aspiration that the information would be available by October . We are at the back end of November. Do you have final specifications?

No, in a word. We were informed at the end of last week by P ort of Dover that the EU has still not made clear the type of spec that it need s to follow in terms of the kiosks. T here is an immediate obstacle in terms of planning installation . T he EU ha s not as yet confirm ed exactly what is required.
Q14 Are you doing all of your engagement —I will ask Mr Smith first — through Dover ? Is that the primary engagement , or are you having direct engagement yourselves ?

It is a significant partner in terms of engagement , but I have to say that, in terms of operational communications, the Home Office has been running readiness workshops for this . I have been to about three of them . They have been very useful . They are in the same position ; t hey are relian t on the information they can extract from their colleagues in the EC.

Q15 ABTA is in exactly the same position . D o you have your own direct engagement? More importantly, we were told in July that the final specification would be available in October. Do you have any sense today of when the final specification will be available?

Luke Petherbridge : My understanding on the specification is no different to Phil’s . We are still waiting for the final details . That impacts not just the ports and operators at the juxtaposed borders but everybody, including the airlines, which will need to put systems changes in place to facilitate these as well. T hat is a very significant challenge for the entire travel industry .

I n terms of our engagement , w e engage politically directly, but when it comes to the operational matters , we rely on the carrier associations, people like Phil , Dover and those that are going to be operationally impacted . As I mentioned earlier, our members are primarily intermediaries . They are one step back ; they are not operating the ferries or airlines themselves.

Q16 K nowing what the final specification is w ould allow you and us to discern what roll - out periods, trial periods and flex ibilities there may be with in this. In all of the engagement either of you have had up until now, do you have any sense of where those considerations may land , albeit not in a final form, or do you see this as a moving feast , where there will be change s in each of those parameters?

There are two points here. First, it was made pretty clear to us a few months ago that it is unlikely this will happen before the Paris Olympics next summer. T he consistent theme has been October 20 24.

More recentl y , there has been some suggestion that there might be trials, but it has been very loose, I have to say. A trial would be very sensible. I do not know how you would do it. Every 10 th coach going through could be subject to a trial , j ust thinking off the top of my head . Again, it seems to be very unclear whether this will definitely happen in October . I f so, where will the vehicles go in Dover to be processed ? W ill the P ort of Dover have all the necessary information to move this project forward before autumn 20 24?
Q17 Do you agree with that?
Luke Petherbridge : The latest information from Frontex is that it will be late 20 24 for entry/exit checks . ETIAS, which is due to come on six months later, would then be mid -20 25 .

Q18 At this stage, h ave you crystallised in your mind what sort of lead-in period you would require , if this is to go live ? W hat is the industry saying ? Do you need a trial period of six months, eight months or nine months ?

Luke Petherbridge : O ur members have expressed concern with any implementation period below 12 months . We have a secondary concern, which is that six months after the entry/exit s ystem scheme is switched on , we will also have ETIAS . T hat window of six months is also a concern for the industry. It would prefer a longer lead - in time between the two systems.

Port of Dover is certainly on record as saying that it would have liked 18 months. It was saying , “W e need specifications now ” back in July. A s we have said, we still do not have that specification yet.

I did not completely hear you r question, but it is fair to say that, in terms of the lead-in for EES, yes, trials would be good . S econdly, as soon as we know exactly what is required of our operator members and our passengers, we can start working out ways of making coach passengers and users aware of the changes , and getting everybody into the mindset of what will happen, how it will happen and where it will happen on arrival at the f rontier. At the moment, we cannot tell anybody anything because everything is so fluid.
Q19 G ood afternoon. Just for the viewers and for me , if I am a passenger on a bus, what bio metric information would the border guards need e xactly ? You would have to show your passport.
Yes.
What else?

A gain, we have not seen a practical demonstration , but fingerprint taking is involved . I am making an assumption , but presumably, as well as the ir passport going into the sca nn er at the booth for it to be re a d and for all the personal data to be downloaded into the EU’s database, a passenger will have to put the ir hand in as well , so it can take the ir fingerprints .
It will happen at the same time as they take your photograph .
Indeed, yes.
Q20 It will be rather like the things you go through now at airports . You put your passport in , and it takes a photograph of you. It identifies you and then through you go.

Luke Petherbridge : It is a very similar system to the US ESTA. Y ou are looking at facial recognition, biographical information from your passport and your fingerprint . It uses your fingerprint because that is something that belongs to you and is completely immutable.

Q21 Will it be practical? Let us say you are a bus passenger . To do all that, 50 people have to get off the bus into a t erminal where there are lots of check-in points , you hope . T he driver go es through his or her own little checkpoint. T he cars keep going . You go through and re join your bus. Is that the sort of thing that will happen?
That i s effectively what will happen . That is kind of what happens now, but it is the additional time that these extra requirements will take to process.

R eturning to the C hair ’s earlier point about pre - validation, if we could get to a position where the passport is sca nn ed before somebody even leaves home , for example, or the driver has the ability to sca n the passport by way of an app , it could save a great deal of time at the f rontier . I t may then just be a case of facial recognition , which is somebody staring at a camera , and putting their hand in the scanner to get the ir fingerprints . That would potentially take out about 50% of the time of the process.

Q22 Mr Smith, you are saying that t he impact on a family or person from a non-Schengen area country going through border control to enter the EU or S c h engen area from the UK is very hard to gauge right now. You cannot answer the question. Is that fair ? It will certainly go up .

Yes, it will increase. We were given an estimate by one of the Home Office workshops . T hey forecasted that the initial transaction would be 1.25 minutes per person. That assum es that they do not make mistakes during the induction process.
Q23 For a bus load of 50 people, that is nearly an hour .
Yes. Again, it depends how many booths you have.
Yes, and how many buses you have .
Yes. On M aundy Thursday there could be 250 coaches.
Q24 It sounds like there is the potential for a nightmare.
Luke Petherbridge : Yes. T hat is where you get into the capacity issues and the infrastructure at the port . T here simply is not the s pace to store that number of coaches.
Q25 You are not going to have 50 border guards , are you? These are French border guards.

T o be fair, we have been seeing at peak time six and seven border guards on the existing system . O ne of the issues in the spring was that there were not enough frontier supervisors . B etween them , Port of Dover and the French authorities address ed that. W e have largely seen the delays disappear since th en, but EES brings a whole new set of challenges into the mix.

Q26 For those who have given th eir biometric data, do you have any idea how long it will take them to go through within the three-year period? Will it be quicker? Will they say , “You can just keep going ” ?
No, we have not been given an exact time amount, but we are assured it will be significantly quicker the second time a round .
Luke Petherbridge : I t is quicker once the initial registration has taken place.

Q27 B ased on the period of three years , on a year -by-year basis , how many people who travel with your members will be repeat travellers and how many will need to register for EES for the first time ? Many bus travellers travel quite frequently . It is almost an annual event, is it not?

T here will be a demographic split . When a lot of the school groups are going through, you will find that they will be first - time rs. W ith the tourists, who are predominantly people of a more mature demographic who tend to be regular travellers , other than issues like mobility and things that sometimes happen with older people , y ou might find that after the initial trip through the border , the subsequent trips become a bit quicker because they do it so often.

We have to bear in mind that the times we have seen these issues with processing people at the border have been when the schools are on the move. M y forecast is that a lot of those will be first - time rs. For example, we would hope that , when this system comes in, it will be embedded in time for when the ski se ason starts, which is when a lot of school groups travel to the continent . We would not want it to come in at the start of that.

Luke Petherbridge : T hat is a really important point. That switch ‑ on point and how this is time d with the peak periods for travel will be really important for the initial implementation of the scheme . W e are going to have a b ulge of first-time travellers initially because they have never had to do this before.
Q28 The moral of the stor y is : d o not be on that first bus .

Luke Petherbridge : The message we would give is : t urn it on at the correct time . D o not turn it on at peak travel period s . T hat applies to both regimes, the entry/exit scheme and ETIAS. Avoid turning them on at peak periods .

Q29 Just finally, you have six to 10 or how ever many buses in a queue waiting to get through . T here are six border guards . Y ou have 50 people in each bus . Maths was not my strong point. You are looking at several hours for that last bus load to get through.
Again, I would refer you to my earlier answer regarding the number of kiosks , because the critical thing here is how many kiosks are actually available .
Q30 These are French-manned.
On this side, at Dover, yes.
These are French people who are on the kiosks.
Luke Petherbridge : At the juxtaposed borders, yes.
Q31 I am just wondering whether they are going to be willing to put a lot of checkpoints on this side.

Hang on. T here are two things here. The first issue is the kiosk s , which will be standing infrastructure . It is my understanding that P ort of Dover will be responsible for install ing and providing th ose. I t will really depend on how much money for investment it has available and , crucially, how much space it has to install w hat is perceived to be the right number of booths .

Frontier staff is a French issue. In fairness, after we ha d the initial problems in the spring, there appear to have been fewer issues with the number of French border officials in situ at the juxtaposed border since. It would be my view that , post EES, because the bo rder guards still have to supervise all this and sca n passports, if it is busy , there will be six or seven of them with six or seven sca nn ers to make sure that the flow of people coming through the kiosks happens in an efficient way.
I have encroached slightly on the next question, so I am going to hand back.

Q32 Dame Andrea Jenkyns : We h ear d in July—t his is pre my time ; i t is my first time today — that for juxtaposed border controls in the UK , there was limited physical space, which poses an issue in preparing the infrastructure required. Are certain types of traveller s more likely to be impacted by the EES, especially when they primarily travel by coach or ferry, for example? I know you have mentioned children going on school trips.

Luke Petherbridge : At the juxtaposed borders, the primary concern is going to be coach passengers . There are some large demographics , such as school children and, as Phil mentioned , the elderly . Those would be the two demographic groups. That is the concern at the juxtaposed borders .

As you suggested in the question — it was covered in July— there are significant capacity problems at both Dover , where there simply is not the space to increase the checks around the port , and the Eurostar terminal . A nyone who has been through St Pancras will realise that it is a very busy international station.
Q33 Dame Andrea Jenkyns : Will people be dissuaded from travelling in the future ?
Luke Petherbridge : This is why we need both the Governments on the other side of the c hannel in the European Union and the UK Government to increase the political prioritisation this is given.
Q34 Dame Andrea Jenkyns : Both sides need to get their acts together , do they not?
Luke Petherbridge : We need solutions that do not require all these checks to occur at the border . I f they do, you are looking at serious slowdowns . Yes, that would then dissuad e people .

I would reiterate what I have said already about having as much pre-departure processing as possible. I f there w ere an option for coach drivers to sca n passports en route to the c hannel port , the amount of time it would take the passengers to go through the kiosks and present themselves to the frontier official would be significantly reduced.

During the whole EU exit process , t here has always been lots of talk about making the best use of the technologic al advances that have been made in the last 10 years or so . T his is a classic example of where technology could go a long way to solving this issue.

Q35 Yes, I c ompletely agree. As we know, the EU is planning to introduce the European travel information and authorisation system , which is an additional travel credential . T he UK has just introduced the electronic travel authorisation system. It is a real mouthful .

Is there a concern in the travel industry that the proliferation of new systems will dissuade people from travelling ? A re you aware of any co - ordination between the UK Government and the European Commission on the introduction of these new systems ?

In terms of ET A , that is relatively straightforward . W e are generally satisfied that HM Government are taking a measured and cautious approach to its introduction. It is an issue for our members that are involved in the inbound tourist market . P eople who are coming into the UK have to have one of these . Ultimately, it will be for every country whose citizens do not require visa s . It is being done in such a way that they can iron out any issues that arise. So far I am not aware of any coach operators having any difficulties with it. W e are reasonably relaxed about ETA .

With the other one — I also have to get the initials in the right order — ETIAS , which is the EU version of ETA , has been subsumed a bit by the juggernaut , no pun intended , of EES . M y understanding is that it is going to cost €7. P eople technically will have to apply two working days before travel . That is fine ; they can do it at home. Even if they do not do it at home, it is potentially achievable to apply when you are on the coach . A s long as you are not an international criminal of some description or wanted in a particular country, you should be able to get a successful application.
We ought to be challenging them when they come over to us .

I agree with Luke’s point that we have to be cognisant of it . A t the end of the day, if it was just ETIAS that was coming down the track, we would be relatively comfortable about how we explained that to our passengers , making sure that it went out in marketing material and publicity . “For next summer , you have to do this ” . It does not have the time constraints that EES imposes.

Luke Petherbridge : I would primarily agree with that assessment. ETIAS is very similar to the US ESTA and the Canadian eTA . We have two concerns around ETIAS . One is consumer awareness . As we saw with the passport validity problems post Brexit , this can catch travellers out . W e do need to ensure as an industry —and Government also have a role in this — that UK travellers are aware of it before they travel for the first time o nce the system is turned on.

The other aspect of ETIAS where we would have a slight concern is around fraud . That is essentially about online scams and people offering to sell ETIAS to UK t ravel l ers when the system is not live yet. If you go online now and search for “ ETIAS ”, you can be sold ETIAS online although it does not exist. Again, there is a role for the Government to play around consumer awareness.
Q36 Greg Smith : My question is for Mr Petherbridge . I would like to talk about air travel. Do you represent any airlines?
Luke Petherbridge : W e have airline - owning tour operators , such as Jet2 , T UI , E asyJet and Virgin Atlantic.

Q37 Greg Smith : We have had evidence — in fact , you have touched on this already — that United Kingdom airports are less likely to be affected by E ES because there are no juxtaposed controls. However, British travellers will be travelling into European airports in the Schengen area. How big of an issue will EES be for British passengers flying into the Schengen area?

Luke Petherbridge : Again, there might be a pinch - point issue w hen it is first turned on, particularly if that is done at periods where there are large volumes . This may cause queues at smaller regional airports where they do not have the physical infrastructure to cope with large volumes o f travellers or airports where there are very large volumes of UK travellers arriving in Europe . I would not expect those queues to be anywhere near the length we see at the juxtaposed borders because airports are more used to dealing with these issues , but, yes, we do have some concerns around initial disruption and initial queues .

Q38 Greg Smith : You mentioned the smaller regional airports . A number of British and Irish airlines , Ryan air in particular , fly to these so-called secondary airports, which I would have thought were less able to cope with the pressure of EES. I t would be a pretty significant capital investment for those airports. Are they going to be able to discharge that?

Luke Petherbridge : I suspect they will, but it will require the Government in destination to be alert to this problem coming. S ome airports in Europe have already adopt ed measures to help the flow of UK travellers . For example, in s ome Portuguese and Spanish airports where there are large numbers of UK travellers, there are already additional border checks . They will allow a minimal check and then verification by a border guard. Y ou already see some attempts to smooth the border flows . I suspect you will see that in destination s with large volumes of UK t ravel l ers.

Q39 Gentlemen, we have talked about specifications and how much preparation and planning you can do with the lack of specifics you have at this stage. K nowing that there will be a process and knowing that your members are the ones that will be receiving the ire of the public , s hould it prove problematic, do you have a moral obligation or a responsibility to indicate in advance what is required and that there may be disruption? Do you have plans in place with your partners or members as to how that may be rolled out? I f you do , can you share those with us?

Luke Petherbridge : Yes, ABTA has quite a well-known consumer brand . W e absolutely see it as part of our role to inform customers about changes to travel. We are looking at putting up information on our website for consumers to make them as aware as we can at this point that these systems are coming . I ndeed , for the UK ETA we already have some advice for inbound travellers as well . We will be doing that from a UK travel industry perspective.

Where I would slightly push back is that w e do not know the specs ; w e do not know exactly what is required yet ; w e do not know the date this is coming into entry , so it is difficult. We cannot give much information at this point , but w e absolutely see a role for industry , as well as Government , in getting those messages across.
Q40 That point about the Government is really important . Have you had discussions with them about making t ravel l ers aware of the new requirements?

Luke Petherbridge : Yes, we have very strong relationships with the Foreign Office and the Department for Transport. We are making these points to them. In fairness, we do not have a switch - on date yet , so t here is not an ability to do that, but we will continue to make that case.

T hat is really helpful and very interesting . It has given us a new dimension of your industry to look at. I was in Madrid airport yesterday. I was surprised at how few people there were around. It s truck me as very odd . I could not quite understand why. That is not really your problem , is it?

It is strange that you say that . I was in London yesterday . W hen I travelled home to the n orth ‑ west , the train was quiet and Euston was quiet , and I thought c entral London was quiet given that it was a weekday in November. I do not know .
There might be some other reason . A nyway, thank you very much for coming . I t has been very interesting and informative.

sessions.iT: Pre-appointment Hearing: Chair of the Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL)
sessions.w: Douglas Chalmers (Committee on Standards in Public Life)

segs.tx: Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Pre-appointment Hearing: Chair of the Committee on Standards in Public life, HC 243
Wednesday 29 November 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 29 November 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Mr William Wragg (Chair); Ronnie Cowan; Jo Gideon; John McDonnell; Damien Moore; Tom Randall; Lloyd Russell-Moyle.
Questions 1 - 29
Witness
I : Douglas Chalmers, the Government’s preferred candidate, Chair of the Committee on Standards in Public Life.
Examination of witness
Witness: Douglas Chalmers .

Q1 Good afternoon and welcome to the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee. Today the Committee is holding a pre-appointment hearing for the Government’s preferred candidate for the role of Chair of the Committee on Standards in Public Life, Mr Douglas Chalmers.

The committee was established by John Major in 1994 to advise Prime Ministers on ethical standards in public life , and continues to be a cornerstone of the framework governing the behaviour of those in public life. The Committee would like to take this opportunity to express our thanks to the previous chair of the committee, Lord Evans, for his hard work and dedication in the role , and to wish him well for the future.
Good afternoon, Mr Chalmers. Please introduce yourself for the record .
Douglas McKenzie Chalmers, currently Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

Q2 Thank you very much indeed. The first question comes from me. You have confirmed, Mr Chalmers, that you were encouraged to apply for the role by the Cabinet Office. Who specifically made that approach?

I will take a step back a little bit. I think I was entering my third year in the college , and many ha d advised me that around that time I should look for a second string — something to take me outside the college bubble , so that I can keep creativity and bring something else to the college community. I had not started looking actively at that stage.

I received a pretty anodyne , staff-level email from the Cabinet Office that had some numbers on it. That brought the committee to my attention. I was aware of the committee from my time in Whitehall before , and of the Nolan principles . I started to look a bit further. I saw the advert in things like LinkedIn. I then spoke to a number of others , such as the secretariat , to confirm that the two appointments might work together. Then I decided that this was something I care d deeply about , and decided to volunteer , and I entered the application process.
Q3 Were you given any indication as to why you particularly were encouraged to apply for that role?

I don’t know for sure , but I think, as you will have seen , there was an extension to the pull to get candidates in at that point . I believe that it was Jeremy Quin in the Cabinet Office, who I had worked alongside in the Ministry of Defence — not in the same area , but he was aware of me — and he was the Minister for the Cabinet Office, I think, at that stage. I am guessing that he put my hat in the ring when they were looking for people to email.
Q4 Other than those you have mentioned, was there anybody else in G overnment who you spoke with before applying?
Not before applying.

Q5 As you said in your introduction, you are currently Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, having previously spent your career in the British Army. What experience have you had of standards in public life and of the Nolan principles?

I will start with the Nolan principles. As I mentioned, I was aware of them , because I had a sabbatical year in which I d id an M p hil , and my thesis topic was on the problems of co-ordinating Government Departments. In the process of that research, I came across the Nolan principles and the committee. It resonated because my research took place at the time when the Army was reviewing its values and standards — in about 2007, 2008. That is what brought me to it.

As I started to move through my career and worked more with civil servants, the awareness of the Nolan principles in particular struck m ore . There was that alignment. For example, there are values of selflessness and integrity in both sets of values and standards. I was very fortunate to be part of a national leaders cohort that went through the National Leadership Centre . T hat allowed me to have a better look at those principles , and the committee’s work as it applies to other parts of public life , in the main . That is how I became aware of the values and principles of public life.

On my own understanding of them, as I mentioned, I had 37 years in the services , and the importance of values and standards has been taught to me from the beginning. As I have gone through my service, particularly after they were refreshed in about 2008, I found them really helpful . I would write them down at the front of my notebooks. Particularly in some pretty turbulent and chaotic times, I found them really helpful to refer back to , mainly because they allowed me to attain perspective ; they pull ed me out of the moment . Also, setting standards around them, and talking about them regularly, allowed me to set a good framework for empower ing commanders in other units that were working with me.

All of that is on top of what I passionately believe, which is that the consistent application of values and standards is the bedrock of trust and confidence. For any unit I have been in, that is absolutely critical if innovation and initiative is to be allowed to go further forward.

That is my military service. I am now obviously in a very different world , but I have found that the need for values and standards, among students and academics, still remains very strong.
