segs.tx: Communications and Digital Select Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Large language models
Tuesday 2 8 November 2023
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Stowell of Beeston (The Chair); Baroness Featherstone; Lord Foster of Bath; Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie; Lord Griffiths of Burry Port; Lord Hall of Birkenhead; Baroness Harding of Winscombe; Baroness Healy of Primrose Hill; Lord Kamall; The Lord Bishop of Leeds; Lord Lipsey; Lord Young of Norwood Green .
Evidence Session No. 1 2 Heard in Public Questions 112 – 129
Witness
I : Professor Dame Angela McLean DBE FRS, Government Chief Scientific Adviser, Government Office for Science .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
This is a corrected transcript of evidence taken in public and webcast on www.parliamentlive.tv .
Examination of witness
Professor Dame Angela McLean .

Q112 This is the Communications and Digital Committee. We are continuing our inquiry into large language models. This is our final public hearing. We have two witnesses today. The first is Professor Dame Angela McLean, the Government’s Chief Scientific Adviser. Later, we will be joined by Viscount Camrose, the Minister responsible for AI. Clearly, with Dame Angela, we are looking to ask questions of the leading expert advising the Government on the various aspects of large language models , on the Government’s proposed policy and approach to it , and on the way in which they intend to take this whole area forward. We will be talking to the Minister later about the policy choices and decisions that the Government are making. Let us get going straightaway . I turn to Lord Kamall to kick us off with the first question .

Q113 T hank you, Dame Angela, for appearing before us today. I want to start by talking about some conversations that I have had with some of my friends who live in European Union countries , who, w hen they look at technology, often feel that the precautionary principle is given more consideration than the innovation principle. In looking at the UK’s emerging policy on large language models and AI more generally, we have heard from witnesses that the UK’s policy seems to have pivoted away from innovation and is now heavily focused on risk. Do you agree with that comment? Do es there need to be a greater focus on innovation , or have we got the balance right?

I can see where that comment comes from , because we—certainly the bit of government that I sit in—spent so much of the summer preparing for, running and, in the case of some of us, attending this thing called the AI Safety Summit. As part of that summit , the Government announced the setting up of this thing called the AI Safety Institute. Let me say that my colleagues in DSIT and the Foreign Office did a terrific job; they ran a summit that we can all be proud of.

However, I do not think that show s that we have stopped paying attention to other things. Of course, you are right , and w e need to keep three things in balance : short-term safety worries, by which I mean safety issues like bias and misinformation and disinformation, all of which we live with already; longer-term safety issues, including the sorts of things that were discussed more at the safety summit and have been discussed rather widely over the past 12 months; and the massive opportunities. There is plenty of focus , and plenty of us in government are very keen to keep those three things in balance.

Q114 Thank you for that. When you think about the UK’s role in the world and in new technologies—AI, large language models, et cetera—what do you think is needed when you look at the current landscape of the UK for us to compete internationally? I am thinking of things such as advanced computing facilities. Wh at do you see from your perspective? What do you think we should be doing more of and who should be doing it ? Should it be the Government, the private sector or others?

First, I see more compute; I think there is more compute on the way. We are already in a very good position i n having well-curated data pertinent to the questions in hand . That is an incredibly important asset and one that we need to make sure we make good use of.

What else? Good and wise regulation. That reminds me: we have a whole thing called the science and technology framework, which I have brought with me. It was written by my predecessor, Patrick Vallance, so I can laud it. It is all about exactly this set of questions. If you have a big science and technology advance, what do you do so that you can use it to drive prosperity, security , terrific jobs—all the things you want for your country? I will not go on about it for too long , but if you do not have a copy, take one of my cards . It will take you to where the framework is on the internet. It is 30 sides long and is about what we used to call the 10 big things. It is a great long list of all the things you need to do in order to drive commercial and public sector advances when you have an exciting new technology at your fingertips.
When you look at those 10 things—I admit that I have not looked at them yet— is anything missing, or potentially missing, in order for the UK to play a major role in this?

It is always skills—at least, skills is the first one. The whole point of the framework is that it says, “It is never just one thing”. W e have sometimes struggled to generate wealth from the brilliant inventions we make because of systems failure. There are lots of things that we do not get quite right. Nevertheless, I would go back to my immediate answer: with th e very rapid advance in platform technology—a technology that you can use for lots of things— we all, not just children, need to up our skills.
When you talk about skills, is that domestic plus immigration?
It is about making sure that our kids are properly skilled, that we reskill , and that we are a tremendously attractive place for the most able people in the world to come and work.

I know f rom speaking to my eldest son—he is 22—that a lot of his friends have done different degrees. Many of them are excited by AI and want to go into data science , but most of the jobs advertised are looking not for entry-level graduates in STEM but for people who have some experience. How do we tackle that gap?

That is a really interesting question. We used to talk about this a lot, actually . I used to work in the MoD and we used to talk about this being a potential way for it to grow its own skills resource and contribute to the country’s skills resource. Basically, we as government need to accept that we need to get a load of people in and train them up in doing this stuff, and that many of them will leave. That is okay , actually, because we need a country that is awash with this set of skills —it is not that expensive —and s ome of them will s t ay ; we have fantastic questions in government , and w e need to set things up so that government is a marvellous place to work if you are skilled at data science. A s I mentioned earlier, we have rich data assets , and that is rare if you are a data scientist asking, “Can I get at the data that will let me answer the question I want to answer?”

It is not just us. We need to ask industry to play a role in imparting the skills that are needed. T here is a whole range of skills. We do not need everybody to be able to write brilliant new algorithms. W e need people to learn about this new skill called prompting and to get really good at that. For me, the most interesting question concerns talking to a person with a problem and thinking about how to turn it into an issue where I can use data science and AI to help.

Can I push you a bit on that data skills gap? Lots of young people want to get into it , but do not have experience when all the jobs ask for experience. You are saying that g overnment should step up there, I suspect. How do you convince government and the private sector , because they do not like paying for training and they are losing people?

That is a great question. The Government take in a lot of graduates. In my own bit of government, we have a new graduate scheme, which is a terrific way for us to access very skilled and able people. We lay on training specifically for them. As I am sure you know, the fast stream is our premier entry route into the Civil Service. I honestly think that we should be expanding all those things and acknowledging that many of those people will leave. O ne of the four things that I have always said in my post is that we clearly need a more scientific Civil Service.

Q115 Generally, from a government perspective, there is lots of public and government data out there. How do we make sure that as much of that data as possible is available to large language models for training?

That is a great question. I know we have a thing called the Open Data Institute, which was established by Mike’s colleague and mine, Nigel Shadbolt, and by Tim Berners-Lee. I am pretty sure that that was set up to help with that. I know that people inside DSIT are working right now on making sure that , at the same time as making the data available, we value it properly. Some of our data assets are extraordinarily valuable , and we need to make sure that we do not underprice them when other people come along and do fantastic things with them.
There are obviously some concerns about sharing data, such as health data. How do you address those concerns ?

I would refer my health colleagues to specialist advice. The Council for Science and Technology , which is the Prime Minister’s group of science advisers, prepared advice on precisely this question about exploiting public data. That has now become a strand of work inside DSIT to make sure that it is done properly.
Thank you. If you have any further thoughts, please send them to our committee staff.
Q116 My colleagues are probably not as ignorant as I am, but what is prompting?

Prompting is asking questions. You are sat there with your large language model and you ask it a question. I might say to it , “Where was Angela McLean born?” and it will give me the wrong answer, which is not tremendously interesting. There is a skill to how you ask questions that can be learned so that you get more useful answers out of it. You would have heard of the version of large language models that you interact with directly, such as ChatGPT.
Would somebody who is good at prompting also be able to tell when a machine is hallucinating?
I think not . I might refer you to your specialist adviser on that.
You mentioned a moment ago the underpriced nature of some of our valuable public sector data assets. Can you give us an example or two of which data assets you are thinking of?
Did I say “underpriced” or “not priced carefully enough”?
I wrote down “underpriced”.
Underpricing would be an error. I cannot give you an example of where they have been given away.
I interpreted what you said as their value not being sufficiently recognised.

I share the view with DSIT, which has taken advice on this from Saul Klein, a member of the Council for Science and Technology, that it needs to be careful to avoid underpricing our data assets. I do not have an example off the top of my head, but do you want me to find one and send it to you?

Yes, it would be helpful to have an example that illustrates that point. My ears just pricked up and I thought, “Where are we undervaluing something that is clearly a precious asset?” So, yes, it would be great if you could do that. Thank you.

You also referred to systems failure alongside skills that has perhaps led to us not exploiting some of the opportunities that emerge from our research. Other than skills, is there another aspect to the systems failure? Are we learning from the past with large language models so that we avoid missing out in this context?

Absolutely, we are. It would be worth sitting down and thinking about the S&T framework, which was published in March last year. I will give you a few of them; I am not going to read out all 10 of the big things . Thing 3 is to invest in R&D. Thing 4 is skills. Thing 5 is spending money for little S&T companies. Thing 6 is one of my favourites; it is using government procurement to encourage innovation. It goes on . T here is a list of 10 things , as I said . It would be super-interesting to sit down and think about what the S&T framework means for how this country is going to generate prosperity and security using LLMs.
Procurement has certainly raised with us before as an opportunity that we do not exploit sufficiently .
I heard you say that we need a more scientific Civil Service. What would it look like , and would it be at the expense of something else?

I would say no t . A real strength of our Civil Service is the idea of the generalist. We have people who run the Civil Service and could write you a single page on almost anything, but , at the moment, very few members of our senior Civil Service, most of whom work as generalists, come from what I call a deep science and technology background and have worked for, say, 10 years in science and technology. In my head, that could have been in industry, universities , or one of our government labs.

We need to create a pathway so that some of those people can come in, learn how to be a civil servant, which is a skill of its own, and join the senior Civil Service as generalists but generalists with a deep experience and expertise as scientists. Let me give you an example to explain why. I want people who can just look at an experiment and say, “That will not do”. That may be completely obvious to people who have spent parts of their lives working as scientists. It happened to me the other day. I will not tell you where, but somebody showed me an experiment and I said, “There are no replicates in that experiment. Every treatment is different, so you are not able to interpret the results”. That was not because I knew about that bit of science, but because I have spent a lifetime teaching science to 21 year-olds.

Q117 Dame Angela, thank you for coming today. The consensus of our witnesses has been that large language models will make things easier, better, quicker and more exciting, but a variety of witnesses have also talked about risks. Can you give us an understanding of what the Government know about risks? How robust is their understanding of risks , and can you articulate the short-term immediate versus the longer-term potentially more existential risks?

Rarely do I find myself able to say, “ I think we’re in a good place at the moment”. That’s because w e were so busy on this over the autumn, so we have an articulation of what the risks are, which might be called a sort of call to arms. That paper was written in the run-up to the safety summit , and I commend it to you.

Even further, I commend its appendix, which was written by my office, the Government Office for Science. Instead of being a call to arms, I would call it a piece of honest brokerage. It really tries to say, “On the one hand , some people think this . On the other hand , some people think that”. Other people have described it as one of the most balanced expositions of this problem that they have seen coming out of government. I am very proud of that piece of work and the people who wrote it, some of whom are sitting behind me.

The Government’s risk register about LLMs was published at the same time. Those three documents are publicly available. Of course, this is a fast-moving field , so things go out of date as quickly as you write them. However, one of the things that happened at the safety summit was the commissioning of a document that will be called , I think, the S tate of the Science, which will be authored by a man called Yoshua Bengio. It will be an even more up to date explanation of the risks. The countries that attended the summit have been invited to nominate somebody to sit on the board of advisers for that document; I will sit on it for the UK. I will not be a writer but one of the advisers helping to guide what comes out of that.
I s that enough?

Q118 I would like to ask a little more. Do you think that, here in the UK, we have credible warning indicators for full risks? Yes, the AI Safety Summit looked at this from an international consensus viewpoint, which is exciting and helpful , and well done to you and your colleagues for bringing together the risks : “These are the risks on the one hand , and these are the risks on the other ” . But where are we going to land? Where should we land, and who , for the UK, should be responsible for where that landing strip is?
What are dimensions of this landing strip?
In other areas, whether health or something like that, we have indicators of pandemic, catastrophic loss, threat to life—
The Chair : —w eather, and that sort of thing.
Yes. For this space, should we have those indicators?

We cannot have those yet, because we do not have what I would describe as an engineer’s description between here and the catastrophic risk. Pandemics happen to be something that I might know about. If I wanted to tell you what would happen between today and, let us say, yesterday’s swine flu case becoming a pandemic, I could spell that out for you in very specific detail.

We do not have that spelled out for the more catastrophic versions of these risks. That is part of the work of the AI Safety Institute: to make better descriptions of things that might go wrong , and find scientific descriptions of how we would measure that. By “scientific”, I mean things like properly designed experiments, properly described work , and an absolute emphasis on reproducibility. If the rest of us in science do an experiment, write it up and publish it, and someone comes along and says, “I couldn’t reproduce what you did”, that is shameful for us. It is like saying that you really messed up, that you are a bad scientist. At the moment, that is not a tradition of this part of science. One of the things that came out of the “What should scientists do” panel at the safety summit was that this needs to become seriously scientific, and reproducibility is a core of the scientific method. So you have not seen those, I would say, because they do not exist for the more catastrophic end of the risks.

Do we have good ways of measuring things that are nearer term? There is much more on misinformation and disinformation; we are better at measuring those. I do not think we are very good on accuracy of these models, so those are things that we ought to be developing now.

I want to paraphrase what you have said. Am I right that the AI Safety Institute will therefore work on developing a framework to address quantitatively new risks? Meanwhile, the current risks, the immediate risks, of large language models are from threat actors or misinformation—that is, things that we know about. Who is responsible for setting out the framework to address those? Is it the Government’s central risk function? Is it regulators? Who is leading?

I will check with my colleagues, but I am pretty sure that it is the NSC(R)— the National Security Council (Resilience)—people who came up with the risk register that I told you was the third document that is available. [1] That is a risk register in the sense of a bunch of things that could go wrong, how bad they would be, some vague sense of how likely they are. So we have that, and it sits firmly inside R esilience.
On things like what bad actors might do, work that was started as part of the work done in preparation for the safety summit will continue . That happens behind wires.
Q119 Do you think that the regulators that we currently have are sufficiently able to understand the risk register and the fast-moving nature of this area?

That is a great question. This is something that we have thought about quite a lot in the Government Office for Science. It started before I came. We had this set of what we think of as innovation-friendly regulation, but in the process of doing that work it becomes very clear to us that it is hard for regulators to attract and retain the kind of extremely valuable talent that is required if you are to be a regulator in a very fast-moving and prosperity-generating domain like this.

We made some suggestions about what to do about that. One was that there should be freedoms—I might have to choose my words quite carefully: “Regulators should be granted greater flexibility to develop a cadre of technical experts and determine the right pay and conditions to attract talented individuals”. The other was that surely the regulators needed ways to facilitate secondments so that people could move in both directions, both in and out of the regulators, to help us to build what I would call SQEP—suitably qualified and experienced people—inside the regulators.
So, in a nutshell, the regulators might need more money and more skills.
I would agree with that, yes.
To clarify, are you talking about people moving in and out of regulators from the regulated industries or from government?
No, I meant from the regulated industries. We would like the movement to go both ways. You will be a much better regulator if you really understand the industry that you are regulating.
That is true, but it also presents different risks to do with regulatory capture and the sufficient independence of the regulator.
I do not deny that, but the need for qualifications and experience is great enough that we need to think about how to manage those other risks.

Again, just so that I can be clear about what you have been saying in response to these questions, is it your view that the Government are in a pretty good place in their approach to the risk management of the near-term risks, but that there is still work to be done on the longer-term risks, which would be done by the AI Safety Institute?

I would say that we are in a pretty good place on identifying risks, and some of them we are taking very seriously. We are all extremely worried about the risks for next year’s election — and we are not the only ones ; t he whole world is very worried about what will happen in next year’s election — and we are in the process right now of thinking about what to do about it. We have hints from other areas where people worry about misinformation and disinformation—the two biggest ones are climate change and medicines in general, vaccines in particular. There is stuff that we can learn from those topics about how you can help people to be prepared to be bombarded with misinformation.
I would not say that I am completely happy that we are doing enough about it, no.
What do you think should be done that is not being done?

This is my personal opinion; you had better not take this as a GO-Science opinion. Right now may not be the right time, but I think we need a public information campaign to let people know what form misinformation and disinformation might take in the run-up to our own upcoming election.

Q120 The AI Council had an ethicist on the board and the AI Safety Institute does not. Yet much of what you are talking is what I would call functional. It is fascinating stuff, but what is the role of ethics—the question of why we are doing this, and why we say yes to some stuff and no to other stuff.

That is a really good point. I completely agree. This question has technical elements, but it is fundamentally a socio-technical question. This is about how we collectively wish to use this technology. Shall I go away and suggest to my friends in the AI Safety Institute that they need an ethicist and I know a good one?
That would be marvellous.
If you know a good one, let me know. I think that is a great idea.

I am fascinated by this thing about attracting sufficient capacity to the public regulators and so on in the face of private firms that can pay a lot of money. This is partly about the psychology of the people you might get. Are there lots of technically adept people who think, “I would love to serve the public interest by working for a public regulator”? Some of those people are very good; some are less good, ethically. Are there such people around , or do you have to match—well, you cannot match what Bill Gates gets—what a successful entrepreneur might get in order to attract people to public service at all ?

I know extremely clever, very able people who have worked in the regulation of medicines for most of their lives. They were not paid anything like as much as they would have been paid if they had worked in a drug company. There is no question that that is possible. We do not have an AI regulator at the moment, so I cannot say in relation to that specific issue, but there are other regulators.

This country is renowned for having fantastic regulators. Let us not fall into the trap of thinking that we can have either regulation or innovation. You probably know better than I do that good regulation drives innovation. Clear, rapid, well-informed, proportionate regulation, particularly if it is stable, creates a terrific environment in which to innovate.

I would like to ask a bit more about the public information campaign. I know this is your personal view, but we are all worried about the general election and misinformation. If you were to give a brief on what that public information campaign should be, from where you are sitting, what should we be really worried about?

I can tell what I would do: I would go away and talk to the experts I already know who work on disinformation and misinformation in other arenas. My understanding is that they would tell me: “Show people what the tricks are. Show people how they would be tricked”. I do not know what those are off the top of my head .

You mentioned that there is no AI regulator today. The AI White Paper is very clear that the Government do not want one and, instead, want existing independent regulators to cover their areas with—these are my words, not the White Paper’s—a light-touch central risk function. Should we be concerned , because, as far as we have been able to discover so far , that light-touch central function does not exist yet? Are we wrong ? D oes it exist? If it does not, should it?
I will pass on that question. I am really sorry; I do not know. Could I ask you to ask Viscount Camrose?
I will be doing exactly that in an hour’s time.
He is a much better person to ask than I am. Forgive me.
No problem.

When you were answering questions from Lord Kamall and a subsequent question from the Chair, you talked about making health and science data available for, among other things, LLM training. At the same time, you stressed the importance of valuing it and went on to talk about how we must avoid underpricing it. Do I take it from that that you believe that LLM developers should pay for the use of this data?
It depends on who they are doing it for. If they are developing something that is just for the public’s use, then no , but if they are developing something that they will se ll , then yes .
In your view, should that apply to all other forms of data?

I see where you are going. I have already written about this and said that it requires an ongoing dialogue about where we are with copyright and how we want to manage copyright to properly balance the rights of creators and the ability to move forward with new technologies.

Q121 We talked earlier about the balance between innovation and safety, and I suppose we are now talking about the balance between innovation and copyright holders. You said that you want to go away and think about it, as more thought should be given to this . We are very keen to put something in our report about it. Your predecessor, Patrick Vallance, was very clear about his belief that text-mining and data-mining exceptions should be extended to make it easier for people to get the data to innovate with LLMs and so on. Do you share that view , or are you saying just that it needs more thinking about?

I will find you something that I have already said, so that I am at least consistent, if you will forgive me. I think this is in the hands of the Intellectual Property Office at the moment, and I would be inclined to await further comment from me while the IPO works on it. I said : “The government response … confirmed that a code of practice would be developed to enable AI innovators and the creative industries to grow together in partnership”. My understanding is that those recommendations currently sit with the IPO.

The problem with the code of practice is that it has been suggested that it will be voluntary. A lot of copyright holders, who are vital to the creative industries, are often small individuals who do not really know how they are able to exercise any of rights they might have . If the code is voluntary, there is no way of knowing whether people have abided by it or not. It is not really a solution. Do you think that a voluntary code is really the way forward?
Can I read another bit?
Yes, please do.

“While the development of a voluntary code of practice is an important, pragmatic step in resolving these tensions, it should not run counter to IP value creation, as IP is central to the sector accruing value and its capacity for growth”.

I strongly share that view and I am very pleased that you have written it, but it means that we need to do more than is happening currently. Surely we need clarity as to where the law actually stands, because there are lots of LLM developers scraping data, which definitely have not paid for it, do not have licences for it and so on, and our creators are losing out. That may be the price we pay for innovation, but that is a decision that people have to make. We are very keen to know your view on it, but I think you are saying that you do not have one at this stage.
This “should not run counter to IP value creation, as IP is central to the sector”. That looks like a view to me. I have told you what I have written . I look forward to seeing what you write.
Okay. Thank you very much. That is it.

Q122 The answers that you have been giving touched on advice, as of course you would, but could you pull together your views on expert, external, scientific advice to the Government? This year, we have been through the Foundation Model Taskforce, which morphed into the Frontier AI Taskforce , and now we have the AI Safety Institute, which is focusing much more on risk. Do you think that the right balance is being achieved in the expert scientific advice to the Government? Are there gaps or places that you think will not be covered by the institute? Should we and the Government be worried?

It is very much part of my job to make sure that advice to g overnment comes from a broad spectrum of opinion. That means commercial opinion , academic opinion , opinion from our own experts in government labs , and opinions from across the spectrum. That means opinion from people who think that truly dreadful things might happen and from people who say, “I just don’t see a pathway to that”.

I opened by describing the work that my office did, which was very careful to say , “Here ’ s the range of opinion. Please don’t think that one side of this opinion sits in the commercial world and the other sits in the academic. That is not where the split lies”. One reason why there is room for so much opinion is that there is not that much evidence. Some of this will be resolved with the acquisition of evidence. For example, as next year plays out, we will see what kinds of capabilities are generated in the next round of these very large models.

Q123 The AI Safety Institute has a brief. I am interested that you describe your role a s bringing in people to add to the pool of thinking, which must be very interesting and exciting. What parts of the bigger picture is the AI Safety Institute not looking at, which you have to make sure are promoted and pushed within government?

We are extremely interested , for example, in helping the Government themselves to get ready for these huge changes that are coming. We have a document that describes five different scenarios for 2030. It says, “Imagine these five different ways in which things could pan out”. They are basically stories that we will take across government to different departments and say, “ Look at this. If this happened, how would you r department react? What would it mean for you? If the world were like this in 2030, what might your bit of government do to make it better before we got there , o r, if it ended up like that, what would you have to do to manage in a scenario like that?”

That is a F oresight report, which is a standard product from GO-Science . I think it is great. I did not write it; my team wrote it. We did its first run-through with some Permanent Secretaries last Friday and had a full and interested discussion. So that is one thing. Of course, this is not particularly about safety; safety is one of five big dimensions that we think about here.
This is more about innovation.

It thinks about capability and adoption. When we imagine these things, we ask, “Are they more closed models or is it an open model?” We think about the geopolitical context in which all this plays out. Those five things are there as guides for thoughtful but busy people to ruminate, in what we hope is a structured and helpful way, on how a technology will change the working lives of those of us who lead in government.

We also suggest people to the AI Safety Institute. We help it to draw up its rosters of experts who can advise it. I chivvy my mates , the other GCSAs in other countries , to join the expert panel to help with the State of the Science report. Those are main things that we are involved in.
I go back to the science and technology framework , because all the things that are happening across government with it ought to help with the commercialisation of these technologies.

To go back to the scenario and what you did with the Perm Secs, that is a good way of getting organisations to think hard beyond the everyday stuff that they tend to think about constantly. What was the worst scenario? What was the scenario that pushed them the most and made them think the most?

We put them into three separate groups , so it was not a proper experiment; there were no replica te s. My least favourite scenario is AI disappointing us—that is, it being just another damp squib , and it turns out that we never managed to sort out the hallucination problem so we can n ever use it and we have to go back to Excel spreadsheets and Google. That is my least favourite scenario . I have not brought them with me. Did you ask for the worst?
I asked for the most challenging.

Probably the AI Wild West , where things that are fairly safe are all driven off open models and the idea is that somehow the open LLMs win the competition and become the best models. So instead of there being four of five companies that we can squash when they are bad, there is an anthill of LLM providers , and then we have to think about how we will have the invisible hand of the market regulate this mess.

As you can imagine, we had a super-interesting discussion where one person sat back and said, “This is fine . The market will sort it all”, and another person said, “No, we ’ ll have to be really clever regulators and design some AIs to regulate the AIs”. We had a very rich discussion , but that was just the start. I hope that we will have more interaction, using those scenarios, right across Whitehall in the coming year.

This sort of points to the view that civil servants are very open to the sort of advice they need from you and the people you bring to them. Is that right , or are there still patches of greater difficulty?

So long as the problem is not too difficult. This was a very open discussion. It was in a session that had been designed specifically so that there would be time for people to put away the difficult problem of today and have a day to think about AI. I gave one of the talks, actually.
Is it about having a more scientific Civil Service—that is, a more scientific top of the Civil Service? Presumably, that includes politicians and Ministers too.

That is for the electorate to decide. I do not think I can change that , but I can try to help. There are two things here. One is that everybody should just be more scientific , because it is fun and interesting . Another is that being a top civil servant is a rare skill. Really good civil servants do amazing things. We have these things called CSA networks where you pluck out people like me, plonk them in and say, “Get on with it”. But we have to have loyal wingmen to whom we say, “I’d like to do this thing”, and then they operate the machine. I want there to be a career stream for people like that who will go on to be part of the senior Civil Service.
And that is what they are aiming for .

Yes. I would like there to be a whole bunch of them. I have loads of wonderful colleagues who would be fantastic senior civil servants — I used to be the CSA for the MoD , so I know loads of scientists who work at D stl, the defence lab —but I do not think that they could do it tomorrow ; t hey would have to come and learn. I do not know what the magic is , because I am not a career civil servant , but they would have to spend a couple of years learning how to be a top-class civil servant.
Thank you. That was f ascinating .
I could comment on that , but I will resist.

That was a fascinating answer. Obviously, the scientific approach is a strong one, but what has struck me in listening to months of evidence is the sheer degree of disparity of view, particularly about risk s . At one stage, we had one lot of people signing a letter saying that we must have a six-month pause in all this—some of them did it for commercial reasons , but some of them did it because they believed it—and, on the other hand, we have had people being completely liberal about it, relatively speaking, and worrying about regulation being a way of blocking innovation. Maybe this is true of the early stages of any scientific development , but this degree of disparity seems to make the challenge of dealing with it all much harder than it otherwise would be , even before we know what happened with Sam Altman.
Yes, it is difficult. I agree with your statement , but I am not sure what your question is.
The question is : do you agree?
I do.

Q124 You mentioned your international counterparts. From your conversations with them, in your opinion, which countries have really thought about this? Whe re have you thought, “Gosh, we really need to do a lot more thinking in this area”? Whose thinking do you admire , and h ave you thought, “We need to think more like them and think about the issues they have raised”? Have I thrown too much at you there?

No. Clearly, the Americans have given this a lot of thought. Actually, the Europeans have given it a lot of thought and have come up with a different answer. I have not read what they think , but I am told that Singapore is very front footed on this. To be honest, the equivalents that I know best are Australia, Canada, the US and New Zealand , because we are in a sort of club together. One of the points of the safety summit was to draw together international discussion on this issue. We cannot do this on our own. We can regulate it until we are blue in the face , but what happens then? It is quite interesting to read about the Chinese attitude towards regulation too .

Q125 You have given us some bedtime reading in that case. I have a second question. You probably do not want to go into too much detail on this—I apologise—but one debate that we are looking at is whether there is enough public ly available data to train the models. If not, are you concerned about a scenario in which a lot of the trainers decide not to access copyrighted material because it is too difficult, meaning that the models are less effective because they have not had the fullest dataset possible?

You are getting into a very technical area that is beyond my expertise. Rather than give you a silly answer, I should say that I am not best placed to answer that question. However, my understanding is that, for more limited tasks—for some in government, our tasks are quite limited—what matters is having the right data, particularly in the later stages of training.

Q126 My last question is about transparency. People say that they want to see more transparency, which means transparency of algorithms and of datasets. Even if we have that transparency, will people understand what that means?

I think experts would tell you that you always have to trade efficacy against transparency , and is that really what you want? I might add that we have plenty of medicines that work but we do not know why, and we have other ways to make sure that they are safe enough and to keep track when surprising things go wrong. There are other situations where we use technology without complete transparency about why it works.

Q127 I have a couple of questions that are both linked and come at the sort of issue that Lord Lipsey raised but from a slightly different angle. You said earlier that one of the influences on the broad range of opinion was the lack of evidence. I thought that was interesting, because is there not sufficient evidence from the way in which other technologies have developed that ought to inform what people think about the balance of risk and opportunities or , indeed, how this technology should be regulated? That is my first question.

My question to add to that would be whether we can think of an example of a technology with such broad application , where we get a step change in apparent capability, such that even the people who have built it cannot articulate exactly how it works.
Does that not apply to the internet?
I do not think so, no.
Why?

Because t he internet is a very large network of information across which various capabilities, particularly in trade, emerged in interesting ways that can be studied pretty openly by anybody. I am happy to debate this further, but I do not see that as a close analogy. I thought you were going to say the published book.
Is that an example you want to draw a comparison with ?

I am not a historian , but an interesting comparison would be to look at what the fears were, because my understanding is that there were a lot of fears. I bet there are some historians here who could tell me about the fears about what would happen if we democratised all that information and made it available, because it all used to be locked away.

That is a really interesting question. If you find out more, let me know. The question is basically how a fundamental technology like this emerges. It is a super-interesting question. The internet is one and the book is another. I am thinking about the Industrial Revolution and the agricultural revolution, which we all studied so much at school.
What about nuclear physics and energy?

Nuclear physics is totally engineered, is it not? Every step inside our application of nuclear physics is understood to the point of being able to describe it, very accurately, with an equation. That is not true of this technology.

Q128 T his question is connected. I want to follow up on your comment that there are medicines that work but we do not understand why, and yet we have a regulatory regime for safety. If you take that as a good analogy for the regulation of large language models, what does it really mean us doing?

I have had it vigorously argued to me that the way we regulate medicines is not a good model for LLMs. But suppose we did it that way: we would have trials. I have had interesting discussions with people in the AI Safety Institute about what stage this is at. If we take that model, the stage we are at at the moment is to think about what we go through for a new medicine. First, we do tests in a test tube, then on some sort of model animal, usually, and then on very tiny numbers of people. We do not even have the equivalent of those tests yet , and that is the stage that the AI Safety Institute is at at the moment : it has to devise the equivalent of in vitro tests, in vivo tests and phase 1 or first-in-human tests. What would the equivalents b e for those three? That is quite an interesting analogy , even if we did not end up having phase 1, 2 and 3 trials in the wild.
I was thinking about social media being just as powerful, in its way, and the challenges that there have been in trying to regulate it.
I regret the things that we did not do already , don’t you think?

I see this as another challenge. I was fascinated by the Sunday Times article on the sacking of Sam Altman and that organisation, and the reinstating of him and the arguments within the organisation about impact. There is no absolute answer when we are trying to assess risk against innovation.
I am sure you are right, but we await your wisdom.

Q129 My final question goes back to th e broad spectrum of opinion and your view that there is a lack of evidence. I am intrigued to know how you, as a scientist, view the debate — among technologists or scientists — on this technology as it exists at the moment and effective altruism. Have you considered and taken a view on this?
No. I would leave effective altruism out of it.
In what way would you leave it out of it?

The question of how we are going to benefit from the promise of generative AI is sociotechnical , and we must figure out how to benefit from it, while first knowing and then protecting ourselves from the risks. It is a huge question. I view effective altruism as a side issue about lifestyle.
That was very helpful. Professor Dame Angela McLean, thank you so much for your time and your answers to our many questions.
[1] Added by witness: The Government confirmed this document was HMG's pre-Summit publication, not an NSC(R) risk register, but that DSIT plan to publish an AI Risk Register in 2024.

segs.tx: Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Pet Welfare and Abuse , HC 161
Tuesday 28 November 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 28 November 2023.
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sir Robert Goodwill (Chair); Steven Bonnar; Ian Byrne; Dr Neil Hudson ; Mrs Sheryll Murray ; Ca t Smith .
Questions 333 - 435
Witnesses

I : Rt Hon the Lord Benyon, Minister for Biosecurity, Marine and Rural Affairs, Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs ; and Marc Casale, Deputy Director for Animal Welfare, Department for Environment , Food and Rural Affairs .
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Rt Hon the Lord Benyon and Marc Casale .

Q333 Welco me to this session of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee . It come s hot on the heels of yesterday ’ s debate in Westminster Hall on the issue of XL B ullies, which had an almost unprecedented number of petitioners calling for that particular deb ate . I know that the Minister ’ s s tand - in , Mark Spencer , was representing him in the Commons, but th is is your area of expertise.

T h is is the fifth of five sessions held by the Committee for our p et w elfare and a buse r eport . F irst of all , I ask the Minister, Lord Benyon, who is an old friend of mine and of the Committee as well, to introduce himself .

Thank you. I am the DEFRA Minister in the Lords . O ne of my areas of responsibility , for the time being a nyway — there is a slight shake - up going on, as you are probably aware — is animal welfare.
Thank you . Mr Casale .
Marc Casale: I am the D eputy D irector for A nimal W elfare in DEFRA .

Q334 Thank you very much indeed. T here was quite a lot of consternation in June when the A nimal W elfare (K ept A nimals ) Bill — as I think most people know it — was withdrawn and the Government stated its contents would be taken forward a s single - issue B ills o r SI s , or maybe even picked up as private M embers ’ B ills . W hich single issue B ills a re you taking forward and how do you plan to do so?

T hank you, Chair . We are taking forward the ban on live exports as a Government Bill . T hat was announced in t he King ’ s Speech. We are also doing one measure that was in the k ept a nimals Bill that we feel we can do as secondary legislation , wh ich is banning keeping primates as pets .

T he other measures that we are in discussion s with a variety of different p eople to see how and whether we can take those forward — and we are reasonably confident we will be able to get all the manifesto commitments in law and indeed some others — includ e , we hope, legislation to tackle livestock worryi ng , raise standards in zoos, bring in a new offence of pet a bduction . W e think we can e xceed our ambition by doing those as well.
Q335 There is not much going on at the moment with the export of animals for slaughter . I think since the farmers ’ ferry ceased operating, there is not a great deal —

The number of livestock that have been exported for slaughter since Brexit is zero . However , there is the possibility that it could be started again if e conomic situations changed and infras tructure that currently does not exist did exist and markets were created . There is a very clear view that we want to ensure that that does not happen . I t is no t a pressing issue but it is one that we want to get on the statute books .

Q336 Dr Hudson : I will chime in on that , Minister . O ver the last two or three years, there were still large numbers of horses exported to Europe, not under the guise of slaughter but illegally transported under the auspices of sport or recreation. Do you agree that the Government bringing forward this Bill would try to stop that loophole ? P art of that is improved equine identification , which I know you are working on as well , but this Bill would close that loophole.

We want to ensure , first of all on the livestock , that you can still export animals for breeding purposes —t hat is a very important export for this country — which is b ulls and other high - end p rime livestock . We want to make sure that that market continues . T hat is , of course , long established, but you are talking about the export of horses for slaughter, which are not listed as such under the export.

Q337 Dr Hudson : Yes , under the pretence that they ar e being exported for sport or movement for s port and breeding . W e want horses to be able to move freely for breeding and sport but w hat is happening is that horses are being illegally exported to Europe u nder cover of another excuse. This tightening up on not being able to be transported for slaughter should hopefully close that loophole.
Yes, that is the plan.

Q338 I thou ght that t here was a minimum value on horses, which was aimed to catch that particular problem . H orses going to slaughter are not the same value as racehorses , eventers and breeding stock and that should have prevented that happening . I s that the case ?
Marc Casale: Tha t is a really old piece of legislation that has a value of a horse that cannot be exported.

I would be wary about tying that into the legislation because horse v alues change, and what was considered a valuable horse in 1990 is chicken fee d today compared with the costs of some of the elite sport animals. However, t here must be a perfectly c lear legislative route to try to weed out precisely the sort of abuse that —

Q339 M y worry is , given that you have said that no animals have been exported for slaughter , or certainly no sheep or cattle , since Brexit, that this may not be very high on the Government’s priority list for getting legislation through the House , g iven that the election may be coming up sooner than we think.

Chair , you have great experience of trying to get B ills into King ’ s S peeches . We had to make a decision about what we thought we could take forward ourselves and get that through t he relevant cross - G overnment discussions , and what we thought could be delivered by other means — c learly , private M embers’ Bills , and having some oven - ready measures that we think can deliver our ambitions . We are working hard to achieve that b ut , as you know, the ballot ha s just been announced and w e are working closely to try to get those t hrough .

Q340 I wish you l uc k. I know that when people get high up in the ballot they are inundated with suggestions for legislation , but certainly a hand - out B ill from the Government would have its way eased by the Government . A lot of the work would be done by officials in the Department s . Let’s hope that those get picked up by M embers who a re fortunate .

T he strength of a private M ember ’s Bill i s when it ha s u niversal support . I think that banning live exports has universal support across the H ouse, but we think that t here are different ways of getting these measures through.

Q341 Dr Hudson : One that you did not specifically mention, Minister, was potentially the one involved with puppy smuggl ing and heavily pregnant dogs and dogs that have had their ears cropped . Stopping those would potentially come in as a private M ember ’s Bill , would n’ t it ?
Yes , absolutely .
Dr Hudson : G reat. Thank you.

Q342 The Dogs Trust has told us in its evidence that it estimate s around 90% of dogs that are purchased in the UK are from unlicensed breeders. I s this an acceptable situation and how are we addressing the risks that this poses?

Lord Benyon : I t is quite difficult to assess the ratio of lice nsed to unlicensed dog breeders in England. N o official data exists on the number of unlicensed breeders . O ur annual data return from local authorities , which are the key r egulator here , shows that there were 2 , 296 dog breeding licences in place in April o f this year i n 261 local authorities.

However, some sector groups, including the Dogs Trust, have attempted to estimate the ratio. For example, in 2015, prior to the introduction of the current l icen s ing scheme, we estimated that about 10% of dogs sold ori ginated from licensed breeders. Sorry, it was estimated — I am not saying that was DEFR A. A number o f different groups have come up with these ratios.
Q343 I n your perception , Minister, between the numbers coming from licensed and unlicensed, do you find this to be an acceptable ratio or split?

W e want to get as many as possible f rom licensed breeders and that is what we are striving to do , b ut that is only half the story. The other story is about having proper standards in place so that we can ensure — and there is existing legislati on that prevents some of the bad practice s that we have all heard about , but w e want to try to improve t his. Marc , is there anything you would like to say?

Marc Casale: A nyone who is breeding on a commercial basis has to have a licence. Anyone who breeds three or more litters a year needs a licence . T he unlicensed people who are basically breeding would be pure ly hobby breeders and w e expect t hat they do not have the same incentives a s people who are breeding on a commercial basis.
Q344 Is the Department confident that the law is being adhered to?

Marc Casale : W e have had the gener al protections in the Animal Welfare Act for providing for the welfare needs of animals and also not to to lerate cruelty. The y apply to everyone who is involved in the breeding of any animal.

Q345 S ome of the other witnesses we have heard from as part of this inquiry have recommended that a register for all dog breeders should be introduced . T hat would be all dog breeders, not just the ones who are currently licensed . W hat assessments has the Department made about the merits of that proposal ?

Lord Benyon : We are currently finalising our post - im plementation review of the A nimal W elfare (L icen s ing of A ctivities I nvolving A nimals ) ( England ) Regulations 2018, which we hope to publish soon. The 2018 regulations introduced a licen s ing regime , which Marc has just mentioned , for eight animal a ctivities , including dog breeding . I t is clear from the responses to this post - implementation review that there r emains, as you accurately say, a considerable concern across the sector about the welfare aspects of dog breeding that they do not currently re quire a licence . S tud dog services , w help ing services and canine fertility businesses are examples of area s where we —
We are c oming along to the canine physicality clinics later.

Q346 I suppose I am asking , Minister , if the recommendations do not includ e a register for all dog breeders, is there anything else that could be introduced that would help the traceability of breeders and puppies?

I think w e have said before — for example, in the p et t heft t ask f orce report — that having a register for those who are bree ding , who do not meet the licen s ing threshold conditions , is something that we are considering. As the Minister said, we have the five - year review of the regulations that is due to come out soon . T hat may also s ay something about th is is sue.

Q347 S ome of these so-called unlicensed breeders are just people with family pets who want to have a litter , maybe , so that t he y have a puppy for when their dog dies. W e had a Patterdale bitch . We had a litter and my brother-in-law got one , m y cousin got another and w e sold a couple to people we knew . You are not suggesting bringing people like me , who might just want to have one litter in the dog’s lifetime , m aybe a couple , within a licen s ing regime ? S urely , it is for the people who are a commercial operation o r maybe having more than three litter s but not really needing to declare it because there is no policing.

O r me, Chair . T he stress of having eight spaniel puppies last year is what will prevent me from trying to b reed from my bitch again — but absolutely not . W e could not possibly regulate to that degree and w e would not want to. It is a fairly bureaucratic process of registering them with T he Kennel Club and things like that. Of course they are now compulsorily microchipped and there are various other measures that a responsible owner has to take , and w e want to continue that. The idea that we we re going to register every hobby breeder, even if it is once in a decade like me , w ould be impossible.
T here are also unplanned pregnancies that happen in the canine world , as well as e lsewhere, which you would not want to get caught up with .
Q348 Mrs Murray : I have to declare an interest as the c hair man of the a ll - p arty p arliamentary g roup on c ats and also the owner of two beautiful cats .

Minister , the Cat Protection Society has argued that licen s ing c at breeding under the LAIA regulations would safeguard cats and kittens against poor breeding conditions. Do you agree with that assessment?

Lord Benyon : We work very closely with them and other organisations. As I said before, we are reviewing the post - implementation. We have the post - implementation review that is looking at precisely that . We are working with others t o see whether the impacts on breeding of cats are being faced properly by legislation and regulation today .

The response that we have had indicate s that there are some g eneral reasons to be concerned about the situation for breeding cats. These include the health and we lfare problems associated with certain breeds and other issues relating to breeding for particular aesthetic purposes . We want to ensure that there are proper regulations i n place.

Q349 Mrs Murray : Thank you. G iven your answer, what assessment have you made of the potential merits of introducing more robust breeding regulations for rabbit s , which are becoming far more p opular ?

W e do not have any plans to implement a requirement for licen s ing the breeding of rabbits . T here is existing legislation under the Animal We lfare Act 2006 , which says it is an offence to cause any animal unnecessary suffering or to fail to provide for its w elfare . T he A nimal We lfare ( Sentencing ) Act of the year before la st amended the 2006 Act to deliver the Government’s manifesto commitment to increase sentences available to the courts, and that certainly includes keepers of rabbits .

W e are happy to l ook at taking positive action to look at welfare and advice is availabl e to educate pet owners on providing for welfare needs of rabbits. This includes the British Rabbit Council ’ s codes of practice , which I think is a very g ood way of doing it. T hese are people who really know what they are talking about and they have produced the G ood P ractice C ode for the Welfare of Rabbits , which I recommend to any keeper of rabbits.
Q350 Mrs Murray : You mentioned the post - implementation review of the 2018 regulations. Can we expect publication before the end of this year?
I t is a very good question.
Very soon I would say . Q uite when , I am not sure we have a date but—
Lord Benyon : I f I say “ very soon ” in the House of Lords there is a groan that goes up around the whole Chamber . I would probably say at your end—
In t he fullness of time.
In the fullness of time, y es. I do not want to sound too prescient here . W e are working it through , and w e will publish it soon. It is a very important piece of work.
Mrs Murray : Are we talking months?
Lord Benyon : If it is not this side of Christmas, it will be t he other side of Christmas . I t will be early in the n ew year.
Mrs Murray : Thank you very m uch , Minister .
I am tempted to say that breeding rabbits must be one of the easiest jobs there is .
T hey tend to look after themselves i n that d epartment .
T hey do .

Q351 Dr Hudson : Minister and Marc , through the course of this inquiry we have been looking at various practice s and things that have increased in recent times and in parallel there have been a few media investigations in to some of t hese . T he first that I want to mention briefly is that ITV News uncovered and brought to the Committee’s attention , prior to one of our ses sions , the incidents of puppy yoga classes where underage puppies are brought in to yoga classes under the guise of it being a lovely , cuddly thing to do but actually t here are significant welfare concerns for those young , under - age, perhaps un vaccinated puppies to be used in a workplace like that. Do the Government ha ve that on their radar to look at moving forward to see what can be done to improve the animal welfare implication s ?

I am aware of this . I mean I am aware of that pi ece of work that ITV did, but we do not have any plans to legislate against it. T here must be a common - sense element here where providers of yoga c lasses can realise where they are doing harm and t here is endless guidance available in what you should and should not do with an unvaccinated puppy . I t is very difficult to legislate for stupidity — and the stupidity of some people who think that they can take a very young puppy into that sort of setting and move it around in the way that they do is just n uts, but I do not know whether w e have —

Q352 Dr Hudson : I take your point . I t is difficult to legislate , but if the Government say , “W e have this on our radar. W e are aware of it ” , i f guidance can come out from DEFRA , the Home Office and so on to police authorities and local government , who are the people potentially involved in policing or being called out to that , so t he y have guidance that th is unacceptable , that will help them stop some of these practice s .

Ma rc Casale: W e do monitor animal activities that are not currently licensed . You have things like cat cafés as well, and various things that are not licensed and not covered by the LAIA regulation s . We work closely with the can ine and fe line s ector g roup to work out what is the best way of getting the right messaging out there , to encourage certain things and discourage other things.
Q353 Dr Hudson : Can you assure me and the Committee that puppy y oga is o n the radar ?
It is definitely on the r adar . Absolutely , yes .

Q354 Dr Hudson : Thank you. Can I get on to the main question ? I n one of your previous answers , you touched on canine fertility clinics . T hat is something that we have taken a lot of evidence on, and w e have increasin g concern about , as do many of the animal welfare charities and the veterinary bodies. The number of canine fertility clinics rose from 37 in 2020 to over 400 today . T he British Veterinary Association has reported that about 93% of vets are concerned about the pet safety and animal welfare implications of the increased number of these unregulated c linics. Do the Government share these concerns — and I think we interrupted you, Richard, in your answer —and w hat steps are the Government taking to look at these unregulated canine fertility clinics?

T he first thing I w ill say , which I hope will be music to your ears , a lthough we have discussed this many times , is that I think we need to reform or replace the Veterinary Surgeons Act 196 6 . S ince that time , a whole lot of complementary and highly necessary and very efficacious treatments are delivered by people who are not v eterinary surgeons . T hose good people , and the veterinary surgeons in whose practice s they operate, want proper regulation in this field. I think that that leads into your question because some activities in these canine fertility clinics have been carried out by people who have no qualification to do th at .

I t is absolutely vital to say that t he actions that are being taken need to be done by a qualified veterinary surgeon un til we have a proper regulated world where some of the ancillary activities can happen . T hese canine f ertility clinics offer a ran ge of services , which can include stud dog services , s upply and shipping of semen, ultrasound scanning, whelping assistance, progesterone testing, and artificial insemination. S ome of these services offered by these businesses, including the methods of und ertaking canine artificial insem ination , constitute acts of veterinary surgery . I think it is really important to say that and it is illegal for laypeople to perform them .

I f we do get into reforming this A ct, there will be a very detailed debate that will require people with real knowledge in both H ouses t o ensure that we are g etting this right . F ertility services can present risks to welfare to the adult dogs used for breeding and their progeny . T hese risk s may relate to the nature of the procedure, the condition of the dog, the competency of the personnel and a variety of other contributing factors.

Q355 Dr Hudson : Thank you , t hat is very helpful. You raised the issues of these acts of veterinary surgery being performed by non- veterinarians — things like taking blood samples and artificial insemination . We had one vet before us as who said there is a concern that potentially things like c aesarean sections are also being per formed. I take your point and I think the veterinary profession will be encouraged that there are plans afoot to reform the Veterinary Surgeons Act 1966 .

T hat is not an easy thing to do in q uick t ime and t here is the concern that these canine fertility clinics are out there now with these procedures tak ing place. What can be done? A s you rightly say, under the Veterinary Surgeons Act, I think there is a penalty for £100 if they find something is being done t hat is not performed by a vet. That is potentially not a huge deterrent for some of the unscrupulous people involved in these practice s . Bearing in mind that, yes, the Veterinary Surgeons Act can be reformed, what can be done in the short term to address these issues to protect animal welfare ?

T o underline what you say, I think that the b usiness model is a fairly recent one. When we brought it in — as recently as February 2020 — more than a year after the 2018 regulations came into force, the British Veterinary Association suggested that there were fewer than 40 canine fertility businesses in the UK . W e know since then that the number has increased significantly , with e stimates su ggesting more than 300 businesses in operation in 2022. W hat can we do? T here is existing legislation where you could take it through on an A nimal W elfare A ct basis and secure a proper prosecution , but some of it would be a fairly niche area of activity an d may n ot be covered by the Act. Are there t hings that we are doing now , Marc ?

A couple of things. One is that a s part of the LAIA five - year review we licensed dog breeding . W e can re consider what the definition of dog breeding captures , whether that should be broader , to include some activities that are not vet activities but they ought to be subject to licen s ing. That is one thing we can do in the near future .

Secondly, at the moment, our expert evidence c ommittee, the a nimal w e lfare c ommittee , is looking not just at where we are with fertility clinics and those kinds of activities for dogs, but also looking at cat breeding that we spoke about a minute ago , j ust to understand where the welfare issues lie, where the biggest risks are and what we want to do about it, including from the LAIA licen s ing perspective. That is under active consideration right now for cats and dogs and fertility clinics.

Q356 Dr Hudson : Can you assure us that there is joined - up thinking across G overnment ? T he BBC “ Panorama ” investigation , which highlighted some of the canine fertility clinics , suggest s that potentially in some of these places there is a n organised crime element , so I guess giving the police force the capability and the intelligence that there are animal welfare implications for what can be done. A re you talking across G overnment a bout what can be done to try to stop s ome of this ?
T he re are close links not just on the breeding side but al so for imports and puppy smuggling, organised crime , police a nd those kinds of gangs as well. Th ere are close links already.

Q357 Dr Hudson : C oming back to the point about private M embers ’ B ills, if pet smuggling , ear cropping and heavily pregnant dogs are covered in legislation , that will give t he police and local authorities more teeth to potentially h it some of the intended consequences from that as well .

T hese are obviously devolved issues. We work on this very closely wi th the dev olv ed G overnments to make sure that we get join - up right across the UK . T hat means that there w ill not be a geographic shift of illegal activity to one country that h as slightly softer laws than ours. We all want to ensure that we are listening not j ust to the usual stakeholders who want high er animal welfare standards but also to the police if criminality is ha ppening .

There is some really good work being done on responsible dog ownership. I am sure we will come on to talk about XL B ullies and that part of it, but we t hink there is a job to be done to educate people more about where they buy their dog from . I think we always imagine a pub carpark. I am not quite sure how many dogs are actually sold in pub carparks, but people are still buying a nimals—not just dogs, cats as well—without any knowledge of where it came from or what the parents of that dog went through t o get that p u ppy into their arms . It is a really important piece of work that we have to continue to push.

Q358 Dr Hudson : I welcome the fact that the Government had the P etfished campaign. Has there been an assessment o f the benefits and the implications of the Petfished campaign in improving people’s awareness of how they source their p ets ?

W e had an internal evaluation of that, which was really quite posit ive , and that was an investment that we b asically had for a couple of years at least . A lso , we worked very closely with the main animal welfare organisations and their campaigns, which have different audiences as well , s o in a combined way , and a lso with t he devolved A dministrations . W e constantly seek to get the message out a bout how to source your dog , w atch out for the person selling it rather than b eing distracted by the fluffy puppy itself . T hat tends to work w ell .

C oming back to your earlier point , we should not forget HM Revenue and Customs , who are very important partners in helping to tackle some of these criminals . N ot just the police but HM Revenue and Customs give s us some really good leaders.

Q359 Dr Hudson : I t is welcome that t here has been an internal ass essment but , as you said, Richard, the climate has evolved rapidly in the last few months, so can the Government reboot some of these campaigns ? Th e bottom line is increasing public awareness —w e are a nation of animal lovers — to make sure that people know that they are getting their animals from the right place and they know how to look after them. Is there a chance to reboot some of th e a dvertising campaign to help that ?

P etfish ed was an example of how to run a campaign in the modern w orld. There used to be a time when a Minister would make a speech and it would be reported . T here was a time when events like this would probably have got much more coverage in getting a message across . I think we have to reflect how people get information and at what point in their life t hey might consider owning a dog or cat, or indeed any other animal, for the first time, because that very often is the time to get to them .

We think that Dogs Trust , th e RSPCA , Blue Cross , Cats Protection and other organisations like them are probably the best way . W ho does n’t remember the words , “A dog i s for life , not just for Christmas ”? T hat came from the Dogs Trust . That is the kind of messaging that we in G overnment have to work with and enable and use our resources where we can , but recognise that we have to get to a wider group of the population , because bad things are still happening and w e want to make sure that they are not.

Q360 Thinking about the law of unintended consequences , some of the procedures that we are talking about in these canine fer tility clinics are procedures that farmers would carry out on their own livestock . F or example, I have put a prolapse d ewe back and stitched it in , delivering lambs, giving injections, all that stuff that farmers do. I n fact , AI g uys come round to farms and do those sorts of procedures. People do foot trimming, that sort of thing . I s it the element of paying for something that is the issue ? W ill there be any suggestion that some of these procedures which farmers are currently doing might be made veterinary only ?

Lord Benyon: U nder our animal health and w e lfare pathway, farmers now get access to a free vet visit a year , which is very popular . It is going down really well , because t he relationship they have with a vet tends to be a crisis relationship . A p erson comes on to the farm because an animal is sick . T h is is where they sit down and look at all aspects of livestock rearing on that farm and walk round with the vet and they make suggestions about how they move animals, where they put their livestock, some good biosecurity measures and p recisely those kinds of issues .

On the h andling of animals , it is absolutely vital that farmers still do that, continue to do it , and w e are not expecting to impose any new costs on farmers and requiring people with particular q ualifications to do things a s basic as the ones you have list ed . A bsolutely, AI on my farm is done by people on my farm , so that must continue .

We are talking about more specialist action with small animals and pets . We are a ware of some real, genuine concerns about animal welfare and it is extraordinary how this b usiness has just appeared in recent years . We are t rying to understand the financial reasons why they have been created , to ensure that we have safe places and that people who love their pet know that they are not part of an activity that does not have the highest welfare standards.

Q361 O ne of the points that we talked about when we were at the Dogs Trust was the automatic neutering of pets — the sort of breeding that happens on your farm and on our farm with dogs just does not happen because so many dogs are neutered . S hould we be thinking about discouraging some of the neuter ing going on so that people can breed fr om their own pet ? I t is good news for vets because at the slightest thing they will get the vet in. Is that something that we have bypassed i n many c ommunities that previously would automatically just have a couple of litters from their dog and probably have them in the house ?

I have a figure of 10 million or 12 million dogs in this coun try . A percentage of them will not have very nice lives, but one hopes it is a fairly small percentage. I do not know whether it is a G overnment ’s job to regulate such things. W here we apply neutering requirements it i s to deliver a very specific outcome , and that is in a reas like dangerous dogs—

Q362 It is t he rehoming charities that automatically neuter. I f you want to have a pet to rehome and you think that it would b e great to have some puppies at some point , they will not countenance that .

Lord Benyon : W e have a concern about some aspects of importation of r escue dogs , when there are so many in our own s ettings here that are in need of homes and that can be properly identified and paired up — the right keeper with the right dog — and an after - service with the charity that will ensure that that dog has a great life.

P eople’s h eartstrings are plucked by pictures of animals from other parts of the world . They pay hu ndreds of pounds to get that dog here, which has biosecurity risks for us , while there is a dog still in a domestic c harit y kennel that could have been rehomed for next to nothing . We want to make sure that we are looking at those charities.
I was talking specifically about our domestic charities , but thank you . Ian , can we come on to your questions, please?

Q363 B uilding on what the Minister and Marc ha ve said , w e have heard of a rise in demand for designer pets bred for extreme traits that compromise the ir health , and w e have had some heart breaking written evidence . T he RSPCA says that the health and w e lfare of these animals is likely to be so poor that they will experience a lifetime of ill health and suffering. What assessments have you made of the scale of this problem and could the 2018 LAIA regulations be st rengthen ed to improve protections ?

I think we share those concerns . I f breeding parents are not screened and selected adequately, animals can be bred with an inherited disease or confirmation traits known as extreme breeding, and this may also lead to serious ongoing health p roblems . T hese include the brachycephalic obstruction, obstructive airway syndrome, a long - term condition that can require regular veterinary treatment and / or corrective surgery, and very often a shorter life span for t he dog .

A number of health and w e lfare issues can be associated with extreme breeding . We support the work of the UK Brachycephalic W orking G roup, whose aim is to protect dogs kept as companion animals from the health and welfare harms of this condition . We are looking through this post - implementation review at other things we can do . Do you want to a dd some colour to that , Marc, or have I done it all ?
Marc Casale : No, that was e verything.
