Q364 T ouching on that , I am delighted with w hat you have just said about agreeing with the premise of the question, but how many successful prosecutions ha ve there been for the individuals who contravene the schedule o f the regulations, which prohibits the breeding of dogs where there are reasonable expectations that genetics or health would lead to welfare problems ? We have seen it. It is there . I t is happening. H a ve there been any successful prosecutions of anybody doing it knowingly ?

Marc Casale : I n practice , if you have a licensed breeder who is engaging in activities that are not along the right lines, they are likely to have their licence suspended or revoked rather than a criminal prosecution being pursued. That is what tends to happen in practice , so we do not have figures about prosecutions themselves.
Q365 Do you h ave any figures on licences that have been suspende d , t he scale of the problem , if you have not had any actual prosecutions?

W e can come back to you on that one . We will double - check because that will be taken forward by local authorities individually. We would have to c heck with them individually, but let’s come back to you on that one .
Q366 Okay. Just to finish on this, is the Department seeking to increase the elements of prose cution? I s that something where we are looking at to tighten up the regulations ?

Y es, we are working with organisations like The Kennel Club on very clearly defined a ttempts to breed out the kind of a esthetic and other related issues that have cause d so many problems . I will always want to increase the number of prosecutions where we think there is an increased amount of abuse, but what people always seem to be looking at and saying is, “D o we need mor e legislation to do this? ” I think our review of the 2018 regulations will be an opportunity to assess that, but my instinct is probably no. I think we need to ensure that we are doing e nforcement properly.

Q367 On s ome of the enforcement elements that you touched on , S am G ain e s , the head of the companion animals team at the RSPCA , s aid we could look at Scotland as a good example b ecause it is difficult for local authorit ies and forces to understand the guidance. In Scotland they list the breeds of dogs for which it is unlikely that a licence will be given for the breeding of individuals. W e can look at t he Scottish model .

Marc Casa le : Yes , I think it is part of the five - year review . We are definitely looking at the detail of our current guidance and regulations . We work very closely with colleagues in Scotl and , Wales and Northern Ireland about what the y are doing to make sure that we are learning from one an other. A bsolutely, that is something that will be covered under the u mbrella of the five - year review.

Q368 That is good to know, Marc . To finish w hat we have just talked about, what are we doing to educate the public on the welfare issues and the h arm s of these so-called designer pets? My esteemed colleague , Dr Hudson, is always quite rightly talking about how certain films now encourage the images of pets that have had this done to them . We m ight come on to that in a later q uestion, but what mo re could be done from a public perspective to di spel the narrative of w hat we are seeing — that these are a good thing ? I know my own daughter looks at the se design er pets —it is only when you g et into where we are and the harm that th at is done that you see something different — so h ow do we dispel that narrative ?

I emphasise what I was saying earlier about the work that we are doing on responsible dog ownership . I t is not just about responsible dog ownership . I t is about the processes you ne ed to go through before you are an owner , finding out where a dog has come from, how it is bred and whether it will have life limiting —
Yes, the impact of that.

T he impact that has on you . It is one of the most important things in people’s lives, and they are miserable when they see it suffering . We are supporting animal s , and w e want them to have a good experience, but also people who become very attached to these animals . We want to do that and t hat is where G overnment work best with —

Q369 Ian By rne: A lso , if you are going to choose a dog for the first time, you need an understanding of how that dog has been br ed, the impact that will have on it s life. A lot of people just do not have that information to hand or understand t he difficult ies they will have .

Lord Benyon : I will give you an exam ple . O n social media, people often post pictures of lanterns, night lanterns —w hat ever they are called —and y ou and this Committee , w e all know that can be a terrible thing because cattle and wild animals , like deer , e at them and suffer terribly .

T here is a huge back lash now on Twitter and other platforms w hen somebody does that or if people go to a wedding and they see all these things going up , v ery often people comment . I t is becoming socially unacceptable , as socially unacceptable as smoking became before it was banned. I think that is the bes t way to go to make sure that people understand. “ Have you seen my n ew dog ? ” “W hy have you bought that dog ? Y ou made a terrible mistake . Y ou have lined the pocket of somebody doing a bad thing. ”
I agree completely with that, yes .
I think that is the most effective way.
Q370 H ow do we get t o that ? T hat is what the question is, is n’t it?

We get to that b y the G overnment doing what they need to do in a regulatory and legal capacity but understanding that the real power of communication lies with s ome pretty well - resourced charities and campaig n groups .
We cannot just leave it to them.
No, we cannot just leave it to them.
Q371 It has to be a joint effort , surely .

It absolutely has to be a joint effort. We put resources into it . The Government can do things like the Petfished campaign . I am not throwing it back to you, but it is a fantastic thing for a constituency MP to do , t o run a campaign on some of these things , and G ov ernment should support what you are doing in your constituen cy . I am sure you are already doing it , but there will be some new MP s coming in here and these are the sort of campaigns where an MP can give good local leadership , a s can the local authority.

Q372 Ch air: I am going to a sk a little bit about mutilations . We have some very tough laws in this country on ear cropping . T ail docking can only be carr ied out in very limited situations and by a veterinary surgeon. I t ha s been two years since DEFRA consulted on prohibiting the importation o f dogs with cropped ears and docked tails. When will that consultation be published a nd is DEFRA committed to closing t his loophole?

Yes, we are learning more about this problem. Interestingly — I do not want to diminish it — we do not have evidence for the overall number of crop ped dogs entering Great Britain , but w e do have statistics for cases where a cropped or docked d og has been detained due to being illegally landed . It was 115 in 202 1 ; in 2022 it was 2 9 ; and so far , up to the end of last month , 21 this year .

T he PDSA a nimal w elfare r eport is a n ational survey , and the sample of cat and dog owners suggested that about 3% of dog owners who got their pet from abroad d id so because they wanted a dog with cropped ears. T hat is quite a large number of a nimals .

Q373 The breeds, I guess, where it is fashionable, made popular in popular culture and cartoon s . Dr Hudson mentioned in the debate yesterday in We stminster Hall that some children ’s cartoons are featuring dogs with cropped ears, making them an attractive thing for people to desire.

Lord Benyo n : Yes , and I think we have people , particularly at the s hort s traits , who are working with carriers and Border Force to identify i ssues where there is a potential problem and stopping them, but that will only ever catch a proportion of them , because it is hard to see into the back of a van or a car . We want to ensure that we are doing as much as we can to s top them .

Q374 We have not yet banned the importation , t hat is the problem . If you see an animal that ha s had its ears cropped in another country , it is not illegal to import it yet, is it? T hat is what I think we are trying to suggest might be a good idea for the Government to take acti on on .

W e have had the private M ember ’s Bill ballot recently and very soon we will see what happen s with the Bills that Members wish to take forward. In light o f that , I think various things will become apparent, including where we are with the response to that consultation.
Q375 You are optimis tic that one of the lucky raffle ticket winners in the private M embers’ Bill draw might pick this one up?
Marc Casale : Discussions are ongoing .

Q376 Excellent. S pecifically on the declawing of cats, which is a particularly cruel process , y ou mentioned the PDS A survey . It reckoned that about 5% of cat owners acquired cats abroad because they wanted a declawed cat. Do you recognise these figures , and would you support a ban also on the i mpor tation of declawed cats ?

Lord Benyon : Definitely —y es, w e would. I have never met a person who has made that choice. It seems an extraordinary thing to do in this day and age , but it exists. It is a problem , and w e definitely want to ensure that we stop it happening.
Marc Casale : On the figures , it is harder to detect a declaw ed cat , but definitely, as the Minister says, we look at all these mutilations in the same abhorrent light .
T hat could be part of the same Bill . It could be included in that same p rivate M ember ’ s Bill .
It w ould be optimistic .

Q377 We are told it is fairly easy to purchase the tools for ear cropping or tail docking to do it here in the UK. Is there anything that G overnment could do to restrict t he ownership o f these tools, which can be bought online , w e are told ?

There must be a way of doing that without it being a heavy-handed primary legislative route, but there may well be, and it is something we will certainly look at. I have seen in museums some horrendous things for docking horses ’ tails or dogs ’ ears — they were heated in a f ire and the animal must have gone through unbelievable pain . The se things must exist in folklore . We want to ensure that they rema in in museums and not become available on the i nternet for bizarre people who want to carry out such abhorrent actions .

Q378 T he dogs that are imported with cropped ears come from countries where ear cropping is also illegal, which indicate s those animals may have originated from places like Serbia . There fore , banning the im por tation of dogs with cropped e ars might also close a loophole in animal health. There are countries where rabies is prevalent or certainly occurs . Is DEFRA aware of any figures for where dogs are originating ? We are going to come o n to controls at the port later, but is this an animal - health loophole that needs to be closed, which might be part of the picture?

Lord Benyon : The re is European legislation . T here is the European Conventi on for the P rotection of P et A nimals , w hich ban s surgical operations for the purpose of modifying the appearance of an animal. As of October, this c onvention has been ratified by 26 countries across Europe, including Romania, Cyprus, Bulgari a , a nd Greece , s ome of the locations from which a number of the se dogs have appeared . T hey have had to ratify t hat to transpose that into their domestic legislation.

However, there is no dat a available on the source country of mutilated pets currently coming to GB. As we touched on earlier—and I think you are probably coming on to this —t here could be a win-win here if we we re reducing the risk of importation of dogs that might have conditions, the diseases that we want to keep out of this country, bearing down on mutilations in imports, and perhaps getting some of the people to whom those animals are coming to look at a better regulated, high - integrity , closer - to - home rehoming operation from one of our many reputable charities .

Q379 I almost had a fall - out with one of my friend ’ s d aughters , who had rescued a dog from Serbi a a nd I ha d to point out it was probably just a street dog. It may even have been stolen from a family . U nfortunately , people seem to think they are doing the right thing by rehoming some of these dogs, which does not really help the dog, or certainly the rehoming charities here , which have no shortage of dogs, as we found out at Batterse a , a nd at The Dogs Trust in Kent.

P eople need to think of the wider implications of what they are doing . By spending so much money importing that dog , t hey are leaving another one without a home —one that possibly has had a terrible experience and could benefit from a good family home . I think that w hen you take people through t hat conversation they can quickly see it . A s I say, people have their heartstrings pulled by the p itiful sight of dogs in miserable circumstances and we want to make sure—there is a consumer rights issue here—that they are getting the full story and that they understand the wider implications of what they are do ing .

Q380 Mrs Murray : I will turn now to pet importation incidents and smuggling , Minister . I n 2020, Lord Goldsmith told this Committee that the Department does not know how much smuggling is happening and that the data it has is not reliable. Three years on , d o you hold better data and what does it show?

Lord Benyon : If something, whether it is a b ottle of drink or a packet of fags — or sadly , in this case , an animal — is successfully smuggled , n obody tends to know about it, and so there will always be a data deficit. We can assess trends and where we are seeing an increase in an activity we can c hange the risk profile of that and put more resources into doing it. We do have some details. I can give you t he number of animals detained. We have the figures for animals , dogs and cats , and animals detained , identified as welfare non -c ompliant, detained under a rabies order, detained for TARP or health attestation other than rabies , p regnant an imals that have been seized , commercial disguised as non- commercial , a bandoned during detention, which is a n issue , and transited through Europe but originating i n a non- EU coun try .

W e have identified over 6 , 190 non- compliances between January and August of this year . T his non- compliance is on certificates accompanying commercially imported dogs, cats and ferrets from EU countries ; 364 dogs were detained in quarantine following unsatisfactory check s at Dover , under both the commercial and non- commer cial pet travel regime, and about 95% of these a nimals were dogs . T his included 19 pregnant dogs, including two b asset h ound bitches that had 19 puppies between them. We will leave this data with you.

Q381 Mrs Murray : Thank you very much. To continue, in 2021 , the Committee welcomed the Government ’ s proposals to reduce the number of animals an individual can bring into the UK f rom five to three per individual, with a limit of five per motor vehicle . W hy have these measures not been brought in yet?
Lord Benyon : This was a k ept a nimals B ill measure and one that we hope to be bringing in before the end of t his Parliament .
Q382 Mrs Murray : W hich piece of legislation will it be brought in under?
W e will find out after the —
Mrs Murray : Is it something that the Government can bring in or a private M ember’s Bill ?
To be frank, this will be coming through the private M embers’ Bill direction . W e are in discussions. We cannot be more specific because we cannot rely on i t .

Q383 I f you are not fortunate in attracting a colleague who c o me s out in the private M ember ’s Bill ballot, will there be potential for bringing forward a DL or could this be covered by a simple measure in C ommittee ?

That is certainly what we are doing with p rimates as p ets. I will look at any way of avoiding primary legislation . We all have the scars on our backs of the Christmas - tree effect of that and how sometimes , i n seeking to make the perfect , it finally becomes the enemy of the good . I will look at any secondary legislation route or indeed try to hook it on to another piece of primary legislation , which has been quite successful in the past. O ur minds are always open to that . We want to get a ll our measures — in fact, more than our measures that were in the manifes to — on to the statute book.
Q384 By the way , f or anyone watching and wondering what a Christm as tree Bill is, that is a Bill where lots of people hang things on —

Lord Benyon : Yes , I always explain that you have a piece of le gislation with a clear purpose and then in its journey to and from both H ouses it gets decorated like a Christmas tree and ends up a monster , f alling over.

Q385 Mrs Murray : Thank you, Minister . Wh ile the official figures state that around 40,000 cats came into the UK last year , Cats Protection , in its 2022 Our C a ts and T heir S tats survey , estimates that the figure i s closer to 80,000. How do your account f or this disparity and what are you doing to improve your data and address the problem?

We have been working closely with Cats Protectio n regarding its figures , because there is difference between its estimates and our estimates . I t is quite hard to pin down what the most accurate figure is, but it is something that our economists , analysts and statisticians are engaging with it about.

Lor d Benyon: W e ought to say that the vast majority o f those are cats that are well looked after , which are coming back here because , for whatever reason , the family are moving back to the UK , having been posted abroad or whatever, but not in every case . We want to make sure t hat we are able to identify where we think abuses are happening and that we are dealing with it .
Q386 Mrs Murray : Thank you. What is your estimate of how many puppies are being smuggled into Great Britain each year? Do you h ave any estimates?
As I say, it is an impossible figure to get. However, we can start seeing from the data that we have where we think there is a problem and we can pivot resources into doing it.
Q387 Mrs Murray : Can you give us any idea of the trend? I am not asking for disti nct numbers, because I do understand. However, is it increasing or is it reducing?

On commercial movements—not smuggling figures but actual commercial movements—the trends were increasing quite a lot. With dogs, overall we had about 40,000 in 2019, going to 60,000 in 2020 and then almost 75,000 in 2021. Since then , we have introduced a regime that licenses import and they have fallen back down to about 40,000. Most of the imported commercial dogs come from places like Romania and we have a l icensing regime in place, since the beginning of the invasion of Ukraine, which initially prevented imports from Romania and now it licenses them. That has enhanced compliance with our requirements and at the same time reduced the number of imports from th at particular country and others. It is very hard to get figures on the illicit activity by its very nature.

I will give you an example. You may have had letters from constituents when we did that. I certainly got a lot as Minister saying, “ It is terrible that you have done this. We are in the process of importing this dog from Romania, please let it come.” I investigated and we were getting 5,000 or 6,000 a month coming from mainly Romania. That is a hell of a number. The regime that we brou ght in dealt with a particular problem and we have now eased it a bit , so we are seeing a return to slightly more sensible figures.

Q388 Mrs Murray : Thank you very much. We have heard concerning reports of cats and dogs being imported when they were 90% throu gh gestation. Do the Government still plan to introduce legislation to ban the import of heavily pregnant dogs? If so, what is the timeframe?
The same measure as part of what was in the kept animals Bill , which would ban the importation of a n animal in its final trimester of pregnancy.
Q389 Mrs Murray : Finally, have you made an assessment of the potential merits of prohibiting the import of heavily pregnant cats?
Yes, that would be in exactly the same measure.

Q390 We are talking about pet importation. Transport providers and carr iers are responsible for pet importation checks. Is this acceptable and can we be confident they are striking the right balance between speed, checks, profit and identifying non-compliance?

Carriers are a very important partner in this. It i s entirely justified that they should be working in close association with the Animal and Plant Health Agency and Border Force. Our relationship with Border Force is now closer than ever, with what we are introducing through the targeted operating model fo r borders and particularly what we are doing on the s hort s traits. We want to make sure that we are identifying risks and using all players to help us in this, and carriers are important.

Q391 Undoubtedly, but are you confident in the fact that the re is no G overnment body involved in that? The onus is on the transport providers and carriers. I say this because Tim Reardon, who we took evidence from, said, “There are some things that could be done better. The emphasis of a government body, whatever t hat looks like, has the benefit of animal welfare and animal health being right at the top priority for how they are operating, as well as ensuring that consistency...and capacity.” Is there a potential call for a different model or are you happy with it a s it is now? Are you confident?

Some carriers will be better than others. We want to make sure that we are not just thinking of the heavy workload of carriers across areas like the short straits , but are also making sure that other ports aro und the country have a similar standard of intervention. Is there anything more on working with carriers that I am missing?

We think that the model as such is the right approach. We do work with carriers to make sure that it is applied as we ll as possible. However, in general, in how far should the state get involved versus leveraging in some resourcing and input from carriers in the private sector, we have a good balance.
Q392 How often is that reviewed?

It is ongoing. We make sure that there are no major problems and that if there are they come to us. We have seen also in the farming sector that we have farm assurance schemes where it is not always the state that sets regulations and has to monitor and regulate everyth ing. We want to get that joint buy-in and joint responsibility. That also helps with some of the messaging. If a message comes from the Government people might not listen to it or wilfully do the opposite, whereas if some messaging around how to comply and how to do it in the right way comes from the carrier or from other parties, sometimes it works better.
Q393 Effectively, that model is always under scrutiny.
It is ongoing, yes. We constantly monitor how well all the pet import meas ures and controls we have are working.

Q394 We have heard serious concerns about the robustness of a pet importation system, which follows on from what we are talking about, that is based on 100% documentary checks with absolutely no requirement to visualise the animal. Do you share these concerns when we are talking about the review and what are you doing to address them?
We do have 100% documentary checks, but we can do physical checks as well, and we do. We will work on a risk-base d, intelligence-led system where we can.
Q395 Are they piecemeal?

I am sure you are not suggesting that we should do 100% physical checks , because it would be impossible. What is enough and what is good? I do not claim that our syste m is perfect, but it is well resourced and professional. The 100% documentary check does sift out a lot of the wrong kind of transporters. I will be interested to know what your report says on this, because you have been talking to a variety of different p eople. We are open to any suggestion. I am interested to talk to the person who gave evidence. We think that carriers are very important and we want to make sure that at every level of their employ, rather like at every level of our people, they are tuned into identifying where they think there may be a problem.
Q396 That is a good answer. The people who we have spoken to were professionally aware and are dedicated and it would be good to speak to them after you have seen the report.
At airports it is 100% physical checks. They are met by an APHA indivi dual. However, it is the ports—
Q397 It is the ports, yes, but there is a concern about what is potentially getting through. T here is always room for improvements on that aspect, isn’t there?

On penalties, the maximum penalty for illegal animal im portation is 12 months. Do you consider this an adequate deterrent, particularly in the scale of what we see regarding criminality and criminal gangs?
I do not know what actual penalties have been dished out for illegal importation.

It comes back to the earlier point that for some of the people involved on a more criminal basis, to be caught by Revenue and Customs measures and to have sig nificant financial penalties is more of a deterrent. It is around which enforcement measures have the best impact.
Q398 Is that linked up? Are we seeing that between different Departments, different agencies?
Yes, we do work with the police and with Revenue and Customs on puppy smuggling.

Q399 Dr Hudson : I want to t urn to biosecurity. We touched on this a little earlier in the session. We did an inquiry a couple of years ago on movement of animals across borders, where we looked at some of these issues. Some of these issues hopefully will be addressed in the upcoming legislative S ession with some of the Bills coming forward.

However, first I want to talk about Brucella canis. There has been an increase in cases from 14 in 2020 to 75 in 20 22. This is a disease of dogs , but it is also a zoonotic disease that can go to people and there have been incidences of it being transferred to people in this country as well. In answer to Mrs Murray’s question about heavily pregnant animals coming in, on e of the real risks is heavily pregnant dogs coming in and whelping in this country. Potentially when people are exposed to birthing fluids they can be affected. We have seen the increased number of cases and a potential spread to people. Are we doing enou gh to help our animal health in this country and our public health with our biosecurity? What can we do to mitigate this?

We recommend prospective owners make sure that any dog imported from an area where Brucella canis is present is tested before arrival. Our future policy is guided by risk assessment. You are absolutely right that as of July this year two laboratory-confirmed cases of Brucella canis human infection have been identified in the UK. Risk assessment was undertaken and published in August this year and the probability generally across the UK is considered low to very low.

I was very upset, having been given assurances by the person trying to import dogs during the Afghan Kabul evacuation that they were all healthy, that we found that some of them had Brucella canis. There was even a case of leishmaniasis. We take this very seriously and APHA vets at borders and visiting these dogs are extremely aware of this disease. We are concerned about the disease risk of imported dogs general ly and we are taking measures to improve compliance and reduce risk. Highlighting it to breeders and vets to encourage testing is very important.

We are seeing an increased number of suspect canine cases of Brucella canis. These have been reported by priva te vets and APHA laboratories. As awareness across the UK vets has increased, imported dogs have been tested while clinically well, in part due to protocols put in place by some vet practices and companies for health and safety reasons. We are keen to make sure that this does not get here. We have been rabies free for 100 years and we want to make sure that we continue with that. There are other pathogens that worry us , but Brucella canis is a very important one.

Q400 Dr Hudson : You are recommending pre-importation health checks. Could we go stronger than that and insist on having pre-importation health checks on dogs coming, certainly pregnant dogs at least ? Is there something that we can do, rather than just recommending it, to go stronger?

We would need to consider exactly what kinds of checks and measures would be taken by whom and where , whether they are mandatory or recommended and for which cases. In light of the recent risk review that we are considering at the moment, definitely. We want to have a targeted but also a balanced and proportionate approach.

Q401 Dr Hudson : I understand that. Equally so for another species, there has been a concern about cats in Cyprus with a type of coronavirus causing feline infec tious peritonitis. What are the Government doing? Is that on your radar in trying to stop that coming in?
That is a recent phenomenon that has come our way and we are actively looking at that. There has been quite a lot of intense considerat ion in the past week or so.

Q402 Dr Hudson : So the Government are moving in a live monitoring situation, potentially restricting the movement or import of animals from areas where there are diseases that we currently have , but also diseases that are exotic in this country. Are the Government prepared to put in import restrictions to protect the UK population of people and animals?

We have ramped up the whole biosecurity noise, as well as real things that we are doing, in recent years. We have ex ercised for outbreaks of diseases that would cost this country billions if they got here. It is an opportunity to say how impressed I am with the Animal and Plant Health Agency. It has tackled major issues, not least a huge gap in the number of vets, which it seems to have filled to a large proportion— but not enough—and the ability to understand diseases like this. It maps the genomics of it and can turn things a round very quickly. That leads to an active response time when a problem occurs. I am usually ta lking about something like bluetongue, but in pets it would be catastrophic if some of these diseases got here. The ability to contain them is very important to us.

Q403 Dr Hudson : Thank you. We have a question on APHA coming up. I echo your thanks to APHA fo r keeping us safe from these diseases coming in, whether they are infectious disease outbreaks of things like avian influenza or, heaven forbid, things like foot and mouth or African swine fever, but also on an individual basis of pets moving in.

Now that we have left the European Union , we are able to strengthen our borders for biosecurity. The European Union stopped the mandatory treatment for things like ticks and tapeworm coming in. We have the capability now, as an independent sovereign state, to do th at. There was a case in the last couple of years of a dog in Harlow in Essex that contracted babesiosis, a tick-borne disease. That dog had never been out of the country, so it had contracted the disease from a tick that had probably been brought in on ano ther dog, dropped and then the dog picks it up. We can use that Brexit dividend, as the British Veterinary Association, the Dogs Trust and many groups are calling for, to reinstitute mandatory tick treatment and tapeworm measures to protect the population of animals in this country. That is very simple for the Government to do. Is it something that we can do and will do?

We are measuring tick burdens across the country and there is an increase, and will continue to be an increase, with changes to climate and large aeras being covered by species like bracken where ticks thrive and people walk their dogs. They spread them around and the problem continues. Very often these have human health implications, not just Lyme d isease but other incredibly unpleasant diseases that come from them.

Keeping our borders secure is important , but is only part of the issue. It is important that we exercise across agencies when these outbreaks occur and we learn from cases, such as the on e that you identified, to try to trace it back to how it got here. It is almost impossible to do , but you can sometimes do it.

Q404 Dr Hudson : If you reinstituted the tick treatment and/or the tapeworm treatment, it would protect that. That could be done, rev ersing what the European Union did a few years ago. The UK could strengthen measures .

We have specifically covered, in pet travel legislation, a tapeworm called Echinococcus multilocularis—I will call it EM—which has a serious impact on publ ic health. Strict animal health requirements for rabies apply to non-commercial and commercial movements of dogs and cats, and making sure that the tapeworm EM is listed in that way is vital.

Q405 Dr Hudson : These were discussed during the kept animals Bill, at the Committee stage . With t hese Bills coming forward, simple recommendations and clauses being added could sort this. You mentioned rabies. One of the things that people are calling for is extending the waiting time post-rabies vaccination to 12 weeks. That will help us in mitigating the risk of rabies coming in, as will increasing the age of animals that can be imported. These things can be addressed. Can you give us the assurances that they will be?

We have to stay flexible on this and w ork with latest scientific advice and best risk assessments. APHA is one of the partners, one of the agencies, that is doing this. The monthly biosecurity meeting that I chair specifically goes into detail on an emerging risk basis. Also there are horizon scans that look to see what is happening in other parts of the world that might come here. As you rightly say, it is not just our nearest neighbours in Europe. We can see patterns of disease movement, like African swine fever and Xylella in trees and vario us other things. However, we live in a globalised economy and people are bringing stuff here, and animals and plants here, and we have to be ahead of the game.

Q406 Dr Hudson : Before I hand back—I know that you will get on to APHA—you mentioned bringing stuff back. With the target border operating model there is a fear that there could be a dispensation for people to bring up to 2 kg of meat products or animal products with them. Is that on your radar to say that that loophole could put us at risk from things like African swine fever?

We have dropped it to an amount that relates to personal use only, recognising that a disease like African swine fever can come in on a pork chop. We want to make sure that people are aware of this. We will have muc h more visual campaigns. However, the target operating model operates under a prenotification system. What is vital as well is the activity in the port. It is not just Dover but elsewhere as well.

We may be getting off the case, but there is an extraordina ry cultural import at the moment of home-slaughtered sheep and pigs from certain parts of Europe that are driven across here in a van and attempted to be smuggled through. We are absolutely on to this. This is high, high risk to our disease security here, to our cybersecurity. We are doing everything that we can to clamp down on it.

Q407 Dr Hudson : We discussed this at the Committee a couple of weeks ago. Even for personal use, once you have finished with it and someone chucks it out of the car window or it is fed to a pig or gets into wild boar or whatever, it has gone. That is the issue. Even smal l amounts for personal use could put our country at risk.

Every country. Even countries that have a biosecurity system that I would love to have here, like Australia or New Zealand, allow a certain amount of prepackaged— as long as you declar e it. It is impossible to stop someone bringing a ham sandwich in with them. However, greater awareness and reducing the amount to what is as near to safe as you possibly can is very important.
Thank you very much indeed. I had to remove a tick la st year, but that was a combination of deer and bracken. We have far too many deer in certain parts of the country.

Q408 I have a few questions on APHA. The APHA chief executive recently told us, “We are on the precipice now of the need for investment into that Weybridge site”. Do you agree with that assessment and are the Government committed to providing the funding for t he essential improvements?

Absolutely. When any new Minister arrives at DEFRA, the first group of civil servants to come to see them is to talk about SCAH, which is science capability in animal health. The reason is that it is such an eye - wa tering amount of money that every Minister says, “Do we really need to do this?” particularly if they are in the run-up to a comprehensive spending review. What I would say to any future Minister, any of you and anyone else, is to go down to Weybridge and look at it. You have, I know, and I am grateful that you did, because you can keep the importance of this going in Parliament.

What you see there is amazing people doing amazing things, but we want them to have equally amazing facilities to do it in. We wa nt them to have the high-containment units that they need and to have a work environment that respects them for their skills and for what they do for this country. I think that it has been moved to the right on budget spreadsheets for too many decades and we are determined to grasp it. We have allocated £198 million to deliver tranche 1 through to the end of 2024-25. That budget is being spent on finalising the delivery, contracting and mobilising the delivery of resources and getting ahead with enabling wo rks to prepare the site for the main construction stage.

The next stage of SCAH will be defined , based on a further programme business case next year. At that point , a decision will be made over the balance of funding that will settle the scope and overall funding for the next spending review to progress towards the main construction stage starting in 2027. The current estimate is that the new science hub will be complete, licensed and commissioned by 2033-34. I urge us all to try to keep future Governments ’ feet to the fire on this. It is really important .

Q409 Thank you. You spoke in your answer about the amazing people working there. My question is about whether or not that is an adequate number of people. On an average day in 2023, 12 Animal and Plant Health Agency staff are based at the P ort of Dover. If we assume that that is three shifts of four people, that leaves weekends, bank holidays and nights covered with on-call duty team. Are you comfortable with that level of staffing and do you think that smugglers perhaps are aware of the weaknesses in staffing levels and when a good time to sneak through would be?

I would always like more. We are working so well with Border Force and carriers and various other agencies that we are abl e to operate particularly on a risk-based model. We can surge those numbers if we detect, for example, that people think that the weekend is when they can try to get something through, and we have done. We have certainly exercised on that elsewhere as well . The new operating BCP at Sevington will increase the ability to do speedy but thorough checks. There is a proper equine unit, for example, and a variety of different other facilities there that can help. It is very important that we support them with get ting turnaround of scientific data where we can. That is why the Weybridge site is important.

Q410 You have touched on different agencies working together. One of the agencies that has not been mentioned so far is local councils. We have heard alre ady that the financial situation faced by many local councils negatively impacts their ability to be able to undertake prosecutions, investigations and enforcements. Do you agree with that assessment?

Yes, and I have done some work on this w ith the target operating model, which required asymmetric negotiation internally in government, with devolved Governments, with local authorities that are the main arbiter of delivery mechanism here and, importantly, with stakeholders, people who are tradi ng and bringing food into this country that we all need, and other services.

Local authorities are very important. For example, a local authority can share port staff if two ports are close enough together. However, what was made very apparent to me by the Welsh Government was that having the same port staff operating across two ports with a three-hour drive is difficult. Therefore, they have to be resourced to do that. We have to make sure that ports, even small ones, are still viable, even if they have on e or two trips a week, unlike a port like Dover, which has a huge number 24/7. I am impressed by the skills of local authority officials, who know what they are looking for, know their way a round the legislation and are doing a good job, but we will contin ue to work with them to make sure that they have the resources that they need.
Q411 What about, say, local authority dog wardens? Do they have the capacity that they need to be able to use enforcement measures?

I remember being shout ed at when I was an MP by somebody who said that there was a stray dog, and it was all because of Tory cuts that there were no dog wardens. I said that we have not had a dog warden in west Berkshire since about 1970. There was an arrangement with the Dogs Trust based in west Berkshire. It provided what most people refer to as a dog warden service , where they worked with the police and picked up a stray or dangerous dog and it was dealt with through a partner like the Dogs Trust. In many other areas , it is t he RSPCA. Some local authorities do have dog wardens and I know they do in London boroughs, for example, and they do a great job. However, many areas like mine have not had a dog warden for decades.
Q412 Are you comfortable with that, Minister?

Lor d Benyon: It does not worry me whether they are employed by a charity and contracted to a local authority or whether they are a direct employee. I just want to make sure that they are doing what is needed to keep animals and people safe.
Q413 Is there an adequate number in local authorities across England?
I am not sure. I do not have any data on how many local authority-employed dog wardens there are and how many, like my local authority, contract that service.

We have not been specifically approached about this. Also, when we think about the Dover staffing and resourcing requireme nt, we like to think about the whole system—upstream what requirement should be placed on people before they leave their country to come here. We mentioned the licensing scheme for dogs coming from Romania. What checks can we require upstream, including by vets in those countries? Then what do we have at the border? At Dover we also have the Dogs Trust, which plays an important role in helping to deal with illegal imports. After that we have the post-import checks, which can be at the point of destination. We need to think about the whole system, where it is best to place the resources and how we have a risk-based approach that means that we get best value from those resources.
I am conscious that I may stray into the territory from dog wardens to XL Bullies, and I will hand back to the Chair.

Q414 Mrs Murray : To pick up on your council area employing the Dogs Trust and my council area in Cornwall employing dog wardens, are there any checks to make sure that the services operate in a consistent way?

That is a very good question. There are certain parameters in which local authorities are mandated to deliver this kind of service. I believe in local democracy. If they are not doing that, they should be held to account. Do we have any reg ulatory role over the delivery of such services?

We have the responsible dog ownership taskforce group that was established about 18 months ago, which includes local authorities, the police and animal welfare groups. That includes considerin g how local authorities can use their resources to most effect, and the powers that they have, including their preventive powers and their community order powers. That is mainly for responsible dog ownership , but also dog wardens and stray dogs. That is on e aspect of being a responsible owner, if you let your dog stray. As we have seen with livestock worrying, 80%-odd of the attacks come when people let their dogs escape from their property. The owner is nowhere to be found i f the dog has chased the livesto ck or scared them. We have that wider regime that has been doing some good work.

Q415 Mrs Murray : The other reason I ask is that it was one of the criticisms with primates, where local authorities perhaps did not have people who were qualified to assess prima tes kept at home. That was behind the question that I asked.

We will be publishing our statutory instrument on this very soon and I will be interested to know what you think about it. We are trying to say that this is the basic minimum-sized space that you should require for a primate and these are the features that should be within it. If you cannot provide that within your house, it is illegal for you to do it. That is why there are no dolphinariums in this country, because we created rules that made it impossible for them to exist. The idea of someone keeping primates in a small house or flat is, of course, impossible to envisage after we have done this statutory instrument.
Mrs Murray : Thank you, Minister. I will be interested in that, h aving Wild Futures in my constituency where most of the primates that are seized end up.

On the issue of dog wardens, if anyone missed it, in one of our earlier evidence sessions we had an inspirational lady from Worcestershire working across a nu mber of local authorities in the west m idlands. Her enthusiasm shone through and the limitations placed on her, particularly the cost of housing dogs if they are confiscated. It was an excellent piece of evidence, and I would certainly recommend anyone wat ching to scroll back and have a look at that.

Q416 Dr Hudson : We are coming on to the imminent American XL Bully ban, Minister and Marc. Our Committee has looked at this very closely with our emergency session and there was the debate in Westminster Hall yesterday. I was on a panel at the London Vet Show a couple of weeks ago speaking about this. You will be aware that there is a lot of high emotion on both sides of this debate. With the ban coming in there has been some disquiet in the veterinary sector and the animal health sector about some of the implications of how the ban will work. I have been very much trying to encourage those sectors and Government to stay around the table in this iterative process to make things work moving forward. There are questions about veterinary capacity and the implications for neut ering and euthanasia. In your discussions, are you confident that you are still staying around the table to address some of the issues that are being flagged, almost daily, from those sectors?

Yes, and I am grateful, particularly to the vete rinary profession but others—local authorities and the police—that have been part of our working group. The most important thing was to identify the breed, which has been quite a technical process. It is now posted on the gov.uk website and it does give pe ople an indication as to whether or not they have a dog that falls within the legislation. Marc might be able to give more detail about it , because he has been at these meetings with different stakeholder groups and how we want them to continue.

Marc Casal e: We are hugely grateful to all of the groups for engaging with us. We know that there are strong feelings on both sides of the argument. S ome groups that have stated that their position is that they firmly oppose what we are doing, but will keep workin g with us to help us to make sure that we minimise any unintended consequences , which is hugely appreciated. We meet at least weekly with all key groups , and we separately meet on an ad hoc basis to look at specific issues such as neutering and the like.

W e had a group that came up with the specification of an XL Bully dog. That included working very closely with the police as well, who will be applying it in practice. We have a description and some photos, which should help people to identify whether they have a dog that meets the requirements.
Dr Hudson : We will come on to identifying them in the Chair’s subsequent question.

On the neutering side of it , there are questions around vet capacity and when is the right time to neuter an XL Bull y. The legislation has different timings so that neutering is not expected when the dog is too young, which is quite important. Definitely it is something that we have done as inclusively as we possibly could, including with the devolved Administrations.

Q417 D r Hudson : Can I push you on the identification—the Chair is going to follow up on it—so that other dogs are not inadvertently caught up i n this? In identifying the type of dog, the capacity to do that at a local authority level and with dog legislation o fficers, because asking vets to do it is perhaps not the way forward, owners will have to come forward and identify their dogs. Are you confident that you have that support with dog legislation officers being trained to be able to facilitate enabling the p ublic to identify their dogs?

Absolutely. We are working very closely with the police on their capacity requirements and on training their dog legislation officers on how to identify an XL Bully. We are working with them and with the Home Of fice on their resourcing and providing them with extra resourcing to enable this to happen. The definition was drawn up very closely with the police to ensure that it was workable in practice.

There will be dogs with some of the characterist ics of an XL Bully breed, but we hope that we have defined it to a degree where the margin of error will be small. It is a serious attempt at identifying a new breed.

Q418 Dr Hudson : Can I press you on the neutering point? If people come forward and their dog is classified as an XL Bully, that will be an exempted dog and they will be able to keep the dog so long as it is neutered, insured, kept on a lead in public and muzzled and so on. If the animal is less than a year old on 31 January 2024, it must be neute red by the end of December 2024. If it is older than one year old on 31 January 2024, it must be neutered by 30 June 2024.

Last week , the British Veterinary Association wrote to the Chief Veterinary Officer, Christine Middlemiss, with what I believe is a very sensible solution, that if these dogs are kept on a lead and muzzled, that is trying to mitigate harms to people and other animals. We ultimately do not want these dogs to be breeding. After December this year , it will be illegal to breed from these d ogs. These large-breed dogs, if you neuter them too young, potentially under 18 months, it may increase their risk at a later date in their life of developing diseases such as developmental orthopaedic diseases or other medical conditions, cancers and so on. Th erefore, a reasonable suggestion coming forward is if you could extend the deadline for dogs that are under seven months of age on 31 January 2024 to the end of June 2025. All that is doing is adding an extra six months, but if these dogs are on a lead and muzzled they are deemed safe.

Would the Government look at that? If you move to meet a very sensible and scientifically and clinically indicated suggestion, you will help the hearts and minds of the veterinary profession. I know from personal experience, having spoken to many vets, that they are struggling with this. There are a number of vets who, like me, support the ban, but there are a significant number who are against it. I firmly believe that if you work with them and adopt sensible recommendations that are not going to change the safety of the implementation of the ban, you will have more success with that. Can you take that on board?
It is certainly something that I will discuss with Christine Middlemiss. Were you aware of this?
Mar c Casale: It was a relatively recent letter.
Dr Hudson : It was a letter last week to Christine Middlemiss.
Yes, so it is under consideration.

We need to take this forward. If a small change can be made that carries more pe ople in the profession with us, I am very happy to look at it. There may be other factors that have created the particular dates that we have, but I want to make sure that this is as smart a piece of legislation as we can deliver.

Q419 Dr Hudson : Thank you. I t is reassuring that you will consider that. The other concern, and something that I keep saying to people, is that if these dogs are deemed safe people can keep them. They will be licensed and they will be able to keep them under certain conditions. That is why I said in the debate yesterday that we need to be very careful not to be using the language of cull or kill and things like that. However, something that will happen from this is that the dogs that are not deemed safe and are not able to be kept, ul timately a number of them will be euthanised moving forward. That has created a lot of disquiet in the veterinary profession but also in the animal welfare charity sector as well about capacity and what that means for the mental health of the staff involve d with that. Again , can I encourage you to keep those organisations around the table and move a little with them? The ban is coming and we need to make it work , but we need to make sure that people o n the frontline impacted by this are supported through th is as well.

I will certainly keep them in mind and I will keep discussing with them, as I will the heart - rending stories of people who have been severely injured and families of people who have been killed. This is an issue that has caused a bsolute outrage among large numbers of the population. No form of legislation will be perfect. Most of these animals are still going to be around , but the number of them that exist in the community means that the Government have to act. I think that it is a real shame that it is not happening right across the UK. However, I want to make sure that we are working with people, understanding that it is not the dog’s fault that it has this congenital condition that can sometimes, in some cases, change its charac ter in a nanosecond and it can do horrendous things. We have to be humane and we have to work with the keepers of these animals to understand that we are just trying to keep our communities safe. There is a perfectly good middle path, where they will keep the dog alive, subject to certain conditions.

Q420 Dr Hudson : Thank you, Minister. As you quite rightly say, we need to bear in mind public safety and the safety of other animals. Some people say that we should be judging the animals on the deed not the breed , but as far as I and many people are concerned, once that deed is committed it is too late. A child or adult is maimed, if not worse, so we have to try to find, as you say, that middle ground to keep people and animals safe. What I am urging is to keep th e stakeholders around the table so that we can make this ban work compassionately, sensitively and practically.

Some key groups have already been helping with messaging to get to different audiences and with guidance on how to use a muzzle i n the right way and how to train your dog to use a muzzle. That has been very supportive.

Q421 Certainly when we considered this measure as a Committee , you had the unanimous cross-party support of this Committee in what you are bringing forward. Some of the stories that we have heard about people being attacked, and dog-on-dog attacks, much of which is not reported, mean that these measures needed to be brought forward.

One question was raised in the debate yesterday that I do not think that Minister S pencer addressed comprehensively. It was the bit about defining the breed. You have said that you have laid out parameters stating that the dog meets a substantial number of various physical characteristics to be in scope. There may be some case law where people challenge some of these assessments. When you say a substantial adherence to the definition, are we talking about 50%, 90%? How are we going to measure whether this is an XL Bully if people challenge it?

That term is currently used, for example, for the application of the G overnment specification for a P itbull T errier. There is not a particular figure attached to what “substantial” means. It provides the police with some flexibility. Definitely with an XL Bully , one absolute requirement is the minimum height, which is specified in the definition. If that minimum height is not met, the dog is not an XL Bully, irrespective of whether everything else in the definition is met. You have things called p ocket b ul lies, which are the same but just a bit smaller. They look the same , but they are smaller. They are not covered by it. For the rest of it, it has never been specified whether “substantial” means 50% or 90%. In practice it is a significant majority. Trained dog legislation officers know what they are looking for. They have told us that they think that it will be a lot simpler to identify an XL Bully than a P itbull T errier, for example.

Q422 When I was looking on the internet at dogs for sale, or offered free to a good home in many cases, they were described as XL Bullies, the photographs looked as we would expect an XL Bully to look and in many cases they showed photographs of the parents of the dogs and in some cases the grandparents as well. While there may be people challenging some of these definitions, most people out there know what an XL Bully is. When the Committee was at Battersea, they had some XL Bully pups and they had no compunction in describing these almost newborn pups as XL Bullies. In mos t people’s minds , I suspect that they will know what one is, but you will, I guess, receive some challenges.

There may also be people who are scared that their dog might fall within the definition and they do not want to become a criminal by not registerin g it, or other people who are confident that their dog does not and then subsequently the police intervene and say that it is. Are we clear that we will be able to reassure people who have dogs that do not meet the definition that they will not fall foul o f the law, particularly looking at the old - time bulldogs, which was raised with me by a colleague earlier?

If you have a type of dog that is known by another name because it is a different breed, that is not an XL Bully. We have had people w riting to us that they have a Rottweiler that meets many of the specifications, is it an XL B ully. The answer is no, it is a Rottweiler, as you have told us. If it is known to be a different kind of breed, it is not an XL Bully. It is as simple as that.
Q423 Do you think that there are people who might think that they do not want to fall foul of the law so they will register it anyway to be on the safe side? is that possibly going to happen?

Normally you would type one of these dogs whe n they are old enough, which might be when they are 18 months old. If somebody had a younger dog or a puppy and they were not entirely sure, such as those puppies that you saw at Battersea, they could choose to get a certificate of exemption and, in effect , to decide that they are an XL Bully. In due course if they had doubts that it was an XL Bully because it grew up and did not necessarily accord too closely with the photos and the definition, we are exploring what the mechanism would be for them to dereg ister.

Q424 That is something that we had not been aware of before. That might reassure some people who might want to be on the safe side, but do not want to have to muzzle a dog and restrict its freedom in a way that if it was a Bully they might have to.

Yes. We have encouraged people to adopt a cautious approach, to apply for a certificate of exemptio n at the outset, by adopting that approach. In due course , we will have to consider what the arrangements are if someone’s dog clearly is not an XL Bully once it grows up. I may have seen the same puppies that you saw, and it was not evident to me that the y were going to be XL Bullies.
Q425 That is quite reassuring for people who have raised concerns. Who would make the assessment that the dog was not an XL Bully?
The owner.
Q426 The owner themselves could decide to deregister?
Marc C asale: No, we have to further clarify how that aspect of the process would work , but initially it is for the owner to decide whether their dog is an XL Bully or not.
Q427 Your advice would be to err on the safe side and register and when the dog is f ully grown possibly deregister. I am asking would it be just the owner’s decision or would a vet be able to help?
Dr Hudson : The British Veterinary Association has said that it does not want vets to be the people adjudicating. It would be dog legislation officers. Do you have the capacity to help owners?

That is what we are working on at the moment with the police and their capacity , and the capability and the training. We are looking 18 months ahead, so that aspect of the process is still being ironed out.
That is very helpful for the people who have contacted us.

Q428 Dr Hudson : It might be more urgent, because it will perhaps be ironed out as those animals get older, but in the next few weeks people will have to be clear whether the y have a Bully or not. One of the things that the veterinary sector has been pushing for is will the owners have the support to identify whether they have one of these dogs, with the dog legislation officers?

Dog liaison officers are proceed ing with training right across police authority areas. These are starting to answer some of these questions. Ultimately, the responsibility rests with the owner. If the owner does not comply, they will be contravening the law.

Q429 Minister, you have m ade it clear that this is not a mass cull of XL Bullies and that there is a procedure that people can use. However, there is a £200 compensation claim available for people who euthanise their XL Bullies. Given that the cost of registering would be the cost of the neutering, the public liability insurance and the £92.40 fee for a certificate of exemption, is there a risk that you are creating an incentive for euthanasia of these dogs with this compensation package?

I really hope not. I know th at this is a difficult time for owners of these dogs , and they will be looking to see the breed guidelines and whether their dogs comply and what it will cost. I do not think so. That is not our evidence. Our evidence is that most owners will want to keep their dog alive at all costs, will want to stay withi n the law and will comply. That has been the experience of the other four breeds that are on the dangerous dogs register. It is an attempt to be as near to perfect as we can be , but we are not going to sit in front of you and try to pretend that this will be the end of this problem. There will be people who will sit outside the law or there will be other breeds that will emerge and we could be looking at amending this in the future. We want to make that for this breed and the particular issues that have bee n caused because of it that we are doing all that we can to prevent any more attacks.

Q430 Do you think that Scotland is playing a very dangerous political game in this area, given that if there is an attack next year from a dog that is out in public w ithout a muzzle, that could be as a direct result of a political decision made at Holyrood?

I do not know what reason it had for not following what Wales is doing, what we are doing here and in Northern Ireland. It must be held to account fo r decisions that are devolved and it is for it to take. However, it would be a great help for all of the people involved — the expertise of the police, which will be shared across different police authorities, the experience of local authorities, the experie nce of the veterinary profession — if there was a UK-wide determination to tackle this problem. I am not going to presume that there is some political motive for just wanting to be different. We work very well with the devolved authorities on many of these i ssues, and secondary legislation is something that we are constantly trying to get agreement on, and usually do across things like UKIM and other areas. It is a matter of huge regret that Scotland has decided not to go down this route.

Q431 If an Engli sh XL Bully owner who has registered their dog quite correctly decides to take it for a walk in Scotland, will they still be required to muzzle their dog and keep it on a lead in public areas?
That is a very good question. I do not think tha t they will.
Not in Scotland.
No, they would not. They could take a dog from England and walk it in Scotland and it would not be under this legislation. Therefore, the answer is that they would not have to muzzle it.

Q432 What about the other way round, where a dog that does not need to be registered in Scotland is brought to England? Would that dog be allowed to run free in England or would that dog not be allowed to be brought into the English jurisdiction?

If they brought it to England for whatever reason, it would have to comply. It would have to be registered, neutered and subject to all the other measures to fulfil the exemption. That is what currently exists.

Q433 If they want to come on holiday to north Yorkshire, for example, and bring their XL Bully with them, they will not be able to do that? They will have to leave the dog in kennels in Scotland, in effect.
Yes.

Q434 Minister, you touched on the Christmas-tree effect of am ending legislation so much that it fail s . I have had many constituents raise the subject of the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991. Indeed, many organisations we spoke to and took evidence from outlined how defective a piece of legislation it is. The Association of D ogs and Cats Homes said that it was a byword for poor legislation and done in haste, and evidence points to this. Dog bites alone went up 70% in Alder Hey Children’s Hospital in my constituency , and 10,000 people needed hospital treatment nationally. Can y ou reassure us that by bolting on XL Bully legislation to this flawed framework it will not be counterproductive to improving public safety and that we will not get the Christmas-tree effect that you spoke about before?

This is a genuine attempt to tackle a problem that has emerged since the Dangerous Dogs Act. There were no XL Bullies until a relatively few years ago. Is this going to be the end of it? I suspect not, because there are people breeding dogs in all parts o f the world. One of the dogs on the dangerous dogs register is the Dogo Argentino. That was obviously bred in another part of the world and identified as being a problem here. We want to make sure that we are fleet of foot, if we start seeing other attacks from other species of dogs, that we can do this. I cannot sit in front of you and say that this will resolve the problem. It is a fact that the four breeds that are on there, am I right, there has not been—
No dog on the list—Pitbull Terrie rs, Dogo Argentino, Fila Brasileiro and the Japanese Tosa—has been involved in any fatality or any attack.
That is a tempting-providence thing to say.
Q435 You think that this is the best way to cover the legislation. Is there any way it could have been made more effective? We know that it is a flawed piece of legislation.

You can go through all Acts and have a long list of improvements that w e could make, including this one. There is a question mark around what you would put in its place that was any better and how long it would take to do that and whether fundamentally it would still be a regime that seeks to place restrictions on the riskies t dogs that generate the highest risks for public safety.

I entirely understand where your constituents are coming from, but I would throw it back to them and ask: what do we do? All of us have a responsibility to keep people safe. If this l egislation is wrong, what is the alternative? What exists out there to prevent some of these awful experiences from happening? We are happy to look around the world. We are not exclusive. We have more dogs per head of population, second only to Ukraine, or is Ukraine second to us? We have a very high number of dogs per people here, some of them living in extremely close proximity to large families and dense populations. We are learning every day, every year, from experts about this but we do not have the fi nal answer. We think that this is the best way and it is the responsible action to take.
Good answer, thanks.
Thank you very much, Minister, for your evidence today, and Mr Casale, for coming along and helping where necessary, which w as not very often. Thank you very much indeed.

sessions.w: Nigel Huddleston (House of Commons); Doug Stoneham (HMRC); Matthew Henty (HM Treasury); Zoë Nettlefield (HMRC)

segs.tx: Economic Affairs Committee
Finance Bill Sub-Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Draft Finance Bill 2023-24
Wednesday 29 November 2023
Watch the meeting
Members present: Lord Leigh of Hurley (The Chair); Lord Altrincham ; Lord Palmer of Childs Hill; Lord Roborough; Lord Rooker; Lord Stevenson of Balmacara; Baroness Valentine.
Evidence Session No. 6 Heard in Public Questions 71 - 9 3
Witnesses

I : Nigel Huddleston MP, Financial Secretary to the Treasury and Member of Parliament for Mid Worcestershire; Doug Stoneham, Deputy Director of Policy and Technical , Counter Avoidance Directorate , HMRC; Matthew Henty, Deputy Director, Enterprise and Property Tax, HM Treasury; Zoë Nettlefield, Deputy Director, Strategic Data Policy, HMRC.
Examination of witnesses
Nigel Huddleston, Matthew Henty, Doug Stoneham and Zoë Nettlefield .

Q71 Welcome, everyone, to the evidence session with the Financial Secretary to the Treasury and his colleagues from departments . We are dealing with four issues this morning: the measures dealing with promoters of tax avoidance ; the measures increasing the maximum sentence for tax fraud ; the measure merging the two existing R&D schemes and the introduction of a new R&D scheme for intensive SMEs; and the measure that requires taxpayers to provide additional data to HMRC. I invite the Minister and colleagues to introduce themselves and then we will start the questioning.

Good morning. It is a pleasure to be here. I am the relatively newly appointed Financial Secretary to the Treasury ; I was appointed just two and a bit weeks ago in a somewhat busy period. Therefore, it is with great relief that I am at this committee with some excellent members of the team from the Treasury — I know how you go into the details— and I will invite them to introduce themselves.
I am the deputy director for enterprise and property tax , and within the team we have R&D tax credits.
I am the deputy director for policy and technical in HMRC’s Counter Avoidance Directorate.
I am deputy director for strategic data policy in HM Revenue and Customs.

Q72 Thank you. Can we start off with promoters? Generally, there has been a warm welcome to the direction of travel and the proposals. Some witnesses felt that there was a strong case for letting the civil measures , which have been out for a while, bed down before moving to a criminal sanction. Would you agree? Would you not like to spend a bit more time finding out how the civil regime goes before you go on to other sanctions?

Civil can work in many cases , but the criminal element elevates it to show how important the issue is and how seriously we take it. Across this whole thing — we will probably talk a lot about this today — we want to make sure that , when we have incidents of avoidance in this area, particularly given its large scale , it very clear that it is not the taxman who is suffering here ; it is the taxpayer. It is having a huge impact on public service provision and looking after the most needy in society. Therefore, the criminal side is very important. That does not mean that we are ignoring other processes, but it is important to elevate it to show how importantly we are taking this and why , therefore, we are bringing the new system in.
You do not feel the need to see how the civil system goes before moving to criminal .

As always in these things, we will carefully monitor the situation and see how it goes. I do think it is important , because it elevates and signals the importance. The signalling is important as well as the process.

Q73 Witnesses we heard from are concerned that the introduction of a criminal offence for promoters of avoidance schemes who do not comply with a stop notice gives HMRC more powers without additional safeguards. In particular, they feel that some independent oversight of HMRC’s decisions is necessary. Will you amend the legislation to provide for this?

I will ask Zoë to come in here in a minute. We will constantly monitor the situation. That will be a theme that you hear from me throughout today. However, we have decent systems and processes in place already that we are broadly comfortable with. HMRC takes its responsibilities very seriously and the people are incredibly professional. I am comfortable that if we do have incidents that are of concern, I will look at that in my ministerial responsibility as well as with HMRC.
Could someone touch on the safeguards that you have in place within HMRC?

We have a number of safeguards in place within HMRC in relation to the issuing of a stop notice in the first place. Technical experts and senior managers have to agree that it is appropriate to issue a stop notice. Once that process is complete, HMRC solicitors may need to be consulted, but the final decision on whether to issue a stop notice is taken by an independent senior civil servant in HMRC, so outside the Counter Avoidance Directorate where the work is being carried out.

Promoters can appeal to HMRC against a stop notice. If HMRC does not agree to withdraw the stop notice, the promoter can go to the tribunal to seek to have the stop notice withdrawn. It is also worth stressing that if we were to move into the criminal side of things on any of this work, that work would be taken forward in a different area of HMRC, its Fraud Investigation Service. Obviously, the decision to prosecute or not would be taken by the appropriate prosecuting authorities rather than in HMRC. Obviously, HMRC can seek to prosecute , but it would be for the Crown Prosecution Service in England and Wales or the appropriate authorities in Scotland and Northern Ireland to take the final decision to prosecute. There are a number of layers of governance in place.

We recognise that there are some concerns here and we are planning to publish a document setting out all the various safeguards that are in place. We can share that with the committee if that would be helpful.

Q74 Lord Roborough : My question is more for HMRC. Witnesses that we heard from were sceptical about the effectiveness of the criminal offence when so many promoters operate offshore. HMRC has said that international treaties can be used to bring them to book , but this seems to depend on extradition and the offence having a parallel in the other jurisdiction. Is the reality that the offence will not be effective against promoters based offshore?

We feel that introducing the new powers in the stop notice measure and the director disqualification measure gives us greater scope in the offshore space to utilise the network of tax treaties that you referred to. It is also worth suggesting that the vast majority of avoidance cases, or avoidance schemes coming through , that we see are still related to disguised remuneration schemes, where there will almost always be a UK footprint in place so that the UK company is able to offer employment services as part of the process.

So we feel that there is a multistrand approach that we can take, where , going down the criminal route , we have the director disqualification measure that is being introduced, which would apply offshore and well as onshore , and there is the ability to go after the UK-based element of it. We have a range of different powers in place that enable us to tackle the offshore side of things , but w e recognise that it is an area of concern.

Q75 I hope you can hear me . I apologise for not being present. We have heard evidence that a number of promoters are appointing stooge directors who have no direct knowledge of the business but would be under risk of criminal prosecution and disqualification. Would you consider amending the legislation so that it focuses more on the controlling minds behind the avoidance activity , and provide a reasonable exemption for those who might be called stooge directors?

It is a good point , and I have discussed this with the team since I was appointed. We want to make sure that the right people are targeted here. We probably all share the concern that there are probably some naive, young individuals who are trapped or taken advantage of , and this can be pretty harsh treatment for them. But the reality is that anybody taking on these roles has a responsibility to know what they are letting themselves in for. There will probably be a mechanism for a bit of leniency in the processes and in any criminal sanctions at a later stage.

However, we need to take this seriously, and there are too many stooge directors. We have seen that across a range of sectors. Again, I think we have the balance right . The mechanism will allow us to go after the shadow directors and controlling minds as well, but s tooge directors are a real problem , and it is not one or the other; we now have a mechanism to go after all.
My question is a simple one. I can see a stooge director being taken on the first time. Might I suggest that you think about what happens when they do it more than once?

To be honest, t hat is the point here. We need to get tougher on the s erial offenders of worst abuses, because there is a perception of too much leniency at the moment. I wanted to give some level of sympathy to the real edge case that we could all have on a human level when I made those comments a few minutes ago, but the reality is that the vast majority of people know exactly what they are doing in these cases and are trying it on, to call it sympathetically.

Q76 I have a question for the Minister on the maximum sentence. HMRC does not seem to have any evidence about what deterrent value the maximum sentence for fraud may or may not have . In fact, it has only just begun research on this. Is this measure more of a statement about the Government’s attitude to tax fraud rather than an effective additional deterrent?

It was a manifesto commitment, which is important in terms of parliamentary process and the way the country is run. We endeavour to implement manifesto commitments wherever possible. However, similar to the answer I gave earlier, it is an important signal of how seriously we take these crimes and offences, because there is an impact.
