In a fully decarbonised economy, we are looking at up to 500 million tonnes, roughly a five times increase, and potentially up to 800 tonnes when you take into account high-case assumptions. It is a very significant increase in the volumes we need.

I agree that there are lots of places where we can use it, and I very much agree that , in the long term , supplying it will be the challenge. In the short term, however, I think the challenge that we face is a challenge on the demand side. At the moment, while costs are starting to come down towards $2 a kilogram —that is a threshold that a lot of the people who are very excited about the hydrogen economy are looking at, because when we reach $2 a kilogram it unlocks a lot of other uses — in order to get there, there is very much a green premium in using hydrogen versus the fossil alternative.

In steel production , for instance, if you want to do green steel hydrogen direct reduction, with green hydrogen, there is a premium of around 30% versus the fossil alternative; I can double-check this and come back to you. [1] That is very significant from a business-to-business perspective. It is relatively trivial when you pass that all the way through to the end consumer in terms of what the price of that increase in steel cost does to the price of a house. Once you filter it through the economy it is low, but from a business-to-business perspective it is significant. In unlocking the hydrogen economy, for other sectors and for hydrogen in the electricity system, it will be an absolutely crucial role.

The demand-side policies that effectively enable people to start using it now, even though there is a green premium, can be a form of contracts for difference or buyers’ clubs ’ voluntary green premiums ; we have seen a lot of industry clubbing together to say that they will pay more. If it is carbon price and carbon taxes that bridge that gap, in the short term we know that we can start producing either blue or green now. There are lots of projects going ahead. In the short term, it is who will pay for using it when it is a higher cost. That is absolutely the chicken and egg. We need to start using it in order to drive down the cost.
Baroness Neville-Jones : It is the politicians’ problem.

Q41 Assuming that how you see the future is correct, could you set out the regulatory issues with novel projects such as long-duration energy storage, which you have been talking about, entering the grid? Which regulatory or planning authorities have a key role to play in enabling long-duration energy storage to be deployed on the grid?

As a subsidiary, because we are short of time, are those regulators actually doing enough? Is there sufficient capacity in the regulators at present to assess, and indeed develop, commercial and regulatory arrangements for different storage technologies? A very short answer, please.

I would like to raise and then pass on from one very quickly, which is the planning system. It is not an area in which I am an expert, but it is a major obstacle to any large-scale energy infrastructure.
To anything, actually .

I have no magic silver bullet for it. I spent some time on the board of a company that was trying to develop a natural gas storage site in north-west England using old ICI salt caverns, and I was absolutely staggered at the extent of local resistance for a facility that, once built, would be pretty well invisible. Essentially, it was an objection to any development on the rural landscape. That is a major blockage to most large-scale energy projects. I have to mention it, but I have no particular experience or bright ideas.

If we switch to the other obvious area, which is energy regulation, we may need a change in mindset. Ofgem has, in the past, tended to regard storage projects as a user of the system. There was a big debate about whether a storage facility, for instance, should be charged both on input and export from the site: that is, as a consumer and a producer. That has tended to be rationalised so that we avoid double paying, but there is an argument for saying that storage is part of the energy system rather than a commercial user of it. You could imagine a world in which storage assets of whatever sort do not pay transmission and distribution charges at all, and T&D charges are paid by people who inject the energy into the system at first use, essentially, and by consumers who take it out.

There is room for some quite radical thinking on that, but it needs a policy direction, which probably is not there, to push the regulator into it. One of your subsidiary questions was about policy. It is not so much about policy; it is a strategy. We need a national strategy that says, “This is what we think hydrogen is for. Here are the priority uses. Here is what we think might be the volumes”. That gives commercial developers the framework to work within when planning things, and the regulator the framework to think about how you achieve potentially radical changes. Regulation tends to be much better at dealing with incremental change than radical change; you have to think differently about transformational change. So I think we probably need to do some thinking about the overall approach.

I want to pick up another point , because Ita has mentioned it. People talk about the use of surplus renewables as a really good way of making hydrogen. That is absolutely true . It is really irritating to have large quantities of wind generation stuck behind transmission constraints and unable to be used, but the volume that would come from that is not enough. We must not just think of hydrogen manufacture as a way of making use of cheap renewable energy that would otherwise be unused. We need to set up the system so that we can make it in larger scale than that, and have the electrolysers located where they need to be rather than necessarily right next to a wind farm. Those would be my starters.

I absolutely agree on the planning and permitting. The strategic vision point that you made is also crucial for that planning and permitting. They all fall together. The difference is that a lot of our regulatory systems, given the system that has been operating for the last 30 or 40 years, have reasonably assumed a steady state, but our electricity usage in the UK has been declining, not doubling. It is a radical mindset shift for that system. At the same time, we have a new strategic objective, in the sense of wanting to decarbonise. That is an additional directive. In that context, where we are looking at a system that might need to double in size versus the steady state that has been operating, where we are talking about a fundamental shift of the technologies, the strategic vision is really important .

The only other piece I would add is that the capacity market is important from a storage perspective. We need to make sure that the capacity market can allow all technologies to compete, including demand-side response storage and generation into the capacity market. We also need to make sure that it recognises that some of the long-duration storage options—for instance, pumped hydro , which can play an important role in the middle—have much longer timeframes. At the moment , the capacity market allows for bids to deliver up to four years in advance. That is not going to cut it for pumped hydro. Within that strategic vision, what are the different timeframes that will allow us to have the optimum mix of technologies?
That is very helpful . T hank you.

Q42 I would like to ask the witnesses about possible business models for generating long-duration energy storage because of the large upfront capital investment and the fact that the assets may only be used in certain circumstances, as you have already described. W hat sort of business models ought the Government to consider, and what factors should they take into account in fulfilling their commitment to provide a business model by the beginning of next year?
Are there examples of successful market arrangements that the Government could learn from? Would a national energy company, as proposed by Labour, be useful? What would it do if it were useful?

Can I enlarge on my experience with gas storage in the context of the business model? We spent many years modelling like mad the prospects for a large-scale gas storage plant. That was 10 years ago. It was in a period when gas prices were relatively stable and had been for some years. That continued through to 2019 or thereabouts. There was not enough revenue from the level of volatility in the market to give you the confidence to go ahead with a very big, very long-term investment. In particular, there was not the evidence to persuade debt providers. Essentially, it became an equity proposition and was much too risky for any likely provider of equity.

As an aside, had we built it, it would have made enough money in the last two years to pay for itself many times over, given the level of volatility we found we had, as opposed to what we could predict and rely on at the time. That makes the point. Commercial models will work over the long term, but they probably will not get built unless you provide some support to give the confidence to go ahead. At the very minimum you need to provide a commercial model that allows the developer to recover enough money to pay debt costs. Then you need an incentivisation, in the form of equity return, to use the asset at its maximum optimum efficiency. So you need to think about it in those terms.

It is not a new problem. We have come across it in various areas. We have a range of ways of getting things done. We have used contracts for difference for renewa b l e generation. We use a cap and floor regime in the electricity and gas interconnectors. We use the capacity market for generation. We do not necessarily need to invent anything new, but we need to think constructively about how to achieve the desired effect for an asset that is very long term and not necessarily used very often. Of the things I have mentioned, the best starting point for a regulatory model to produce a commercial proposition is probably the cap and floor regime, because it absolutely addresses the basic point that you need to pay for the debt. Then it provides a sensible balance of return for the equity holder.

I would do it slightly differently. I would not have an absolute cap. I would have a sliding scale so that the benefit is more and more to the consumer the more the asset gets used. None of these projects will be developed without an explicit or implicit consumer guarantee. Essentially, it is the consumer that pays. Things get built on the basis that they will : either through a RAB model, a contract for difference or whatever. If you are giving a very long-term deal to an unpredictable asset, you need to make sure that the more it is used, the more the benefit goes back to the consumer. A cap and floor regime that protects the debt return and then thinks constructively about incentivising efficient long-term use is probably the right sort of idea.

I will throw in another little special interest. As you said, I am chairman of Mutual Energy in Northern Ireland, which is a mutual company. It owns the interconnectors between Scotland and Northern Ireland, and it owns a chunk of the gas transmission system. It has a very straightforward arrangement. The company can pass through all its costs to the consumers. There is an absolute guarantee from the regulator that that is the case. In return, they expect us to be efficient and, when we make money, to return it to consumers.

That works really well . With that backstop to the consumer, we can raise very cheap long-term debt finance. It has been a very good way of financing the interconnectors to Northern Ireland. I can see potentially quite wide-ranging use of it as a business model in doing long-term assets. It would not remove the need for something like a cap and floor regime, because you have to remunerate the debt providers, but it is a different way of thinking about it that I think would be worth going into.
Ita, would you like to add anything?

Yes. T hat was incredibly useful. Keeping the system vision in mind when thinking about the cost to the system, as you move towards a renewable-dominated system, what we should be seeing, and are seeing, at the system level for generation is that costs decline. As penetration of wind and solar— n ow the cheapest form of generation—increases, the costs decline relative to the existing system. All the way up to about 80% penetration levels those costs continue to decline, and the system gets cheaper. Once you hit that 80%, you turn a curve in the cost of delivering the generation , because you are meeting the seasonal and daily storage gaps, which are more expensive. The assets that you need to meet that challenge are themselves expensive. Therefore, you need to use the right mechanisms to make sure that you can pay for them. At a system level, the system as a whole is probably in many cases still cheaper than the alternative—today’s system.

When we are talking about that and understanding what we are doing, we are effectively finding mechanisms to have a small number of quite expensive assets balanced by a very large number of cheaper assets. At a system level, we are therefore better off for consumers and for the users of energy. That is a useful context.

There was a supplementary about examples of it being done. The gas industry has always been very good at producing storage to support consumer demand. If companies have customers and need to supply them, they do that quite effectively. Where it becomes more difficult is when you have a strategic need, either for security of supply or now for the increasing requirements brought in by decarbonisation. It is hard to think of good business models around the world that already exist for doing that.

Do you think it is feasible to have the same business support model to support the predictable seasonal element of the storage as you have for the unpredictable climate-dependent wind/drought, where you do not know whether the strategic storage will be needed or not?
It goes back to what I have just said, essentially. The commercial approach to storage will tend to deal with predictable fluctuations in consumer demand, but it will not go beyond that unless—
You are saying that the same model will not work for both of those two elements. You will have to think differently about them.
Yes. You could bring it all together, but they are two different things , and it may or may not be sensible to do them in the same way.
With the really unpredictable storage needs , the strategic reserves model is also a model we can look to. As I say, we have done that before , but largely not in a commercial model.
You could, of course, have the same facility providing some of both—some of the long-term strategic and responding to the seasonal.
Large-scale cavern storage will do both.
How do you incentivise two business models on the same asset?

We have that already. Obviously, we are talking about long duration here, but in the shorter duration market we already have revenue stacking, where the same projects might bid into multiple different markets. We have the capacity markets. We have multiple different markets now and we have the same projects that take their revenue from the merchant market over their project lifetime, potentially some from CfDs and others. We have examples where developers will look at multiple different mechanisms to make the economics of the project add up.

The way to do both is to combine commercial arrangements to cover the predictable stuff with some sort of mandated requirement for the strategic element of storage. You see that in the European gas market now. People have worked out that storage needs to be full for the winter, so there are mandated levels of storage in the run-up to winter. You could have something similar applied to otherwise commercial storage sites, dealing with the more predictable variations.
Is deciding on the business model one of the most difficult elements in the whole issue of setting up storage, or do you think it is pretty solvable if people put their minds to it?

It was a question about commercial arrangements. The arrangements for storage in that sense are a relatively complex but solvable problem. The blockages at the moment are more about creating a clear, credible long-term strategy and dealing with the time delay problem, particularly planning but also all the stuff you get with big, long-range infrastructure projects.

Q43 My question is partially about planning and the use of the national grid. One of the major concerns we have heard from previous witnesses is the long wait times that exist for being connected to the national grid. Are we progressing fast enough? Are we getting grid and electricity infrastructures ready for future demand? What do you think about the policy areas that need focus to reduce the waiting times? That is one set of questions.

The other set concerns planning. Some people say that the connection queue is a long-standing problem and that some proposals are the result of the project’s place in the queue rather than when it was actually submitted . Is that a real issue? Generally, do you think that the planning system is a barrier to developing long-duration energy storage and the necessary supporting infrastructure? From what has just been said, I suspect that the answer is yes. Could you tackle that group of questions?

I will take the first one, which is essentially about the queue. That has been a problem for as long as I have been involved in energy regulation—20 years—and it has got longer because we have never introduced a prioritisation system, as it was quite hard to tell which were credible projects and which were not. Once you start interfering with the queue it becomes very contentious. If we are to make the transformational change that we are talking about, we will have to rethink that. Nick Winser produced a report for the Government on the whole question of transmission investment and so on, which I will not bother going into.

One addition to that is that we need a way to prioritise the queue. When I arrived here today there was a very long queue, but I was given a pass that allowed me to go to the front, otherwise I could have been late. We need to introduce some sort of assessment of consumer benefit in projects. When Ofgem receives a proposal for an interconnector project, one of the things it does is a cost-benefit analysis. It looks at both ends of the interconnector. If the numbers add up on an overall consumer benefit scoring system, it tends to give approval for the project. You need a way of fast-tracking high consumer benefit projects through the connection queue. Again, the technology exists. We know how to do the economic analysis. It might be contentious , because people who are in the queue will not want to be overtaken.

One idea I heard was to prioritise in terms of delivery date. That is not the answer. That would simply prioritise short-cycle projects. You need something that says, “This project is really important . It needs a connection on such-and-such a date. It will get it”.

I refer back to the idea that we have been developing around system transformation versus BAU. The grid processing queue was developed in a world where there might be two, three or four major thermal plants a year. Now, the E SO is receiving around 1,600 applications a year. I understand that there are 390 gigawatts of clean power projects currently in the queue. To meet the 2030 targets as set out, we would only actually need 140 of those gigawatts to come through, but they are all still in the queue and the queue is not moving fast enough .

There is potentially a need to look at the queue as it stands today to manage that backlog. I absolutely agree that the idea of queue management is critical. It is a holistic assessment that comes back to having a clear strategic vision of what the system needs as a whole not only in the generation that has been added but, critically, in the storage. As we said, that was not something we were looking at in the past. A key strategic piece that might be part of that is the regional view, looking at projects within a region. Are they important projects from a system balancing perspective? Are they col l ocated so that we could do something at the same time? Is there a group of projects that could be moved forward together?

That aligns to thinking about networks more broadly and the importance of having a strategic vision for where generation and consumption will be in the future, allowing us to think potentially about a more strategic approach to building transmission and distribution. If we know that we want to connect 20 projects in an area of the sea over the next 15 years, we can build that transmission line in anticipation of those projects, rather than each of those projects having to submit individually to connect back to the grid.

It is a critical issue. It is a barrier to storage projects and generation projects, but the answer will require going back to what we are trying to do and the period of time in which we are trying to do it, and therefore which of the projects meets the priority. We should work with those first.

Do I understand you to be saying that the adequacy of National Grid’s capacity is itself related to other questions that need to be solved, and that it is not a question that you can answer in isolation from having decided its relationship to the strategy that we do not have?

A strategy or policy statement that actually covered , in a convincing fashion, what the Government see as the requirements would give a context that would make it much easier for National Grid and the regulator to solve the queue problem.

Related to that, if we are building the renewable system of the future, we need to think of it as a system. Generation is part of it. Transmission and distribution become critically important when you have a renewable-dominated system, because where the wind blows best might not be where the consumption is. You have to move the electrons around more. As we have talked about at length, the storage is critical. Without that storage, the system does not balance.

The power network, storage plans and generation plans need to be planned together holistically. Currently t here is a network that is gradually iterated and built upon , there are some generation plans and then there is a storage plan. If you do not design the plan to think across those three, you will not get a system-optimal result. You will not get some of the benefits that the system can bring. It will not be as cheap and it will not be as reliable for consumers and users. The design of that system must be less siloed than it has been in the past.
Is it feasible to develop business models for the individual elements that will drive the market to do the right thing to give you an integrated system?

It is absolutely feasible. We have been doing it on many different elements. The step that we need to take is a clearer strategic vision. For instance, there is a strategic vision at the overall policy level that allows the regulators to take a strategic approach—
What is in the strategic vision? You keep saying that there is a strategic vision. What precisely does the strategic vision spell out?
It would effectively cover how we think the system would optimally evolve to meet generation needs in 10 or 20 years.
It would specify what the system is made up of.

It would specify the types of technologies that we believe we need. It would give us the framework by which further work can be undertaken to understand for instance spatially where that might be. We know we want this much offshore wind and we have said we roughly think this is the right amount for our system. Where are our options? Where do we think we would need to develop? Okay, there are these different sites. The network would then need to be able to connect to those sites. Where would we place storage to optimise the storage uses against those? Effectively, there is a spatial element to the plan that we perhaps do not have at the moment . It would also allow the grid provider to think about anticipatory investments.

At the moment , the grid can think primarily only about what the system needs are now . Even if the system might need double that in a particular location in 10 years, it cannot take that into account in current decision-making on developing an asset. Allowing it to take into account where we think this will go will be a critical part.

I have used the word “strategy” here quite deliberately. In my mind, a strategy is very different from a plan. I think what is needed is a strategy. It is a vision. It is what sort of energy system we expect to have by 2040 or 2050, as op posed to a detailed plan for getting there, but it needs to set out the big building blocks that we expect to have: “This is the order of magnitude of renewable generation. We expect it to be located roughly here. We expect to need this much hydrogen storage”, et cetera, as opposed to, “Here’s a very detailed road map”. It is an overarching vision of what the system will need to deliver by 2030, 2040 or 2050, and then a request, please, to get on with it that I do not think we quite have in place.
Do we think the future system operator will be able to deliver that? In a way, it is going towards a plan. It says what our system looks like and where it is by 2050.

It will help in the context of the electricity system, but what I am talking about is much wider. The question of where we use hydrogen, and whether it is best used in electricity generation, domestic heating or industrial heat, will not be addressed by a future system operator. It will want to think about it, but that is more a political strategy or vision question.
But do you think, in the electricity part of it, the future system operator has the right powers and tools to deliver it?

To be honest, I have not looked in enough detail at how it has been set up to answer that. The concept is a good one. We need rather more planning in the system operation than we have had, as opposed to day-to-day operation.
Ita, do you have any thoughts on that?
No. Indeed, I have not looked in enough detail at exactly what is being proposed for the overall need for additional management of the system. I will leave it there.
Q44 This nicely leads on from what you have been saying. You have answered quite a lot of it in looking at the strategy, vision and possible lack of it.

The current Government have a target of a fully decarbonised electricity grid by 2035, and the Opposition have that ambition by 2030. Are developments currently on track in any shape or form to achieve the long-duration energy storage necessary for either of those? If they are not, what would your priorities be to make those goals feasible?

Overall, I would say that we are not fully on track. If we are to hit those 2035 and 2030 requirements, and if we do it in the lowest-cost way and using the wind and solar resources that we have available in the UK, we are probably not on track to have sufficient storage operational, both short and long term.

Part of that is the planning and permitting queues that we have been talking about. Quite a lot of projects are being discussed, but they are just not getting to connect. On the long-duration side—we have alluded to this—I have spoken about the excess electricity, but beyond the potential for curtailed electricity, we will need wind and solar for green hydrogen production. We are not yet at the pace where we are confident that we will be able to hit the wind and solar needs for direct electricity generation. On the 50 gigawatts, we would need to do eight gigawatts a year in the next three auction rounds in the UK, which is quite an ask, given that the latest auction round had zero. That is only to meet the direct electrification requirements. We would probably need additional wind and solar for the production of green hydrogen that could then be used for long-duration energy storage. So w e are not quite on track, although we are making a lot of progress.

In terms of the key policy priorities, we have talked a lot about planning and permitting and the grid. The power market design reforms of the types that we have been discussing will be crucial to provid ing that long-term business model. There is probably a piece around using hubs and cluster approaches as a potential location to support some of the long-duration energy storage, alongside the other industry users that we have talked about.

I agree that we are not completely on track. We are on track to get quite a long way towards those targets, but I do not think that competitive bidding for a date to decarbonise electricity is a particularly good way to think about it. We are already at dates when our ability to deliver the necessary infrastructure, particularly storage, is questionable. We have discussed the things that need to be done for storage. Insisting on targets for decarbonising the electricity network that run ahead of our ability to deliver the necessary storage is probably not very constructive. To get to 90% of the targets is relatively doable, but getting to 100% is much more expensive and might be better done later with better technology and so on. I would focus on storage and then have the target for decarbonising electricity related to our ability to put in place the flexibility systems generally that are needed to go with that.
Do you get any sense that either grouping, as it were—the current Government or possibly a future Government—is coming to the conclusion that you have just indicated?
I am sorry, I missed the question.
Are you seeing any indication that either the current Government or any future Government realise that they need to be approaching it in that way in order to achieve the long-term goals?
I do not think I am close enough to be able to answer as to how the Government are thinking. I think practical constraints bite in the end , and we are facing them.
Ita, do you have any view on that? Are you getting any sense that they are seeking to approach it in the way that has just been described?

There is a sense that, in general, it is being taken seriously. The right discussions are being had. I understand the challenge on the vision and having a date. The other thing about a date is that it sets a clear direction and aligns a lot of disparate actions around it. If you set a date, the question then becomes whether you are willing to understand what is between you and that date. For me, the date is less of a problem , but that is also because the date is largely dictated by what we must do if we are to meet the climate challenge. The power system must run ahead of the other areas of the economy to allow us to decarbonise via electrification.

At the ETC, we really push for having that clarity, but behind the clarity you must have the strategy. What does it look like? What are the different components of the system? How would they need to work together? What do we need to do to overcome the very real barriers that are making the dates very challenging? To the extent that there are discussions on how we think about a future energy system operator or think about more strategic energy system operations, looking at what we might do with planning and permitting and on jobs and skills, there are lots of noises and the right conversations coming out, but we need to continue to move to concrete policy recommendations and actions. Certainly, the discussions are there.

Q45 Viscount Stansgate : Apart from the cost—leave that aside—what would you say are the major barriers to a successful scaling up of long-duration energy storage? If I can answer my own question immediately, I think I am right that you will probably refer to the planning process, which you have done already. Are there other issues, apart from that, although emphasise that if you wish, that may arise in relation to the scaling up of long-duration energy storage, apart from the cost element?

My answer would not be specific to long-duration storage. It is more a general one about decarbonisation and its resources in terms of supply chain and people, most obviously engineers. We need to train lots and lots of people to do that. I have never understood why electrical engineering is not seen as a much more attractive option for universities than it is. It is clearly a growth business. Hydrogen engineers — we can go through the whole range of technologies that we have talked about — need expertise.

We will need to think about supply chains for electrolysers. We will need to think about the construction industry, if we are looking at large-scale cavern storage. There are all sorts of things that I could put on your list. The critical ones are planning and the commercial and regulatory arrangements.

Viscount Stansgate : Thank you. You have answered a question I had not yet asked, which was what more you could tell us about the range of skilled individuals needed to be able to deliver this system in the future. You mentioned electrical engineers, and that is obviously one. Where do we need to focus our training and recruitment efforts to get the numbers and the types of people that we will need to make it possible?

I have always struggled with how you do that in practice. The idea that we would need — to take a very specific example — more electrical engineers has been obvious for decades. The industry was privatised with quite an old workforce profile. A lot of those people have retired, and the more interesting things have been outside the main electricity system, so they have tended to attract the better graduates. It is hard to come up with a policy that produces the personnel resource, the technically qualified people you need, for this kind of big transformational change. I do not have any bright ideas, I am afraid. I just think it is a real problem.
Viscount Stansgate : Any thoughts?

I absolutely agree about the engineering challenge that has already been identified. I understand that there are 200 linesmen in the UK, but National Grid estimates that 1,400 will be required by 2030. There is a training time that has to be built in. There is also an infrastructure perspective. I believe there are only two training centres in the UK where they can train. There is a whole practical mapping out of what is needed.

What feels different is the power system, but it is also the larger energy transition. We have a range of areas where we know that we will have locally specific jobs. There is the power system side. There is also the retrofit of residential homes to enable electrification of heating. There is a whole range of jobs where perhaps people do not fully understand the vision and the connection of those roles with meeting the decarbonisation challenge that we face.

Alongside the difficult work of trying to break down exactly which roles and therefore which training absolutely need to be done, there is a piece around linking more clearly for people that some of these roles are critical to delivering net zero. They are the roles of the future. They are the roles that will allow us to meet the climate crisis. That is an exciting and perhaps a different way of talking about some of those roles than previously. Harnessing that vision can be really helpful .
Viscount Stansgate : You referred to salt mines in Cheshire. If you fill them with hydrogen, what do you think the reaction would be from the people living above them?

I went to Luleå in northern Sweden, about a year and a half ago, where SSAB built the first pilot hydrogen direct reduction plant to make fossil-free steel five years ago. It is a huge achievement from an R&D perspective. As part of the complex in Luleå , they have also developed rock cavern storage. A salt mine is cheaper , because it already exists and we can just put it in, but for people who do not have them there are rock caverns. Drilling out in rock is probably what people will use.

As part of the R&D they developed a rock cavern to test it. There are a lot of questions around hydrogen storage and hydrogen cavern safety. There are lots of risks. It was very interesting talking to them. One of the biggest pieces of work that they needed to do, for the planning and permitting of that project and that site, was to discuss rock cavern storage and safety, what the risks were, how they were manufacturing it and what specifications they were manufacturing to. They were manufacturing rock cavern storage to very high specifications because of people’s concerns about the risks.
Viscount Stansgate : Did it go ahead?
Yes. It is in production. It is being built.

We have a storage specialist coming to give evidence at a subsequent session, so perhaps we can pick this issue up then. I would like to thank both of our witnesses in this session. We have worked you extremely hard and we have very much appreciated the input you have given. If you think of anything else that we would find useful, we would be very pleased to receive it as formal evidence after this event. Thank you very much indeed.
[1] There is a premium of +40% per tonne of crude steel versus the fossil alternative. Please see ETC: Making the Hydrogen Economy Possible (2021) for further details.

sessions.iT: The environmental sustainability of the Department for Education
sessions.w: Department for Education; Department for Education

segs.tx: Environmental Audit Committee
Oral evidence: The environmental sustainability of the Department for Education , HC 1839
Wednesday 18 October 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 18 October 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Philip Dunne (Chair); Barry Gardiner; Dr Matthew Offord; Chris Skidmore; Cat Smith; Claudia Webbe.
Education Committee Member present: Mr Robin Walker.
Questions 1 - 5 8
Witnesses

I : The Baroness Barran MBE, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State (Minister for the School System and Student Finance), Department for Education ; and Dr Jonathan Dewsbury, Director of Capital Operations and Net Zero, Department for Education.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: The Baroness Barran MBE and Dr Jonathan Dewsbury.

Q1 Good afternoon . W elcome to the Environmental Audit Committee for our one-off inquiry into the sustainability of the Department for Education and all its entities. Be fore I introduce the Minister , to whom we are very grateful, I would like to welcome Robin Walker, who is the C hairman of the Education Select Committee and formerly an Education Minister , who may have had some part in much of what we will discuss. Welcome, Robin. In particular, welcome to Baroness Barran, the Minister for the Department for Education. Perhaps you would be kind enough to introduce Jonathan Dewsbury.
Absolutely. Jonathan, do you want to go ahead and introduce yourself?

Yes ; t hank you for having me, Committee. My name is Jonathan Dewsbury , and I am the director of capital operations and net zero. I have had that role from 11 September. Prior to that , I was the chief sustainability officer at D FE, so I prepared the strategy on behalf of Education Ministers and started to oversee the implementation of it.
Q2 Excellent , thank you . I think that you wanted to say one or two words to set the scene from your perspective. We are happy for you to do that.

Thank you, Chair. I wanted to set today ’ s evidence in the context of our wider climate change and sustainability strategy. T he school estate is an incredibly important dimension , but the way that we are approaching this is to say that we are in a unique position to influence 16 million students of differing ages i n their attitude to wards sustainability and climate change, their knowledge , and the skills that they develop.

In the strategy, we have set out our plans for climate education, for green skills, for estates, for digital infrastructure , for the supply chain, and for the international dimension. Forgive the snappy titles, but we are aiming to inspire first, particularly with young people through the curriculum, as well as through their participation with a National Education Nature Park and the Climate Action Awards. We are doing a great deal of planning so that when we get to the action, we make sure that we execute as well and as effectively as possible. This is not to diminish where I think the focus of the Committee ’s questions today will be — on the estate and decarbonisation — but it is to set this in a wider context of how we see our role as a Department in the future of the planet.

Q3 We very much welcome the work the Department is doing to introduce climate education within the curriculum in different ways. I think that when Robin was in the Department , he recommended that we should reintroduce na tural history O-level as an option in the curriculum and I am very pleased that that has happened. We admire what you are doing in that respect.

As you say, t his inquiry is focused more on the sustainability of the built estate , for which you are responsible. A s a Committee , we are gently working our way around Government Departments focused on this. We have the support of the National Audit Office, which has written its report on this , which has informed the work that we are doi ng in this session. That is the context from our side.

The strategy that was published 18 months ago gives you about eight years to deliver on the significant ambitions and set of commitments within it . From the work that the NAO has done, it seems to us that you spent much of the first year and a half out of eight trying to come to grips with the governance arrangements for how you will deliver this strategy. Could you start by confirming whether or not the governance is now set and clear , and has been communicated throughout the Department and its bodies?

Yes, thank you. The short answer is that I think that we have made really good progress since the NAO visited and wrote its report. The role of c hief s ustainability o fficer has been con firmed at director level and we now have a deputy director as the senior responsible officer for delivery in this area. That gives us more capacity so that our CSO can get involved across g overnment in all the inter- departmental and cross-departmental work that is happening. We have senior civil servant sponsors from every part of the Department who are involved in the governance of this . T he permanent secretary appointed the DG of our strategy group to be the champion among our direc tor s- general. T his sits in my ministerial portfolio , and one of our non-exec utives , Jack Boyer, is very involved and attends the cross- g overnment C limate N on- E xec utive B oard M ember s L iaison F orum.

The other thing that has happened is that all our DGs have received training on the new environmental principles legal duty. Training is happening for Ministers and our private office s . About 1,550 staff across the Department have engaged with the environmental principles, either through direct training or piloting of resources . We have also done an all -staff broadcast on the principles, which reached about 2,500 members of the Department.
Q4 Staying within the Department for a moment, is it a regular agenda item on the Department ’ s board to review delivery against strategy?

On the board, we tend to take a deep dive on different topics. It is certainly something that I regularly review in my role as Minister . I worked out my top m inisterial priorities with my private office and this is one of them. That is not to say we would not do a deep dive on the board ; we might. I also make sure that I update the Secretary of State in our bilats and have regular meetings with the team to make sure delivery is on track.

Q5 Given the wide rang e in size , number and variety of properties within the Department —the school estate, the university estate and so on —do you have a good handle on delivery against your objectives and the strategy mechanisms to be able to influence what is happening across the estate?

As I am sure you are aware, we do not own and control the school and university estate in the way that other Government Departments might own and control their estate. I am sure that we will come on and ta lk about this a bit more, but on the one hand , we definitely have a role in encouraging the behaviour that we want to see on the ground from those who are responsible.

If I start with our schools, whether that is local authorities , academy trusts or dioceses, there are ways that we can influence their behaviour and work out what levers we have. At the same time, we believe that it works better to have that distributed responsibility rather than us controlling everything from the centre. There are certain things that obviously we do control, such as the delivery of the school rebuilding programme, for example . For schools that are applying for funding for condition improvement, they now have to demonstrate their environmental sustainability audits. We are trying to weave this in and use those levers at the right intensity, if I can put it like that.

The other bit —again, I am sure we will cover this in more detail —is that we are in the process of doing a few different things, including testing and piloting a number of approaches and getting absolute clarity and consistency in how we measure the risk in the school estate so that we start from a clear and solid base from which we measure progress.

On the baselin ing of the education estate in terms o f emissions, we have worked with the higher education and further education system to set a standardised way for them to report emissions. We published that in January ’ 24 , and that did a baseline of the emissions—
January of?

Of ’2 3, sorry — I am getting ahead of myself. On the emissions for the school and nursery estate, we have shared our draft standardised reporting framework with the union groups and our user group, and we are hoping to publish that later this year . This sets the baseline of how the sector should report and , therefore , allows us to quantify the emissions more accurately to then be able to set some scientific targets moving forward.

Q6 On delivery levers, I can see that where you are providing funding for new build or for refurbs on the properties that have been subject to RA AC and other issues , where you have to undertake a rebuild or a new build, you will have influence. What levers do you have for the existing built estate in addition to establishing the baseline ? How can you help them to apply for the public building decarbonisation money that has been available , for example?
We do a few different things . Jon is much closer to the decarbonisation scheme than I am, so I will let him pick th at up.

The other thing that we offer is a service that is free to all schools, called the school resource management service. Included within that is all sorts of practical advice on procurement , management of energy bills, and in particular, maintenance of the school estate. That is an optional service. Schools do not have to take it, but I gather that interest has increased in that , understandably, given what has happened to energy prices. Do you want to say a word about the decarbonisation scheme?

Yes. The Committee will be aware that the p ublic s ector d ecarbonisation s cheme is consistently oversubscribed. We have worked closely with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to make sure that the education sector is getting its fair portion from that pot. That portion is defined by the percentage of emissions from education in the public sector. It is between 30% and 35% of that pot. We have seen £342 million from the p ublic s ector d ecarbonisation s cheme from phase 3. We recognise the challenges—
Did you say £342 million?
Yes .
Had you had any from previous phases?
We will have had some from previous phases.
It would be very helpful if you could send us a note of how much you have received, both in absolute terms and as a proportion since it began.

Yes ; w e will write to you with that. We recognise the challenge for , particularly , small schools or a single academy trust accessing the p ublic s ector d ecarbonisation s cheme. We are working collaboratively with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to look at how phase 4 might be changed. For phase 3 , we moved the application window out of the summer holidays in conjunction with DESNZ and we ran webinars with Sa lix, the organisation that run s the loan scheme, to help schools with their applications.

Q7 I think that we will come on to some more questions on that in a minute . I have a final question about the overall governance. Your strategy had 143 different commitments. Do you now have a delivery schedule for when you will meet each of those commitments and how?

We certainly have a delivery schedule for them all, but some are inevitably much more precise than others. Some are contingent on others. I would say that for the next 18 months to two years we have a pretty detailed plan. Inevitably , it becomes higher level beyond that . I suppose I would be more worried if it was super - precise in a way. I think it is realistic in its ambition.

Q8 Following on on the point of delivery schedule, how do you know if you are on track to deliver all your sustainability commitments? Historically, the Department has been able to make some eye-watering commitments. For example, I think that Dami a n Hinds promised to get rid of all single-use plastics in schools by 2022, but we all know teachers ’ tendency to laminate things and I do not think that was ever a realistic promise. How d o we ensure that these will be measured and delivered on?

The NAO report highlights confidence in delivery of statutory environmental obligations from May . T here is at least one issue on water efficiency, which is highlighted in red in terms of the Department ’s confidence there , so w here you come across issues like that, how do you address them and how do you make sure that you are confident?

Our overall risk rating on the delivery plan is amber - red. I was slightly surprised at that when I went through it with the team. T here are seven commitments that are off track out of 143. It felt a bit harsh to me . I think that the real reason is that this is a long-term plan and we are relatively early in it. W ithout going into the niceties of how different people use and understand risk registers, I think that it is the length of time ahead and how early we are in the process that is the big determinant of this. It is an eight-year delivery timescale for the st rategy and obviously we are early on in that.

Going back to the questions around governance, clearly it has been important to put in place senior civil servant sponsors to make sure that that risk is managed. I think that the biggest risk, which is why we are here today, is making sure that we can prioritise funding — working with colleagues in the Treasury — for decarbonisation and for adaptation of the education estate, which , as you will understand very well , is incredibly important. Our belief is that the more detailed and the more accurate the analysis we carry out, the more reasonable our case will be for additional funding to address this. There are some commitments that are off track. I do not know if you want to talk about any of those in particular.

Q9 I think that it is just water efficiency that is particularly highlighted in the NAO report. Obviously , this is a statutory obligation that comes into effect in November this year , as I understand. We already talked a bit about training senior officials in those environmental principles and that is very welcome, but if there are issues that are liable to be missed or red-rated, what is the process for trying to put those back on track?
Do you want to say a word about water efficiency?

Yes. First of all, we are working with Ofwat and M arket O perat or S ervice s L t d to make sure that 10,000 of those schools are more water - efficient. I n our specifications for buildings — which is not just new builds ; it is also refu rbishment or replacement of blocks , and that standard is used by other responsi ble bodies who deliver in other ways — we have a metric against the total water use and thus water efficiency. We are clear that any future standard we set for how our buildings ar e refurbished or retrofitted hits those water efficiency targets —l ess than 10 litres per day per person.

The Minister mentioned the education estate being devolved and there being over 3,000 responsible bodies. One of the ways we are trying to instigate action is through the c limate a ction p lan s. T he ask is for all education settings to have a c limate a ction p lan in place by 2025, where they need to outline their approach to decarbo nisation, their approach to adaptation resilience—this is where water efficiency would come—their approach to biodiversity, and their approach to climate education and green careers. We are in the process of tendering for the service to support schools in delivering those. That will go live from next year. That is accompanied by a network of ambassadors, which calls on experts from universities and engineering companies to go out to support schools and make sure that they have the right resilience plans in place to deal with the challenges we will face.

Q10 Will you work with trust boards and the National Governance Association — organisations like those— to make sure that they have the capacity they need to play their part in formulating those plans?

The NGA sit s on our user group, and we test all our policies and delivery plans with that user group. We will absolutely work with trusts. In delivering these c limate a ction p lans , we will approach trusts to see how they work best with their particular school network.

Q11 Baroness Barran, in your opening comments , you mentioned that the strategy went more widely than just the school estate. I played a small part in feeding into some of those curriculum and qualification commitments in the strategy and declare my interest in that respect. Can you give any update on the progress of the natural history GCSE, the nature pathway and the contribution of that as a primary science model curriculum and the emphasis on green jobs? Is there anything useful for the Committee to know in that respect?

We aim that the natural history GCSE should be taught first by 2025. As you will know, introducing a new GCSE is a complex exercise, so we are working very hard at the moment on the subject content and curriculum , and working hard with the exam board. We will do a full public consultation on it next year when we have those ideas clearer. Forgive me, you also asked about green skills, I think.
It was about green skills and the primary science model curriculum , which was due to look at that broader nature pilot through schools as well.
Yes. Do you want to take the primary one and I can take the skills?

Yes. The other commitment in that space was the science C PD . That has been delivered with climate change and sustainability in science teachers ’ CPD. The primary science model curriculum has been delivered through Oak National Academy and it plan s to roll out the curriculum map between this autumn and September 2024. It is working with the University of York and CAPE, the Cl imate A dapted P athways—I cannot remember what the E stands for, so rry. That sits alongside the curriculum material we are delivering through the National Education Nature Park .

The other question you had was on the National Education Nature Park. This is the concept where we consider the whole of the education estate as one national park and empower learners and young people to look after it like a national park. If we increase the biodiversity and resilience of it to the effects of overheating, drought and flood, we can make a big difference to the landmass of the UK. That was soft-launched on 4 October. That is now live. You can look at what schools are engaging with it. In the initial challenge, the hidden nature challenge, we had over 2,000 uploads from students. We have had 164 schools start mapping out their estate already. We plan to do a more formal launch with more communications around that later in November in th e build-up to COP because the Minister and the Department have ambitions to use the National Education Nature Park as an inspiration on an international level, not just a national level.

One of the thoughts we have is that children could maybe compare the biodiversity of their schools across countries, not just within the UK. I f anyone gets a chance to go and visit their local primary sc hool getting involved in all this, it is a very uplifting visit.

On green skills, you will be aware that there is huge ambition within the net zero strategy and the energy security strategy that we should create 190,000 green jobs by 2025. We have already had 100 green apprenticeships in different industries approved. [1] We have a Green Jobs Delivery Group, which will publish an action plan in this area in 2024.
Q12 Can I interrupt for a second? Could they include in that delivery plan a definition of what they mean by—

By a green job? Okay. I think that is a very fair challenge. The other thing that the Committee will be aware of is our investment in institutes of technology where we bring together local colleges, universities and employers focusing on some of the technical challenges that we face . E nergy and agritech are both big parts of that.

The other thing , with a different approach , are the skills bootcamps, which are free — typically 16-week skills training. For example, there are boot camps in the installation of solar panels, heat pumps and so on. We are getting very good feedback from those. I suppose that this is not something that explicitly intends to address green skills but I think it will do. You will all be aware of the lifelong learning entitlement. That legislation will allow people to upskill and reskill through their careers in more bite-sized chunks and access the funding to be able to do that. Obviously, as skills demands evolve, hopefully that will provide the funding to facilitate a lot of people to get the right training.

Q13 Thank you. I want to return to the public sector decarbonisation grant. You mentioned t hat you are working closely to try to increase the share that the Department gets to more like its share of emissions. I think that 37 % is the share of emissions from the education estate, and it is getting slightly less — 30% on rounds to date according to the NAO report. Within that, though, is there not a particular challenge in that the HE sector has punched above its weight and schools have punched below their weight in previous rounds of the bidding for public sector decarbonisation? Is there not a particular challenge because of the shape of the school estate and its very devolved nature that we probably need to go further to address?

I do not think we would disagree with you. The numbers speak for themselves, but I think that it is also fair to say that that has improved a lot in recent rounds. As Jon said earlier, we are working very closely with DESNZ on the next phase of the funding, trying to make sure that it works better for the school estate. The example we hear is that the first -past -the -post system for funding just does not work very well for schools. We do not know what the final outcome will be, but I think that it is fair to say we will be in very constructive conversations. The aim is to get the right share to schools in a way that works for them.

Q14 Would you be able to provide the Committee with any figures, either historical or in the current round, o n th e breakdown within the education estate of where public sector decarbonisation grant is going? I think that that will be interesting and valuable from the perspective of scrutiny.
Absolutely and that ties in, does it not—

I can give you the breakdown for phase 3B, which was 2023 and was 122 education settings. There was £ 168 million in total— £ 51 million to schools and academies, £ 84 million to higher education and further education, and £ 33 million to school- only. Y ou sugge sted that the contribution from the PS D S was less than 30%. We get it to 30% [2] because we include £ 55 million from phase 3B that is allocated through local authorities, so w here the education sector applications are mixed with local authority grants.

The Minister might want to also speak about recognising where the p ublic s ector d ecarbonisation s cheme is . W e have been thinking about the approach we have set out for how we transition the estate — to innovate, test and invest. One way of investing is through the p ublic s ector d ecarbonisation s cheme. Another way we have been looking at is how we might use some of our capital more strongly through something we call the net zero a ccelerator s ervice. We have just tendered for five organisations to test the feasi bility of that, which is that if we aggregate groups of schools together , we could introduce fabric / condition improvements and local energy generation, and we could see the reductio n of energy costs paid back to reutilise that money further forward.

Barone ss Barran: Part of the hypothesis behind the net zero accelerator scheme —as Jon said , we are in the feasibility stage that finishes in December. Depending on the findings of that, we would aim to go into a larger trial from the spring of next year . We know that in the private sector , there is a huge amount of capital that wants to come into this area , and we are seeing whether there is a way that we can access that in the interests of speedier decarbonisation , but not in a way that crosses any Treasury red lines. That is what we are working for , and if it works , it would have a huge potential , but we are in the early stages of that . We think that it is an important thing to test out.
Q15 Thank you. Picking that up , before I ask Matthew Offord, would that apply both to the academy sector as well as the currently maintained schools?
Yes ; I think it would in some ways be easier to do in academies than it would be in maintained schools.
We are expecting a vote. The Minister is on his feet in the Commons, but we will start Matthew Offord ’s question.

Q16 I will be brief. Given that the Department is not expected to set the emission targets for the best part of another two years, and that by 2032 the Department will be expected to reduce emissions by 50% and by 75% by 2037, do you think that is enough time for the Department to play its part in the carbon neutral agenda?

That is a huge question. What I suppose is behind that is our ability to secure sufficient funding principally from the Treasury to carry out the required decarbonisation. The work that we are doing is to establish a climate risk framework for every school . We will launch that in January 2024 , with it being fully embedded by January 2025. That will allow each individual school to be able to assess their risk in relation to temperature increases, risk of flooding and risk of drought. We need the clearest possible picture and this is one route to us getting that. We will also have a lot of information from the National Education Nature Park , from the digital uploads of the biodiversity within each individual school estate. We will get a much richer picture quite quickly— [ Interruption. ]
Minister, I am sorry but a D ivision has been called.
I will hold my breath and finish —
If you would not mind concluding that.
Briefly—
Very briefly, or we could come back in.

I am happy to cover it in more detail. Clearly , there is a major financial commitment that needs to be made both in school rebuilding and in retrofit, but I think that our responsibility is to be as accurate as possible in what is needed.
W e will come back to that in a minute , and I will call a halt for the moment.
Very good.
Sitting suspended.
On resuming—
Q17 Where we left off , I think, Minister, you had not quite completed your answer to Matthew Offord.

Than k you very much, Chair. On whether we have enough time to deliver, we are clear on what the targets are. I think that we would agree that the trajectory to get there is extremely challenging and we know from the UCL model that its estimate is that about 80% of the school estate will require significant investment.

On t he things that we are doing in addition to the climate risk assessment framework, which I mentioned before the vote, we have a number of pilots and pathfinder projects — i f I may give a couple of examples. I am happy to send the Committee the full list, but there are 285 schools trialling innovative energy management systems. There is work going on with 550 schools who are at risk of surface water flooding to mitigate that risk, and we have 22 schools replacing gas, coal and oil boilers with ground and air source heat pumps. [3] Some of this is important, as the Committee understands, because we are such a large client in the UK construction indu stry that what we do and the standards we set will have ramifications more broadly.

The other thing that I think is interesting is the behavioural change aspects. About 44% of schools that we tracked had smart met ers , and that is leading to a significant change in their behaviour and energy usage . As Jon and I both said earlier, we think that the c limate a ction p lans will also lead to a change. None of this is to diminish the scale of the challenge. The Committee is absolutely right to focus on that and so are we.

Q18 I am grateful for that because I share your concern that you will be able to achieve that. In the written answers that I have received from the Education Minister, he said that he has not estimated the cost of retrofitting the maintained school estate and he has also not made an assessment on the percentage of maintained schools that will be retrofitted by 2050. In addition, he says that by December 2023 he will be able to produce a report on the implementation of progress for the Department for Education ’ s sustainability and climate change strategy. Unless you know something that I do not or that indeed the Minister does, I am very concerned that you will not be able to achieve the results in that time. The 2050 target is obviously even longer than the target that we have just mentioned — by 2032. You mentioned earlier targets and the reported stage of those. I think that you indicated that they would be at the individual level of each school. Is that correct?

We will have a framework where each school will be able to assess their risk. In our understanding of the school estate, you will be aware that we do the condition data collection survey. We do a visual survey of every school in the school estate. We have that picture and that is shared back with schools. Jon, are there other elements that I have forgotten?

At the start of the session, the Minister talked about the overarching approach of inspire, plan and act to deliver our strategy. The act bit is also accountability. We are setting up a net zero reporting system that plays back the emissions to schools so that they can use that data usefully to know where they need to intervene on a loca l level. That is done through the c limate a ction p lan , so we are giving them ambassador support from university and engineering experts. We are helping them by giving them planning tools and also by play ing back that data on climate risk, overheating, floo d and drought, and also their emissions so they can see what thing they can do first to make the right steps.

On target setting, we will collate that information nationally to make sure we hit those targets. One thing to say is that the strategy has been a big catalyst in trying to drive the movement towards this. We have seen an increase in P V in schools, presumably because of not just strategy , but other energy issues — from 19% from our emission data collection to 26% from the partial data collection we ha ve had so far. We have seen heat pumps go up from 14% to 17%.

I think that the Minister has outlined one of the barriers as investment between 2025 and 2030, but what we are doing is removing the other barriers that are in this space, such as the supply chain and the technical standards required to deliver those buildings. We published specification 21 for our building standards, which meets the RIBA 2025 sustainability guidance. The pilots we are carrying out right now are designed to give us the data and information to make sure that we hit the RIBA 2030 standards. Then we have started the school resilience programme, which is making sure —as well as past emissions, we are also dealing with the increased flood, overheating and drought risks that face the estate.

If we think about that as a continuous improvement cycle, we set the standards that we are trying to deliver ; make sure we can fund that through the spending review envelope that we have ; support that delivery through our building programmes ; measure that quality ; and then draw on that experience to set the next standard to drive up. We are leading the way in our building standards in the education system.
Q19 Does it apply to individual schools?
We will not set individual targets for schools. We will support them, making sure they get—

Like your biodiversity target for each school, will you be able to say their biodiversity performance, or will we be able to look at an individual school ’ s climate emissions —so n ot flood, not climate change, not drought, just emissions ?

Yes. Initially when we baseline, we will take the data from the condition data collection , from their display energy certificate or from our VMFI, which is our financial tool where they report their energy costs. So w e initially will be centrally quantifying or calculating their emissions at that level. We will then start playing the emissions back to schools so they can see where to take, and then we will get that two-way play through our net zero emissions board and then use that to test—
Like school league tables, I will be able to say that a local school in my area is not performing environmentally or sustainably in the way another school is, for example.

I would not use the word league table. I say that we would be comparing them so that if you are a standard 6FE secondary, how do you compare to another 6F E secondary ? Are you performing in the same way? It has an impact on your energy bills and your contribution to net zero.

Q20 I realise you would not use the word league tables, but the press do , and I would expect and anticipate the press would do the same with this or , indeed , others would do that . As you say, it is very difficult to compare like for like , but would there be baselines where assessments would be able to be made at an individual level ?

To be fair , through the VMFI financial insights, a school can already benchmark a number of elements of financial performance and their energy consumption , and they know their square meterage and so on . They can already bench that against most similar schools. There are already tools to do that. Going back to the school resource management, that is also something they do on a more personal, tailored basis.
Q21 Thank you. Finally, I understand that the Department is looking for the current requirements of the g reening Government commitments. When are you likely to meet those?
B aroness Barran: The g reening Government commitments for us apply just to the Department ’s estate. Forgive me, I have it written down somewhere —h ere we go.
It is five core buildings and eight minor tenancies.
That is right. We are on track to meet our overall greenhouse gas emission target by 2025.
Q22 What about water neutrality?

I do not have details on water neutrality. I know that we have already hit our waste reduction and recycling targets. I do not have the details with me. Forgive me on water neutrality, but we can come back to you on that.
That is great. Thank you very much.
Q23 What are your plans to improve the school -level data collection to show us about the sustainability across the school estate?

I think that we have already touched on a bit of that. We will be initially defining with schools what we see as climate risk, particularly in relation to overheating, flood and drought. We already have school-level data from the condition data collection survey. Through the c limate a ction p lans , we will also have detailed information about their emissions, water usage and so on , and will work with them and local experts supporting them to come up with their own plan to address and improve their sustainability.
Q24 That is several things that will happen. Minister, could you put any timescale on that or give us an indication of when you expect that to happen?

The risk assessment framework is being introduced in January 2024 and will be implemented fully by January 2025. W e will start work on the climate action plans next year and they need to be returned to the Department in 2025. This is all within the next couple of years.

Can I add the steps we are taking on reporting emissions? It is important we are clear with the sector about what we want them to report. We started with the higher education sector , defining the standard of what we want them to report, which was published in January 2023. We have the draft of s cope 1, 2 and 3 emissions that we want schools and nurseries to report being tested with the union groups and our user group.

That feeds into our discovery work for our emissions reporting system, which is built in with our digital support hub that supports the climate action plan. While we are keen to get the message out, we are not asking for reporting for the sake of reporting. We are asking for emission data to help play it back to schools, to help them make the right choices within their funding envelopes. The two-way information sharing will come through the climate action plan support hub, which has been tendered , and we are about to appoint the successful delivery partner organisations.

That also links to the earlier questions around governance and delivery plan, because clearly it is one thing to say that you have done certain things , but what we want to measure is the impact and the benefits of those actions. That is now beginning to move into action.

Q25 T he NAO report—I am particularly looking at figure 7—detail s the plans that the Department has. I am also aware that the Department told the NAO that it is limited in its capacity to analyse and use that information due to resource constraints. What plans do you have as a Department to find that expertise, or are you confident that you now have the expertise to be able to manage that data and make it usable?

Certainly in the risks presented to me, some of the changes that we talked about at the beginning , in terms of governance and increasing capacity in the team, as well as building our wider data and analytical capabilities, mean that we will be able to deal with that.
Q26 Does the net zero strategy remain deliverable, given the uncertainty in funding and particularly that there are other pressing priorities ? W e have heard about the RAAC, for example .

This comes back to the question about the trajectory and whether we are going to get there . We are clear on where we have to get to. Resources are always a challenge across government, but I am confident that the work we and the team are doing will give us the most robust possible case, not just for the absolute amount of money but for the mix of activities.

For example, you will have seen that the Government audit department projected 650 school retrofits a year, if we keep the school rebuilding programme at 50 schools a year. Clearly , that mix could change, and we need to look at the detailed need out there and the best value for money to make that happen.
Q27 What sustainability information is missing that would enable you to strategically allocate funding to schools?

There are a number of things. There is so much innovation in this area. We want to be sure that the solutions that we decide to scale across the school estate work for schools in their context, hence our pilot and pathfinder approach. We will gather very valuable information from that.

The other big thing is hearing from schools what they believe are the solutions. When we bring those two things together, I think we have a very powerful case not just for having confidence that we are doing the right thing , but having confidence that it will be deliverable and work and be implemented and adopted on the ground.

T he purpose of our National Education Nature Park, the net zero reporting system, the climate action plan and then the climate risk framework is to give us that strategic picture of where the emissions are biggest on the education estate and where the risks are on the education estate.

We could probably already say that schools in particular sites of the country are more likely to be affected by flood, as opposed to others more likely to be impacted by drought. We want to be able to create that strategic view in the centre, to be able to support schools locally, by pulling the granular detail through the climate action plan digital hub or through our net zero reporting emissions tools.

Q28 I suppose some of the difficulties are about understanding whether there is a clear grasp on the funding that is required to achieve the level of sustainability to achieve net zero. You have been doing some work with University College London in developing a digital model. Why have you not yet used the developed models to inform your funding approach?
I am not sure I quite follow. Can you give me an example?
Out of the University College London digital models that you have developed — there are some models that have come out of that. Why not use some of those models to inform?

Jon will be able to go into the detail of the technicalities of the models . But the closer we can get to , as Jon just described , a detailed actual understanding of the school estate based on the facts of individual schools — that will be much more powerful than using models in isolation. Maybe you want to say something about how the models work.

We would agree with the intention that we would want to use a UCL model to help us allocate funding towards sustainability and climate change risks , but with any model we need to be confident of the accuracy of the data going into it, which is why , currently , the UCL model is simulated off seven building types. It is a simulation rather than a data model. We want to make sure we have all that information that we outlined through the nature park — so the biodiversity coming through that, the emissions data coming through our climate action plan and the risks coming through that to feed that model to make sure we are making accurate strategic investment.

Q29 In the Public Accounts Committee session held on 11 September, the DFE’s permanent secretary, Susan Acland-Hood, stated with respect to RAAC , “We have agreed with the Treasury that as we look at negotiations for the next SR , this will be our first priority for the capital spend.” That seems to suggest that sustainability funding would be deprioritised.
