Like members of the Committee, I am surprised at the extent of the collections of the British Museum and other comparable institutions, but given its 270-year-old age, I understand the challenges in documenting the collection, although there are different patterns among the departments of the British Museum and among the different museums with which DCMS works. Like everybody, I am surprised and dismayed that what, according to the allegations, appears to be an inside job has occurred. That is fortunately very rare in the museums sector, but it is a deeply troubling matter to hear about.

Q47 Are you treating this as an isolated incident just affecting the British Museum? We have had 560 objects logged as missing from the Imperial War Museum, for example. Is this issue wider than just one or two museums?

We are not treating this in isolation. We have written to our other national museums and some other of our arm’s length bodies, as you would expect us to, to ask for assurances about their processes. Through that and through the inquiries that they are getting from the outside world, they are being forthcoming about items that are missing or unaccounted for in their collections, but there are a variety of reasons and explanations for that. I think it is important on behalf of the sector to stress that some of those numbers should not cause immediate alarm. Dr Balshaw can explain some of the context from her experience in the sector.

We have written to our other organisations to seek their assurances. The majority of museums and galleries in this country are not directly arm’s length bodies of DCMS—we have a more distant relationship with them—but I still visit them when I am around the country, and I am yet to find a museum or gallery that has not, at its board of trustees level and its executive level, thought about its own processes in the light of the reports that have emerged about what took place at the British Museum.
Q48 Thank you. Dr Balshaw, has the Tate suffered theft that you are aware of?
The Tate has not lost or had any object stolen from any of its stores or collections.
Jane Stevenson: Ever?
In terms of the time that I have been here and records that we have preceding my time as director. We have no recorded instances.

Q49 Are you looking at the museums sector and seeing that certain collections are more vulnerable to theft? Do you think certain types of exhibit are more open to theft and to being targeted than others?

There is a distinction to be made between items on exhibit and items in store. What is alleged to have taken place at the British Museum did not concern items that were on public display. Those are harder to steal—they are behind protective cases; there are security guards; there is CCTV. The allegations about the British Museum concern items that were not on public display and were mostly for academic research and study. We await the outcome of the independent review and the police investigation to see what lessons need to be learned, but it is clearly in that area that lessons need to be learned for the British Museum and perhaps, therefore, for others.
Q50 Will you be asking other national museums to consider their entire security of storage items?

We have already written to the other ones to seek assurances about the processes that they have in place, and we are pleased by the assurances that we have been getting from them. As more details emerge from the independent review, we will continue to have those conversations with the museums and galleries, but I know that they are having those conversations internally already.

Q51 Finally, we have seen internationally some protests in museums and damage to paintings. Do you think that the museums sector has to respond to a world that is a bit more open to protest at the moment? Dr Balshaw, are you taking any steps?

The reassuring thing that I can share with the Committee is that there are probably more attempts to make protests and damage objects than are ever actually realised. Our security is based on the principle of observing before something happens, so I would want to give reassurance that that is under continual monitoring by museums large and small. We share information and best practice on how to ensure that our collections are safe.
Q52 Lord Parkinson, are museum staff being trained to look out for this?

Yes. There is a long history, sadly, of protesters down the centuries, for various reasons, targeting cultural institutions and works of art to try to make their points. It is an issue that the sector has been grappling with for a very long time. As those trends change, they consider it as well. Certainly, in my discussions with museums big and small, I have been asking them about the steps that they have been taking. But it is part of a long history, sadly.

Q53 Maria, you were very definitive a moment ago when you were asked whether the Tate had ever lost anything from its collection. Given what we have heard today about how the British Museum denied that items had been lost or were unaware that items had been lost for quite a considerable period of time, how can you respond so reassuringly? How can you be so sure?

As Sir Mark Jones pointed out earlier, the size and type of collections that museums hold vary hugely. In Tate’s case, we routinely audit our collection. It is a little under 80,000 objects, so its scale is quite different from the British Museum’s, and every object has a record, which is in our collection. We have a complete catalogue—an inventory of items—which means that we know where things are and could therefore identify if they were lost, misplaced or even stolen. Our records demonstrate that that has not happened since we have had that catalogue in place.

Q54 Good morning. Lord Parkinson, I want to go back to an answer you gave to Jane Stevenson. You said that after the event you had written to other museums and were satisfied that everything was fine. If you had written to the British Museum before this happened, would you not have received such a reassuring answer then as well?

Through our sponsorship of the museum, we talk to them in a number of ways, but of course, the facts that have come to light beg a number of questions that it is worth asking of them, but also of other institutions.

Q55 I am just concerned; writing a letter and receiving a letter back saying, “Yes, everything’s fine” does not to me sound that thorough. It does not seem to be pushing—to say, “Well, why do you think this?”—or was that what the letter was about?

For the other institutions, it is about asking the immediate questions that spring to mind when we see what appears to have gone wrong at the British Museum, but that is in the early stages. There is the independent review, which is looking into this in detail. I am sure that that will throw up other questions that other museums and galleries will want to ask themselves. We will ensure that they are asking those questions and that, for those we work with and sponsor, we have the answers and are assured about them.

In relation to the British Museum’s own inquiry, we are meeting the joint chairmen of the independent review. We have seen its terms of reference and have taken some further steps, including having senior DCMS representation on the museum’s audit and risk committee to make sure that we are watching closely the steps that it is taking as it carries out that review.

Q56 Dr Balshaw, you have mentioned how the Tate ensures the safety and preservation of its collection by the way you have things catalogued and the audits and so on and so forth. How much of the national collections do you think are appropriately catalogued?

I am not able to speak about the details of the individual institutions that make up the national museums because I simply do not have access to all that information. What I would say is that the events at the British Museum, of course, have meant that all those national museums have reviewed their own situation.

The fact that, as your colleague was able to point out earlier, the Imperial War Museum is aware that 559 objects are currently lost or misplaced suggests that they are across their recordkeeping and are aware of the extent of any movement within a collection that is 33 million objects. That gives me some reassurance that they too are aware of their responsibilities in terms of maintaining catalogue and proper records and the safe care of the collections.

Q57 Are there any institutions that we could look at—museums or other institutions across the world—as exemplars of how you do this? Are there any places that you can think of that we should be looking to?

Often the UK museums are looked at as the standard for how you should maintain collections. The UK Spectrum standard s and accreditation , which underpins the way in which we look after all our national and most of our regional collections, is often used as the standard by which other international museums work. So we have very clear parameters that we all strive to work to.

Some museums’ collections are so large and continually evolving that a proportion of them are not yet catalogued, but I think we have a very clear sense of the standards that we should be aspiring to.
Q58 Is there a case for a unified catalogue of our national collections?

There is an ongoing project funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council called Towards a National Collection, which is looking at the opportunities and potential for digitising all the nation’s collections and linking those up using AI and emerging new technologies. It is an immensely complex job because of the incredibly varied nature of collections across the UK.

Having a single library-like catalogue for all the nation’s collections might sound like a simple thing, but some museums hold oral histories, some hold objects and some museums are effectively forms of community practice. That variety of museum work is what actually makes UK museums stronger. As a sector, I think we are doing the research to allow our collections to be accessed and used for research and for the public benefit already.

Having every single record of every single type of object—large, small, valuable or not valuable—is perhaps not quite what is needed. Actually meeting the standards that we clearly have in place is what we should all be doing as museums.
Q59 Lord Parkinson, what is your view on a unified catalogue of national collections?

The Government does support museums in cataloguing. For instance, we are contributing £200 million towards the Natural History Museum’s Unlocked project. They have a collection of 80 million items and they are digitising them and sharing them, so that scholars and academics but also curious members of the public from around the world can interact with that incredible collection, wherever they are.
We are keen to see more digitisation and wider sharing of the UK’s national collection. It is for the enjoyment and education of people around the world.

Q60 Lord Parkinson, I know you’re a music fan, because I saw you at a concert the other evening. You might therefore know the great George and Ira Gershwin song, “A Foggy Day in London Town”, which has the memorable lyric, “I viewed the morning with alarm / The British Museum had lost its charm”. What damage do you think this has done to the reputation of the British Museum?
As the museum itself has said, this is—was—a sad day for the British Museum.
Q61 Would you describe it as a disaster for their reputation?
I think it is deeply regrettable. It has caused dismay and concern across Government and across the sector.
Q62 You don’t think it’s a disaster?

I would like to see the outcome of the independent review before making final judgments about the scale of what has happened and the reasons why. But the British Museum is a world-class institution; it has a long and proud history. As I heard the chairman of trustees and the interim director explaining, it is continuing doing its excellent work while also asking the questions of itself that it needs to ask in light of this very concerning incident. So we are concerned about it, but we await the outcome of the independent review and the police investigation before, I suppose, I choose my adjectives.
Q63 Let us put it this way, then. Do you think that it has potentially wider implications for the reputation of the UK museums sector across the piece?

As I say, it is mercifully very rare for what appears in this case to have been an inside job to happen; that is a rare occurrence in museums, not just in the UK but around the world. It has caused dismay across the profession. Lots of people move between different institutions. They know the British Museum well and are concerned to hear about it. But, as I say, we—with our other arm’s length body museums—have written to them about the processes they have in place. We see no reason to be concerned that what seems to have happened at the British Museum may have happened in other museums.

Q64 Maria, you mentioned that UK museums are looked at as a place where you can expect to find high standards that international organisations, or other organisations in other countries, would wish to replicate. Is that reputation under threat from this scandal?

I think it is fair to say that the international museum community was both shocked and deeply dismayed that something like this could have happened; at the same time, they are also aware that the museums in the UK maintain very high standards for the care of their collections. We at Tate, along with colleagues at the V&A and the National Gallery, are in very active conversation with our international peers.
Theft by somebody who works within the museum is probably the most shocking thing that any of us could ever anticipate, and I think that across the profession there was really deep dismay.
Q65 Do you think there are any implications for attracting items on loan to UK museums as a result of this scandal?
I have not encountered that. We are still able to borrow and lend objects from Tate’s collection.
Q66 And have you heard from anyone else in the sector that they are having any problems in that regard?
No, I haven’t.
Q67 You don’t anticipate that being an issue at all?

No, I don’t think that will be an issue. I think that the larger concern is the shock and surprise for very hard-working museum professionals who pride themselves on putting the care of the collection first, in terms of their own professional standards. There is just dismay that one of their number could have done this.

Q68 Beyond this scandal, is the UK currently successful at being able to attract items from around the world ? Are there any other issues about that the Committee ought to be aware of in our work looking into and taking an interest in museums?

You might see newspaper reports today that there is a Rothko show currently in Paris to which Tate lent Rothko’s extremely important S eagram murals . We lend internationally to very prestigious institutions, and we also borrow from extremely important collections and institutions. Our processes to allow that to continue are very thorough and highly respected across the sector. That is the case for the museums within the national portfolio, as it is with museums across the UK.
Q69 This is slightly boring question, but has Brexit made any difference to that process?
No, it hasn’t. The trust and reciprocal relationship between European and UK museums is as strong as it has ever been.

Q70 As you will know, other cultural institutions that we have taken evidence from have had problems with the movement of objects, people and so on. But it is not an issue for you in the museum sector?
It has not caused us issues at Tate.
Q71 Have any of the other members of the body you represent reported any issues of that kind to you?
I can’t answer that question, I’m afraid.
Q72 Well, you can answer it. You can say that they haven’t.
I don’t know.
Q73 Exactly. I wasn’t asking you whether you knew; I was asking whether anyone had said anything to you about it.

Can you also briefly explain the indemnity scheme that the Government runs around insurance? Perhaps, Lord Parkinson, it would be appropriate to ask you about that. Does any of this have implications for that?

We run a Government indemnity scheme that saves museums around £100 million a year in commercial insurance costs. It is another instance of the way that the Government support the sector. It allows museums big and small to be able to take part in that exchange of items on loan, which means that people can see collections from around the world and also compare things to works of art and cultural objects from different time periods and civilisations.
Other than to mention that St Fagans Museum in my constituency won museum of the year just before the pandemic, that is all from me.
Q74 Well done—nice plug!

You both heard the evidence from our previous witnesses. From some of what they said, I took the impression that despite the trauma of everything that has happened, it actually has shone a very useful light on the situation up until now—the need for things to be digitised and recorded effectively and the benefits of having items, rather than being locked away in dusty strongrooms, actually out there in different corners of the country and the world, being appreciated by those who would like to see them. Is that experience unique to the British Museum, or do you feel that other parts of the sector will have picked up some learnings from what has been experienced by the British Museum?

I think an incident of this seriousness asks all museums to look again at the safety and security of their collections. That is what we did at Tate. Our trustees had their last meeting in our large collection store, and were walked through every aspect of the handling, care and access of objects, so that they could check, with me, that we had all the appropriate measures in place—which we will always continue to strengthen.

Nearly all national museums lend generously to collections across the UK. At Tate, we have more than 50 organisations that work with us as part of a sharing network called Plus Tate, whereby they have privileged access to the national collection so that they can use those objects in their own exhibitions. They are in institutions in places that are as varied as Shetland, Llandudno, Penzance or Middlesbrough, and that is part of our national role. The V&A, the Science Museum and the Imperial War Museum all have locations outside London, and they lend to many other regional collections. The reciprocity across those collections is one of the great strengths of UK museums.

Q75 I think you were in the room to hear the British Museum team say they were very keen for a new arrangement for what I grew up calling the Elgin marbles, and which I observe the museum itself now calls the Parthenon sculptures, which makes it clear where they think they belong. Is there a Government position on what should happen on that?

We call them the Parthenon sculptures because that is where they came from. As the chairman of the museum explained, they were legally acquired, and this issue has been the subject of debate ever since that purchase. The Government is clear: the British Museum Act 1963 prohibits the museum from deaccessioning items—that is, permanently removing them from their collection—and we have no plans to change that law.

But the Act does not prohibit the museum from generously lending items to institutions throughout the country and around the world; it does that all the time. It has done that with some of the Parthenon sculptures in the past. It lent to the Hermitage Museum in Russia when we had better relationships with the Russian Federation than we do today. We support the museum in making loans to other institutions that recognise the museum’s ownership of them, and they do that for many items in their collection.
Q76 As you say, they were talking about the possibility of a loan. You would support that.

Across all the items in their collection, if they wish to loan them, there is no prohibition in law and that would not concern me. But for a loan to take place, the recipient of the loan obviously needs to acknowledge the British Museum’s ownership of the item, and it needs to be a loan that is returned.

Q77 That is precisely the nub of where I was going to get to. Call me cynical, but it feels to me that if the Parthenon sculptures ever get back to being displayed at the Parthenon again, the chances of them coming back to this country are quite remote.
That would be a matter for the museum and the Greek Government to discuss and to reassure each other and His Majesty’s Government about.
Q78 I am still not quite clear. Would you support them in that?
They have loaned some of the Parthenon sculptures to museums in other countries in the past, and we have supported that.
But not in Greece.

If a museum in Greece accepted the British Museum’s ownership of them and it was clearly a loan that would be returned, I would see no reason to say that that is contrary to the British Museum Act 1963, but, like you, I would have lots of questions about how it is described and how that is assured.

Q79 The British Museum Act 1963 is often cited as the reason why things cannot be disposed of or shared more broadly, particularly when it comes to contested items. You said there are no plans to change that piece of legislation, but it is quite old. Is there an argument for reviewing the legislation and seeing if there are ways it could be brought more up to date?

In between my two stints at DCMS, there was an interesting debate in the House of Lords about the National Heritage Act 1983, which, like me, turned 40 this year. Turning 40 is a moment for introspection, and for looking forward and back. We have no plans to change any of the laws that cover the national museums in this area but, as I said in that debate, it is important to remember that we have 15 national museum groups, which are covered by various Acts of Parliament. Some of our national museums are covered by different statute—for instance, the Horniman Museum, and that didn’t prohibit it from returning legal title of some of the Benin bronze material in its collection. The pattern is varied, and most museums around the country are free to do what they, their trustees and their leaders think within the context of charity law and other statute. The pattern we have allows for freedom for the majority of museums in this country, while protecting a national collection from de-accessioning. I think that balance is the right one.

Q80 The Museums Association issued a statement at the time this was all in the media, saying: “ Theft by members of public — as in any other sector — does happen, but ‘inside jobs’ are extremely unusual. ” Lord Parkinson, you have said that it is very difficult for the public to steal because when things are behind display cabinets and so on they are more secure, but they are more vulnerable when they are in storage. So which is it? Are we being a bit complacent here? I get the feeling that we are being ushered along and being sold, “Nothing to see here. There’s not a problem; it’s just this one-off character. Let’s get on with it.”

No, not at all. There is no complacency. We are deeply concerned by what has occurred at the British Museum and the allegations that are being investigated. I make the point that there is a distinction between the allegations there, which concern items in the collection to which only members of staff have access: it is very rare, as we have heard, for members of museum staff to be involved in theft in this way. That is different from items that are on public display, which of course have additional levels of protection and assurance because they are on public display. But we are not complacent about it, and nor are museums across the country.

Q81 I think you were in the room when I read out the quote from Morgan Belzic, doctor in archaeology at the French archaeological mission in Libya, who is quite scathing about the situation in London. I will read it again: “ The London art market is one of the most involved in antiquities theft and looting…It can move objects very easily and quickly out of the country. It’s one of the least controlled markets in the world. There’s a lot of complacency, a lot of negligence and, of course, some dealers are directly involved with the illegal trade ”. Do you recognise that description of London? Isn’t there a danger that the antiquities that are in storage in our national museums are vulnerable to that illegal trade?

No, I do not recognise that picture. There are deeply committed professionals across the art trade. As the chairman of the British Museum said, there are people like Dr Gradel who are part of that wider warning system and protective ecology for museums. There are codes of ethics by which they do their business. The UK is a party to the UNESCO 1970 convention on combating illicit trade, and Government Departments and agencies work very closely with the sector to tackle illicit trade where it occurs. Border Force and HMRC both play an active role in that, and the Metropolitan Police’s arts and antiques unit is consulted by police forces from around the world for its expertise. That is not because there is a large problem in London, but because they are vigilant partners in ensuring that there is not.

Q82 Were all those measures in place before these antiquities were being sold from the British Museum? It took a whistleblower who was receiving them at the other end as a buyer to alert them to the fact that all the items had been trickling out over a long period of time from the British Museum, so it doesn’t seem that those checks and balances are very effective.

Like the chairman of the British Museum, I want to wait for the police investigation and the independent review before going into considerable detail about it. But, like him, I would say t hat t he fact that Dr Gradel, who is a scholar and buyer, was concerned by what he saw and reported it, based on the professional code of ethics to which he and others adhere, shows that that is working, and would make also the distinction between the art trade and museum collections. The point is that the items that have allegedly been stolen in this instance should not have left the museum’s collection. That is nothing to do with the art trade in London: that is to do with problems at the British Museum.

Q83 I am implying no criticism of Dr Gradel whatsoever. None the less, what was going on was not picked up, was it? It took him—as an expert—recognising these items were for sale in the market and alerting those authorities that you said are being so vigilant. It was right under their noses and they didn’t spot it. Going back to my original point, aren’t we being too complacent here? What is happening to try to prevent this being allowed to happen in the future?

I do not think we are being too complacent. All of us are keen to see the outcome of the independent review and the police investigation, which may throw up further questions that we want to ask and want to see answered.
Q84 I will leave that there. Can I come to Maria Balshaw? What other issues face the museum sector that we should be aware of?

The most chronic issue that museums across the UK face is the diminishment of core funding, particularly from local authorities, but also within the higher education sector and across the independent museum sector. That reduction in funding means that they are less able to deliver the public benefit they would wish to see from their collections, which includes activities like schools visits and community engagement work—the use of the collection by the people who are supposed to benefit from it. Museums are facing such stringent budgets and reductions in staffing levels that they are not really able to fulfil the public service that they would like to.
Q85 Would you like to see more Government support for these museums?

I think that Lord Parkinson and I would absolutely share the view that investing in the nation’s museums and, through local authorities and higher education, investing in the regional museums most especially, would be of huge benefit to the UK public.

Q86 You mentioned local authorities. To pursue that very quickly, before we finish, local authority funding has been hit extremely hard through austerity. Are you saying that there should be some form of direct funding and that you shouldn’t have to rely on local authorities—which immediately start to fund their statutory duties, protecting that funding, so that museums, youth services and other things get squeezed?

I am certain that everyone on the Committee will be well aware of the strain on local authority funding and will also know that Arts Council England, as well as the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, invests very significantly in museums. Of course, as a museum director among a group of really committed and active museum directors, I think we would like to see renewed funding for the benefit that museums can give. I have no particular view on the mechanism by which that funding should come to us.

Q87 You heard from the previous witnesses about the challenges of the stewardship of large listed buildings. They are homes to many of our national galleries. I wondered more broadly about the Department’s attitude to the protection of our heritage assets, and whether any work is ongoing on that. In my constituency, it feels that there is literally no responsibility whatsoever for maintaining the standard of listed buildings that fall within the curtilage of MOD property. There seems to be an approach of managed decline which, in layman’s terms, suggests that listed buildings and other assets of national significance can just rot without anybody caring. More broadly, when buildings are in private ownership, the restrictions are imposed so punitively that it actually negates the ability to restore them and bring them back into use. Is the Department aware of that? Is it aware that the listing rules and the rules around renovation and repair are being imposed in such an unpredictable and scattergun way? Are there any plans to look at that?

I have a lot of conversations about this topic. Last week, I was at the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth, where there is an accredited museum, and I heard about the complicated structures they have with the Defence Infrastructure Organisation to look after that building. At the start of the week, I was speaking to the Heritage Trust Network in Newcastle, with more than 200 local community groups, civic societies and others who look after a variety of properties. I speak to the Listed Property Owners Club, and I was at the parliamentary breakfast yesterday for the Historic Houses Association , which obviously represents people with significant historic properties in private ownership. We talk about all these things.

Through the Levelling-up and Regeneration Bill, we are trying to make sure that the planning system gives the protections for heritage assets that we all want to see and, with colleagues across Government, we are taking part in a review of the energy efficiency measures that might be taken to future-proof those buildings and to help them to play their part towards achieving net zero while balancing the protections for their heritage significance. We have those conversations.

Q88 Conversations do not really solve the problem. To what extent are you talking to the heritage bodies about over-imposing punitive restrictions on people who genuinely want to save buildings from falling into disrepair and being lost?

I chair the Heritage Council, which brings together a number of heritage bodies that have different views on this. Conversation is a part of it, because it allows them to explore where there are differences of opinion and why, and it allows us to reflect those in the reviews that we conduct and the legislation that we bring forward, such as the Levelling-up and Regeneration Bill.
I think that is something we might want to look again at as a Committee. Thank you very much, both of you, for your time. Is there anything that you would like to add before we let you go?
No. Thank you.
In which case, thank you very much for your time and patience with us today.

sessions.w: Rt Hon Mark Drakeford MS (Welsh Government); Des Clifford (Welsh Government); Piers Bisson (Welsh Government)

segs.tx: Welsh Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The First Minister of Wales, HC 1890
Wednesday 18 October 2023
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 18 October 2023 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Stephen Crabb (Chair); Simon Baynes; Ruth Jones; Ben Lake; Robin Millar; Mr Rob Roberts.
Questions 1-4 4
Witnesses

I : Rt Hon Mark Drakeford MS, First Minister of Wales, Des Clifford, Director of the Office of the First Minister, and Piers Bisson, Director of European Transition, Constitution and Justice, Welsh Government.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Mark Drakeford, Des Clifford and Piers Bisson.

Q1 Good morning. Welcome to this session of the Welsh Affairs Committee. We are delighted to be joined virtually from Cardiff by the First Minister of Wales, the right hon. Mark Drakeford MS; by Des Clifford, director of the Office of the First Minister; and by Piers Bisson, director of European transition, constitution and justice.

As ever, First Minister, we are very grateful to you for giving us your time. You are under no obligation to a House of Commons Committee, but as a courtesy you give us these sessions, and we find it very useful to talk to you about issues that intersect between the UK Government and the Welsh Government.

Perhaps I could start my line of questioning by asking about something you said last November, on the previous occasion you appeared in front of the Committee—this was following another change in Prime Minister at the Westminster end. You said that you were looking forward to “a return to normality” in your relationship with the UK Government. That was following the appointment of Rishi Sunak as Prime Minister. Has there been a return to normality?

Well, in some ways I think that would be correct. We certainly no longer inhabit the world of active hostility to devolution, which I think was characteristic of both Mr Sunak’s predecessors. I have met the new Prime Minister twice, I think, in the last 10 months, and I would say that the conduct of relations is at least on a more respectful footing than would have been the case in the previous period.

In other ways , you probably could not quite say that things are back to normal, because the machinery set out in the IGR review is still really to operate in the way that was intended. To be frank, Chair, I have an impression of a Government that knows that it is coming towards the end of the current parliamentary term and whose energy to invest in reviving intergovernmental relations is at a relatively low ebb. Things are better than they were, but you could not describe intergovernmental relationships as characterised by a great deal of energetic determination to make the system work to its optimum.

Q2 When you have had these meetings with the Prime Minister, are they to discuss points of interest? Are there actual resolutions to be made and disagreements to resolve? Can you give us a flavour of what the business of a meeting between the First Minister of Wales and the Prime Minister consists of?

There is usually an ostensible purpose for the meeting. The second meeting that I had with the Prime Minister was at Holyhead in north Wales. It was to mark the agreement on freeport arrangements in Wales, so there was a topic that we were both engaged in and therefore needed to discuss. The remainder of that meeting was probably more me raising with the Prime Minister a number of issues that I thought were important to draw to his attention. I did so because in the previous meeting that I had had with him, when I had raised issues, there was clear evidence that he had pursued them—that he had gone away and asked his officials to look into and do further work on some of the matters that I had raised with him. That gave me a bit of confidence that if I did the same again, those issues would be pursued in the same way.
That is helpful. It is probably consistent with how we see things—very business-like administration. I am going to move the questions on by bringing in Rob Roberts.

Q3 Thank you, Chair. Good morning, First Minister. We appreciate your time. You mentioned a lack of energy or will. In more general terms, do you feel that the structures that are in place for intergovernmental relations are working adequately? Are they the correct structures, regardless of the amount of energy that is being put into them, or does anything need to change?

I should say first of all that a great deal of time and effort went into constructing the new arrangements. They were nearly four years in discussion. I was very glad when we managed to secure a four nations agreement to them.

It is difficult to answer Mr Roberts’s question, because I don’t think that the machinery has ever been fully tested. You know it has three tiers to it. The working tier is the tier in which individual Ministers meet with their counterparts at Westminster. My impression there is that where there have been reasonably good relations in the past, those relations have transferred into the new structure and that part of the machinery is working. Where there is less of a history or a more unhappy history, I don’t think you could say that there is a great deal of evidence that the new structure has managed to put that right.

Then there is a middle tier, which is a Finance Ministers meeting and an inter-ministerial group that is more general. The FISC—the Finance Ministers meeting—I think does work. Again, that was picking up an arrangement that had been in place for quite a long time, but it has continued and has come to be useful. The other meeting, the inter-ministerial group, has been more sporadic and harder to pin down. There is a meeting of it to happen this week, but I do not think you could say yet that it is working at full steam.

The top tier, the Council of Ministers, has never met, really. It met once when the new Prime Minister, Mr Sunak, took office, but it was a mixture of in-person and virtual, and it did not have anybody from Northern Ireland in the room because there was no Northern Ireland Executive to take part in that meeting, and it has not met since. So I don’t think you can say that that part of the intergovernmental machinery has been properly tested.
Q4 Mr Roberts : In May you advocated a “solidarity union” of the UK. What does that mean in practical terms? Would that solve any of the issues that you have just highlighted?

I think it could well go some way to addressing them. I was trying to make the case for the United Kingdom. I am a believer in the United Kingdom, but I want a United Kingdom where people in all parts of the United Kingdom want to belong to it and do not feel that they are somehow obliged to belong to it even though they are not satisfied with it. I want a United Kingdom where people in Wales would say, “That’s a country that I want to belong to.” For me, the idea of a solidarity union captures that. It would explain to people the things that they get as a result of their membership of the United Kingdom—the rights that come as a result of citizenship. One of those rights would be to live in a country where people know that the things that apply only to the part of the United Kingdom that they live in are decided upon by people who live in that part, and then we would pool our sovereignty to discharge those things that we do better together—foreign affairs, defence, macroeconomic policy and so on.

Q5 Mr Roberts : Thank you. Those are very comprehensive answers. On a slightly different element of IGR, you told us last year that Sue Gray was leading work to improve the Sewel convention process. Do you have an update on what the outcome of that work was and how that has gone?

I am afraid that is one of the least good parts of the picture. It is true that Sue Gray, when she headed up part of DLUHC, was working on an improvement to Sewel. I don’t think that work has been picked up by anybody else since her departure. I might have said in my original answer to the Chair’s question that one of the parts of intergovernmental activity that has been at a pretty low ebb in the last 12 months has been the part played by DLUHC. There was a time when Mr Gove took a very active, leading role in intergovernmental matters. That is why his Department ended up looking at the Sewel convention. I have only met Mr Gove once in this calendar year, which is pretty extraordinary and demonstrates, as I said originally, that energy has gone out of this agenda at the Whitehall end.

Unfortunately, where Sewel is concerned, I think it has now become a broken piece of the machinery. It is designed to make sure that the UK Parliament only legislates in devolved areas with the consent of devolved legislatures. That convention was observed without breach for 20 years—1999 to 2019. Now it is broken absolutely routinely. Routinely, when the Welsh Parliament votes not to give legislative consent, UK Ministers just go ahead anyway. I am afraid that Sewel is now completely unfit for its original purpose. I think that more radical solutions will be needed than the ones that Sue Gray might have been anticipating, and I believe that those solutions are best found in the Gordon Brown report: a report—commissioned, of course, by Keir Starmer—that deals directly with the Sewel convention and would solve these recent problems in a more radical way.
Q6 Would you happen to have any details to hand, First Minister, about how many times the Sewel convention has been disregarded?

Seven times, I think, just recently. It is routine. The first time the Sewel convention was disregarded, the UK Government made a case that the circumstances were not normal because that is what the Sewel convention allows for. That was in Brexit legislation. Although I did not agree, I could at least see the case that the UK Government were making—that these were not ordinary circumstances and they were dealing with the UK’s fundamental relationships with our European neighbours. You could at least recognise the case that was made. Now the convention is broken in absolutely routine pieces of legislation, where I do not see how a “not normal” argument could possibly be justified.

Q7 In the latter half of my short time, I want to ask a few questions about the 20 mph speed limit. I appreciate that the issue is devolved, so I ask you whether you mind me asking such questions before I do; it is not an area that the Committee necessarily deals with.

Chair, of course I want to be helpful to the Committee, but you said in opening that the invitation to give evidence was to deal with things where there is a genuine overlap between responsibilities held in Wales and responsibilities discharged in Westminster. I am not sure that I see where the 20 mph limit fits into the remit that you set out at the start of the meeting. I will do my best to answer, but I do not think this is quite in the spirit of the invitation to appear before you.

Q8 I will cut out a huge number in that case, but I will get one or two in, if I might. First Minister, what is your position on the petition that, as of 9 o’clock this morning, has 462,000 signatures—more than voted for the entire manifesto in 2021?

We will take the petition seriously, of course. The petitioner has chosen, as is his right, to keep the petition open for the full six months, so the Senedd will not be able to make any response to the petition probably until March next year. But the petitioner can choose at any moment to close the petition, at which point it would get considered.

The way petitions are handled in the Welsh Parliament is that first of all they go to the Parliament—to the Petitions Committee. It decides the process by which it wishes to respond to the petition. The Welsh Government will take the petition seriously and look to respond to it when that happens, by which time we will have had six months or more of experience of the new regime. That will help us in responding to the points made.

Q9 This is my final question, First Minister. You mentioned recently when questioned—I think you were being interviewed at the conference—that it is up to local authorities to determine where they apply exemptions. Is that exactly correct? I asked our local authority and an officer came back to me to say that although it is correct that the powers to implement speed limits do sit within the individual local authority, local authorities do not have the ability to disregard specific criteria and can apply an exemption only if it fits within your quite narrow parameters of what would be allowed. It is not really up to them, is it?

It is up to them. It is not an unfettered right to disregard the law; they have to act within the parameters set down, but within those parameters, it is local authorities that make decisions on whether to exempt individual roads from the default 20 mph position. One of the reasons why I think six months-worth of experience will be useful is that I think you can already see that different local authorities are taking different approaches to how they navigate their way through those criteria to a final decision. I think that in a sensible world, with experience, local authorities will want to look again to see whether they got those initial judgments right, and there may be some fine tuning and adjustments to the designations on individual roads in the light of experience and learning from how different local authorities have deployed the criteria that they must operate within in making what is, in the end, their decision.
My time is up.

Q10 Thank you very much. On this point, and very briefly, First Minister, I understand that some of the emergency services have expressed concerns about the new speed limits. May I ask how you are engaging with them in Wales and what your response is to them about whether the concerns about potential delays to responding to critical emergencies are real?

Some individual voices in some services have expressed concern. The services themselves have not. Of course, we work very closely with them. The rules are no different on a 20 mph road than they are on a 30, 40, 50 or 60 mph road. Emergency services are able to travel above the speed limit where there is a case for them to do so. None of that has changed. I think a number of these concerns are concerns in advance of the facts. When it comes to operating the system on the ground, I don’t think that those fears will materialise.
Thank you very much. I am going to bring in Robin Millar.

Q11 Good morning, First Minister. It is good to see you again; it has been a couple of years. I apologise: I missed our last opportunity to speak. It is good to see you again, and thank you for your time.

First Minister, one of the things I particularly enjoy is your interest in the constitution. I know that you are conducting a commission on the constitutional future of Wales, but given time constraints, may I jump straight to the matter of Senedd reform? In particular, how do you foresee that Senedd reform will affect the Welsh Government’s relationship with Westminster?

I don’t think it will do in a fundamental way, because Senedd reform is just a matter of making sure that the Senedd itself is properly equipped to discharge the responsibilities that it discharges. So there will be more capacity in that sense, but I don’t think intergovernmental relations have been affected by capacity issues; those have not been the source of concerns in recent years. I doubt there will be any impact of the sort that you have identified.

Q12 Thank you. Electoral reform was not in the manifesto, as I understand it, and not part of the plan, but that is part of the programme moving forward. When, back in 2011, the UK Government was formed as a coalition, one of its manifesto pledges was for electoral reform, so a referendum was brought before the people of the UK. Why do you feel that it is not a good idea to have a referendum on electoral reform in Wales?

Senedd reform was in the manifestos of my party, Plaid Cymru and the Liberal Democrats. I don’t think anybody who looked at what was being promised in the 2021 election could have been unaware of that. We operate within the rules set down by the Conservative Government’s Wales Act 2017. That does not require a referendum. It does require us to secure a two-thirds majority on the Floor of the Senedd for reforms. That is the safeguard that that Act puts in place, and we operate within the rules created for us.

Q13 You are absolutely correct to say that a referendum is not required, but there is also a cost to these reforms—over £100 million in the course of the next Senedd period. I am curious why that is the choice of the Administration when public services are struggling in Wales. You have the lowest educational attainment in the UK, the worst-performing health service and the highest unemployment rates—and you spent £100 million on electoral reform, First Minister.

Chair, I am not going to litigate in front of this Committee all those matters for which the Committee has no responsibility, as it has no responsibility for Senedd reform. However, we will complete, I hope, the journey on which we set off 20 years ago, when the Richard review, carried out by Lord Ivor Richard, concluded that the then Assembly required more Members to discharge the responsibilities that were to be exercised in Wales. Over those 20 years, the scope and depth of the powers exercised in the Senedd has grown; those powers include new powers transferred to the Senedd under the leadership of the Chair of your Committee. I am confident that a new Senedd, properly equipped to do its job, will save money time after time, and far more than pay for itself. That is why democracy is important.

Q14 I acknowledge the importance of that scrutiny; hence my interest in referenda. I will return to the issue of intergovernmental relations and the health service. As you are aware, I am in north Wales, and Betsi Cadwaladr has had significant challenges. The last time we spoke, we talked about the offer that the UK Government made to cut waiting lists during the pandemic. That offer was declined. As we both know, since then, the UK Government have made a further, supplementary offer to help reduce waiting lists in Wales. What progress has been made on that?

I don’t think a great deal of progress has been made, but that is because waiting lists in England are growing far faster than waiting lists in Wales. The capacity of the English system to offer treatment to Welsh patients when you cannot satisfy the demand from English patients is inevitably constrained. That does not mean—as I think you, Mr Millar, will acknowledge—that there is not a great deal of cross-border treatment, with patients who live in England receiving treatment in Wales, and patients who live in Wales receiving treatment in England. I am a big supporter of that. I regularly defend the fact that patients who live in Wales get treated in England when that is the right thing for them. Is there scope to do more of that when every health service is under enormous pressure? I think the scope for that is inevitably limited.

Q15 Thank you, Mr Drakeford. I understand, of course, that the English health service is outside your responsibilities, but the offer was made none the less. Before you make a decision on that, will you speak to any patients on waiting lists who are waiting to receive essential, life-changing treatment and would benefit from such an offer of help from the UK Government?

It is not a matter of a decision for me. The offer was made by the English Secretary of State. If he is in a position to offer us not just, “We will help”, but “Here is capacity that could be made available for you, and Welsh patients could take advantage of it,” of course we will be open to that conversation, just as we in Wales provide for English patients—thousands of them—every day of the week.

Q16 Thank you. I will take that as a cautious positive, and we will pursue that at this end of the line. Finally and briefly, I move to the very good news we had in north Wales recently of £1 billion of investment for the electrification of the north Wales main line. Of course, that follows more than £700 million in metro South Wales. I was disappointed, and I know that many residents were perplexed, by the response from the Welsh Government spokesperson, who said that this was not a priority for Wales.

There are two answers there. First, the so-called promise unravelled very quickly indeed when the Secretary of State for Transport in the UK Government said that this was merely an illustrative list, and nobody was to take it as meaning that this was actual money for actual activity. I doubt whether a single penny will be spent on this scheme during the lifetime of the current Government. In fact, it will be a 10-year project, if it is to happen at all.

Our Minister here pointed to the joint committee made up of representatives of the Welsh and UK Governments that prioritises plans for rail investment in north Wales. That committee, with UK representatives on it, had not put electrification of the main line at the top of its list of investments. The announcement was made with no reference to the group that had been established between two Governments to draw up priority plans. There is a list of priorities currently agreed, but instead, in a conference announcement designed, I am afraid, for headlines rather than for real activity, something was pulled out of a hat. There is very little confidence among people in north Wales that the investment will ever happen, because they saw the experience in south Wales, where we were told twice that there would be electrification of the main line, and twice that plan was reversed.

Q17 We won’t talk about promises on infrastructure projects while the M4 hangs over our heads, First Minister, but I will say that the Transport Secretary confirmed from the Dispatch Box on Monday that £1 billion has been allocated for north Wales. I am delighted by it. At the back of that, really, is the point that north Wales is tired of being left out or left behind, and the sense that decisions made in Cardiff extend only as far as Welshpool, perhaps.
I am afraid that that is a tired old trope, and I am sorry to hear it rehearsed again this morning.

Q18 Thank you, Robin Millar. Before I bring in Ruth Jones, may I follow up on the issue of Senedd reform, First Minister? I will raise an aspect that touches on our role as Members of the Westminster Parliament. Across Wales, there are sets of constituencies, and Members of the UK Parliament or of the Welsh Senedd are elected as representatives of specific constituencies; you are the Member of the Senedd for Cardiff West, First Minister. The MP and the MS will often work together on constituency issues; even if they are of different parties, their offices will pass on information and cases. Often the two politicians will appear together at local events, and will work on projects together. If I am not mistaken, the proposal being taken forward for Senedd reform is to no longer have one Member for a Senedd constituency; instead, large constituencies will elect multiple Members of the Senedd, often from different parties. There will be no single MS to represent a particular constituency. Is that the correct perception?
Yes, in one way, but let me be clear: I am not the only Senedd Member for Cardiff West.
Q19 But you are. You are the elected Member for Cardiff West.

But there are also two Conservative Members of the Senedd who represent the region in which Cardiff West is to be found, and a Plaid Cymru Member as well. It is not the case that we simply have a Westminster system here in Wales.

Q20 I did not say that there is a Westminster system; I am saying that in both systems, an individual elected politician represents a constituency. Yes, there is the dynamic of the relationship with the Westminster MP, but there is also the visibility of the individual MS. There is accountability and scrutiny that comes from being the person for that community. When there were the Ely riots, you were approached for comments by the press, as the local Member of the Senedd. With the move to a larger Senedd with more Members, and a system in which there is no longer one Member for a constituency, is there not a danger that there will be less accountability, and instead just a noisier, fuzzier Senedd system?

I do not agree with that, and I very much doubt that the Members in the Conservative group at the Senedd who are elected on the list system—more than half—would agree with it either. They would certainly argue that they are no less accountable than any other Member of the Senedd.

It is true that in future we will pair to Westminster constituencies. There will be six Members elected for that constituency. One of the great advantages of that is that constituents who might rather take their case to a Conservative Member of the Senedd, rather than a Labour Member, will be able to exercise that choice. There will be a greater plurality of representation, and through plurality will come a great sense of accountability as well.

Q21 One of the golden rules for Members of Parliament is that you treat every constituent as an equal, whether they voted for you or not. What you seem to be hinting at, First Minister, is a system where a Plaid Cymru MS or a Labour MS will deal with Labour voters or Plaid Cymru voters, and you get a segmentation of the constituency, which I think is really unhealthy.

That is absolutely not what I said. I completely take the same principle as you do: anybody who comes to the door of my office gets the same service—I never want to know how people’s political preferences have been exercised—but individual voters will have choices, not Members of the Senedd. Individual citizens will have choices about who they think would be the most effective person to take up their case. I think that is a good thing.

Okay, but personally—to get this on record—I think it is a recipe for fuzziness, confusion and less accountability and scrutiny. I do not think it will lead to a more effective Senedd, but that is a personal view. Simon Baynes?

Q22 Thank you for your time, First Minister. To pick up on that point, particularly with casework, there will be a real problem with people knowing where to take their case, if they have six different people they can go to. The benefit of having a constituency representative is that you know where to go with your casework. For instance, in my constituency of Clwyd South, where I work very well with my opposite Labour Member, Ken Skates of the Senedd, I know where to send casework that might be applicable to him, and my constituents know whether to go to him or me, according to whether it is a Senedd matter or a Westminster matter. I hear what you are saying, but I think in practice it will be very confusing for them to know where to take casework.

Mr Baynes, I am afraid that these questions, which are actually nothing to do with the responsibilities of a Westminster MP, are very much a view of Wales through the Westminster end of a telescope. We have 25 years’ experience of having regional Members who represent a range of different constituencies. In my constituency, people who are looking for help from a Senedd Member do not have to come to me. They have two Members from your party who also represent that area in the Senedd, and they have other Members as well. We are much more used to this system than you are, and we see that it is capable of working. In fact, far more Members of the Senedd from Opposition parties arrive through the list system than do Labour Members. I don’t think that they would share your point of view.

Q23 Good morning, First Minister. Thank you for your time this morning. It is good to see you. I will turn back to rail infrastructure, but given that my constituency is Newport West, I will concentrate on south Wales. I had a meeting with Transport for Wales last week. I declare an interest, as my son lives in Manchester, and he uses that train very often. We have had a few issues over the last couple of years. It will obviously be in the ownership of the Welsh Government, going forward. I am wondering about customer satisfaction and developments. Could you outline what will happen in the next year or so?

The improvements , which we will hear about from Transport for Wales in the coming months , will be the accelerated delivery —we hope—of new rolling stock, which was expected to have arrived in Wales already. By today, we were expecting to have 77, I think, new trains that would run on that south Wales to Manchester line. For many complex reasons—the pandemic is certainly part of the picture—the manufacturer has been able to deliver only 33 of those trains to date. That means that Transport for Wales has had to keep running rolling stock that it had planned to retire and replace with new stock. I am sure you will have seen some of the new trains, Ruth Jones; they are of a very different calibre from the trains that are being retired.

The good news is that a new train is being delivered to Transport for Wales every seven to 10 days, so the ability of Transport for Wales to substitute the old rolling stock with the new will accelerate. The performance of Transport for Wales trains has improved through September and into this month, and Transport for Wales is confident that that improvement will continue through the rest of this calendar year and into 2024 as it becomes able to deploy the new trains that we expected to have been here and operating already.

Q24 We are looking forward to those improvements very much. We had the reports by Lord Hendy and Lord Burns on the M4 alternatives. Five new railway stations are planned between Cardiff and Newport—or maybe a bit further, if we include Magor . How do you see the calling-in of the Cardiff Parkway planning application? Obviously, we are a little bit anxious that that might stop developments along that line. How do you see the timescales for that calling-in?

I must not get drawn into the call-in itself, because ultimately that decision could end up on the desk of Welsh Ministers, and anything I said about it would be material to any legal challenge to the call-in consideration, so forgive me if I do not get drawn directly into that.

There is a wider point, which the Member for Newport West made: the UK connectivity review—the Hendy review—has, as far as I can tell, completely disappeared out of sight. We did receive, and I was grateful for it, some relatively modest but important funding from the UK Government to further develop the Burns proposals for bringing the second main line back into more effective use through south Wales; that includes the five stations that Ruth referred to. However, there is a real radio silence on the outcome of that UK connectivity review.

As you represent Newport West, you will remember very well that Sir Peter Hendy said that this was one of the proposals that was closest to being able to be put into practical effect, and it would meet all the criteria of the review with regard to improving UK connectivity, but we have heard nothing since, and that is a big disappointment. A billion pounds for north Wales was plucked out of a hat. That leaves people in that part of Wales wondering when we will hear about the investment that we need to upgrade the line, and to improve connectivity from south Wales to England and beyond.

Q25 I share your disappointment with the lack of action on Lord Hendy’s report, but the electrification of the south Wales line is a grave disappointment as well, given the promises we were made. James Price, the chief exec of Transport for Wales, told us that he expects that Network Rail will be “ eking out ” existing rail infrastructure , rather than investing in enhancements. Do you agree with that evaluation, and what do you see as your priorities for national infrastructure projects?

I’m afraid that is Network Rail’s own assessment as well. The arrangements for the next seven-year period have just been concluded. They put Wales at the bottom of the league table for investment, and it is a picture of managed decline. I think Network Rail have said that it will lead to longer delays and more breakdowns in infrastructure. It is not a good outlook when we depend so much for services in Wales on Network Rail’s ability to invest. This is not Network Rail’s fault; I am not criticising them. This is the remit that they have been given—the funding that they have been offered—but it puts Wales where we have been for far too long: at the foot of the league table of UK Government investment in rail infrastructure.

If my colleague from Swansea West were here, he would give you the figures. We have 10% of the rail and only 4% of the funding, so I agree with your assessment there. Thank you very much. I will hand back to the Chair.

Q26 Thank you very much. On the point that Ruth Jones raised about rail, you talked, First Minister, about infrastructure being a reason for breakdowns and delays. When James Price, the chief executive of Transport for Wales, appeared in front of this Committee, he was very frank in explaining why rail services in Wales have been so appalling in recent months. He talked about rolling stock, where there have been some problems, and also the issue of driver absence due to illness post covid and other reasons. Are you satisfied, First Minister, that since the Welsh Government took over running those rail services under Transport for Wales, you have put in place a plan to improve services not just for communities around Cardiff and the cities, but for places like Pembrokeshire in west Wales?

Services are not as good as we want them to be, and Transport for Wales has a job to improve the services. James Price will have explained to you some of the reasons why the improvement in services that we had hoped for has not yet been realised, but there is a clear plan there to address that, and some of the reasons are beyond the control of Transport for Wales itself, particularly in the delivery of the new rolling stock on which it was planning that improvement. That is a separate issue from investment in the infrastructure itself, which is not the responsibility of Transport for Wales. It is the responsibility of Network Rail, which does have an impact on Transport for Wales’s ability to run a service of the sort that we would wish to see for people in Wales.

Q27 First Minister, in talking about rail infrastructure, you were very much pointing a finger of blame at the UK Government, and they do hold responsibility for decisions about rail infrastructure investment. Do you think there is an issue here with the Welsh Government always ducking taking responsibility for things that you are responsible for? If we are looking at the quality of rail services in the round, there is a large measure of responsibility for the Welsh Government right now, isn’t there?

I think I answered your question about whether we were satisfied that Transport for Wales had delivered the service of the sort that we wish to see, and I have accepted the responsibility for that not being delivered in the way that we had intended. I am very determined to take responsibility for the things for which we are responsible. Decisions about Network Rail investment are not made by the Welsh Government, but they have a material impact on the responsibilities that we exercise.
Q28 Diolch yn fawr i chi, Prif Weinidog. Mae’n dda iawn eich cael chi yma bore ’ma. (Translation: Thank you very much, First Minister. It’s very good to have you with us this morning.)

I would like to ask you a few questions on the fiscal framework, if I may. I understand that the Finance Minister, in detailing some of the plans for changes to the Welsh Government’s budget yesterday, referenced the way in which the existing fiscal framework makes a challenging situation even more challenging to navigate. The Scottish Government has recently updated its fiscal framework agreement and has increased its borrowing powers. Is this something that the Welsh Government is engaging with the Treasury on? Are there any discussions for similar changes for the Welsh fiscal framework?
Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn . (Translation: Thank you very much for the question.)

I was the Finance Minister, at the time, who negotiated the fiscal framework with the then Chief Secretary to the Treasury. The problem with it is that the figures that we agreed back in 2016 have been frozen ever since. We agreed in 2016 that we needed a Welsh reserve of a certain quantum, that borrowing powers were necessary for the Welsh Government, up to a certain level, and other technical ways in which the fiscal framework operated.

Those figures have never been uprated, so their real-terms value today is about 20% lower than when they were struck originally. All we are asking for is a simple uprating of those figures so that they retain the value today that they had when they were first agreed. That would make a material difference to our ability to manage a b udget of £20 billion—a budget that is considerably larger than it was in 2016. That case has been made by our Finance Minister to the current occupant of the Chief Secretary’s chair. I think that is the seventh person that has been the Chief Secretary to the Treasury since she became our Finance Minister, so we have to keep making this case afresh quite regularly. That is in essence what was agreed for Scotland, together with more flexibility about how we use our own funds.
Q29 And so you would be looking for similar changes to the Welsh fiscal framework as the Scottish fiscal framework has seen. Is that right?

The Scottish fiscal framework has been renegotiated in a more thoroughgoing way. I myself don’t see the case for taking long months to renegotiate a fiscal framework that, actually, for the most part, is working effectively. What we are looking for is something much simpler—something that the IFS has called for in a number of reports—and that is just an indexing of the figures within the fiscal framework so that they retain their real value. I don’t think that that requires us to have a root-and-branch review of the whole framework.

It was different in Scotland, where there were other things at play, because they agreed a fiscal framework that had some different components from ours, particularly in the way in which population was treated. That isn’t a problem in our framework, and I don’t think that there is a strong case for a wholesale review. There is a case for a simple keeping up to date of the framework, which would be helpful to us in the way that we manage our budget.

Q30 Thank you, First Minister; that is very useful. The other aspect, of course—something that the Finance Minister outlined yesterday—is that the Welsh Government have made a request of the UK Treasury to allow some capital budget to be brought over to revenue in order to help navigate some of the fiscal challenges that we find ourselves having to deal with, particularly to meet inflationary pressures in-year. To what extent does the package and the changes detailed yesterday depend on a favourable response to that request of the UK Treasury?

As you as the Member for Ceredigion will know, we have had to fill a gap of £900 million between what we have and what we were set to spend through the Welsh Government and the wider Welsh public service. A capital-to-revenue switch is an important part of that. It is over £100 million that we would look to switch. Just to be clear with members of the Committee, we are not asking for money here; this is our money now. We are just looking to be able to use it in a more flexible way. That is routinely done for UK Departments. It was done for the Department of Health in successive years in far greater quantums than the sum of money that we are looking for.

We continue to be in discussions with the Treasury about it . One of the real challenges that we face is that on some of the aspects of our plan that do depend on actions at the UK level, we are unlikely to know the outcome of that probably until February next year, which is perilously close to the end of the financial year to deal with the outcome of those discussions.
Q31 Thank you, First Minister. It is clear that a speedy response from the Treasury would be very well received.

It would be very gratefully received. It would help us a great deal in managing the in-year position. I was grateful yesterday that the Conservative spokesperson on this matter supported that part of the package and said that they would want to see that resolved in the way that we have asked. We will make sure that we continue to have those discussions.

Q32 Finally, the Finance Minister made very clear yesterday the challenges facing the Welsh Government budget due to inflationary pressures and outlined some sound principles as to how to try and navigate them—protecting frontline services as best as possible, supporting households who are hardest hit by the cost of living crisis and prioritising jobs. She also detailed an increase to the Transport for Wales budget of £125 million this year. I beseech the Government to consider ways of allocating a portion of that funding for bus services. Sadly, in many rural areas we found services cut quite significantly due to inflationary pressures and of course it is having a serious impact on households who are trying to navigate the cost of living crisis.

I thank you for those important points. You will know that the Welsh Government identified a sum of, I think, £48 million earlier in the financial year to go on supporting bus services now that the emergency funding post covid has run out. Buses, like trains, have not seen a return of passengers to pre-pandemic levels, so the problem is the farebox. Public subsidy in buses and trains is at an all-time high. What we do not have are paying passengers in the way that those industries saw them back in 2019. Investment in the bus services has not been reduced as part of this very painful exercise over the summer. That extra money was found and has been kept.

The £125 million is mostly to help with rail services because the fixed costs in rail are very, very hard indeed to reduce. It costs you what it costs you to run a railway whether there are trains on it or not. A period where the passenger, or the farebox, as it is called, simply has not recovered means that we are having to find extra money to sustain public transport in Wales—trains but buses as well.

Q33 Thank you again, First Minister. I want to ask you about the Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales. This might be a question that you cannot answer at this stage, but could you give us some idea of what you expect to be the output of the commission? We had a meeting with them here and I was somewhat surprised to see that there was no business representative or north Wales representative on the commission. Can you address that as well?

I am quite sure that Albert Owen, the former MP for Y nys Môn , would certainly take exception to the idea that there is no representation from north Wales on the commission. There are certainly people on the commission who have had wide experience of different aspects of Welsh life. What I expect in terms of the outcome will be a report that puts flesh on the three basic constitutional futures that the commission set out in their interim report. Members will remember that the commission at the end of its first year said that they thought there were three broad constitutional futures for Wales. There was entrenched devolution; there was a move to a more federalist United Kingdom; and there was independence in which Wales no longer was a member of the United Kingdom. I expect that its final report will rehearse in more detail the arguments for and against those three potential constitutional futures.

Q34 But it seemed to me to be quite a gap to have no business representative on the commission, given how important business is to the economy, and also that this is a cross-border issue to an extent, given that a large number of people from Wales go to work across the border in England. So, I was very surprised that you had no business representative on the commission.

The membership of the commission was inevitably constrained. There are many, many interest groups who would make a claim for being represented on the commission. I think the commission has worked hard to make sure that, where it feels it needs to strengthen the evidence that it has, or the voice that it hears, from different aspects of Welsh life, it has taken that evidence and heard those concerns.

But I am meeting the joint chairs of the commission tomorrow, and I am certainly willing to put that point to them, as to whether they feel they have had an adequate opportunity to hear from business voices.
Q35 Moving on to the UK Government’s involvement with devolved policy areas, do you see any potential for further discussion with the UK Government on UK financial support for coal tip safety?

I think it is very much an area where those conversations are needed. You will know that Wales has 40% of all the coal tips in the United Kingdom—40% of coal tips and 5% of the population—and in an era of climate change, some of those coal tips are not as secure as we would wish them to be, or as secure as they probably were when the arrangements were first put in place, 30 or 40 years ago. It is about trying to ensure that we respond to the changing nature of severe weather events and check the coal tips to make sure they are as safe as they need to be. That will involve, not in the short run but over the medium term, a significant need to invest in new drainage, and other more modern forms of protection, to make sure that these places are fit for the future; because those communities are very closely overhung by coal tips—they can see them from their own front doors. And to make sure of that, we look for some further support from the UK Government.
Q36 Obviously, the responsibility for safety lies with the Welsh Government, but that ought to be backed by extra funding from the UK Government. That is fair enough.

To go slightly off at a tangent, when you last came before us I asked a question about the Ffos-y- f ran coal and its application for steam engines—a particular interest to me for the Llangollen steam railway. When I asked you the question, you said you would give it consideration. Now, obviously, the Government have come up with their decision not to extend the licence, which I understand. But do you not feel that that is possibly one of those areas where, if we did extend the licence, it would be better environmentally, because it would mean that railways did not have to import the coal to supply to the steam engines?

I am sympathetic to the case for making sure that railways of that sort go on having a supply of coal, and preferably coal that isn’t imported.
